sections.summary: God creates light, separates it from darkness, and names them Day and Night marking the first day.
God forms the firmament to divide waters above and below, calling it Heaven the second day.
Dry land appears, named Earth; seas are gathered; vegetation is created third day.
God sets lights in the firmament sun, moon, and stars to govern day and night fourth day.
Sea creatures and birds are created and blessed to multiply fifth day.
Land animals and mankind are created; man is made in God’s image and given dominion sixth day.
God finishes creation and sanctifies the seventh day as a day of rest.
A detailed account of man’s formation; God plants the Garden of Eden and places Adam there.
Adam is commanded to tend the garden and warned not to eat from the tree of knowledge.
God creates Eve from Adam’s rib; they are united as one flesh and unashamed in their innocence.
The serpent tempts Eve; she and Adam eat the forbidden fruit and become aware of their nakedness.
God confronts Adam and Eve; they confess and shift blame.
God pronounces curses on the serpent, the woman, and the man introducing pain, toil, and death.
Adam names Eve; God clothes them and expels them from Eden to prevent access to the tree of life.
Cain and Abel offer sacrifices; God accepts Abel’s but not Cain’s, warning Cain to master sin.
Cain murders Abel and is cursed to wander, yet God marks him for protection.
Cain’s descendants are listed; civilization develops through city-building, music, and metalwork.
Adam and Eve bear Seth; people begin to call upon the name of the Lord.
Adam’s genealogy begins; he lives 930 years and fathers Seth.
Descendants from Seth to Jared are listed, each living centuries and bearing sons and daughters.
Enoch walks with God and is taken by Him he does not see death.
Methuselah, Lamech, and Noah are born; Noah is prophesied to bring comfort from the cursed ground.
As humanity multiplies, the 'sons of God' take wives from the 'daughters of men'; Nephilim appear mighty men of old.
God sees mankind’s wickedness and regrets creating them; He declares judgment to wipe out all living things.
Noah finds grace in God’s eyes; he is described as righteous, blameless, and walking with God.
The earth is filled with violence and corruption; God tells Noah He will destroy all flesh.
God gives Noah detailed instructions to build an ark and gather animals and food for survival.
Noah obeys all that God commands him.
God commands Noah to enter the ark with his family and animals; Noah obeys.
At age 600, Noah enters the ark; the flood begins with 40 days and nights of rain.
Noah, his family, and the animals enter the ark; the Lord shuts them in.
Floodwaters rise, covering mountains and destroying all life outside the ark; the waters prevail 150 days.
God remembers Noah; the waters begin to recede and the ark rests on the mountains of Ararat.
Noah sends out a raven and then a dove to test for dry land; the dove returns with an olive leaf.
The earth dries; God commands Noah to leave the ark with his family and the animals.
Noah builds an altar and offers sacrifices; God promises never again to curse the ground or destroy all life by flood.
God blesses Noah’s family, commands them to multiply, and institutes respect for life and justice for bloodshed.
God establishes a covenant with Noah and all living creatures, using the rainbow as a sign.
Noah becomes drunk; Ham dishonors him, while Shem and Japheth respectfully cover their father.
Noah curses Canaan, blesses Shem and Japheth, and lives 350 more years after the flood.
Descendants of Japheth are listed; they spread across coastlands and form various nations.
Descendants of Ham include Cush, Mizraim, and Canaan; Nimrod becomes a mighty ruler and city-builder.
Descendants of Shem are listed, including Eber, from whom the Hebrews descend.
These are the clans of Noah’s sons, from whom the nations spread across the earth after the flood.
All people speak one language and settle in Shinar; they begin building a tower to reach heaven and make a name for themselves.
God confuses their language and scatters them across the earth; the city is called Babel.
The genealogy from Shem to Abram is recorded, tracing the line through Arphaxad, Eber, and Nahor to Terah.
Terah’s family is introduced: Abram, Nahor, and Haran; Haran dies, and Terah takes Abram, Sarai, and Lot toward Canaan but settles in Haran.
God calls Abram to leave his homeland and promises to bless him, make him a great nation, and bless all families through him.
Abram obeys, travels to Canaan, and builds altars to the Lord as God reaffirms His promise.
Due to famine, Abram goes to Egypt and tells Pharaoh Sarai is his sister; Pharaoh takes her, but God afflicts his house, and Abram is sent away.
Abram and Lot return from Egypt with great wealth; their herdsmen quarrel due to limited land.
Abram offers Lot first choice of land; Lot chooses the fertile Jordan plain near Sodom.
God reaffirms His promise to Abram of countless descendants and land; Abram settles in Hebron and builds an altar.
Four kings wage war against five kings in the Jordan plain; Sodom and Gomorrah are defeated, and Lot is taken captive.
Abram hears of Lot’s capture, gathers trained men, defeats the kings, and rescues Lot and the goods.
Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, blesses Abram; Abram gives him a tenth of all.
The king of Sodom offers Abram the goods, but Abram refuses to take anything, trusting only in God.
God reassures Abram of His protection and promises him a son; Abram believes, and it is counted to him as righteousness.
God confirms His promise of land; Abram prepares a covenant sacrifice.
God reveals that Abram’s descendants will be enslaved for 400 years but will return with great possessions.
God seals the covenant with a smoking furnace and flaming torch; He promises Abram’s offspring the land from Egypt to the Euphrates.
Sarai, barren and impatient, gives her maid Hagar to Abram to bear a child; Hagar conceives and tension arises.
Sarai blames Abram for Hagar’s contempt; Abram allows Sarai to deal with her, and Hagar flees from harsh treatment.
The angel of the Lord finds Hagar in the wilderness, tells her to return, and prophesies about her son Ishmael’s future.
Hagar names God 'El Roi' the God who sees; she returns and bears Ishmael to Abram at age 86.
God appears to Abram, changes his name to Abraham, and establishes an everlasting covenant to make him father of many nations.
God institutes circumcision as the sign of the covenant for Abraham and his descendants.
Sarai is renamed Sarah; God promises she will bear Isaac; Abraham laughs and pleads for Ishmael, who is also blessed.
Abraham obeys immediately, circumcising himself, Ishmael, and all the males in his household.
Three visitors appear to Abraham; he offers generous hospitality and prepares a meal for them.
One visitor promises Sarah will bear a son; she laughs in disbelief, and God affirms His power.
God reveals His plan to judge Sodom and Gomorrah, acknowledging Abraham’s role in guiding future generations.
Abraham intercedes for Sodom, pleading for mercy if righteous people are found; God agrees to spare it for ten.
Two angels visit Lot in Sodom; the men of the city demand them; the angels strike them with blindness.
The angels urge Lot to flee; he escapes with his wife and daughters to Zoar, but his sons-in-law stay behind.
God destroys Sodom and Gomorrah with fire; Lot’s wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt.
Lot’s daughters, fearing extinction, get him drunk and bear sons by him Moab and Ben-ammi.
Abraham travels to Gerar and again claims Sarah is his sister; King Abimelech takes her.
God warns Abimelech in a dream, revealing Sarah is Abraham’s wife and threatening judgment.
Abimelech confronts Abraham, who explains his fear and partial truth about Sarah being his half-sister.
Abimelech restores Sarah, gives gifts, and God heals his household, lifting the barrenness caused by Sarah’s presence.
God fulfills His promise Sarah gives birth to Isaac, and both parents rejoice at the miracle in their old age.
Conflict arises when Ishmael mocks Isaac; Sarah demands Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, and God assures Abraham of Ishmael’s future.
Hagar and Ishmael wander in the wilderness; God hears their cries, provides water, and promises to make Ishmael a great nation.
Abraham makes a covenant with Abimelech over a well at Beersheba; he plants a tree and calls on the name of the Lord.
God tests Abraham by commanding him to sacrifice Isaac; Abraham obeys, trusting that God will provide.
Abraham prepares to sacrifice Isaac, but an angel stops him; a ram is provided as a substitute.
God reaffirms His covenant with Abraham, promising blessings and multiplied descendants.
News arrives of Nahor’s children, including Rebekah future wife of Isaac.
Sarah dies at 127 years old; Abraham mourns her in Hebron.
Abraham negotiates with the Hittites to purchase the cave of Machpelah from Ephron as a burial site.
Abraham secures the field and cave legally and buries Sarah there his first owned land in Canaan.
Abraham sends his servant to find a wife for Isaac from his homeland, not among the Canaanites.
The servant prays for guidance; Rebekah appears and fulfills the sign by offering water to him and his camels.
Rebekah’s family consents to the marriage; she agrees to go and departs with the servant.
Isaac meets Rebekah in the field; he brings her into his mother’s tent and takes her as his wife.
Abraham marries Keturah and has more sons; he gives gifts to them but leaves his inheritance to Isaac.
Abraham dies at 175 and is buried by Isaac and Ishmael in the cave of Machpelah.
The genealogy of Ishmael is listed; he fathers twelve princes and dies at 137.
Isaac and Rebekah have twins Esau and Jacob; God foretells that the older will serve the younger.
Esau sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of stew, showing disregard for his inheritance.
A famine strikes the land; God tells Isaac not to go to Egypt but to stay in Gerar, reaffirming the covenant made with Abraham.
Isaac, fearing for his life, claims Rebekah is his sister; Abimelech discovers the truth and warns his people not to harm them.
Isaac prospers greatly in Gerar, causing envy among the Philistines; Abimelech asks him to leave.
Isaac reopens Abraham’s wells and digs new ones amid disputes; at Rehoboth, he finds peace and worships God.
Abimelech seeks peace with Isaac, recognizing God’s blessing; they make a covenant and Isaac’s servants discover a new well.
Esau marries two Hittite women, bringing grief to Isaac and Rebekah.
Isaac, old and blind, asks Esau to hunt and prepare food so he can bless him before dying.
Rebekah overhears and instructs Jacob to impersonate Esau to receive the blessing instead.
Jacob deceives Isaac and receives the blessing meant for Esau.
Esau returns, discovers the deception, and pleads for a blessing; Isaac gives him a lesser one.
Esau plans to kill Jacob; Rebekah urges Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran.
Isaac blesses Jacob again and sends him to Paddan-aram to find a wife from Rebekah’s family.
Esau, seeing his parents’ disapproval of Canaanite wives, marries a daughter of Ishmael.
Jacob dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven with angels ascending and descending; God reaffirms His covenant.
Jacob sets up a stone pillar at Bethel, vows to serve God, and promises a tenth of all he receives.
Jacob arrives in Haran, meets Rachel at a well, and is welcomed by Laban.
Jacob agrees to work seven years for Rachel’s hand in marriage, driven by love.
Laban deceives Jacob by giving him Leah instead; Jacob agrees to work another seven years for Rachel.
God sees Leah is unloved and blesses her with four sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.
Rachel, barren, gives her maid Bilhah to Jacob; Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali.
Leah, also ceasing to bear, gives Zilpah to Jacob; Zilpah bears Gad and Asher.
Leah trades mandrakes with Rachel and bears Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah.
God remembers Rachel; she conceives and bears Joseph.
Jacob negotiates wages with Laban and uses selective breeding to grow his flocks and wealth.
Jacob hears Laban’s sons grumbling about his wealth; God tells Jacob to return to Canaan, promising His presence.
Jacob explains to Rachel and Leah how Laban has deceived him, but God has blessed him; they agree to leave with him.
Jacob secretly departs with his family and possessions; Rachel steals her father’s household idols.
Laban pursues Jacob and confronts him; God warns Laban in a dream not to harm Jacob; Rachel hides the idols from Laban.
Jacob rebukes Laban for years of mistreatment and declares that God has seen and defended his cause.
Jacob and Laban make a covenant of peace at Mizpah, setting up a stone witness and parting in peace.
Jacob encounters angels and names the place Mahanaim, meaning 'two camps'.
Jacob sends messengers to Esau and learns Esau is coming with 400 men; he divides his camp in fear.
Jacob prays earnestly for deliverance, recalling God’s promises and his own unworthiness.
Jacob prepares a large gift of livestock to appease Esau, sending them ahead in waves.
Jacob wrestles with a mysterious man through the night; he is renamed Israel and walks away limping.
Jacob meets Esau, bows seven times; Esau embraces him and they weep together in reconciliation.
Jacob introduces his family and insists Esau accept his gift as a sign of peace.
Esau offers to travel with Jacob, but Jacob declines and journeys slowly to Succoth.
Jacob arrives in Shechem, buys land, and builds an altar to God named El-Elohe-Israel.
Dinah is violated by Shechem; Jacob’s sons are outraged while Jacob remains silent at first.
Shechem and Hamor propose marriage and alliance; Jacob’s sons deceitfully demand circumcision.
The men of Shechem agree and are circumcised, hoping for unity and shared wealth.
While the men are in pain, Simeon and Levi kill them all, rescue Dinah, and plunder the city.
Jacob rebukes his sons for endangering the family; they defend their actions as protecting Dinah’s honor.
God tells Jacob to return to Bethel; Jacob purges idols, builds an altar, and worships.
Deborah dies; God reaffirms Jacob’s name as Israel and renews the covenant promises.
Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin; Jacob buries her near Bethlehem and sets up a pillar.
Reuben sins by sleeping with Bilhah; the twelve sons of Jacob are listed by mother.
Jacob returns to Isaac; Isaac dies at 180 and is buried by Jacob and Esau.
Esau’s wives, sons and daughters are listed; he moves to Mount Seir.
Chiefs of Edom Esau’s descendants are named.
Horite clans in Seir before the Edomites are catalogued.
Eight kings who reigned in Edom before Israel are recorded.
Second list of Esau’s tribal chiefs by clan and territory.
Joseph, Jacob’s favored son, provokes his brothers by sharing dreams.
Two prophetic dreams increase his brothers’ jealousy.
Brothers seize Joseph; Reuben saves him from death, casts him in a pit.
Judah sells Joseph to Midianite traders for twenty shekels.
Brothers deceive Jacob with Joseph’s blood-stained coat; Jacob mourns.
Judah marries a Canaanite; sons Er and Onan die for wickedness.
Tamar deceives Judah as a prostitute and conceives by him.
Tamar exposes Judah’s items as proof; twins Perez and Zerah are born.
Joseph prospers in Potiphar’s house; is put in charge of all.
Potiphar’s wife tries to seduce him; he flees, leaving his garment.
False accusation lands Joseph in prison; God is with him.
Joseph oversees prisoners and finds favor with the warden.
Pharaoh’s cupbearer and baker offend him and are jailed with Joseph.
Joseph interprets both dreams restoration for one, death for the other.
Cupbearer reinstated, baker executed; cupbearer forgets Joseph.
Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven gaunt ones and seven plump grain heads devoured by withered heads.
The chief cupbearer recalls Joseph’s gift; Pharaoh summons Joseph from prison.
Joseph interprets the dreams: seven years of plenty then seven of famine, and prescribes grain storage.
Pharaoh elevates Joseph to second-in-command, renames him Zaphenath-paneah, and gives him Asenath as wife.
Joseph oversees the gathering of grain; as famine strikes, Egypt and surrounding nations buy from his storehouses.
Famine in Canaan drives Jacob’s sons (except Benjamin) to Egypt for grain.
Joseph recognizes his brothers but conceals his identity, accuses them of spying.
Brothers protest innocence; Joseph demands they bring Benjamin and detains Simeon as guarantee.
On their way home they find their silver returned, sparking fear and guilt over Joseph’s charge.
Severe famine forces Jacob to send Benjamin; Judah assures his safety and Jacob consents.
Jacob loads their vessels with best gifts and double money to appease the Egyptian official.
Brothers dine at Joseph’s house under his steward’s hospitality, unaware it’s Joseph.
Joseph beholds Benjamin, weeps, then orders a special feast seating his brothers by birth order.
Joseph instructs his steward to refill the brothers’ sacks and secretly place his silver cup in Benjamin’s.
Steward accuses them of theft; brothers deny and offer to become slaves if guilty.
Sacks are searched oldest to youngest; cup is found in Benjamin’s, and they tear their clothes.
They return to Joseph’s house; Judah pleads for Benjamin’s life, offering himself as substitute.
Joseph orders all Egyptians out and reveals his identity to his astonished brothers.
He explains God’s providence in sending him to Egypt to preserve life and invites them to Goshen.
Joseph kisses and weeps with Benjamin, hastily prepares wagons and provisions for Jacob’s family.
Brothers return to Canaan with Joseph’s gifts and news; Jacob rejoices at the report of Joseph alive.
Israel offers sacrifices at Beersheba; God appears in vision, assures him about going to Egypt.
Jacob and his family journey to Egypt in wagons provided by Pharaoh.
Genealogical listing of Jacob’s descendants who moved to Egypt, totaling seventy persons.
Jacob meets Joseph in Goshen and prepares his sons before audience with Pharaoh.
Joseph presents his family to Pharaoh; they settle in Goshen.
Severe famine leads Egyptians to exchange money, livestock, and land for food; Joseph’s protocols centralize Egyptian land under Pharaoh.
Israel prospers in Egypt; Jacob requests burial in Canaan.
Jacob prepares to die and adopts Ephraim and Manasseh, promising them inheritance.
Jacob crosses hands to bless Ephraim over Manasseh, prophesying their future greatness.
Jacob seals the blessing, gives Joseph a portion of land in Canaan.
Jacob summons his sons to prophesy over them, beginning with Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.
Blessings and prophecies for Zebulun, Issachar, Dan, Gad, Asher, and Naphtali.
Joseph’s rich blessing and Benjamin’s description as a ravenous wolf.
Jacob instructs his burial in Machpelah and then dies.
Mourning and embalming of Jacob; Joseph secures Pharaoh’s permission for burial in Canaan.
Brothers fear reprisal, Joseph reassures forgiveness and acknowledges God’s sovereignty.
Joseph lives until 110, instructs his burial with the patriarchs when Israel returns to Canaan; then he dies.
Jacob’s descendants settle and multiply in Egypt, filling the land
A new Pharaoh, fearing Israel’s growth, enslaves and oppresses them with forced labor
Midwives Shiphrah and Puah defy Pharaoh’s command to kill Hebrew boys and are blessed by God
Pharaoh orders all newborn Hebrew boys to be cast into the Nile
Moses is born, hidden by his mother, placed in a basket, and adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter
Moses kills an Egyptian overseer, fears reprisal, and flees to Midian
In Midian Moses defends Jethro’s daughters, marries Zipporah, and they have a son Gershom
Israelite suffering rises, their cry reaches God, and He remembers His covenant
Moses encounters the burning bush at Horeb and hears God call his name
God promises to deliver Israel from Egypt and commissions Moses as leader
Moses objects; God reveals His name as I AM WHO I AM and assures His presence
God instructs Moses on confronting Pharaoh, giving signs, and plundering Egypt
Moses expresses doubt; God gives the rod-to-snake sign
God gives the leprous-hand and water-to-blood signs
Moses protests his speaking ability; God reassures He will guide his words
Moses asks for help; God appoints Aaron as his spokesman and confirms the signs
Moses returns to Egypt with his family; God warns Pharaoh his firstborn will die if he resists
God seeks to kill Moses; Zipporah circumcises their son, averting divine wrath
Aaron meets Moses, they perform signs before Israel’s elders, and the people believe
Moses and Aaron demand Israel’s release to worship; Pharaoh refuses and questions God’s authority
Pharaoh increases Israel’s burdens by removing straw supply and maintaining the brick quota
Israelite foremen confront Moses and Aaron, blaming them for the harsher labor
Moses cries out to God, questioning why the people’s suffering has worsened
God reaffirms His covenant, promises to bring Israel out of Egyptian bondage by mighty hand.
Israelites, discouraged by slavery, refuse to listen; Moses doubts his own speech ability.
Genealogies of Moses and Aaron outline their Levitical lineage and divine appointment.
Moses and Aaron obey but Moses again protests his lack of eloquence.
God appoints Moses as His representative to Pharaoh and warns that Pharaoh’s heart will be hardened.
Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent and swallows the magicians’ serpents, yet Pharaoh’s heart remains stubborn.
Moses strikes the Nile; its waters turn to blood, killing fish and ruining the river.
Egyptians dig for fresh water, but Pharaoh’s heart stays hardened despite the plague.
Frogs cover the land; Pharaoh briefly relents then hardens his heart once they are removed.
Gnats infest people and animals; magicians cannot replicate this plague and acknowledge God.
Flies swarm Egypt except Goshen; Pharaoh negotiates but again breaks his promise when relief comes.
Pharaoh offers sacrifices but refuses to free Israel’s herds, hardening his heart anew.
A pestilence strikes all Egyptian livestock but spares Israel’s, yet Pharaoh’s heart remains hard.
Soot from a furnace causes painful boils on Egyptians and their animals without warning.
Hail, thunder, and lightning destroy crops and livestock outside Egypt; Goshen is spared.
Pharaoh admits sin and pleads for the hail to stop but hardens his heart once the storm ceases.
God warns of a locust plague; Pharaoh remains defiant despite his servants’ counsel.
Locusts devour all vegetation; Pharaoh begs removal but again hardens his heart.
Deep darkness covers Egypt for three days while Israelites have light; Pharaoh refuses to let Israel go.
God announces the final plague: the death of Egypt’s firstborn and promises Pharaoh will then drive Israel out.
Moses delivers God’s warning; no Israelite home is harmed as God distinguishes His people for protection.
The Passover is instituted: select an unblemished lamb, sacrifice it, and mark doorposts with its blood.
Israelites eat unleavened bread and observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days.
Households apply the lamb’s blood as instructed; the first plague of death passes over Israel.
At midnight all Egyptian firstborn die; Pharaoh urges Israel to leave with silver, gold, and clothing.
Israel departs Rameses to Succoth with unleavened dough; Passover ordained as a perpetual observance.
Every firstborn human and animal is consecrated to the Lord as a sign of His redemptive act.
The Feast of Unleavened Bread is commanded to memorialize the Exodus and teach future generations.
Firstborn are redeemed; the law’s commands become a sign on hand and between eyes.
God leads Israel by a longer wilderness route and guides them with a cloud by day and fire by night.
Israel camps by Pi-hahiroth; God sets the stage to harden Pharaoh’s heart for their rescue.
Pharaoh pursues with chariots; Israel finds itself trapped between the sea and Egypt’s army.
In fear they cry out; Moses urges them to stand firm as God prepares to deliver them.
God parts the sea at Moses’ command, creating dry ground with walls of water on both sides.
Israel crosses safely; the pursuing Egyptians drown when the waters return, sealing Israel’s freedom.
Moses and Israel sing the Song at the Sea, celebrating God’s victory over Egypt.
Miriam leads the women in dance and song, echoing the celebration of deliverance.
At Marah the waters are bitter; God makes them sweet and promises protection from future diseases.
Laws for Hebrew servants: six years of service, freedom in the seventh, and provisions if one chooses to stay.
Regulations for giving daughters as servants: rights to food, clothing, and marriage if unloved.
Murder and personal injury statutes: life for life, eye for eye, and compensation for harm.
Liability for animal attacks: owner’s responsibility and restitution for property damage or death.
Theft and restitution: return stolen goods doubled if alive, triple if sold.
Liability for damage by one’s animals or neighbor’s property left in one’s care.
Householder’s responsibility: injury or death of a slave or maid; seduction and marriage duties.
Seduction of virgin: payment of bride-price or marriage; no redemption by price later.
Prohibitions: sorcery, bestiality, sacrifices to other gods; the Lord’s zeal against idolatry.
Justice commands: no false reports, bribes, or oppression of foreigners, widows, or orphans.
Sabbath and agricultural rest: six years sow and reap, seventh year left fallow; Sabbath rest for all.
Three annual festivals: Unleavened Bread, Harvest, and Ingathering; firstfruits and prohibition of boiling young goat in its mother’s milk.
Promise of angelic guidance into Canaan, victory over enemies, and warning against idolatry in the land.
Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders see God; covenant ratified with sacrifices and sprinkled blood.
Elders dine in God’s presence under His feet; no harm befalls them.
God calls Moses to Sinai for tablets; Moses ascends the clouded mountain for forty days and nights.
Call for offerings: gold, silver, bronze, fabrics, and precious stones to build the tabernacle.
Design of the ark of the covenant with mercy seat and cherubim; God’s presence promised above the atonement cover.
Table for showbread: dimensions, materials, and arrangement of twelve loaves before the Lord.
Golden lampstand design and instructions for its accessories; weaving of tabernacle curtains and fittings.
Instructions for making the ten curtains of fine linen and blue, purple and scarlet yarn for the tabernacle.
Directions for constructing twenty wooden boards and their silver bases to form the tabernacle frame.
Design of the inner veil of blue, purple and scarlet yarn with cherubim, separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy.
Specifications for the bronze altar for burnt offerings, including horns and utensils.
Layout of the courtyard: hangings of fine linen, supporting pillars and bases surrounding the tabernacle.
Command to keep pure olive oil continually supplied for the lamp to burn in the tabernacle.
Selection of Aaron and his sons for priesthood and materials needed for their garments.
Making of the ephod: two onyx stones engraved with the names of Israel’s tribes and settings of gold and gemstones.
Crafting the breastpiece of judgment with twelve stones and instructions for its attachment to the ephod.
Weaving the blue robe with pomegranates and golden bells along its hem for Aaron’s service.
Making the turban and golden plate engraved 'Holy to the Lord' to fasten on Aaron’s forehead.
Ordination ceremony for Aaron and his sons: washing, clothing, anointing and sacrifices.
Sin offering with bull for atonement and consecration over the altar.
Ram of consecration: blood applied to the altar and the priests, and anointing oil poured on them.
Second ram offering and use of its blood on Aaron’s ears, hands and feet to sanctify him.
Instructions for the seven-day consecration period and its recurring atonement rituals.
Altar of incense made of acacia wood overlaid with gold; Aaron to burn incense morning and evening.
Instruction for atonement money: each man over twenty gives half a shekel for the service of the tabernacle.
Bronze basin for Aaron and his sons to wash their hands and feet before ministering.
Recipe for the holy anointing oil and aromatic incense; warning not to reproduce these for personal use.
God names Bezalel and Oholiab as chief artisans, filling them with skill to build the tabernacle furnishings.
Detailed list of sacred objects and garments to be crafted according to God’s design.
The Sabbath is instituted as a perpetual sign of the covenant; profaning it brings death.
God gives Moses the two tablets of the Testimony, inscribed by His own hand.
In Moses’ absence on Sinai, the people demand a god; Aaron fashions a golden calf and they worship it.
God threatens judgment; Moses intercedes and God relents from destroying Israel.
Moses descends, shatters the tablets in anger, burns the calf and makes the people drink its dust.
Levites execute judgment on idolaters; Moses offers to have his name blotted out for their sake; a plague follows.
God tells Israel to move on to Canaan but will not go with them lest He consume them for their sin.
Moses pitches the Tent of Meeting outside the camp where he speaks with God face to face.
Moses pleads for God’s presence; God agrees to accompany and grant rest to Israel.
Moses asks to see God’s glory; God passes by, shielding Moses so he sees only His back.
God commands new stone tablets; Moses ascends Sinai early to meet Him.
The LORD proclaims His name and character compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love.
Covenant renewed with promises of blessing for obedience and laws on festivals, firstborns, and idolatry.
Moses spends 40 days with God; he descends with a radiant face and veils it before Israel.
Moses reiterates the Sabbath command, warning against any work or fire on that day.
Call for freewill offerings of gold, fabrics, skins, wood, oil and spices to build the tabernacle.
Skilled craftsmen are invited to construct every part of the tent, furnishings, and priestly garments.
Israelites, moved by the Spirit, bring generous offerings of material and labor.
Bezalel and Oholiab are formally filled with the Spirit to teach and oversee all artistic work.
Bezalel and Oholiab, filled with God’s wisdom, are appointed to oversee the tabernacle work; offerings flood in beyond need.
Artisans make ten fine-linen curtains with blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and goat-hair coverings for the tent.
They construct twenty acacia wood frames plated with gold, each set in silver bases, to support the tabernacle walls.
An inner veil of blue, purple and scarlet with cherubim motifs is woven to separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy.
Bezalel builds the Ark of the Covenant from acacia wood overlaid with gold and fitting rings and poles for carrying.
He fashions the mercy-seat and its two cherubim of beaten gold to cover the Ark.
The table of showbread is made of acacia wood and gold, with utensils and twelve loaves arranged upon it.
A pure gold lampstand with seven branches, cups and ornamental buds is crafted for continual light.
An acacia wood incense altar is overlaid with gold; the sacred anointing oil and incense are prepared.
The bronze altar for burnt offerings is constructed, hollow and portable, with horns and all utensils of bronze.
A bronze laver, made from the mirrors of Israel’s women, is set for priests’ ceremonial washing.
Fine-linen curtains and silver-fitted pillars form the tabernacle courtyard and its entrance screen of blue, purple and scarlet.
An inventory lists the gold, silver and bronze contributed by the people and used in all the sanctuary work.
Priestly garments are woven and assembled: the ephod, breastpiece, robe, tunics, sashes and turban with "Holy to the Lord" plate.
All tabernacle furnishings and priestly vestments are brought to Moses, who inspects the work, blesses the craftsmen, and confirms completeness.
God commands Moses to set up and consecrate the tabernacle and all its furnishings with anointing oil.
Aaron and his sons are anointed and ordained as priests over the altar and the holy place.
Moses erects the tabernacle on the first day of the first month of the second year, following every divine detail.
The cloud covers the Tent of Meeting and God’s glory fills the tabernacle; the cloud and fire guide Israel’s journey.
Instructions for burnt offerings from the herd: unblemished male, hand laid, blood sprinkled, and entire animal burned on the altar.
Burnt offerings from the flock: unblemished lamb or goat, same ritual of laying on, slaughter, blood handling, and burning.
Burnt offerings of birds: turtledove or pigeon, priest removes head, drains blood, tears it and burns it whole.
Basic grain offering: fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense; priest burns a memorial portion, remainder to priests.
Grain offerings baked on a griddle or in an oven or pan: unleavened cakes or wafers of fine flour and oil.
Firstfruits grain offering: fine flour with oil, frankincense, and salt; sweet aroma on altar, rest given to Aaron’s sons.
Peace offerings from the herd: male or female unblemished, hand laid, blood sprinkled, fat and kidneys burned.
Peace offerings from flock or goat: same procedure lay on, slaughter, blood, and burning of designated portions.
Prohibition on eating fat or blood in peace offerings; establishes a perpetual statute of holiness.
Sin offering for the anointed priest: unblemished bull, hand laid, blood sprinkled in sanctuary and on altar, fat burned, carcass taken outside camp.
Sin offering for the whole congregation: identical bull offering for unintentional communal sins.
Sin offering for a ruler: unblemished male goat, same atonement ritual of blood and burning.
Sin offering for a common person: female goat or lamb, identical procedure, showing universal need for atonement.
Guilt incurred by failing to testify, touching unclean things, or making rash vows; confession triggers atonement.
Guilt offerings scaled to means: lamb or goat, or two birds, or fine flour, with confession and sacrifice ritual.
Trespass offerings for desecration of holy things: male lamb or goat, hand laid, blood sprinkled, fat burned.
Restitution for harm: restore value plus one-fifth to the wronged party, bring guilt offering, priest makes atonement.
Guilt offering prescribed for deceit, theft or false oath, requiring restitution plus one-fifth and a ram without blemish for atonement.
Burnt offering regulations: fire on the altar must burn continually; priest removes ashes and keeps the fire alive, including morning provisions.
Grain offering rules: fine flour mixed with oil and frankincense; a memorial portion burned, remainder eaten by priests in a holy place without yeast.
Regular grain offering for anointed priest: daily portions morning and evening; must be prepared on a griddle and burned completely.
Sin offering details: slaughter at the burnt-offering site, designated parts for burning and consumption by priests, and restrictions on contact with atonement blood.
Further instructions on guilt, sin and grain offerings, clarifying that priests eat designated portions in a holy place.
Peace offering ordinances: unleavened cakes, wafers and fine flour with oil; eating provisions by the offerer and priests; timing limits.
Prohibition on eating fat and blood from sacrifices; sacredness of these elements and penalty for violation.
Wave and heave offerings assigned to the priests; statutes made perpetual for Aaron’s sons, affirming their entitlement to parts of sacrifices.
Moses gathers the congregation, washes Aaron and his sons, dresses them in priestly garments, and anoints the tabernacle.
Sin offering for priests: a bull is offered, blood sprinkled on the altar and used for purification, and the carcass burned outside the camp.
Burnt offering: a ram is slaughtered, blood applied to the altar, entrails washed, and the entire animal burned as a pleasing aroma.
Ordination ram and bread offering: blood applied to Aaron and his sons, portions waved, and consecration oil sprinkled.
Command to eat consecration offerings, remain at the Tent of Meeting seven days, and completion of the ordination.
On the eighth day Moses summons Aaron, his sons and the elders; instructions for sin, burnt and peace offerings with promise of God’s appearance.
Aaron performs sin and burnt offerings for himself and the people, following Moses’ commands and rituals precisely.
Aaron presents the people’s offerings: sin, burnt, grain and peace offerings according to the prescribed ordinance.
Moses and Aaron bless Israel; the glory of the LORD appears and fire from the LORD consumes the offerings on the altar.
Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD; divine fire proceeds from the LORD and consumes them as judgment.
Moses explains God’s holiness; Aaron remains silent; Moses directs removal of the bodies and warns priests against mourning.
The LORD forbids priests from drinking wine or strong drink before ministry, commands them to distinguish holy from common and teach this to Israel.
Moses instructs Eleazar and Ithamar to eat the sin offering properly; they initially withhold, citing grief, then obey on Moses’ approval.
Defines clean land animals those chewing the cud and having cloven hooves; others are unclean.
Permits fish with fins and scales; all others in the water are unclean.
Lists forbidden birds predators, scavengers, and winged pests.
Allows only certain flying insects with jointed legs for hopping; all others are detestable.
Contact with carcasses defiles people; they must wash and remain unclean until evening.
After childbirth a mother is unclean seven days for a son, fourteen for a daughter; purification days follow.
On conclusion of purification she brings a lamb (or turtle dove/pigeon) for a sin offering and a burnt offering.
Priest examines skin lesions; initial quarantine for seven days, then reinspection.
Differentiates white hairs, raw flesh, and sore patterns to declare clean or unclean.
Bright spots that fade on shaving are clean; persistent spots are unclean.
Scalp and beard diseases described; white hair in a mole or swelling signals uncleanliness.
White scabs with normal hair are clean; leprous scabs require isolation outside the camp.
Cleansing ritual for healed leper: two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop; blood of one sprinkled, other set free.
Cleansed person shaves hair, washes clothes and body; then declared clean.
Offers lambs, grain offering, oil; priest sprinkles blood and oil seven times, waves offerings.
House defiled by mold must be examined, stones removed, scraped and replastered; if defilement returns, stones dismantled.
Detailed protocol for house purification: new stone, fresh plaster, oil sprinkling; record of statutes.
Any abnormal male discharge makes him unclean; garments and bedding contaminate, washing and offerings required if persistent.
Normal emission of semen defiles until evening after bathing; no offering required.
Woman’s menstrual flow makes her unclean seven days; anyone touching her or her bed is unclean until evening.
Prolonged female discharge extends uncleanness until flow stops plus seven days; must bring offerings.
The community must distinguish clean from unclean; all clothes and vessels defiled by discharge must be washed.
God forbids Aaron from entering the Holy of Holies at will and prescribes the bull sin offering for himself.
Two goats are presented: one sacrificed for a sin offering, the other (the scapegoat) sent to Azazel by lot.
Aaron applies bull and goat blood to cleanse the Most Holy Place, the tabernacle, and the altar from Israel’s sins.
Aaron makes atonement for the people by placing hands on the scapegoat, which bears their sins into the wilderness.
Bull and goat carcasses are burned outside the camp; the sanctuary is purified and uncleanliness removed.
The Day of Atonement is ordained as a yearly Sabbath of rest and atonement for all generations.
All slaughter for sacrifice must occur at the Tent of Meeting to avoid profaning camp and foreign altars.
Sacrificial animals must be brought to the priest; unlawful slaughter incurs guilt and must be reconciled.
Eating blood is strictly forbidden; life is in the blood, so blood must be poured out and covered with earth.
Any carrion or flesh with blood eaten defiles; those with bodily discharges must wash and remain unclean.
The people must obey Israel’s statutes, not the customs of Egypt or Canaan, to live and inherit the land.
Prohibitions against sexual relations with close kin: parents, siblings, in-laws, and extended family.
Further bans on sexual immorality: relations during menstruation, with a neighbor’s wife, and bestiality.
Israel is warned to avoid Canaanite abominations and called to uphold God’s holiness or face expulsion.
Call to holiness: fear God, honor Sabbath and offerings, revere parents, and avoid idols.
Leave gleanings and the corners of fields for the poor and the stranger; do not harvest to the boundary.
Prohibitions on stealing, lying and slander; pursue justice, love neighbor and the stranger as self.
Ban on mixing species, sowing mixed seed and wearing mixed fabrics; rules for vows and fruit trees.
Various statutes: no divination, honest weights, festival observance, and respect for parents and the alien.
Child sacrifice to Molech is punishable by death; the people profane God by these rites and are cut off.
Mediums and spiritists are forbidden and must be cut off; keeping God’s statutes demonstrates life.
Severe penalties, including death, for adultery, incest, homosexuality, and bestiality to purge evil.
Incest with in-laws and relations with animals demand execution to maintain holy conduct.
Obey God’s decrees and ordinances; be holy as God is holy, reflecting His separation from defilement.
Priests must not defile themselves by touching the dead except for close kin mother, father, son, daughter, brother or virgin sister.
They must not shave their heads, trim beards or make bodily cuts; they are holy and must honor God’s name.
A priest must marry only a virgin of his people; his daughter who prostitutes profanes him and is to be burned.
The high priest must not uncover his head, tear his clothes or approach any dead body, nor marry a widow or divorced woman.
Any descendant of Aaron with physical defects blindness, lameness, disfigurement may eat holy food but cannot serve at the altar.
Aaron and his sons must treat sacred offerings with reverence: unclean or blemished priests are cut off and forbidden to eat them.
Only priests, their household slaves or widowed/divorced daughters may eat holy offerings; trespass requires restitution plus a fifth.
Offerings must be unblemished; anyone bringing a flawed animal is to be cut off and cannot eat from the altar.
Young animals must stay with their mothers seven days; firstborn unblemished animals are sacred and not to be mutilated.
The LORD’s appointed feasts begin with the weekly Sabbath as a holy convocation six days of work, one of rest.
Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread mark Israel’s exodus; Firstfruits sheaf offered before new grain is eaten.
Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) follows seven weeks after Firstfruits; bring two loaves and cheerfully present offerings.
Feast of Trumpets on the first of the seventh month and Day of Atonement on the tenth as a solemn rest and affliction.
Feast of Tabernacles for seven days in booths; all male Israelites appear before the LORD and rejoice.
Command to supply pure olive oil for the lampstand so Aaron tends the lamps continually before the LORD.
Twelve loaves of showbread baked on the Sabbath, arranged in two rows, with frankincense as a perpetual covenant.
Incident of blasphemy by a mixed-heritage man; the community stones him outside the camp at God’s command.
Principle of lex talionis life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth applies equally to native and foreigner.
Sabbath year: after six years of sowing and pruning the land rests, its produce feeding all inhabitants and livestock.
Year of Jubilee every fiftieth year: trumpet blast proclaims liberty, property returns to original families and fields rest.
Land sales priced by remaining years until Jubilee; permanent sale forbidden since the land belongs to the LORD.
Kinsman-redeemer restores sold property; poor Israelites can borrow without interest and be freed in Jubilee.
Israelite servants work only until Jubilee and are treated as hired workers; God reminds them He redeemed them from Egypt.
Command to avoid idolatry, keep Sabbaths and festivals as foundational statutes.
Blessings for obedience: abundant harvest, peace, defeat of enemies, and God’s presence among Israel.
Curses for disobedience: terror, pestilence, famine, wild beasts, sword, siege, exile, and ruin.
Promise of restoration: upon confession, God remembers His covenant and restores the land and fortunes.
Reaffirmation that these statutes apply equally to native Israelites and resident aliens.
Valuation of persons vowed to the LORD: pricing by age and gender for redemption.
Valuation of animals and houses: fixed values for consecration of livestock and urban properties.
Valuation and redemption of land: prices set relative to years remaining until Jubilee.
Devoted persons and animals become the LORD’s property and must not be redeemed but sacrificed.
Tithes: a tenth of produce and herds is holy, with no redemption allowed; Levites’ tithe given to priests.
God instructs Moses and Aaron in Sinai’s second year to take a census of men 20 years and older capable of military service.
Tribal leaders are named to assist with the census, one from each tribe.
Each tribe’s population is counted in order from Reuben to Naphtali; totals reveal over 600,000 fighting men.
The Levites are exempted from military service to care for the Tabernacle.
Israel camps around the Tabernacle as God commands, organized under tribal standards.
The LORD directs the arrangement of Israel’s camp around the Tabernacle by tribe and banner.
Tribes of Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun camp to the east under their respective leaders.
Reuben, Simeon, and Gad position to the south with their captains.
Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin encamp to the west under named chieftains.
Dan, Asher, and Naphtali settle to the north; Levites occupy the center to guard the Tabernacle.
Genealogy of Aaron and Moses, noting Nadab and Abihu’s fate and Eleazar and Ithamar’s roles.
The tribe of Levi is set apart to serve Aaron and care for the Tabernacle’s furnishings.
God substitutes the Levites for all firstborn Israelites as holy to the LORD.
Levites are counted by clan Gershonites, Kohathites, Merarites and assigned specific duties.
All firstborn males of Israel are numbered; Levites redeem surplus firstborn by a ransom payment.
Kohathite Levites aged 30–50 are charged with carrying the Tabernacle’s most holy items after priests cover them.
Gershonite Levites transport the Tabernacle’s fabrics and curtains under priestly oversight.
Merarite Levites are responsible for moving the Tabernacle’s structural poles, frames, and bases.
Moses and Aaron oversee the census of Levite clans, totaling 8,580 ready for service.
God commands removal of anyone with skin disease, bodily discharge, or contact with the dead, to keep the camp pure.
Laws of restitution: sinners must confess, repay victims plus one-fifth, and offer a guilt offering if no kinsman.
Ordinance of jealous husband: a ritual with bitter water tests suspected adultery, bringing curse if guilty or vindication if innocent.
Instructions for the Nazirite vow: abstain from grape products, let hair grow uncut, avoid corpses, and bring specified offerings when the vow ends.
Aaronic blessing: the Lord commands Moses to have Aaron bless Israel with words of protection, grace and peace.
Each tribal chief offers six covered carts and twelve oxen for the service of the tabernacle, to be assigned to the Levites.
God directs that Gershonites and Merarites receive the carts and oxen; Kohathites carry the sacred furnishings on their shoulders.
Over twelve days, the leaders of each tribe present identical dedication offerings of silver, gold, grain and livestock.
Moses enters the tabernacle and hears the Lord speak to him from above the mercy seat between the cherubim.
God instructs Aaron to arrange the seven lamps on the golden lampstand so they give light toward the front.
Levites undergo a purification rite shaving, washing and sin offering and are presented before the Lord as a wave offering.
The Levites begin active service at age twenty-five and retire at fifty, though they may assist their brothers thereafter.
Israel keeps the second Passover in the wilderness on the fourteenth day of the first month, at twilight.
Those ceremonially unclean or traveling may observe Passover in the second month; failure to do so brings exclusion.
A cloud covers the tabernacle by day and fire by night; Israel breaks camp or stays put according to its movement.
God commands two silver trumpets for calling assemblies, directing camp movements, sounding war alarms and celebrating festivals.
On the twentieth day of the second month Israel departs Sinai for Paran; the ark leads and tribes march in divinely ordained order.
Moses invites his father-in-law Hobab to join; as the ark moves he prays for the Lord to scatter Israel’s enemies.
The Israelites grumble about hardship; the Lord’s fire consumes the camp’s outskirts until Moses prays and it stops.
A mixed multitude craves meat; Israel weeps for Egypt’s foods, Moses laments his burden, and the Lord promises help.
God appoints seventy elders to bear Moses’ spirit; Eldad and Medad prophesy, and Joshua wishes all were prophets.
God sends quail in wind; as meat fills them, His wrath strikes greedy Israelites with a severe plague at Kibroth-hattaavah.
Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses over his Cushite wife and question his exclusive prophetic role.
God defends Moses’ unique face-to-face relationship, contrasting it with other prophecy by visions and dreams.
In anger, the Lord strikes Miriam with leprosy; Aaron pleads for her.
Moses intercedes, the Lord heals Miriam after seven days of isolation, and the camp waits until she returns.
God commands twelve tribal leaders to spy out Canaan; they explore the land’s people, cities, produce and terrain.
The spies spend forty days scouting; they return with a cluster of grapes, pomegranates and figs as evidence.
Ten spies report giants in fortified cities, stirring fear, while acknowledging the land’s bounty of milk and honey.
Caleb and Joshua urge faith and immediate conquest; the other spies spread a fearful report, likening themselves to grasshoppers.
All Israel weeps at the bad report and revolts, proposing to return to Egypt under new leadership.
Moses and Aaron fall facedown; Joshua and Caleb plead for trust in God and warn against rebellion.
The congregation threatens to stone the faithful spies; God threatens judgment, and Moses intercedes, invoking God’s mercy.
God forgives but decrees that the unbelieving generation will wander forty years and not enter Canaan, sparing only Caleb and Joshua.
The faithless spies die of plague; a failed attempt to enter Canaan ends in defeat by Amalekites and Canaanites.
Laws for offerings upon entering Canaan: supplementary grain and drink offerings accompany burnt and peace sacrifices.
Regulations for unintentional sin: community and individual guilt offerings and atonement procedures.
A man gathering wood on the Sabbath is executed by stoning, underscoring the seriousness of desecrating the day.
God orders tassels on garments’ corners as a visual reminder to obey His commandments perpetually.
Korah, Dathan, Abiram, and 250 leaders rebel against Moses and Aaron, claiming all Israelites are holy.
Moses proposes a test: God will show whom He has chosen by accepting incense offerings.
Dathan and Abiram refuse to meet Moses, accusing him of failing to deliver the promised land.
Korah and his followers gather at the Tent of Meeting; the glory of the Lord appears.
God threatens to destroy the congregation; Moses and Aaron intercede for the people.
The earth swallows Korah, Dathan, and Abiram; fire consumes the 250 men offering incense.
Eleazar collects the censers and hammers them into a covering for the altar as a warning.
The people complain again; a plague breaks out, but Aaron stops it with incense 14,700 die.
God commands each tribe to submit a staff; the one that buds will confirm His chosen leader.
Aaron’s staff buds, blossoms, and produces almonds God’s sign of priestly appointment.
God tells Moses to place Aaron’s staff before the Ark as a sign against rebellion.
The people fear death from approaching the Lord’s presence, realizing His holiness.
Aaron and his sons bear responsibility for the sanctuary; Levites assist but may not approach the altar.
Priests receive portions of offerings, firstfruits, and holy gifts as their inheritance.
Levites receive tithes from Israel in place of land inheritance.
Levites must tithe from their tithes to the priests; both must treat offerings as holy.
Law of the red heifer: a perfect red cow is burned; ashes are kept for purification from corpse defilement.
Anyone who touches a dead body is unclean for seven days and must be purified or be cut off.
Instructions for purifying tents, vessels, and people exposed to death using water mixed with red heifer ashes.
Miriam dies and is buried at Kadesh.
The people complain about lack of water; Moses and Aaron seek God’s guidance.
God tells Moses to speak to the rock, but he strikes it; water flows, but Moses and Aaron are barred from Canaan.
Edom refuses Israel passage through its land, forcing a detour.
Aaron dies on Mount Hor; Eleazar becomes high priest; Israel mourns thirty days.
Israel defeats King Arad after vowing to destroy his cities if God grants victory.
The people complain; God sends fiery serpents; Moses lifts a bronze serpent to heal those who look upon it.
Israel journeys through the wilderness, camps at various sites, and sings the Song of the Well after God provides water.
Israel requests passage through Amorite land; King Sihon refuses and is defeated in battle.
Israel defeats King Og of Bashan and takes possession of his territory.
Balak, king of Moab, fears Israel and sends for Balaam to curse them.
God tells Balaam not to go; Balaam refuses Balak’s first offer.
Balak sends more prestigious messengers; God permits Balaam to go but only speak His words.
God’s angel blocks Balaam’s path; his donkey sees the angel and speaks; Balaam repents.
Balak meets Balaam and takes him to view Israel from Bamoth-baal.
Balaam blesses Israel from Bamoth-baal; Balak is frustrated.
From Mount Pisgah, Balaam again blesses Israel, declaring God’s unchanging favor.
Balak tries a third location, hoping for a different result.
Balaam delivers a third oracle, praising Israel’s beauty and strength.
Balak angrily dismisses Balaam, who insists he can only speak God’s word.
Balaam prophesies a star from Jacob a ruler who will crush Moab and Edom.
Balaam foretells the downfall of Amalek, Asshur, and other nations.
Israel commits idolatry with Moabite women and worships Baal of Peor; God commands judgment.
Phinehas kills an Israelite and Midianite woman, halting a plague that kills 24,000.
God rewards Phinehas with a covenant of peace and perpetual priesthood.
The slain couple is identified; God commands hostility toward the Midianites for their deception.
God commands a second census of men 20 years and older for military service.
Tribes are counted individually; total number is 601,730 fighting men.
Land is to be divided proportionally by tribe size, assigned by lot.
Levites are counted separately 23,000 males but receive no land inheritance.
Only Joshua and Caleb remain from the first generation; all others perished in the wilderness.
Zelophehad’s five daughters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah petition Moses for their father’s inheritance since he had no sons.
God affirms their claim and establishes a new law: if a man dies without sons, inheritance passes to daughters, then to other relatives.
God tells Moses to ascend Mount Abarim to view the Promised Land; he will die there for disobeying at Meribah.
Moses asks God to appoint a successor; God chooses Joshua, and Moses publicly commissions him before Eleazar and the people.
Daily offerings: two lambs each day morning and evening with grain and drink offerings.
Sabbath offerings: two additional lambs with grain and drink offerings.
Monthly offerings: bulls, rams, lambs, and a goat for sin offering at the start of each month.
Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread: special offerings for seven days, beginning on the fourteenth day of the first month.
Feast of Weeks (Pentecost): offerings of new grain, animals, and drink, with no regular work permitted.
Feast of Trumpets (1st day of 7th month): sacred assembly with trumpet blasts and special offerings.
Day of Atonement (10th day): solemn rest, self-denial, and prescribed sacrifices for atonement.
Feast of Tabernacles (15th–21st days): daily offerings with decreasing numbers of bulls, plus rams, lambs, and goats.
Eighth day assembly: final festival offering; Moses records all these commands for Israel’s observance.
Moses instructs Israelites on the binding nature of vows.
Vows made by men stand unchanged.
Vows by married women require husband’s approval or are nullified.
Vows by widows or divorced daughters stand unless a father intervenes.
Father’s or husband’s power to confirm or annul a daughter’s vow.
God commands vengeance on Midian for leading Israel into sin.
Israel defeats Midian, slays kings, and takes captives and spoil.
Purification rites for soldiers and spoil, with offerings to the Lord.
War spoils are divided: tribute to the Lord, priestly share and soldiers’ share.
Detailed distribution of plunder among soldiers, community and tribal contributions.
Reuben and Gad request to settle on the east side of the Jordan.
Moses warns their request will hinder conquest west of Jordan.
They pledge to join the army until all tribes possess their land.
Territories east of Jordan allocated to Reuben, Gad and half-tribe of Manasseh.
Moses records Israel’s journey stages from Egypt as commanded by the Lord.
Israel departs Rameses the day after Passover; Egyptians bury their firstborn.
Forty-two encampments are listed from Rameses to the plains of Moab, including key stops like the Red Sea, Sinai, Kadesh, and Mount Hor where Aaron dies.
God commands Israel to drive out Canaan’s inhabitants, destroy idols, and take possession of the land.
Land is to be divided by lot; failure to expel the Canaanites will result in them becoming a snare to Israel.
God defines the boundaries of Canaan: south from Zin to Egypt’s Wadi, west by the Mediterranean, north to Mount Hor, and east along the Jordan.
Leaders from each tribe are appointed to oversee land distribution; Eleazar and Joshua lead the process.
God commands 48 cities for the Levites, including six cities of refuge, proportionally taken from each tribe’s inheritance.
Cities of refuge are established for those who kill unintentionally, protecting them from the avenger of blood.
Intentional murder is punishable by death; no refuge is granted to the guilty.
Unintentional killers must remain in refuge until the high priest dies; leaving early forfeits protection.
Murder requires multiple witnesses; no ransom is accepted for murderers or fugitives; bloodshed defiles the land.
Leaders from Manasseh raise concern that Zelophehad’s daughters’ inheritance could transfer to other tribes through marriage.
God commands that daughters who inherit land must marry within their tribe to preserve tribal boundaries.
Zelophehad’s daughters obey and marry within Manasseh, keeping their inheritance in their father’s tribe.
These are the final commands given by God through Moses on the plains of Moab before entering Canaan.
Moses begins his final address to Israel in the wilderness east of the Jordan, recounting their journey.
God commands Israel to leave Horeb and take possession of the Promised Land.
Moses recalls appointing leaders to help judge the people due to their growing numbers.
Israel’s refusal to enter Canaan after the spies’ report leads to rebellion and fear.
God punishes the unbelieving generation; only Caleb and Joshua will enter the land.
Israel tries to enter Canaan without God’s blessing and is defeated by the Amorites.
Israel wanders in the wilderness; God tells them to avoid conflict with Edom, descendants of Esau.
God instructs Israel not to harass Moab, descendants of Lot; 38 years pass until the old generation dies.
Israel is told to avoid conflict with Ammon; Moses recounts the history of the Rephaim and other ancient peoples.
God commands Israel to defeat Sihon, king of Heshbon; Israel conquers his land and begins its conquest.
Israel defeats Og, king of Bashan, and takes his fortified cities; Og is described as a giant.
Moses assigns the conquered land east of the Jordan to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.
Moses reminds the eastern tribes to help conquer Canaan before settling their land.
Moses pleads to enter Canaan, but God denies him; he is allowed to view the land from Mount Pisgah.
Moses urges obedience to God’s laws, warning not to add or subtract from them.
Israel is reminded of the Sinai encounter and the importance of teaching future generations.
Moses warns against idolatry, emphasizing that God is a consuming fire and jealous.
If Israel turns to idols, they will be exiled, but God will show mercy if they return to Him.
Moses highlights God’s unique relationship with Israel and calls for obedience and reverence.
Moses designates three cities of refuge east of the Jordan for accidental killers.
Introduction to the law Moses set before Israel, with geographic context east of the Jordan.
Moses reminds Israel of the covenant made at Horeb and his role as mediator.
Reiteration of the Ten Commandments, including Sabbath observance and honoring parents.
The people fear God’s voice and ask Moses to speak on their behalf.
God affirms their request and urges obedience for their prosperity and long life.
Moses urges Israel to obey God's commandments so they may prosper in the Promised Land.
The Shema: 'Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God, the LORD is one.' Love God with all your heart, soul, and strength; teach His words diligently to your children.
Warning not to forget God amid prosperity; Israel must not follow other gods, for the LORD is a jealous God.
Do not test the LORD as at Massah; obey His commands to receive blessing and victory over enemies.
Teach children the story of deliverance from Egypt and explain that obedience brings righteousness.
Israel must destroy the seven nations of Canaan, make no covenants, and avoid intermarriage to prevent idolatry.
Israel is God's chosen people, loved not for their size but because of His covenant; they must obey His commands.
Obedience brings blessings: fertility, health, and victory over enemies.
Do not fear strong nations; God will drive them out gradually. Destroy their idols completely.
Remember how God humbled and tested Israel in the wilderness to teach dependence on His word.
The Promised Land is rich and abundant; Israel is to bless God for His provision.
Warning not to forget God in prosperity or claim credit for success; forgetting Him will lead to destruction.
Israel will conquer strong nations not because of their righteousness, but due to the wickedness of others and God's promise.
Moses recounts Israel’s rebellion at Horeb and the golden calf; he interceded to prevent their destruction.
Israel repeatedly provoked God at Taberah, Massah, and Kibroth-hattaavah.
Moses recalls his 40-day intercession, pleading with God to remember His covenant and spare His people.
God commands Moses to make new tablets after the first were broken; they are placed in the ark.
Aaron dies; Eleazar becomes priest; the Levites are set apart to serve the LORD and have no land inheritance.
Moses recounts his second 40-day fast and God's command to lead the people onward.
Israel is called to fear, love, and serve God; circumcise your hearts, care for the vulnerable, and remember God's mighty acts.
Remember the LORD’s discipline, signs, and wonders in Egypt and the wilderness.
Obedience brings rain and abundance; disobedience brings drought and destruction.
Teach God’s words constantly; doing so ensures long life, blessing, and dominion in the land.
A choice is set: blessing for obedience, curse for disobedience, to be declared at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
Israel must destroy all pagan worship sites and bring offerings only to the place God chooses.
Worship must not be done as each sees fit; sacrifices are to be brought to the central sanctuary.
Meat may be eaten freely, but blood must not be consumed; tithes and offerings belong at God’s chosen place.
Israel must not imitate Canaanite worship; God forbids adding to or subtracting from His commands.
False prophets who lead people to other gods must be put to death, even if their signs come true.
Even close relatives who entice others to idolatry must be exposed and executed.
If a city turns to idolatry, it must be destroyed completely as a burnt offering to the LORD.
Israel is holy to God and must not follow pagan mourning practices.
Clean and unclean animals are listed; Israelites must not eat anything that dies naturally or is forbidden.
Tithes of produce are to be eaten before the LORD or converted to silver; every third year, tithes support Levites and the poor.
Every seventh year, debts are to be canceled; generosity toward the poor is commanded.
Hebrew slaves are to be freed in the seventh year and sent away with provisions; willing servants may remain permanently.
Firstborn male animals are sacred to the LORD and must be offered; blemished animals are not to be sacrificed.
Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread are to be observed in the month of Abib at the chosen place.
Feast of Weeks (Pentecost) celebrates the harvest with rejoicing and offerings.
Feast of Tabernacles is a seven-day celebration of the harvest; all males must appear before the LORD three times a year.
Judges are to rule with justice; bribes and idolatrous practices are forbidden.
Do not offer to the LORD any animal with a defect or blemish it is detestable.
If anyone is found worshiping other gods, they must be investigated and, if guilty, stoned to death on the testimony of two or three witnesses.
Difficult legal cases must be brought to the Levitical priests or judge at the sanctuary; their ruling is final and must be obeyed.
When Israel appoints a king, he must be chosen by God, be an Israelite, not multiply horses, wives, or wealth, and must write and read the law daily to remain humble and obedient.
Levites receive no land inheritance; they are supported by offerings and may serve at the sanctuary equally.
Israel must not imitate Canaanite abominations like child sacrifice, divination, sorcery, or necromancy.
God promises to raise up a prophet like Moses from among Israel; the people must listen to him.
False prophets who speak presumptuously or in another god’s name must be put to death; true prophecy is confirmed when it comes to pass.
Three cities of refuge are to be established for those who kill unintentionally, ensuring justice and preventing innocent bloodshed.
Premeditated murderers must not find refuge but be handed over for execution to purge evil.
Do not move your neighbor’s boundary marker respect property rights.
A matter must be established by two or three witnesses; false witnesses receive the punishment they intended for the accused.
Do not fear superior armies; the LORD fights for Israel.
Men who are newly married, recently built homes, planted vineyards, or are fearful are exempt from battle.
Cities far away must be offered peace; if they refuse, only the men are to be killed, and the rest taken as spoil.
Cities within Canaan must be completely destroyed to prevent idolatry.
Do not destroy fruit trees during a siege; only non-fruit trees may be used for war efforts.
If a murder victim is found and the killer unknown, the nearest city must perform a ritual with a heifer to atone for the bloodshed.
Rules for marrying a captive woman: she must be given time to mourn and cannot be sold or enslaved if later rejected.
A firstborn son’s inheritance must not be denied due to favoritism between wives.
A persistently rebellious son may be brought to the elders and stoned to purge evil.
A hanged criminal must be buried the same day; leaving the body exposed defiles the land.
Return lost property and help your neighbor’s fallen animal; do not ignore their need.
Men and women must not wear clothing of the opposite sex; such acts are detestable to the LORD.
If you find a bird’s nest, you may take the young but must let the mother go to prolong your days.
Build a parapet around your roof to prevent bloodshed by accidental falls.
Do not mix seeds, animals, or fabrics; wear tassels on the four corners of your cloak.
If a man falsely accuses his wife of not being a virgin, her parents must present proof; if guilty, she is stoned.
Adultery with a married woman results in death for both parties.
If a betrothed virgin is violated in the city and does not cry out, both are stoned.
If a betrothed woman is raped in the countryside, only the man dies she is innocent.
If a man sleeps with an unbetrothed virgin, he must marry her and pay fifty shekels.
A man must not marry his father’s wife; it dishonors his father.
Certain individuals (e.g., emasculated men, Ammonites, Moabites) are excluded from the assembly; Edomites and Egyptians may enter after three generations.
Maintain purity in the camp during war; designate a place for bodily functions and keep the camp holy.
Do not return escaped slaves to their masters; let them live freely among you.
No Israelite is to be a cult prostitute; earnings from such acts are not acceptable to the LORD.
Do not charge interest to fellow Israelites; interest may be charged to foreigners.
Fulfill vows made to the LORD promptly; it is better not to vow than to delay.
You may eat grapes or pluck grain from a neighbor’s field by hand, but not harvest it.
A divorced woman who remarries may not return to her first husband; it is detestable to the LORD.
A newlywed man is exempt from military duty for one year to bring joy to his wife.
Do not take a millstone as a pledge it is essential for life.
Kidnapping a fellow Israelite for slavery is punishable by death.
Follow Levitical instructions for skin diseases; remember Miriam’s punishment.
Do not enter a debtor’s house to collect a pledge; return a cloak by sunset.
Pay hired workers daily; they depend on their wages.
Each person is responsible for their own sin; no one is punished for another’s guilt.
Do not pervert justice for foreigners or orphans; remember your slavery in Egypt.
Leave gleanings in the field for the poor, the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow.
Disputes must be judged fairly; corporal punishment must not exceed forty lashes.
Do not muzzle an ox while it treads grain let it eat as it works.
Levirate marriage: a brother must marry his deceased brother’s widow to preserve his name.
If a woman grabs a man’s genitals during a fight, her hand must be cut off.
Use honest weights and measures; deceit is detestable to the LORD.
Remember Amalek’s attack; when settled in the land, blot out their memory.
Bring firstfruits to the sanctuary and declare God’s deliverance from Egypt; rejoice in His provision.
Every third year, give the tithe to Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows; affirm obedience in prayer.
Moses calls for covenant renewal: Israel is God’s treasured people, called to obey and be exalted.
Moses and the elders command Israel to set up large plastered stones inscribed with the law upon entering Canaan and to build an altar on Mount Ebal for burnt and peace offerings.
Moses and the Levitical priests urge the people to listen and obey, affirming their identity as God's covenant people.
Six tribes are assigned to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless, and six on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses.
The Levites proclaim twelve curses for secret sins such as idolatry, dishonoring parents, injustice, and sexual immorality with all the people responding 'Amen' to affirm accountability.
Blessings for obedience: Israel will be exalted above all nations, blessed in city and field, fruitful, victorious, and established as God's holy people.
Curses for disobedience: widespread calamity including disease, drought, defeat, madness, exile, siege, and national ruin culminating in slavery and despair.
Moses reminds Israel of God’s miracles in Egypt and the wilderness, urging them to keep the covenant for success.
All Israelites leaders, families, and foreigners stand to renew the covenant, binding both present and future generations.
Warning against idolatry: anyone who secretly turns from God will face devastating judgment and exclusion from the covenant.
Future generations and foreigners will see the land’s desolation and ask why; the answer will be Israel’s abandonment of the covenant.
God’s secret things belong to Him, but revealed things are for Israel to obey and pass on to their children.
If Israel repents in exile, God will restore them, circumcise their hearts, and bless them abundantly in the land.
God’s commands are not distant or difficult they are near, in the mouth and heart, ready to be obeyed.
Moses sets before them life and death, blessing and curse, urging them to choose life by loving and obeying God.
Moses, now 120 years old, announces Joshua as his successor and assures Israel of God’s presence and victory.
Moses commissions Joshua publicly, encouraging him to be strong and courageous.
The law is given to the priests to be read every seven years at the Feast of Tabernacles to all Israel.
God predicts Israel’s future rebellion and instructs Moses to write a song as a witness against them.
Joshua is commissioned by God; Moses finishes writing the law and teaches the song to Israel.
Moses begins the Song by calling heaven and earth to witness; he praises God as the Rock perfect, just, and faithful.
Israel is described as corrupt and foolish, having repaid God’s kindness with rebellion.
Moses recounts God’s care for Israel: choosing them, guarding them like the apple of His eye, and blessing them with abundance.
Jeshurun (Israel) grows complacent, forsakes God, and turns to idols, provoking His jealousy.
God hides His face and sends calamities famine, beasts, and war as judgment for Israel’s unfaithfulness.
God considers wiping them out but refrains for the sake of His name; He laments their lack of wisdom.
God stores up vengeance and mocks Israel’s false gods who cannot save them.
God declares His sovereignty He kills and makes alive, wounds and heals and promises to avenge His people and atone for their land.
Moses and Joshua recite the Song to the people; Moses urges them to take it to heart as their very life.
God tells Moses to ascend Mount Nebo to view the Promised Land; he will die there for disobeying at Meribah.
Moses begins his final blessing, praising God’s majesty and His kingship over Israel.
Reuben: May he live and not die, and his men not be few.
Judah: May the LORD hear his voice and help him against his enemies.
Levi: Blessed for faithfulness; entrusted with teaching and sacrifices; may his enemies be struck down.
Benjamin: The beloved of the LORD dwells securely between His shoulders.
Joseph: Blessed with land, favor, and strength; his horns like a wild ox to gore nations.
Zebulun and Issachar: Rejoice in trade and worship; they draw abundance from the seas and hidden treasures.
Gad: Blessed with territory and leadership; he executes God’s justice.
Dan: A lion’s cub leaping from Bashan.
Naphtali: Satisfied with favor and full of the LORD’s blessing.
Asher: Most blessed of sons; favored by brothers; his strength endures like iron and bronze.
Moses concludes with praise to God, declaring Israel’s unmatched blessing, security, and salvation.
Moses ascends Mount Nebo; God shows him the full extent of the Promised Land.
Moses dies in Moab; God buries him in an unknown location.
Moses dies at 120 with undimmed vision and vigor; Israel mourns him for 30 days.
Joshua is filled with wisdom through Moses’ laying on of hands; Israel listens to him.
No prophet like Moses has arisen he knew the LORD face to face and performed mighty signs and wonders.
After Moses' death, God commissions Joshua to lead Israel into the Promised Land, defining its territorial boundaries.
God promises to be with Joshua as He was with Moses, urging him to be strong, courageous, and obedient to the Law.
Joshua commands the officers to prepare the people to cross the Jordan in three days.
Joshua reminds the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh of their pledge to help conquer the land before settling east of the Jordan.
The people affirm their loyalty to Joshua, pledging to follow him as they did Moses and encouraging him to be strong and courageous.
Joshua sends two spies to Jericho; Rahab hides them from the king’s men and misleads the pursuers.
Rahab expresses faith in Israel’s God and secures a promise of protection for her family in exchange for her help.
Rahab helps the spies escape through a window and is told to tie a scarlet cord as a sign for her household’s safety.
The spies return to Joshua, reporting that the inhabitants of the land are fearful and that God has given them the land.
Joshua prepares the people to cross the Jordan; the Ark of the Covenant will lead the way.
God promises to exalt Joshua and confirms that the Jordan will stop flowing when the priests step into it.
As the priests carrying the Ark step into the river, the waters stop, and the people cross on dry ground.
Twelve men, one from each tribe, take stones from the Jordan to set up a memorial of the crossing.
The stones are carried to the camp at Gilgal; the priests remain in the river until all have crossed.
God commands the priests to come out; the waters return as soon as they step onto dry land.
The stones are set up at Gilgal as a sign for future generations of God’s power and faithfulness.
Canaanite kings lose heart upon hearing of the Jordan crossing.
God commands circumcision of the new generation; the reproach of Egypt is rolled away at Gilgal.
Israel celebrates Passover; manna ceases as they begin eating the produce of Canaan.
Joshua encounters the commander of the LORD’s army and is told to remove his sandals on holy ground.

God gives Joshua detailed instructions for conquering Jericho: march around the city once daily for six days with seven priests blowing trumpets; on the seventh day, march seven times and shout after the trumpet blast.
Joshua relays God's plan to the priests and people; they begin the daily procession around Jericho in silence, with the Ark of the Covenant leading.
For six days, the Israelites repeat the march around Jericho once per day, returning to camp each night.
On the seventh day, they march seven times; after the final trumpet blast and shout, the walls collapse. Israel charges in and destroys everything, sparing only Rahab and her family.
Rahab and her household are rescued and brought safely outside the city, fulfilling the spies’ oath.
Joshua curses anyone who would rebuild Jericho, declaring they will lose their firstborn and youngest sons. Joshua’s fame spreads throughout the land.
