Achan secretly takes devoted items from Jericho, causing Israel to be defeated at Ai; 36 men die, and the people are disheartened.
Joshua and the elders mourn and question why God allowed the defeat.
God reveals that someone has violated the ban; Israel must purge the sin or face continued defeat.
Achan is identified by lot and confesses to taking a robe, silver, and gold, which he hid in his tent.
Achan and all he owns are destroyed in the Valley of Achor; God's anger is turned away.
God encourages Joshua to attack Ai again, this time allowing Israel to keep the plunder.
Joshua sets an ambush behind Ai while leading a frontal assault to draw the enemy out.
The ambush succeeds; Ai is captured and burned. The king is executed and hung on a tree until evening.
Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal, writes the law on stones, and reads the blessings and curses to all Israel.
Canaanite kings unite to fight Israel.
The Gibeonites deceive Israel by pretending to be from a distant land; Joshua makes a peace treaty without consulting God.
Three days later, Israel discovers the deception but honors the treaty to avoid breaking their oath.
Joshua curses the Gibeonites to perpetual servitude as woodcutters and water carriers for the sanctuary.
Five Amorite kings form an alliance to attack Gibeon for making peace with Israel.
Joshua marches overnight to defend Gibeon; God throws the enemy into confusion and sends hailstones. Joshua commands the sun and moon to stand still until victory is complete.
The five kings hide in a cave; they are captured, executed, and buried under stones.
Joshua leads a southern campaign, defeating multiple cities and kings, leaving no survivors, as God commands.
Jabin king of Hazor forms a massive northern coalition of kings and armies to fight Israel at the waters of Merom.
God assures Joshua of victory; Israel attacks suddenly, defeats the coalition, hamstrings their horses, and burns their chariots.
Joshua captures Hazor, kills its king, and destroys the city; he obeys all commands given to Moses, leaving nothing undone.
Joshua conquers the entire northern region; God hardens the hearts of the enemy kings to ensure their destruction.
Joshua eliminates the Anakim from the hill country; the land has rest from war as Israel takes full possession.
List of kings defeated by Moses east of the Jordan: Sihon of Heshbon and Og of Bashan; their lands given to Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh.
List of 31 kings defeated by Joshua west of the Jordan, from Jericho to Tirzah, marking the full conquest of Canaan.
God tells elderly Joshua that much land remains to be conquered; He instructs him to divide it among the nine and a half tribes.
Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh receive their inheritance east of the Jordan; the Levites receive no land, only offerings.
Territory of Reuben: includes Heshbon and surrounding cities.
Territory of Gad: includes Ramoth in Gilead and cities in the Ammonite region.
Territory of half-Manasseh: includes Bashan and the kingdom of Og; Balaam the diviner is mentioned as slain.
Land west of the Jordan is divided by lot among the remaining tribes; Levites receive no inheritance.
Caleb reminds Joshua of Moses’ promise and asks for Hebron, the land he spied out 45 years earlier.
Joshua blesses Caleb and gives him Hebron; Caleb drives out the Anakim, and the land has rest from war.
Detailed boundaries of Judah’s inheritance, stretching from Edom to the Mediterranean Sea.
Caleb receives Hebron; his nephew Othniel captures Debir and marries Caleb’s daughter Achsah, who requests and receives springs of water.
Extensive list of cities within Judah’s territory, grouped by region: Negev, lowlands, hill country, and wilderness.
Judah fails to drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem; they remain there to this day.
The territory allotted to the descendants of Joseph Ephraim and Manasseh extends from the Jordan near Jericho through the hill country to the Mediterranean Sea.
The boundaries of Ephraim’s inheritance are described in detail, including cities and border towns shared with Manasseh.
The Ephraimites fail to drive out the Canaanites in Gezer, who remain as forced laborers.
The western portion of land is allotted to the tribe of Manasseh, including clans descended from Machir.
Zelophehad’s daughters receive an inheritance among their uncles, fulfilling Moses’ earlier command.
Boundaries of Manasseh’s territory are outlined, including towns shared with Ephraim and cities in Issachar and Asher.
Manasseh fails to drive out the Canaanites, who remain but are subjected to forced labor.
The descendants of Joseph request more land; Joshua tells them to clear the forested hill country and drive out the Canaanites, even those with iron chariots.
Israel assembles at Shiloh and sets up the Tent of Meeting; Joshua urges the remaining seven tribes to claim their inheritance.
Surveyors are sent to map the land; Joshua casts lots before the LORD to assign territories.
The tribe of Benjamin receives its inheritance between Judah and Joseph, including cities like Jericho, Bethel, and Jebus (Jerusalem).
Simeon receives land within Judah’s territory due to Judah’s large allotment.
Zebulun’s inheritance includes twelve cities and their villages.
Issachar receives sixteen cities and surrounding villages.
Asher’s territory includes twenty-two cities along the coast and hill country.
Naphtali receives nineteen cities in the northern region.
Dan’s inheritance includes seventeen cities; they later capture Leshem and rename it Dan.
Joshua receives Timnath-serah as his inheritance; the land division concludes at Shiloh before the LORD.
God instructs Joshua to appoint cities of refuge for those who kill unintentionally to escape vengeance.
Fugitives must present their case at the city gate and remain in the city until trial or the high priest’s death.
Six cities are designated: Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron (west); Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan (east); they serve both Israelites and foreigners.
The Levite leaders request cities and pasturelands as promised by God through Moses; Joshua and the tribal leaders agree to allocate them.
The Levites are divided into three clans Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites and receive cities by lot from various tribes.
The descendants of Aaron (Kohathites) receive 13 cities from Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, including Hebron and Anathoth.
The remaining Kohathites receive 10 cities from Ephraim, Dan, and half of Manasseh, including Shechem and Gath Rimmon.
The Gershonites receive 13 cities from Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and half of Manasseh in Bashan, including Golan and Kedesh.
The Merarites receive 12 cities from Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad, including Ramoth in Gilead and Mahanaim.
In total, the Levites receive 48 cities with surrounding pasturelands, scattered throughout Israel.
God fulfills all His promises: Israel possesses the land, has rest from enemies, and not one of God’s promises fails.
Joshua commends the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and half-Manasseh for their faithfulness and sends them home with blessings and spoils.
These tribes return to their land east of the Jordan, carrying wealth and instructed to share it with their families.
They build a large altar near the Jordan; the rest of Israel fears rebellion and prepares for war.
A delegation led by Phinehas confronts them, warning of the consequences of unfaithfulness like Peor and Achan.
The eastern tribes explain the altar is not for sacrifice but a witness to future generations that they share in the LORD.
Phinehas and the leaders are satisfied; war is averted, and the altar is named 'Witness' to affirm unity in worship.
Joshua, now old, reminds Israel that God has given them rest and will continue to drive out remaining nations.
He urges them to be strong, obey the Law of Moses, and cling to the LORD without turning to other gods.
Joshua warns that associating with remaining nations and their gods will bring snares, traps, and God’s judgment.
He testifies that all of God’s promises have been fulfilled and warns that disobedience will bring destruction.
Joshua gathers all Israel at Shechem and recounts God’s faithfulness from Abraham to the conquest of Canaan.
He challenges the people to choose whom they will serve; they affirm their commitment to serve the LORD.
Joshua warns that God is holy and jealous; the people insist they will serve Him and reject other gods.
Joshua makes a covenant, writes it in the Book of the Law, and sets up a stone as a witness.
Joshua dies at 110 and is buried; Israel remains faithful during his lifetime and that of the elders who outlived him. Joseph’s bones are buried at Shechem; Eleazar also dies and is buried.
After Joshua’s death, Israel asks God who should lead the conquest; Judah is chosen and allies with Simeon. Together they defeat Adoni-Bezek, cutting off his thumbs and big toes.
Judah captures Jerusalem and other cities. Caleb offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever captures Debir; Othniel succeeds and receives land with springs.
The Kenites settle in Judah’s territory. Benjamin fails to drive out the Jebusites from Jerusalem.
The house of Joseph captures Bethel with help from a local man, who is spared and builds a new city.
Several tribes Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali, and Dan fail to fully drive out the Canaanites, who remain in the land and become forced labor.
The Angel of the LORD rebukes Israel for not breaking down pagan altars; the people weep and offer sacrifices at Bochim.
After Joshua’s death, a new generation arises that does not know the LORD or His works.
Israel turns to Baal and Ashtaroth; God’s anger burns, and He allows enemies to oppress them.
God raises judges to deliver Israel, but the people relapse into idolatry after each judge dies.
God declares He will no longer drive out the remaining nations, using them to test Israel’s faithfulness.
God leaves certain nations to test Israel and teach warfare; Israel intermingles and serves their gods.
Israel serves Baals; God allows Cushan-Rishathaim to oppress them. Othniel delivers Israel, and the land has peace for 40 years.
Israel sins again; Eglon of Moab oppresses them. Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, assassinates Eglon and leads Israel to victory. The land rests for 80 years.
Shamgar kills 600 Philistines with an oxgoad and delivers Israel.
After Ehud’s death, Israel sins again. Jabin king of Canaan oppresses them through Sisera, his commander.
Deborah, a prophetess and judge, summons Barak to lead Israel. He agrees only if she accompanies him; she prophesies that a woman will get the glory.
Barak defeats Sisera’s army with God’s help; Sisera flees on foot.
Sisera seeks refuge in Jael’s tent. She kills him by driving a tent peg through his head while he sleeps.
God subdues Jabin, and Israel grows stronger until he is destroyed.
Deborah and Barak sing a victory song, praising God’s power and recounting Israel’s oppression and deliverance.
The song highlights which tribes responded to the call to battle and which did not.
God’s intervention in battle is praised; Meroz is cursed for not helping.
Jael is honored for killing Sisera; her act is vividly described.
Sisera’s mother waits in vain; the song ends with a prayer for God’s enemies to perish and His lovers to shine.
Israel does evil again; God allows Midian to oppress them for seven years, devastating crops and livestock, forcing the people to hide in caves.
God sends a prophet to rebuke Israel, reminding them of His past deliverance and their disobedience in worshiping other gods.
The Angel of the LORD appears to Gideon, calling him a mighty warrior and commissioning him to save Israel; Gideon protests his weakness, but God promises to be with him.
Gideon asks for a sign; the Angel ignites his offering with fire and disappears. Gideon builds an altar called 'The LORD is Peace.'

God commands Gideon to destroy his father's altar to Baal and build one to the LORD; Gideon obeys at night. The townspeople want to kill him, but his father defends him, saying, 'Let Baal contend for himself.'
Midianites and allies gather for war; the Spirit of the LORD comes upon Gideon, and he summons tribes to join him.
Gideon asks for two signs with a fleece to confirm God's promise first dew only on the fleece, then only on the ground. God grants both.
God reduces Gideon’s army from 32,000 to 300 men to ensure Israel won’t boast in their own strength.
God tells Gideon to spy on the Midianite camp; he overhears a dream foretelling Midian’s defeat, which strengthens his faith.
Gideon divides the 300 into three groups with trumpets, jars, and torches; they surprise the Midianites, causing panic and self-destruction.
Gideon calls Ephraim to cut off the fleeing Midianites; they capture and kill the princes Oreb and Zeeb.
Ephraim rebukes Gideon for not calling them earlier; he diplomatically praises their role and calms their anger.
Gideon pursues the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna; Succoth and Penuel refuse to help, and he vows to punish them after victory.
Gideon defeats the remaining Midianites and captures the kings; he punishes Succoth and destroys Penuel’s tower; he executes the kings for killing his brothers.
Israel asks Gideon to rule; he refuses kingship but makes a golden ephod from war spoils, which becomes an idol and a snare.
Midian is subdued; Israel enjoys 40 years of peace. Gideon dies, and Israel quickly returns to Baal worship, forgetting the LORD and showing no loyalty to Gideon’s family.
Abimelech, son of Gideon and a concubine, convinces the leaders of Shechem to make him king. He murders his seventy brothers, but Jotham escapes.
Jotham delivers a parable from Mount Gerizim, warning Shechem of the consequences of choosing Abimelech as king. He then flees.
After three years, God sends discord between Abimelech and Shechem. Gaal stirs rebellion against Abimelech.
Zebul, Shechem’s governor, warns Abimelech. Abimelech defeats Gaal and drives him out.
Abimelech attacks Shechem again, destroys the city, and burns the tower of Shechem, killing about a thousand people.
At Thebez, a woman drops a millstone on Abimelech’s head. Mortally wounded, he asks his armor-bearer to kill him to avoid the shame of dying by a woman. His death fulfills Jotham’s curse.
Tola, from Issachar, rises to save Israel and judges for 23 years in Shamir.
Jair, from Gilead, judges Israel for 22 years; he has 30 sons who ride 30 donkeys and control 30 towns.
Israel again does evil, serving foreign gods; God allows the Philistines and Ammonites to oppress them.
Israel cries out; God rebukes them for repeated idolatry. They put away foreign gods and serve the LORD.
Ammon gathers for war; Israel assembles at Mizpah, seeking a leader to fight.
Jephthah, a mighty warrior and son of a prostitute, is driven away by his brothers and lives in Tob.
When Ammon threatens Israel, the elders ask Jephthah to lead; he agrees after securing leadership promises.
Jephthah sends messages to the Ammonite king, defending Israel’s right to the land; the king refuses peace.
The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah; he vows to sacrifice the first thing that greets him if victorious.
Jephthah defeats the Ammonites decisively.
Jephthah’s daughter greets him; he fulfills his vow after she mourns her virginity. Israelite women commemorate her annually.
Ephraim confronts Jephthah for not calling them to battle; a civil war breaks out. Gileadites kill 42,000 Ephraimites using the 'Shibboleth' test.
Jephthah judges Israel for six years and dies.
Ibzan of Bethlehem judges for seven years; he has 30 sons and 30 daughters.
Elon of Zebulun judges for ten years.
Abdon judges for eight years; he has 40 sons and 30 grandsons who ride 70 donkeys.
Israel does evil again; God delivers them into Philistine hands for 40 years.
An angel appears to Manoah’s barren wife, promising a son Samson who will be a Nazirite and begin to deliver Israel.
Manoah prays for guidance; the angel reappears and repeats the instructions for raising the child.
Manoah offers a sacrifice; the angel ascends in the flame. Manoah fears death, but his wife reassures him.
Samson is born; the Spirit of the LORD begins to stir him in Mahaneh Dan.
Samson desires a Philistine woman from Timnah for marriage, against his parents’ wishes. God uses this to confront the Philistines.
On the way to Timnah, Samson kills a lion with his bare hands. Later, he finds honey in the lion’s carcass and eats it, sharing it with his parents without telling them the source.
At the wedding feast, Samson poses a riddle to thirty Philistine men, wagering garments if they solve it.
The Philistines threaten Samson’s wife, who coaxes the answer from him. They solve the riddle, and Samson realizes he’s been betrayed.
The Spirit of the LORD empowers Samson to kill thirty men in Ashkelon to pay the wager. He leaves in anger, and his wife is given to another man.

Samson returns to visit his wife but learns she was given to another man. In revenge, he burns the Philistines’ crops using 300 foxes with torches tied to their tails. The Philistines retaliate by killing his wife and her father. Samson strikes them down and hides in a cave.
The Philistines come to Judah seeking Samson. The men of Judah bind him and hand him over to avoid conflict.
The Spirit of the LORD empowers Samson to break free. He kills 1,000 Philistines with a donkey’s jawbone.
Samson, exhausted, cries out to God. God miraculously provides water. Samson judges Israel for 20 years during Philistine oppression.
Samson visits a prostitute in Gaza; the Philistines plan to ambush him, but he escapes at midnight, carrying the city gate to a hill near Hebron.
Samson falls in love with Delilah. The Philistine rulers bribe her to discover the secret of his strength. He deceives her three times with false answers.
Delilah persists; Samson finally reveals that his strength lies in his Nazirite vow his uncut hair.
Delilah has his hair cut while he sleeps. The LORD departs from him, and the Philistines capture, blind, and imprison him.
Samson’s hair begins to grow. During a Philistine celebration, they bring him out to entertain them in the temple of Dagon.
Samson prays for strength one last time. He pulls down the temple pillars, killing himself and about 3,000 Philistines. He is buried in his father’s tomb.
Micah, from Ephraim, steals silver from his mother, then returns it. She dedicates it to the LORD and has an idol made.
A young Levite from Bethlehem becomes Micah’s personal priest. Micah believes the LORD will bless him because of this.
The tribe of Dan seeks territory. Five scouts visit Micah’s house and consult his Levite priest.
The scouts find Laish, a peaceful city, and report back. Dan prepares to attack.
Danites return, steal Micah’s idols and priest. Micah protests but is powerless against them.
Dan conquers Laish, renames it Dan, and sets up Micah’s idol. The shrine continues through the time of the kings.
A Levite retrieves his concubine from her father’s house in Bethlehem after she had left him.
They travel to Gibeah in Benjamin. An old man offers them lodging after no one else does.
Wicked men of Gibeah demand to abuse the Levite. Instead, they rape his concubine all night, and she dies. The Levite dismembers her body and sends the parts to Israel’s tribes to provoke outrage.
All Israel assembles at Mizpah. The Levite recounts the crime. The tribes unite to punish Gibeah.
Benjamin refuses to surrender the guilty men. War is declared; Benjamin has 26,000 soldiers, Israel 400,000.
Israel loses the first two battles despite seeking God. On the third day, they ambush and defeat Benjamin.
Israel destroys Gibeah and slaughters nearly all of Benjamin’s army only 600 men survive.
Israel laments the near extinction of Benjamin and the oath not to give them wives.
They kill the people of Jabesh-gilead for not joining the war and give their virgin daughters to Benjamin.
Still lacking wives, the Benjaminites are allowed to seize women from a festival in Shiloh.
The book ends with this refrain: 'In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.'
During a famine, Elimelech moves his family from Bethlehem to Moab. He dies, and later his sons Mahlon and Chilion also die, leaving Naomi and her Moabite daughters-in-law, Ruth and Orpah, widowed.
Naomi decides to return to Bethlehem. She urges Ruth and Orpah to stay in Moab. Orpah returns home, but Ruth clings to Naomi.
Ruth pledges unwavering loyalty to Naomi, declaring, 'Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.'
Naomi and Ruth arrive in Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. Naomi, bitter over her losses, asks to be called 'Mara.'
Ruth goes to glean in the fields and unknowingly ends up in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi’s late husband.
Boaz notices Ruth, learns of her loyalty to Naomi, and offers her protection and favor while gleaning.
Ruth is humbled by Boaz’s kindness. He invites her to eat with his workers and instructs them to leave extra grain for her.
Ruth returns home with abundant grain. Naomi is encouraged upon learning Boaz is a close relative and advises Ruth to stay in his fields.
Naomi instructs Ruth to approach Boaz at the threshing floor and request his protection as a kinsman-redeemer.
Ruth follows Naomi’s plan, uncovering Boaz’s feet and asking him to spread his garment over her.
Boaz praises Ruth’s kindness and agrees to redeem her if a closer relative declines.
Boaz sends Ruth home with barley. Naomi assures her that Boaz will resolve the matter quickly.
Boaz meets the closer relative at the town gate. The man declines to redeem Ruth and the land, fearing it would endanger his estate.
Boaz legally redeems the land and Ruth before witnesses. The elders bless the union, invoking Rachel, Leah, and Tamar.
Boaz marries Ruth. She bears a son, Obed, who becomes the grandfather of David. Naomi is restored through the child.
The genealogy from Perez to David is listed, linking Ruth to the royal line of Israel.
Elkanah has two wives Peninnah, who has children, and Hannah, who is barren. Peninnah provokes Hannah, causing her deep sorrow.
Hannah prays fervently at the tabernacle, vowing to dedicate her son to the LORD. Eli the priest initially thinks she is drunk but blesses her after hearing her plea.
God remembers Hannah; she conceives and gives birth to Samuel, meaning 'heard by God.'
After weaning Samuel, Hannah brings him to the tabernacle and dedicates him to the LORD, fulfilling her vow.
Hannah offers a prayer of praise, exalting God's justice and power. She prophesies about God's anointed king.
Eli’s sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are corrupt priests who exploit the sacrificial system, showing contempt for the LORD.
Samuel ministers before the LORD as a child. God blesses Hannah with more children.
Eli hears of his sons’ immoral behavior but fails to restrain them. Meanwhile, Samuel grows in favor with God and people.
A man of God prophesies judgment on Eli’s house: his descendants will die young, and the priesthood will be given to another.
God calls young Samuel during the night. After three mistaken trips to Eli, Samuel responds, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.'
God tells Samuel of the coming judgment on Eli’s house. Samuel delivers the message to Eli, who accepts it as God’s will.
Samuel grows, and God confirms him as a prophet. All Israel recognizes that the LORD speaks through him.
Israel is defeated by the Philistines. They bring the Ark of the Covenant into battle, but are defeated again. The Ark is captured, and Eli’s sons die.
A messenger reports the defeat to Eli. Upon hearing that the Ark is captured, Eli falls backward, breaks his neck, and dies.
Phinehas’ wife gives birth and names her son Ichabod, saying, 'The glory has departed from Israel.'
The Philistines place the Ark in Dagon’s temple. Dagon falls before the Ark twice; the second time, his head and hands break off.
God afflicts Ashdod and Gath with tumors. The people panic and move the Ark to Ekron.
Ekron also suffers affliction. The Philistines decide to return the Ark to Israel, recognizing God’s power.

After seven months of suffering, the Philistines consult their priests and diviners on how to return the Ark of the Covenant to Israel. They are advised to send it back with a guilt offering of five golden tumors and five golden mice.

To test if their affliction is truly from God, the Philistines place the Ark and offerings on a cart pulled by two cows separated from their calves. The cows head straight to Beth-shemesh, confirming divine intervention.
The people of Beth-shemesh rejoice at the Ark’s return and offer sacrifices. The Levites take charge of the Ark, and the golden offerings are presented as a memorial.
God strikes down seventy men of Beth-shemesh for looking into the Ark. The people, terrified, ask the men of Kiriath-jearim to take it away.
The men of Kiriath-jearim take the Ark to Abinadab’s house, where it remains for twenty years under the care of his son Eleazar.
Samuel calls Israel to repentance, urging them to put away foreign gods. The people gather at Mizpah, fast, and confess their sins.
As the Philistines attack, Samuel offers a sacrifice and prays. God thunders against the Philistines, throwing them into confusion, and Israel defeats them.
Samuel sets up a stone named Ebenezer to commemorate God’s help. The Philistines are subdued, and Israel regains lost territory.
Samuel judges Israel faithfully, traveling in a circuit between Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, and returning to his home in Ramah.
Samuel appoints his sons as judges, but they are corrupt and accept bribes.
The elders of Israel demand a king to be like other nations. God tells Samuel to grant their request, explaining they are rejecting Him, not Samuel.
Samuel warns the people about the burdens a king will impose conscription, taxation, and servitude but they persist.
Despite the warning, the people insist on having a king. God tells Samuel to appoint one, and he sends the people home.
Saul, a tall and handsome young man from the tribe of Benjamin, is introduced as the son of Kish.
Saul is sent by his father to search for lost donkeys. After an unsuccessful search, his servant suggests consulting the prophet Samuel.
They meet young women who direct them to Samuel, who is about to offer a sacrifice at the high place.
God had revealed to Samuel that Saul would come and be anointed as leader. Samuel tells Saul that the donkeys are found and hints at his future role.
Samuel honors Saul at a feast and later speaks privately with him, preparing to reveal God’s message.
Samuel anoints Saul with oil, gives him signs to confirm his calling, and instructs him to wait at Gilgal.
God changes Saul’s heart; he prophesies with prophets, fulfilling Samuel’s signs.
Saul tells his uncle about meeting Samuel but omits the part about being anointed king.
Samuel gathers Israel and publicly selects Saul by lot. Saul hides but is found and presented as king. Some accept him; others despise him.
Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and demands to gouge out their right eyes.
Saul, empowered by the Spirit of God, rallies Israel and defeats the Ammonites with a surprise attack.
Saul refuses to punish dissenters and is reaffirmed as king at Gilgal with sacrifices and rejoicing.
Samuel defends his integrity before the people, who affirm his honesty and justice.
He recounts God’s faithfulness and Israel’s repeated disobedience, including their demand for a king.
Samuel warns that obedience will bring blessing, but rebellion will bring judgment. He calls down thunder and rain as a sign.
The people repent; Samuel assures them of God’s mercy if they remain faithful and promises to continue praying and teaching them.
Saul reigns and forms an army. Jonathan attacks a Philistine outpost, provoking a larger conflict. Saul takes credit for the victory.
The Philistines gather a massive army. Israelite troops panic and hide; Saul remains at Gilgal with a dwindling force.
Saul offers a burnt offering himself instead of waiting for Samuel. Samuel arrives, rebukes Saul, and declares that his kingdom will not endure.
Samuel departs. Saul counts only 600 men left. Philistine raiders spread out to plunder the land.
Israel has no blacksmiths due to Philistine control; only Saul and Jonathan have swords. The chapter ends with a grim picture of Israel’s military disadvantage.
Jonathan and his armor-bearer launch a surprise attack on a Philistine outpost, trusting God for victory. They kill about twenty men, sparking panic in the Philistine camp.
God sends an earthquake, causing confusion among the Philistines. Saul and his men join the battle, and Israel wins a great victory.
Saul makes a rash oath forbidding his troops from eating until evening. Jonathan, unaware of the oath, eats honey and criticizes his father’s command.
Famished troops slaughter animals and eat them with the blood. Saul builds an altar and seeks God’s guidance for further battle.
Saul casts lots to find the cause of God’s silence. Jonathan is identified for breaking the oath, but the people defend him, and Saul relents.
Summary of Saul’s reign: he fights many enemies and gathers strong warriors. His family and military leadership are listed.
God commands Saul to destroy the Amalekites completely. Saul spares King Agag and the best livestock, disobeying God.
God tells Samuel He regrets making Saul king. Samuel confronts Saul, who makes excuses. Samuel declares that obedience is better than sacrifice and that Saul is rejected as king.
Saul admits his sin but pleads for honor before the people. Samuel agrees to accompany him but reiterates God’s rejection.
Samuel executes Agag and departs from Saul. Samuel mourns Saul, and God regrets making him king.
God sends Samuel to anoint a new king from Jesse’s sons in Bethlehem. Samuel arrives under the pretense of offering a sacrifice.
God rejects Jesse’s older sons. David, the youngest, is chosen and anointed. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon him.
The Spirit departs from Saul, and a harmful spirit torments him. David is brought to play the harp, soothing Saul and becoming his armor-bearer.
Goliath challenges Israel to single combat. Saul and his army are terrified.
David visits his brothers at the battlefield and hears Goliath’s taunts. He volunteers to fight.
David convinces Saul and prepares for battle with only a sling and five stones.
David defeats Goliath with a stone to the forehead and cuts off his head. The Philistines flee, and Israel pursues them.
Saul inquires about David’s family. David identifies himself as the son of Jesse.
Jonathan and David form a deep friendship and make a covenant. Jonathan gives David his robe and weapons.
David’s success earns him praise, but Saul becomes jealous and suspicious.
Saul tries to kill David with a spear. David continues to succeed, and the people love him.
Saul offers his daughters in marriage to trap David. David marries Michal after bringing 200 Philistine foreskins. Saul becomes David’s enemy.
Jonathan warns David of Saul’s intent to kill him and persuades Saul to spare David for a time.
Saul again tries to kill David. Michal helps David escape and deceives Saul’s messengers.
David flees to Samuel. Saul sends men to capture him, but they all prophesy. Saul comes himself and also prophesies.
David and Jonathan devise a plan to test Saul’s intentions. Jonathan promises to warn David.
At the feast, Saul becomes enraged when David is absent and tries to kill Jonathan.
Jonathan signals David to flee. They part with sorrow, reaffirming their covenant.
David visits Ahimelech the priest, receives consecrated bread and Goliath’s sword.
David flees to Gath and pretends to be insane to avoid danger.
David gathers followers at the cave of Adullam and moves his parents to Moab for safety.
Saul accuses his men of conspiracy. Doeg reports Ahimelech’s aid to David. Saul orders the massacre of the priests; only Abiathar escapes.
David saves Keilah from the Philistines after seeking God’s guidance.
Saul pursues David, but David escapes with divine help.
Jonathan encourages David and reaffirms their covenant.
The Ziphites betray David’s location. Saul nearly captures him, but a Philistine invasion forces Saul to retreat.
David spares Saul’s life in a cave at En Gedi, cutting off a corner of his robe but refusing to harm him. He restrains his men, declaring he will not strike the LORD’s anointed.
David confronts Saul from a distance, showing the piece of robe and declaring his innocence. He appeals to God as judge between them.
Saul weeps and acknowledges David’s righteousness and future kingship. He asks David to swear not to cut off his descendants. David agrees, and Saul returns home.
Samuel dies, and all Israel mourns. David moves to the wilderness of Paran.
David sends men to request provisions from Nabal, a wealthy but harsh man. Nabal insults them, and David prepares to attack.
Abigail, Nabal’s wise wife, intervenes with gifts and a humble plea. David blesses her for preventing bloodshed and accepts her offering.
Abigail tells Nabal what happened; he has a stroke and dies ten days later, struck by the LORD.
David praises God for justice and marries Abigail. He also marries Ahinoam, while Saul gives Michal to another man.
The Ziphites again betray David’s location. Saul pursues him with 3,000 men.
David and Abishai sneak into Saul’s camp at night. Abishai wants to kill Saul, but David refuses and takes Saul’s spear and water jug instead.
David calls out from a distance, rebuking Abner for failing to protect Saul. He again declares his innocence and pleads for justice.
Saul confesses his sin and blesses David. David returns the spear, and they part ways.
David, fearing Saul will eventually kill him, flees to Gath and seeks refuge with Achish, king of the Philistines. Saul stops pursuing him.
David requests a rural town to live in and is granted Ziklag, where he stays for sixteen months with his men and families.
David raids the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, leaving no survivors. He deceives Achish by claiming he attacked Judah, gaining Achish’s trust.
Achish plans to go to war against Israel and expects David to join him. David agrees, keeping up his deception.
Saul, desperate for guidance, seeks a medium at Endor after God refuses to answer him through dreams, prophets, or Urim.
Saul disguises himself and visits the medium, who is shocked when Samuel actually appears. She realizes Saul’s identity.
Samuel rebukes Saul for disturbing him and foretells Israel’s defeat and Saul’s death the next day.
Saul collapses in fear. The medium and his servants persuade him to eat before he departs into the night.
As the Philistines prepare for battle, their commanders object to David’s presence, fearing he might turn against them.
Achish defends David but sends him back to avoid conflict. David returns to Ziklag, spared from fighting against Israel.
David and his men return to Ziklag to find it burned and their families taken by the Amalekites. The men weep and consider stoning David, but he finds strength in the LORD.
David seeks God’s guidance and is told to pursue the raiders. Two hundred men stay behind due to exhaustion.
An abandoned Egyptian servant leads David to the Amalekites. David attacks and recovers all the captives and spoils.
David insists on sharing the spoils equally with those who stayed behind, establishing a lasting ordinance.
David sends gifts from the plunder to elders in Judah, strengthening alliances.
The Philistines defeat Israel at Mount Gilboa. Saul’s sons, including Jonathan, are killed. Saul, wounded, takes his own life. His armor-bearer does the same.
Israelites flee their towns. The Philistines desecrate Saul’s body, displaying it and his armor in pagan temples.
The men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons, burn them, and bury their bones, mourning for seven days.
An Amalekite brings news of Saul and Jonathan’s deaths to David, claiming he killed Saul at Saul’s request and presenting Saul’s crown and bracelet.
David and his men mourn. David rebukes the Amalekite for killing the LORD’s anointed and has him executed.
David composes a lament for Saul and Jonathan, known as the 'Song of the Bow,' honoring their bravery and mourning their loss.
David seeks God’s guidance and moves to Hebron, where the men of Judah anoint him king.
David commends the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul and encourages their loyalty.
Abner, Saul’s commander, makes Ish-bosheth king over Israel, leading to a divided kingdom.
A battle at Gibeon erupts between Abner’s men and Joab’s. Asahel is killed by Abner. The conflict ends with heavy losses and a fragile truce.
David’s house grows stronger while Saul’s weakens. David’s sons are born in Hebron.
Abner quarrels with Ish-bosheth and decides to support David.
Abner negotiates peace with David and brings Michal, David’s wife, back to him.
Joab, angry over Abner’s past killing of his brother Asahel, murders Abner in revenge.
David mourns Abner publicly, distancing himself from Joab’s actions and affirming his innocence.
Ish-bosheth loses courage after Abner’s death. Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son, is introduced.
Rechab and Baanah assassinate Ish-bosheth and bring his head to David, expecting a reward.
David condemns their treachery and has them executed. Ish-bosheth’s head is buried in Abner’s tomb.
All Israel anoints David king. He begins a 40-year reign 7.5 years in Hebron, 33 in Jerusalem.
David captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites and makes it his capital, the City of David.
Hiram of Tyre sends materials and workers to build David a palace. David’s family grows.
David defeats the Philistines twice after seeking God’s guidance, including a strategic ambush at Baal-perazim.
David gathers 30,000 men to bring the Ark of the Covenant from the house of Abinadab. They place it on a new cart and celebrate with music and dancing.
As the oxen stumble, Uzzah reaches out to steady the Ark and is struck dead by God for his irreverence.
David becomes angry and afraid. He leaves the Ark at the house of Obed-edom, where it remains for three months and brings blessing.
Hearing of Obed-edom’s blessings, David brings the Ark to Jerusalem with sacrifices and joyful dancing. He wears a linen ephod and leads the procession.
Michal, Saul’s daughter, despises David for dancing. David places the Ark in a tent, offers sacrifices, blesses the people, and distributes food.
Michal confronts David for his undignified behavior. David defends his worship before the LORD. Michal remains childless for the rest of her life.
David expresses a desire to build a house for God. Nathan initially approves.
God tells Nathan that David will not build the temple. Instead, God promises to establish David’s house and kingdom forever a covenant pointing to the Messiah.
David responds with humility and gratitude, praising God’s greatness and praying for the fulfillment of His promises.
David defeats the Philistines and Moabites, making them subject to him.
He defeats Hadadezer of Zobah and the Arameans, taking gold, bronze, and shields.
Toi of Hamath sends gifts to David. David dedicates all the spoils to the LORD.
David defeats Edom and places garrisons there. The LORD gives him victory wherever he goes.
David reigns with justice and righteousness. His key officials are listed, including Joab, Jehoshaphat, Zadok, and his sons.
David seeks to show kindness to Jonathan’s family. He learns of Mephibosheth, Jonathan’s lame son, living in Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth humbly appears before David, who promises to restore Saul’s land and honor him.
David assigns Ziba and his household to serve Mephibosheth and grants him a permanent place at the king’s table.
David sends envoys to comfort Hanun, king of Ammon, after his father’s death. Hanun humiliates them, suspecting espionage.
The Ammonites hire Aramean mercenaries. David sends Joab and the army to confront them.
Joab divides his forces to face both enemies. Israel defeats the Arameans, and the Ammonites retreat.
The Arameans regroup, but David leads Israel to a decisive victory. The Arameans submit and no longer aid Ammon.
While Israel is at war, David remains in Jerusalem. He sees Bathsheba bathing, sends for her, and sleeps with her. She later informs him she is pregnant.
David summons Bathsheba’s husband, Uriah, from battle, hoping he will sleep with his wife to cover the pregnancy. Uriah refuses out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers.
David sends Uriah back to the battlefield with a letter instructing Joab to place him in the front lines and withdraw support. Uriah is killed in battle.
Joab sends word of Uriah’s death. David downplays the loss, telling Joab not to be discouraged.
Bathsheba mourns, then becomes David’s wife and bears him a son. But the LORD is displeased with David’s actions.
God sends Nathan to confront David with a parable about a rich man stealing a poor man’s lamb. David is outraged until Nathan declares, 'You are the man!'
Nathan rebukes David, recounting God’s blessings and David’s betrayal. Though forgiven, David is told the sword will never depart from his house, and his child will die.
David fasts and pleads for the child’s life, but the child dies. David accepts God’s judgment and comforts Bathsheba.
Bathsheba bears Solomon. The LORD loves him and names him Jedidiah through Nathan.
Joab captures Rabbah. David takes the crown and spoils, enslaves the people, and returns to Jerusalem.
Amnon, David’s son, lusts after his half-sister Tamar. With Jonadab’s help, he deceives and rapes her.
After the assault, Amnon despises Tamar and sends her away. Tamar is devastated. Absalom, her brother, shelters her and harbors hatred toward Amnon. David is angry but does nothing.
Two years later, Absalom invites all the king’s sons to a feast and has Amnon killed in revenge.
David mourns, thinking all his sons are dead, but learns only Amnon was killed. Absalom flees to Geshur and remains there three years.
Joab, seeing David’s longing for Absalom, devises a plan to reconcile them. He sends a wise woman from Tekoa to present a parable to the king.

The woman tells a story of two sons one killed the other, and now the family wants to execute the survivor. David promises protection. She then applies the story to David’s estrangement from Absalom, revealing Joab’s involvement.
David agrees to bring Absalom back to Jerusalem but refuses to see him face-to-face.
Absalom is described as exceptionally handsome and has three sons and a daughter named Tamar.
After two years without seeing David, Absalom burns Joab’s field to get his attention. Joab arranges a meeting, and David finally kisses Absalom, signaling reconciliation.
Absalom builds his image by positioning himself at the city gate, intercepting those seeking justice, and winning the hearts of the people.
Absalom asks to go to Hebron under the pretense of fulfilling a vow but uses the opportunity to declare himself king. He gathers support, including David’s counselor Ahithophel.
David flees Jerusalem with his household and loyal followers to avoid bloodshed. Ittai the Gittite pledges loyalty and joins him.
Zadok and Abiathar bring the Ark, but David sends it back, trusting God’s will. They remain in Jerusalem as informants.
David ascends the Mount of Olives weeping. Hushai the Archite meets him and is sent back to Jerusalem to counter Ahithophel’s counsel.
Ziba meets David with supplies and claims Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping to reclaim Saul’s throne. David gives Mephibosheth’s property to Ziba.
Shimei, a relative of Saul, curses and throws stones at David. David restrains his men, accepting the humiliation as possibly from God.
Absalom enters Jerusalem. Hushai pretends loyalty to Absalom, positioning himself as a double agent.
Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with David’s concubines to assert dominance. Absalom follows the advice, fulfilling Nathan’s prophecy.
Ahithophel advises a swift attack on David with 12,000 men to kill only the king and bring peace.

Hushai counters the advice, warning that David is too experienced and dangerous. He suggests gathering all Israel for a massive campaign. Absalom accepts Hushai’s counsel, fulfilling God’s plan to defeat Ahithophel’s advice.
Hushai sends word to David through priests’ sons. They narrowly escape capture and warn David, who crosses the Jordan safely.
Ahithophel, seeing his advice rejected, sets his affairs in order and hangs himself.
David arrives at Mahanaim. Allies bring supplies to support him and his weary men.
David organizes his army under Joab, Abishai, and Ittai. He stays behind but commands them to deal gently with Absalom.
David’s forces defeat Absalom’s army in the forest. Absalom is caught in a tree by his hair and killed by Joab, despite David’s orders.
Absalom had erected a monument to himself, having no sons to carry on his name.
Ahimaaz and a Cushite run to deliver news. Ahimaaz arrives first but withholds the full truth. The Cushite informs David of Absalom’s death.
David is overwhelmed with grief, crying out, 'O my son Absalom... would God I had died for thee.'
Joab rebukes David for excessive mourning over Absalom, warning that it demoralizes the troops. David heeds the advice and publicly encourages his men.
The tribes of Israel debate David’s return to the throne. David sends word to Judah, who welcomes him back. He appoints Amasa as commander in Joab’s place.
Shimei, who had cursed David, begs for forgiveness. David spares his life, showing mercy.
Mephibosheth explains his absence during David’s flight, blaming Ziba’s deception. David divides the land between them.
Barzillai, an elderly supporter, declines David’s invitation to Jerusalem and sends Chimham in his place. David blesses him.
A dispute arises between Judah and the other tribes over who has more claim to the king, revealing lingering divisions in Israel.
Sheba, a Benjamite, incites a new rebellion, and the men of Israel follow him, while Judah remains loyal to David.
David confines his concubines who were violated by Absalom, providing for them but isolating them for life.
David orders Amasa to gather troops, but when he delays, Joab kills him and resumes command.
Joab besieges Abel Beth-maacah, where Sheba is hiding. A wise woman negotiates peace by having Sheba executed and his head thrown over the wall.
The chapter ends with a list of David’s key officials, reflecting restored order in the kingdom.

A famine prompts David to seek God, who reveals it is due to Saul’s violation of a covenant with the Gibeonites. Seven of Saul’s descendants are executed. Rizpah mourns them, and David later buries their bones with Saul and Jonathan. God ends the famine.
David’s men defeat four Philistine giants, including relatives of Goliath. David is told not to fight in battle anymore to preserve his life.
David sings a psalm of deliverance, praising God as his rock, fortress, and savior who rescued him from enemies and death.
David attributes his deliverance to his righteousness and God’s faithfulness to the blameless.
He praises God’s strength, guidance, and victory over nations and enemies.
David concludes with praise for God’s enduring mercy and covenant with his descendants.
David’s last words reflect on righteous leadership, God’s covenant with him, and the fate of the wicked.
The exploits of David’s three mightiest warriors are recounted, including their heroic deeds and loyalty.
Abishai and Benaiah are highlighted for their valor and leadership among the elite warriors.
A list of the remaining thirty warriors is given, honoring their service and bravery.

God’s anger is kindled against Israel, and He incites David to take a census of Israel and Judah. Despite Joab’s objections, David insists. Joab and the commanders count the people over nine months and report 1.3 million fighting men.

David’s conscience strikes him after the census. He confesses his sin, and God sends the prophet Gad to offer three punishments: seven years of famine, three months of fleeing enemies, or three days of plague. David chooses to fall into God’s hands.

A plague strikes Israel, killing 70,000. As the angel prepares to destroy Jerusalem, God relents. David sees the angel and pleads for mercy, asking that the punishment fall on him and his family instead.

Gad tells David to build an altar on Araunah’s threshing floor. Araunah offers it freely, but David insists on paying, saying he won’t offer to God what costs him nothing. He builds the altar, offers sacrifices, and the plague is halted.
King David, now old and frail, is cared for by Abishag the Shunammite, a young woman chosen to serve and keep him warm.
Adonijah, David’s son, declares himself king without David’s consent. He gains support from Joab and Abiathar but excludes Solomon, Nathan, and others.
Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba inform David of Adonijah’s actions. Bathsheba reminds David of his promise that Solomon would succeed him.
David orders Solomon to be anointed king by Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet. Solomon is proclaimed king with great celebration.
Adonijah and his supporters hear the news and panic. Adonijah seeks refuge at the altar. Solomon spares him on the condition of future loyalty.
David gives Solomon final instructions: to walk in God’s ways and to deal wisely with Joab, Shimei, and others who wronged him.
David dies after reigning 40 years. Solomon firmly establishes his reign.
Adonijah asks to marry Abishag. Solomon sees this as a threat and has him executed.
Solomon exiles Abiathar, fulfilling prophecy. Joab is executed for past murders. Benaiah replaces him as army commander.
Shimei is confined to Jerusalem but later disobeys and is executed. Solomon’s kingdom is now fully secure.
Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter and offers sacrifices at Gibeon, where the tabernacle is located.
God appears to Solomon in a dream and offers him anything. Solomon asks for wisdom. God grants it, along with riches and honor.
Solomon demonstrates his wisdom by resolving a dispute between two women claiming the same baby. His judgment earns him national respect.
Solomon’s officials and governors are listed, showing his administrative structure and the division of the kingdom into districts.
Israel enjoys peace and prosperity. Daily provisions for Solomon’s household are described, reflecting the kingdom’s abundance.
Solomon’s wisdom surpasses all others. He speaks proverbs and songs, and people from all nations come to hear him.
Solomon contacts King Hiram of Tyre to request cedar for building the temple, explaining that David was unable to build it due to war.
Hiram rejoices and agrees to supply materials. A covenant of peace is established between the two kings.
Solomon organizes a large labor force to prepare materials. Stonecutters and timber workers begin preparing for temple construction.
Solomon begins building the temple in the fourth year of his reign, 480 years after the Exodus. The structure’s dimensions, side rooms, and construction methods are described in detail.
God speaks to Solomon, promising to dwell among the Israelites and not forsake them if Solomon walks in obedience.

The temple’s interior is finished with cedar and gold. The inner sanctuary (Most Holy Place) is prepared for the Ark, with two large cherubim. Carvings and gold overlay adorn the temple. The work takes seven years to complete.
Solomon builds his palace complex over 13 years, including the House of the Forest of Lebanon, the Hall of Pillars, the Hall of Judgment, and a house for Pharaoh’s daughter.
Hiram, a skilled craftsman from Tyre, makes two massive bronze pillars for the temple, named Jachin and Boaz.
Hiram crafts the 'Sea of cast metal' (a large basin), twelve oxen to support it, ten bronze stands, and basins for temple use.
Hiram completes all bronze furnishings. Solomon also has gold items made for the inner sanctuary. The temple work is finished, and David’s dedicated treasures are placed inside.
Solomon gathers Israel’s leaders to bring the Ark into the temple. As the priests place it in the Most Holy Place, a cloud fills the temple, signifying God’s glory.
Solomon addresses the assembly, recounting how God fulfilled His promise to David by allowing Solomon to build the temple.
Solomon offers a long prayer of dedication, asking God to hear prayers offered toward the temple and to forgive His people when they repent.
Solomon blesses the people, praises God’s faithfulness, and urges Israel to remain loyal to the LORD.
A massive festival follows, with thousands of sacrifices and a 14-day celebration. The people return home joyful and blessed.
God appears to Solomon a second time, affirming His promise to dwell in the temple if Solomon remains faithful but warning of exile and destruction if Israel turns away.
Solomon gives Hiram twenty cities in Galilee as payment for materials, but Hiram is displeased with them.
Solomon’s building projects include the temple, palace, and fortified cities. He uses forced labor from non-Israelites but not from the Israelites themselves.
Solomon builds a fleet of ships with Hiram’s help. They bring back gold from Ophir, enhancing Israel’s wealth.
The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon to test his wisdom. She is amazed by his answers, wealth, and court. She praises God and gives Solomon lavish gifts.
Solomon’s annual gold income is immense. He makes golden shields, a grand ivory-and-gold throne, and drinking vessels of gold. Silver is considered of little value.
Solomon amasses chariots and horses, importing them from Egypt and exporting them to other nations.
Solomon’s many foreign wives lead him into idolatry. He builds high places for gods like Ashtoreth, Chemosh, and Molech, turning away from the LORD.
God becomes angry with Solomon and declares that the kingdom will be torn from his son, though not entirely, for David’s sake.
God raises up adversaries against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite and Rezon of Damascus, both of whom trouble Israel.
Jeroboam, a capable servant of Solomon, is chosen by God to rule ten tribes. The prophet Ahijah confirms this with a symbolic act. Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who flees to Egypt.
Solomon dies after a 40-year reign. His son Rehoboam succeeds him.
Rehoboam becomes king. The people ask him to lighten Solomon’s heavy burdens. He rejects the elders’ advice and follows his peers’ harsh counsel, provoking rebellion.
Ten tribes reject Rehoboam and make Jeroboam king. Rehoboam plans war, but God sends Shemaiah the prophet to stop it.
Jeroboam fears losing loyalty to Jerusalem and sets up golden calves in Bethel and Dan. He appoints non-Levite priests and creates a rival religious system, leading Israel into sin.

A man of God from Judah prophesies against Jeroboam’s altar. Jeroboam’s hand withers when he tries to seize him but is healed after the prophet prays. The prophet refuses to eat or drink in Bethel, obeying God’s command.
An old prophet deceives the man of God, claiming an angel told him to invite him to eat. The man of God disobeys and accepts the invitation.
God speaks through the old prophet, declaring judgment on the man of God. A lion kills him on the road, but does not eat him or harm his donkey. The old prophet buries him and mourns.
Despite the signs, Jeroboam does not repent and continues in idolatry, sealing his dynasty’s doom.
Jeroboam’s son Abijah falls ill. His wife, in disguise, visits the prophet Ahijah, who foretells the child’s death and the downfall of Jeroboam’s house. The child dies as prophesied.
Jeroboam dies after a 22-year reign. His son Nadab succeeds him.
Rehoboam reigns in Judah but leads the people into idolatry and immorality, provoking God’s anger.
Shishak of Egypt invades Jerusalem and plunders the temple. Rehoboam replaces the stolen gold shields with bronze. He dies after 17 years and is succeeded by Abijam.
Abijam reigns in Judah for three years, continuing in sin. Yet God preserves his line for David’s sake.
Asa, Abijam’s son, reigns for 41 years. He removes idols and deposes his idolatrous grandmother. He allies with Ben-Hadad of Syria to repel Baasha of Israel.
Nadab, Jeroboam’s son, rules Israel for two years before being assassinated by Baasha, who becomes king.
Baasha reigns over Israel for 24 years, continuing Jeroboam’s sinful ways and provoking God’s anger.
God sends the prophet Jehu to rebuke King Baasha for following Jeroboam’s sinful ways. Baasha’s dynasty is condemned, and God promises to wipe out his house.
Elah, Baasha’s son, reigns for two years before being assassinated by Zimri, one of his officials. Zimri kills the entire house of Baasha, fulfilling Jehu’s prophecy.
Zimri rules for only seven days. When the army hears of his coup, they proclaim Omri king. Zimri sets the palace on fire and dies.
A civil war breaks out between Omri and Tibni. Omri prevails, becomes king, and builds the city of Samaria. He reigns twelve years but continues in idolatry.
Ahab, Omri’s son, becomes king and does more evil than all before him. He marries Jezebel and promotes Baal worship. Hiel rebuilds Jericho, fulfilling Joshua’s ancient curse.
Elijah proclaims a drought to King Ahab. God sends him to the brook Cherith, where ravens feed him until the brook dries up.
God sends Elijah to a widow in Zarephath. Though she has little, she feeds him, and her flour and oil miraculously never run out.
The widow’s son dies. Elijah prays, and God restores the boy’s life. The woman declares Elijah a true man of God.
God tells Elijah to confront Ahab. Elijah meets Obadiah, a faithful servant who had hidden prophets from Jezebel. Obadiah arranges a meeting with Ahab.
Elijah challenges Ahab and the prophets of Baal to a contest on Mount Carmel to prove who is the true God.
The prophets of Baal call on their god all day with no response. Elijah mocks them.
Elijah repairs the LORD’s altar, drenches it with water, and prays. Fire from heaven consumes the offering. The people declare the LORD is God, and Elijah has the prophets of Baal executed.
Elijah prays for rain. A small cloud appears, and a heavy rain follows. Elijah runs ahead of Ahab’s chariot to Jezreel.
Jezebel threatens Elijah’s life. He flees into the wilderness, prays to die, and is miraculously fed by an angel. He travels 40 days to Mount Horeb.
At Horeb, God reveals Himself not in wind, earthquake, or fire, but in a gentle whisper. He reassures Elijah and tells him to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha.
Elijah finds Elisha plowing and calls him to follow. Elisha sacrifices his oxen and joins Elijah as his servant.
Ben-hadad of Syria besieges Samaria and demands Ahab’s wealth and family. Ahab initially agrees, but refuses when Ben-hadad demands full access to plunder the city.
A prophet tells Ahab that God will give him victory. Israel defeats the Syrians, and the prophet warns Ahab of another attack in spring.
The Syrians return, thinking Israel’s God is only a god of the hills. Israel wins again. Ahab spares Ben-hadad and makes a treaty.
A prophet rebukes Ahab through a parable, condemning him for sparing Ben-hadad. Ahab returns home sullen and angry.
King Ahab desires Naboth’s vineyard, which is near his palace. Naboth refuses to sell it, citing ancestral inheritance laws. Ahab becomes sullen and refuses to eat.
Jezebel, Ahab’s wife, devises a scheme to acquire the vineyard. She arranges for false witnesses to accuse Naboth of blasphemy. Naboth is stoned to death by the townspeople.
Jezebel informs Ahab of Naboth’s death. Ahab immediately goes to take possession of the vineyard.
God sends Elijah to confront Ahab. Elijah prophesies judgment: dogs will lick Ahab’s blood where Naboth died, and Jezebel will be eaten by dogs.
Ahab is described as having sold himself to do evil, incited by Jezebel. He is condemned for idolatry and wickedness.
Ahab humbles himself, fasting and wearing sackcloth. Because of his repentance, God delays the judgment until after Ahab’s death.

After three years of peace, Ahab seeks to retake Ramoth-gilead from Syria. He allies with Jehoshaphat of Judah, who insists on consulting a prophet. Ahab’s 400 prophets predict success, but Jehoshaphat asks for a true prophet of the LORD.

Micaiah, the true prophet, initially mocks Ahab but then reveals a vision of Israel scattered and Ahab’s death. He explains that a lying spirit has deceived the other prophets. Ahab imprisons Micaiah.
Ahab disguises himself in battle, but is struck by a random arrow and dies. His blood is washed from the chariot where dogs lick it up, fulfilling Elijah’s prophecy.
Jehoshaphat reigns righteously in Judah, removing some idolatry. He makes peace with Israel and dies after a 25-year reign.
Ahaziah, Ahab’s son, becomes king of Israel. He follows in his father’s wicked ways, provoking the LORD’s anger.

King Ahaziah of Israel falls through a lattice and becomes ill. He sends messengers to consult Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron. Elijah intercepts them, condemns the king’s idolatry, and prophesies his death.
Ahaziah sends three groups of fifty soldiers to summon Elijah. Fire from heaven consumes the first two groups. The third captain pleads humbly, and his men are spared.
Elijah accompanies the third captain and confirms the prophecy before the king. Ahaziah dies, and Jehoram becomes king in his place.
Elijah and Elisha journey together as Elijah prepares for his departure. At the Jordan, Elijah parts the waters. A chariot of fire takes him to heaven in a whirlwind as Elisha watches in awe.
Elisha takes up Elijah’s mantle and parts the Jordan. The sons of the prophets recognize his authority. They search unsuccessfully for Elijah’s body.
Elisha purifies a city's water supply. Later, youths mock him; he curses them, and two bears come out and maul forty-two of them. He travels on to Mount Carmel and Samaria.
Jehoram becomes king of Israel and reigns 12 years. He removes some idolatry but continues Jeroboam’s sinful ways.
Moab rebels against Israel. Jehoram allies with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom. When they run out of water, Elisha provides it miraculously after a musician plays.
Israel defeats Moab and destroys cities. When the Moabite king sacrifices his son on the wall, great wrath falls on Israel, and they withdraw.
A prophet’s widow cries to Elisha for help. He miraculously multiplies her oil so she can pay off debts and live on the rest.
A wealthy Shunammite woman hosts Elisha regularly. As a reward, he prophesies she’ll have a son, and she does.
The child later dies suddenly. The woman seeks Elisha, who raises the boy back to life by praying and lying upon him.
Elisha purifies a deadly stew with flour, making it safe to eat.
Elisha multiplies twenty loaves to feed a hundred men, and there is food left over.
Naaman, a Syrian commander with leprosy, seeks healing from Elisha. After initial offense at the instructions, he humbles himself and is healed by bathing in the Jordan seven times.
Naaman returns grateful, confessing Israel’s God as the only true God. Elisha refuses payment and blesses him.
Gehazi, Elisha’s servant, secretly takes gifts from Naaman and lies about it. Elisha confronts him, and Gehazi is struck with Naaman’s leprosy.
The sons of the prophets begin building a larger dwelling near the Jordan. During the work, a borrowed axe head falls into the river. Elisha miraculously causes it to float, recovering the tool.
The king of Aram plans attacks against Israel, but Elisha repeatedly reveals his plans to the king of Israel. The Aramean king suspects a traitor but learns Elisha is the source.
The Arameans surround Dothan to capture Elisha. Elisha’s servant panics, but Elisha prays, and the servant sees the hills filled with horses and chariots of fire God’s protection.
Elisha prays, and the Aramean army is struck with blindness. He leads them to Samaria, where their sight is restored. Instead of killing them, Elisha has them fed and released. The raids cease.

Later, Ben-hadad of Aram besieges Samaria, causing a severe famine. The situation becomes so desperate that cannibalism occurs. The king blames Elisha and vows to kill him, but Elisha prophesies relief.
Elisha prophesies that the famine will end the next day, with food sold cheaply. A royal officer scoffs, and Elisha declares he will see it but not eat of it.
Four lepers decide to surrender to the Arameans but find their camp abandoned. God had caused the Arameans to flee in fear, thinking an army was approaching.
The lepers realize they must share the good news. They return to the city and inform the gatekeepers.
The king suspects a trap but sends scouts. They confirm the Arameans have fled, leaving everything behind.
The people plunder the camp, and food becomes abundant just as Elisha said. The scoffing officer is trampled at the gate and dies, fulfilling Elisha’s prophecy.
Elisha warns the Shunammite woman of a coming famine. She leaves for seven years and returns to find her land taken. Gehazi tells the king her story, and the king restores her land and profits.

Elisha visits Damascus. Ben-hadad is ill and sends Hazael to inquire about his recovery. Elisha weeps, foreseeing Hazael’s cruelty. Hazael returns, lies to the king, and murders him to seize the throne.
Jehoram (Joram) becomes king of Judah. He follows the ways of Ahab due to his marriage alliance. Edom and Libnah rebel. Jehoram dies, and his son Ahaziah succeeds him.
Ahaziah reigns in Judah and allies with Joram of Israel against Hazael. Joram is wounded in battle and retreats to Jezreel.
Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint Jehu as king of Israel. Jehu’s officers proclaim him king after hearing the prophecy.
Jehu rides to Jezreel and kills King Joram of Israel, fulfilling Elijah’s prophecy. He also wounds King Ahaziah of Judah, who later dies.
Ahaziah flees but is mortally wounded. He dies in Megiddo and is buried in Jerusalem.
Jezebel confronts Jehu from a window. At his command, her servants throw her down. She dies, and dogs devour her body, fulfilling Elijah’s prophecy.
Jehu sends letters to Samaria demanding the heads of Ahab’s seventy sons. The leaders comply, and Jehu displays the heads publicly, declaring God’s judgment fulfilled.
Jehu kills relatives of Ahaziah and all remaining members of Ahab’s house in Samaria.
Jehu deceives Baal worshipers by calling a grand sacrifice. Once gathered, he has them all killed and destroys the temple of Baal.
Despite his zeal, Jehu continues Jeroboam’s idolatry. God grants him four generations on the throne. Jehu reigns 28 years and is succeeded by his son Jehoahaz.
After Ahaziah’s death, his mother Athaliah seizes power by killing the royal heirs. But Jehosheba, Ahaziah’s sister, hides Joash, his infant son, in the temple for six years.
In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada organizes a coup. He reveals Joash to the guards, makes a covenant with them, and crowns the boy king in a public ceremony.
Athaliah hears the commotion, sees Joash crowned, and cries 'Treason!' Jehoiada orders her execution outside the temple grounds.
Jehoiada renews the covenant between the LORD, the king, and the people. They destroy the temple of Baal and kill its priest. Joash begins his reign at age seven.
Joash reigns in Judah for 40 years and does right in God’s eyes under Jehoiada’s guidance, though high places of worship remain.
Joash commands that temple repairs be funded from offerings, but the priests delay. He rebukes them and changes the collection system.
A chest is placed in the temple for offerings. Funds are used to pay workers directly, and repairs are completed with integrity.
King Hazael of Aram threatens Jerusalem. Joash appeases him by giving treasures from the temple and palace.
Joash is assassinated by his servants at Beth-millo. His son Amaziah succeeds him.
Jehoahaz reigns in Israel and continues Jeroboam’s sins. God allows Syria to oppress Israel, but relents after Jehoahaz pleads. Israel is delivered, but remains spiritually compromised.
Jehoash (Joash), Jehoahaz’s son, becomes king and also follows Jeroboam’s idolatry. He reigns 16 years.
Elisha, on his deathbed, prophesies partial victory over Syria. Jehoash strikes the ground only three times with arrows, limiting Israel’s success.
Elisha dies. A dead man is revived when his body touches Elisha’s bones, showing God’s enduring power through the prophet.
Israel continues to suffer under Syria, but Jehoash regains cities from Ben-Hadad, fulfilling Elisha’s prophecy.
Amaziah becomes king of Judah and reigns 29 years. He does right in God’s eyes but not wholeheartedly. He executes his father’s assassins and defeats Edom.
Amaziah challenges Jehoash of Israel and is defeated. Jerusalem’s wall is breached, and temple treasures are plundered.
Jehoash dies, and Jeroboam II succeeds him. Amaziah is later assassinated, and his son Azariah (Uzziah) becomes king.
Jeroboam II reigns in Israel for 41 years. Though he does evil, God uses him to restore Israel’s borders through the prophecy of Jonah.
Azariah (Uzziah) reigns in Judah for 52 years. He does right but leaves high places intact. God strikes him with leprosy, and his son Jotham governs in his place.
Zechariah, Jeroboam’s son, reigns in Israel for six months before being assassinated by Shallum, ending Jehu’s dynasty.
Shallum reigns one month before being killed by Menahem, who becomes king.
Menahem rules Israel for 10 years with cruelty. He pays tribute to Assyria to secure his reign.
Pekahiah, Menahem’s son, reigns two years before being assassinated by Pekah.
Pekah reigns 20 years and continues in sin. Assyria captures parts of Israel. Pekah is assassinated by Hoshea.
Jotham reigns in Judah and does right, but high places remain. He builds extensively and faces threats from Syria and Israel.

Ahaz becomes king of Judah at age 20 and reigns 16 years. Unlike David, he does evil in the LORD’s sight, imitating the kings of Israel. He even sacrifices his son in fire and worships at high places.
Rezin of Aram and Pekah of Israel attack Jerusalem but fail to conquer it. Ahaz seeks help from Tiglath-Pileser of Assyria, sending him silver and gold from the temple and palace.
Ahaz visits Damascus and sees a pagan altar. He has a replica built in Jerusalem and replaces the LORD’s bronze altar with it. He commands the priest Uriah to use the new altar for sacrifices.
Ahaz further alters the temple, removing sacred furnishings and adapting it to Assyrian preferences, showing his disregard for God’s instructions.
Ahaz dies and is buried in Jerusalem. His son Hezekiah succeeds him.
Hoshea becomes the last king of Israel and reigns nine years. He rebels against Assyria, prompting a siege of Samaria. After three years, the city falls, and Israel is exiled to Assyria.

The fall of Israel is explained as a result of persistent idolatry and disobedience. Despite prophetic warnings, the people reject God’s covenant and worship false gods. God removes them from His presence.
The Assyrians repopulate Samaria with foreigners who bring their own gods. A priest is sent to teach them about the LORD, but they continue to mix pagan worship with reverence for God.
The new settlers practice syncretism fearing the LORD while serving their own gods. The chapter ends by emphasizing Israel’s failure to obey God’s statutes and covenant.
Hezekiah becomes king of Judah and reigns 29 years. He does what is right in God’s eyes, removes high places, and destroys the bronze serpent. He trusts the LORD and defeats the Philistines.
The fall of Samaria is recounted again, emphasizing Israel’s exile due to disobedience.
In Hezekiah’s 14th year, Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah. Hezekiah pays tribute by stripping silver and gold from the temple and palace.
Assyrian officials confront Jerusalem and mock Hezekiah’s trust in God. They speak in Hebrew to intimidate the people, urging surrender. Hezekiah’s officials remain silent, as instructed.
Hezekiah seeks Isaiah’s counsel. Isaiah assures him that God will cause Sennacherib to retreat and die in his own land.
Sennacherib sends another message mocking God and boasting of his conquests.
Hezekiah prays in the temple, exalting God’s uniqueness and asking for deliverance to glorify His name.
God responds through Isaiah, condemning Sennacherib’s arrogance and promising that he will not enter Jerusalem. God will defend the city for His name’s sake.
That night, the angel of the LORD kills 185,000 Assyrians. Sennacherib retreats to Nineveh, where he is assassinated by his sons.
Hezekiah becomes terminally ill. Isaiah tells him to prepare for death, but Hezekiah prays, and God grants him 15 more years. A fig poultice is applied to his boil, and he recovers.
As a sign, God causes the shadow on the sundial to move backward ten steps.
Envoys from Babylon visit Hezekiah. He proudly shows them all his treasures. Isaiah rebukes him and prophesies that Babylon will one day carry everything away, including his descendants.
Hezekiah’s deeds are recorded. He dies, and his son Manasseh becomes king.

Manasseh becomes king of Judah at age 12 and reigns 55 years. He does evil in the LORD’s sight, rebuilding pagan altars, worshiping celestial bodies, practicing sorcery, and even placing an Asherah idol in the temple. He leads Judah into greater sin than the nations God had previously destroyed.

God sends prophets to warn that because of Manasseh’s abominations, He will bring disaster on Jerusalem and Judah, wiping them out like a dish turned upside down. The people’s persistent rebellion seals their fate.
Manasseh sheds much innocent blood and continues in idolatry. He dies and is buried in the garden of his palace. His son Amon succeeds him.
Amon reigns two years and follows his father’s wicked ways. His servants assassinate him, but the people kill the conspirators and make his son Josiah king.
Josiah becomes king at age 8 and reigns 31 years. He does what is right in the LORD’s eyes, walking in the ways of David.
In his 18th year, Josiah orders repairs to the temple. Funds are entrusted to the workers, who are known for their honesty.
Hilkiah the high priest finds the Book of the Law during the repairs. Shaphan the scribe reads it to Josiah.
Upon hearing the Law, Josiah tears his clothes in grief and sends officials to inquire of the LORD, fearing divine wrath.
The prophetess Huldah confirms that judgment is coming on Judah for its disobedience. However, because of Josiah’s humility, God promises he will not see the disaster in his lifetime.
Josiah gathers the people and reads the Book of the Covenant. He renews the covenant with the LORD, and the people pledge to follow it.
Josiah purges Judah and Israel of idolatry: he destroys pagan altars, shrines, and high places, defiles Topheth, removes mediums and idols, and fulfills the prophecy against the altar at Bethel.
Josiah commands the people to celebrate the Passover. It is observed with unmatched devotion, not seen since the days of the judges.
Despite Josiah’s reforms, God’s fierce anger remains because of Manasseh’s sins. Judah’s exile is still decreed.
Josiah is killed in battle at Megiddo by Pharaoh Necho. He is buried in Jerusalem, and his son Jehoahaz becomes king.
Jehoahaz reigns three months before Pharaoh Necho imprisons him and imposes tribute on Judah. Necho installs Eliakim (renamed Jehoiakim) as king.
Jehoiakim reigns 11 years and does evil in the LORD’s sight, continuing the cycle of rebellion.

Jehoiakim becomes a vassal of Babylon for three years but then rebels. In response, God sends raiding bands from Babylon, Aram, Moab, and Ammon to attack Judah, fulfilling prophetic warnings. Egypt no longer intervenes, as Babylon controls the region.

Jehoiakim dies, and his son Jehoiachin reigns for three months. Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, and Jehoiachin surrenders. The Babylonians deport the king, his family, officials, craftsmen, and treasures from the temple and palace. Nebuchadnezzar appoints Mattaniah (renamed Zedekiah) as king.
Zedekiah reigns 11 years but does evil in the LORD’s sight. He rebels against Babylon, setting the stage for Jerusalem’s final downfall.

Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem in Zedekiah’s ninth year. After two years, the city falls. Zedekiah tries to escape but is captured. His sons are executed before him, and he is blinded and taken to Babylon.

Nebuzaradan, Babylon’s captain of the guard, burns the temple, palace, and houses. He breaks down Jerusalem’s walls and exiles the remaining people. Temple treasures are taken, and key leaders are executed.
Gedaliah is appointed governor over the remnant in Judah. After he is assassinated, the people flee to Egypt, fearing Babylonian retaliation.
In Babylon, Jehoiachin is released from prison in the 37th year of exile. He is given a place of honor and provided for the rest of his life, ending the book with a glimmer of hope.
The genealogy begins with Adam and traces through Noah and his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth establishing the foundation of the nations after the flood.
The descendants of Japheth, Ham, and Shem are listed, outlining the spread of peoples and nations across the ancient world.
The line from Shem to Abraham is traced, emphasizing the chosen lineage through which God’s covenant will unfold.
Abraham’s descendants are listed, including Isaac and Ishmael, and the sons of Keturah. The focus narrows to Isaac’s line through Esau and Israel (Jacob).
The chapter concludes with the chiefs of Edom, descendants of Esau, highlighting the neighboring nation’s leadership structure.
The twelve sons of Israel (Jacob) are listed, forming the foundation of the twelve tribes.
The genealogy of Judah is detailed, including the line leading to David. Notable figures like Perez, Boaz, Jesse, and David’s brothers are named.
Further descendants of Judah are listed, including Caleb’s line and various clans. The chapter emphasizes the tribe’s complexity and prominence.
David’s sons are listed, distinguishing those born in Hebron and Jerusalem. His daughters and concubines are also mentioned.
The royal line from Solomon to the Babylonian exile is traced, listing the kings of Judah.
Post-exilic descendants of Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) are recorded, preserving the Davidic line beyond the exile.
The descendants of Judah are expanded, including the notable prayer of Jabez, who asks God for blessing and protection.
The genealogy of Simeon is presented, including their settlements and military exploits in seeking new territory.
Reuben’s genealogy is given, noting that his birthright was given to Joseph’s sons due to his sin. The tribes of Reuben and Gad are described.
The tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh wage war against the Hagrites and win with God’s help.
Despite their strength, these tribes fall into idolatry and are exiled by the Assyrians as judgment from God.
The genealogy of Levi is traced through Kohath to Aaron, Eleazar, and onward to Jehozadak, who was taken into exile. This priestly line emphasizes continuity from the tabernacle to the exile.
The descendants of Levi’s three sons Gershom, Kohath, and Merari are listed, showing the broader Levitical family structure.
David appoints Levites for musical service in the temple. The families of Heman, Asaph, and Ethan are highlighted as leaders of worship.
Aaron’s descendants are assigned to offer sacrifices and minister in the Most Holy Place. The line from Aaron to Zadok is detailed.
The cities assigned to the Levites are listed by clan: Kohathites, Gershonites, and Merarites. These include cities of refuge and towns scattered throughout Israel’s tribal territories.
The descendants of Issachar are listed, including their military strength 87,000 warriors.
The genealogy of Benjamin is given, highlighting three sons and their descendants, many of whom were valiant warriors.
The sons of Naphtali are briefly listed.
