The descendants of Manasseh are recorded, including intermarriages and notable family lines.
Ephraim’s line is traced, including a tragic story of sons killed in a cattle raid and the birth of Beriah. Joshua is listed as a descendant.
The tribe of Asher is detailed, with emphasis on their leaders and warriors 26,000 in total.
The genealogy of Benjamin is expanded, focusing on the descendants of Bela, Ashbel, and others. Many are noted as heads of families and warriors.
Jeiel, the father of Gibeon, and his family are listed, including Kish, the ancestor of Saul.
The lineage of Saul is traced through Jonathan to his descendants, highlighting their military prowess and leadership.
All Israel is recorded in genealogies. After the exile, the first to return to their cities were Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants.
The residents of Jerusalem from the tribes of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh are listed.
The duties of priests and Levites are described, including gatekeepers, musicians, and those in charge of temple articles and offerings.
The genealogy of Saul is repeated, bridging the genealogical section with the historical narrative that begins in chapter 10.
Saul and his sons are killed in battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. The Israelites flee, and the Philistines occupy their cities.
The Philistines desecrate Saul’s body, but the men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve and bury it with honor.
Saul’s death is attributed to his unfaithfulness disobeying God and consulting a medium. The kingdom is given to David.
All Israel gathers at Hebron and anoints David as king, recognizing his past leadership and God’s appointment. David makes a covenant with them before the LORD.
David captures Jerusalem from the Jebusites and makes it his capital. Joab leads the attack and becomes commander. David grows stronger because the LORD is with him.
The chapter lists David’s mighty warriors, beginning with Jashobeam, Eleazar, and others who performed heroic feats in battle. Their loyalty and courage helped establish David’s kingdom.
Additional mighty men are named, including Abishai, Benaiah, and the Thirty. Their exploits and dedication to David are honored, showcasing the strength of his support.
Warriors from Benjamin join David at Ziklag while he is hiding from Saul. They are skilled archers and slingers, even though they are Saul’s kinsmen.
Gadite warriors join David in the wilderness. They are described as fierce, lion-faced, and swift as gazelles mighty men of valor who cross the Jordan during flood season.
Men from Benjamin and Judah come to David. Amasai, filled with the Spirit, declares loyalty to David. David welcomes them in peace.
More warriors from Manasseh join David. His army grows daily, becoming like the army of God.
A detailed list of warriors from each tribe who come to Hebron to make David king. They are described as skilled, loyal, and united in purpose.
All the warriors gather with a perfect heart to crown David. They feast for three days, supplied by their families and neighbors, celebrating with joy.
David consults with leaders and proposes bringing the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem. The people agree enthusiastically.
David and all Israel go to Kiriath-jearim to retrieve the Ark. They place it on a new cart and celebrate with music and dancing.
When the oxen stumble, Uzzah reaches out to steady the Ark and is struck dead by God for touching it.
David becomes afraid and leaves the Ark at the house of Obed-edom. God blesses Obed-edom’s household during the Ark’s stay.
King Hiram of Tyre sends materials and craftsmen to build David a palace. David recognizes that God has established his kingdom for Israel’s sake.
David takes more wives and has more children in Jerusalem. Their names are listed, including Solomon and Nathan.
The Philistines attack upon hearing of David’s anointing. David inquires of God, defeats them at Baal-perazim, and burns their idols.
The Philistines attack again. God instructs David to circle behind them and wait for the sound of marching in the trees. David obeys and wins another victory. His fame spreads, and nations fear him.
David prepares a place for the Ark and insists that only Levites may carry it, as God commanded.
David gathers Israel and the Levites. He instructs them to consecrate themselves and carry the Ark properly. The Levites obey and carry it on poles as prescribed by Moses.
David appoints musicians and singers to lead the procession. Specific Levites are named for their roles in playing instruments and guarding the Ark.
The Ark is brought to Jerusalem with great joy and music. David dances in celebration, but Michal, Saul’s daughter, despises him for it.

The Ark is placed in the tent David prepared in Jerusalem. Burnt and peace offerings are made. David blesses the people and appoints Levites, led by Asaph, to minister before the Ark with music and praise.

David delivers a psalm of thanksgiving, urging the people to give thanks, proclaim God’s deeds, and worship Him. The song celebrates God’s covenant with Abraham, His protection of Israel, and His greatness among the nations. It ends with a call to bless the LORD and a communal 'Amen.'

David assigns Asaph and his brothers to minister before the Ark in Jerusalem, while Zadok and other priests continue sacrifices at the Tabernacle in Gibeon. The people return home, and David blesses his household.
David expresses his desire to build a house for the LORD. Nathan initially approves.

God speaks to Nathan, saying David will not build the temple. Instead, God promises to build David a lasting dynasty. This covenant includes the promise of a son who will build the temple and a throne established forever.
David responds with humility and awe, praising God’s greatness and faithfulness. He prays for the fulfillment of God’s promises to his house.
David defeats the Philistines, Moabites, and Hadadezer of Zobah. He captures gold, silver, and bronze, dedicating them to the LORD. Abishai defeats the Edomites.
Tou, king of Hamath, sends gifts to David in gratitude for defeating Hadadezer. David dedicates all the tribute to the LORD.
David places garrisons in Edom and reigns with justice. His key officials are listed, including Joab, Jehoshaphat, Zadok, and Benaiah.
David sends messengers to comfort Hanun, king of Ammon, after his father’s death. Hanun humiliates them, suspecting espionage.
The Ammonites hire Syrian mercenaries. Joab and Abishai divide Israel’s forces and defeat both enemies. The Syrians flee, and the Ammonites retreat.
The Syrians regroup but are defeated again by David. They make peace and refuse to help Ammon further.
Joab captures Rabbah of Ammon. David takes the crown and plunder. The people are put to forced labor.
David’s warriors defeat Philistine giants, including Lahmi (Goliath’s brother) and a man with six fingers and toes. These victories affirm God’s power through David’s men.
Satan incites David to take a census of Israel. Joab protests, but David insists. The census is conducted, though Levi and Benjamin are excluded.
God is displeased and sends the prophet Gad to offer David three punishment options. David chooses a plague, trusting in God’s mercy.
A plague kills 70,000 Israelites. David sees the angel of the LORD and pleads for mercy, asking that the punishment fall on him instead of the people.
Gad instructs David to build an altar on Ornan’s threshing floor. David insists on paying full price. He offers sacrifices, and God halts the plague with fire from heaven.
David realizes this site is where the temple should be built. He is afraid to approach the tabernacle at Gibeon due to the angel’s sword.
David declares Ornan’s threshing floor the site for the temple. He gathers materials and workers, preparing extensively for Solomon to build it.
David charges Solomon to build the temple, explaining that God chose him because David had shed much blood in war.
David blesses Solomon, prays for wisdom, and encourages him to be strong and obedient. He reminds Solomon of the abundant resources already prepared.
David commands Israel’s leaders to support Solomon and urges them to seek the LORD and begin building the sanctuary.
David makes Solomon king and organizes the Levites, numbering 38,000 men aged 30 and above. He assigns them to temple duties, judges, gatekeepers, and musicians.
The Levites are divided by family: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Their descendants and roles are listed in detail.
David lowers the service age to 20 and outlines the Levites’ duties: assisting priests, maintaining the temple, and leading worship during festivals and daily offerings.
The priestly descendants of Aaron are divided into 24 groups under Eleazar and Ithamar. Lots are cast to assign their order of service.
The 24 priestly divisions are listed by name, each assigned to serve in the temple according to their lot.
The remaining Levites are listed by family and also assigned duties by lot, ensuring fairness among all ranks.
David appoints the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun to prophesy with music. They are trained and skilled, totaling 288 musicians.
Lots are cast to assign the order of service for each musical family, from the eldest to the youngest, ensuring equal opportunity in temple worship.

The divisions of the gatekeepers are listed, drawn from the families of the Korahites and Merarites. Lots are cast to assign duties at the temple gates east, west, north, south, and the storehouse. Each family receives a fair and divinely guided assignment.

Levites are appointed as treasurers over the temple’s dedicated gifts, including spoils from battles and offerings from leaders like Samuel, Saul, and David. Shelomith and his relatives oversee these treasures.

Other Levites are assigned as officials and judges in Israel’s territories. 1,700 men serve west of the Jordan, and 2,700 serve east of the Jordan, overseeing civil and religious matters with integrity and strength.
David’s military is organized into twelve divisions of 24,000 men each, serving month by month. Each division is led by a commander, ensuring year-round readiness.
Leaders of each tribe are listed, responsible for civil administration and tribal affairs. Notably, no leaders are listed for Gad and Asher, possibly due to lost records.
David refrains from counting those under 20, trusting God’s promise to multiply Israel. Joab begins a census but does not finish due to divine wrath.
Stewards are appointed over David’s treasuries, vineyards, olive groves, herds, and flocks. Each official manages a specific area of the king’s wealth and resources.
David’s inner circle includes counselors, scribes, tutors, and military leaders. Joab remains commander of the army, and trusted advisors like Ahithophel and Hushai serve the king.
David assembles Israel’s leaders and publicly declares Solomon as God’s chosen successor. He recounts God’s promise and urges the people to obey the LORD’s commands to secure their inheritance.
David charges Solomon to know and serve God wholeheartedly. He reminds him that God searches hearts and will bless or reject based on faithfulness. Solomon is urged to be strong and build the temple.
David gives Solomon detailed plans for the temple its structure, furnishings, and divisions received by divine inspiration. He entrusts Solomon with the sacred blueprint.
David encourages Solomon to be strong and courageous, assuring him that God will not forsake him. The priests, Levites, and skilled workers are ready to assist.
David announces Solomon’s youth and the greatness of the temple project. He donates his personal treasures gold and silver for the temple, setting an example of generosity.
The leaders of Israel respond with generous offerings. The people rejoice at their wholehearted giving, and David is filled with joy.
David offers a powerful prayer, praising God’s greatness and acknowledging that all things come from Him. He prays for Solomon’s faithfulness and invites the people to bless the LORD.
Solomon is anointed king, and the people celebrate with sacrifices and joy. Solomon sits on the throne, and his reign is firmly established.
David’s reign is summarized 40 years of leadership marked by strength and honor. He dies, and Solomon succeeds him. The records of his reign are preserved by prophets.
Solomon is firmly established as king. He gathers Israel’s leaders and goes to Gibeon, where the bronze altar is located, to offer a thousand burnt offerings to the LORD.
God appears to Solomon at night and offers him anything he desires. Solomon asks for wisdom and knowledge to govern Israel. God is pleased and grants him wisdom, along with riches, wealth, and honor.
Solomon returns to Jerusalem and reigns over Israel. He amasses great wealth, including chariots, horses, silver, and gold, making Jerusalem exceedingly prosperous.
Solomon begins preparations to build the temple and a royal palace. He assembles a massive workforce: 70,000 laborers, 80,000 stonecutters, and 3,600 overseers.
Solomon sends a message to King Hiram of Tyre, requesting cedar, pine, and algum logs, as well as a skilled craftsman. He offers wheat, barley, wine, and oil in exchange.
Hiram responds favorably, praising God for Solomon’s wisdom. He agrees to supply materials and sends Huram-Abi, a master craftsman, to assist with the temple work.
Solomon takes a census of resident foreigners in Israel and assigns them to the labor force, totaling 153,600 workers.
Solomon begins building the temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem, where the LORD appeared to David. Construction starts in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign.
The temple’s dimensions and materials are described. The interior is overlaid with gold and adorned with precious stones and carvings.
Two large cherubim are made for the Most Holy Place, their wings spanning the width of the room, symbolizing divine presence.
A veil is made to separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. Two bronze pillars, Jachin and Boaz, are set at the temple entrance.
Solomon makes a large bronze altar and the 'Sea' a massive basin for priestly washing, supported by twelve oxen.
Ten basins are made for washing offerings. Ten lampstands and ten tables are placed in the temple. The Sea is positioned on the southeast side.
Huram crafts various bronze items for the temple, including pots, shovels, and bowls. The sheer quantity of bronze used is beyond measure.
Solomon also makes gold furnishings: the altar of incense, tables for the bread of the Presence, lampstands, utensils, and doors for the inner sanctuary.
Solomon completes the temple and brings in the dedicated treasures. The Ark of the Covenant is brought from the City of David to the Most Holy Place, under the wings of the cherubim.

As the priests withdraw, the Levite musicians praise God with cymbals, harps, and trumpets. When they sing, 'For He is good; His mercy endures forever,' the temple is filled with a cloud the glory of the LORD.
Solomon declares that God has chosen to dwell in thick darkness and built a house for Him to dwell in forever.
Solomon blesses the assembly, recounting God’s promise to David and the fulfillment of building the temple.
Solomon kneels before the altar and begins an elaborate prayer of dedication, asking God to hear from heaven when His people pray.

Solomon prays through various scenarios sin, war, famine, captivity and asks for forgiveness and restoration when the people repent. He concludes by inviting God’s presence to remain and bless His anointed.
Fire comes down from heaven, consuming the sacrifice, and the glory of the LORD fills the temple. The people worship and give thanks.
Solomon and the people offer abundant sacrifices and celebrate the dedication of the temple and the Feast of Tabernacles for seven days.
God appears to Solomon at night, affirms His acceptance of the temple, and gives conditional promises: if Solomon walks faithfully, God will establish his throne.
God also warns that disobedience will bring destruction, exile, and dishonor to the temple, making it a byword among the nations.
Solomon completes construction projects, fortifies cities, and builds storage and military outposts throughout the kingdom.
Non-Israelite populations are conscripted as laborers, while Israelites serve in leadership and military roles.
Solomon moves Pharaoh’s daughter from the city of David to a separate house, honoring the sanctity of the temple area.
Solomon continues regular sacrifices and assigns the priests and Levites according to the order established by David.
Solomon ensures that all temple work is finished and resumes maritime trade with Hiram, bringing in gold from Ophir.
The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon, tests his wisdom with hard questions, and marvels at his riches and governance. She praises God and gives him extravagant gifts.
The chronicler describes Solomon’s extraordinary wealth, trade network, lavish throne, and golden items surpassing all other kings in wisdom and prosperity.
Solomon’s reign is recorded in the books of Nathan, Ahijah, and Iddo. He dies after 40 years, and his son Rehoboam succeeds him.
Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be crowned king. The people request lighter burdens than Solomon imposed.
Rehoboam consults elders and young advisors. He rejects the elders’ counsel and follows the younger men’s advice to increase the burden.
When Rehoboam speaks harshly to the people, they rebel, fulfilling God’s word spoken through Ahijah the prophet.
Israel’s ten tribes reject the house of David and make Jeroboam their king. Only Judah remains loyal to Rehoboam.
Rehoboam prepares for war to reclaim Israel but stops after God, through Shemaiah, tells him not to fight his brothers.
He fortifies cities in Judah and Benjamin, strengthening defenses with weapons and supplies.
Levites and faithful Israelites from the north migrate to Judah, strengthening Rehoboam's reign for three years.
Rehoboam marries multiple wives and has many children. He wisely distributes his sons throughout Judah’s fortified cities.
After Rehoboam becomes strong, he and Israel abandon God. Egypt invades under Shishak, but after they humble themselves, God allows them to become vassals instead of destroying them.
Shishak takes temple treasures. Rehoboam makes bronze shields to replace the stolen gold ones. Judah is spared because they humbled themselves.
Rehoboam reigns 17 years, doing evil because he did not set his heart to seek God. He dies and is succeeded by Abijah.
Abijah reigns in Judah and prepares for war against Jeroboam’s massive army with fewer troops.
Abijah addresses Israel, appealing to God’s covenant with David and condemning Jeroboam’s idolatry.
God gives Judah victory despite being ambushed. Jeroboam is weakened; Abijah grows stronger and reigns three years.
Asa succeeds Abijah and leads Judah into religious reform, removing idols and building fortified cities during a time of peace.
When an Ethiopian army attacks, Asa relies on the LORD. Judah wins decisively and gathers great spoils.
Azariah the prophet urges Asa to stay faithful. He warns of past periods of turmoil when Israel abandoned God.
Asa courageously removes idols and repairs the altar. All Judah and many from Israel unite in a renewed covenant with God, and He gives them peace.
Asa removes his grandmother from power due to her idolatry. He dedicates temple treasures, and the land has peace for many years.

Baasha king of Israel builds Ramah to block Judah, so Asa bribes Ben-Hadad of Aram to break his treaty with Israel. Ben-Hadad attacks northern cities, and Baasha retreats. Asa fortifies Geba and Mizpah with Ramah's materials.
Hanani the seer rebukes Asa for relying on Aram instead of the LORD. He reminds Asa of past victories through faith. Asa becomes angry, imprisons Hanani, and oppresses some of the people.
Asa develops a severe foot disease but does not seek the LORD, only physicians. He dies after 41 years of reign and is buried with great honor in Jerusalem.

Jehoshaphat becomes king of Judah and strengthens himself against Israel. He places troops in fortified cities and receives tribute from Judah. He walks in the ways of David and seeks the LORD, removing high places and Asherah poles from Judah.
In the third year of his reign, Jehoshaphat sends officials, Levites, and priests throughout Judah to teach the people from the Book of the Law of the LORD.
Fear of the LORD falls on surrounding kingdoms, so they do not war against Judah. The Philistines and Arabs bring tribute and flocks to Jehoshaphat.
Jehoshaphat grows increasingly powerful, building fortresses and store cities in Judah. He has a well-organized and mighty army led by capable commanders from Judah and Benjamin.
Jehoshaphat allies himself with Ahab through marriage and agrees to join him in battle against Ramoth-gilead.
Jehoshaphat requests a word from the LORD. Ahab’s prophets predict success, but Jehoshaphat insists on hearing from Micaiah, a true prophet.
Micaiah prophesies disaster, revealing a vision of lying spirits sent to deceive Ahab. Ahab imprisons him.
In battle, Ahab disguises himself but is fatally struck by an arrow, fulfilling Micaiah's prophecy.
Jehoshaphat returns safely and is rebuked by Jehu the seer for helping the wicked, though commended for setting his heart to seek God.
Jehoshaphat appoints judges in Judah’s cities and exhorts them to judge faithfully, fearing the LORD. He also assigns Levites and priests in Jerusalem for legal matters.
Moab, Ammon, and others come against Judah. Jehoshaphat seeks the LORD in prayer and proclaims a fast; the people gather and cry out together.
The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jahaziel, who assures Judah that the battle belongs to God. The people worship in response.
As Judah praises God, the enemies turn on each other and are destroyed. Judah gathers great spoil, and peace follows.
Jehoshaphat reigns righteously but allies with Ahaziah of Israel in shipbuilding, which the LORD opposes; the ships are wrecked.
Jehoshaphat dies. His son Jehoram becomes king and kills all his brothers. He walks in the ways of Ahab, and the LORD does not destroy Judah for David’s sake.
Edom and Libnah rebel. Jehoram builds high places and leads Judah into unfaithfulness.
Elijah sends a letter rebuking Jehoram. The LORD strikes him with a fatal illness. He dies in disgrace, and his son Ahaziah succeeds him.
Ahaziah reigns one year and follows Ahab’s wicked ways. He visits Joram in Jezreel and is killed by Jehu. His relatives are also killed.
Athaliah seizes power and kills the royal family, but Joash is hidden in the temple for six years by Jehoshabeath.
In the seventh year, Jehoiada the priest organizes a coup. Joash is crowned king, and the covenant is renewed.
Athaliah cries treason but is captured and executed outside the temple.
Jehoiada reestablishes proper worship, destroys Baal’s temple, and brings peace to Jerusalem.
Joash reigns well under Jehoiada and restores the temple. Offerings fund the repairs, and the work is completed faithfully.
After Jehoiada's death, Joash turns to idolatry and kills Jehoiada’s son Zechariah for rebuking him.
Aram invades and wounds Joash. His own servants assassinate him for his betrayal, and Amaziah becomes king.
Amaziah reigns and initially follows the LORD. He defeats Edom but brings back their gods.
A prophet rebukes Amaziah for idolatry; Amaziah resists correction.
Amaziah challenges Jehoash of Israel and is defeated. Jerusalem’s wall is broken down, and temple treasures are taken.
Amaziah lives 15 more years but is assassinated in Lachish. Uzziah his son becomes king.
Uzziah becomes king at age 16 and reigns 52 years. He prospers as long as he seeks God, builds up the army, and develops infrastructure.
Pride leads Uzziah to unlawfully offer incense. God strikes him with leprosy, and he lives in isolation while his son Jotham governs.
Jotham rules justly, strengthens Judah, and defeats the Ammonites, receiving tribute. He grows powerful because he walks uprightly before the LORD.
Ahaz becomes king and leads Judah into deep idolatry. Israel and Aram defeat Judah, and many are taken captive, but a prophet ensures their release.
Ahaz turns to Assyria for help rather than God. He shuts the temple, makes altars in every corner of Jerusalem, and increases unfaithfulness. He dies and is not buried with the kings.
Hezekiah begins to reign and immediately works to purify the temple, calling the Levites to consecrate themselves and the sanctuary.
The Levites cleanse the temple and restore all sacred articles defiled by Ahaz.
Hezekiah leads offerings and worship, reinstating musical service. The assembly bows in reverence.
The people bring abundant offerings, and worship is restored quickly, bringing great joy.
Hezekiah invites all Israel and Judah to celebrate the Passover. Some mock, but many respond and come to Jerusalem.
The feast is observed with great unity, even extending seven more days. God hears Hezekiah’s prayer and heals the people.
The celebration continues with joy and music. The priests bless the people, and their voice reaches heaven.
After the Passover, all Israel goes out to destroy idols, altars, and high places throughout Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. They return to their cities afterward.

Hezekiah organizes the priests and Levites into divisions for temple service. He commands the people to provide portions for them, and they respond generously with tithes and offerings, which pile up in abundance.
Hezekiah orders storerooms to be prepared in the temple. Offerings are stored and distributed faithfully by appointed Levites to priests and their families, according to genealogical records.
Hezekiah does what is good, right, and faithful before the LORD. In all his work for the temple and obedience to God's law, he seeks God wholeheartedly and prospers.
Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah. Hezekiah strengthens Jerusalem’s defenses and encourages the people to trust in the LORD, who is greater than the Assyrian army.
Sennacherib’s officials mock God and try to demoralize the people of Jerusalem, comparing the LORD to powerless gods of other nations.
Hezekiah and Isaiah pray, and the LORD sends an angel who destroys the Assyrian army. Sennacherib returns home in shame and is killed by his sons. Judah gains honor among the nations.
Hezekiah becomes mortally ill but prays and is healed. However, he becomes proud, and God’s wrath looms. Hezekiah humbles himself, and the judgment is delayed.
Hezekiah prospers greatly, building treasuries and water systems. But he fails to respond appropriately to envoys from Babylon. He dies and is honored in burial; Manasseh succeeds him.
Manasseh reigns 55 years and does great evil rebuilding pagan altars, practicing sorcery, and even placing idols in the temple. He leads Judah into worse sin than the nations God had destroyed.

God sends warnings, but Manasseh ignores them. He is captured by the Assyrians and taken to Babylon. In distress, he humbles himself and prays. God restores him to Jerusalem, and he acknowledges the LORD.

After returning, Manasseh fortifies Jerusalem and removes foreign gods and idols. He restores the altar of the LORD and commands Judah to worship God, though the people still sacrifice at high places.
Manasseh’s prayer and repentance are recorded. He dies and is buried in his palace. His son Amon becomes king.
Amon reigns two years and does evil like his father’s earlier ways. He does not humble himself and is assassinated by his servants. The people kill the conspirators and make Josiah king.
Josiah becomes king at age 8 and seeks the LORD in his youth. He purges Judah and Israel of idols, altars, and pagan worship sites.
In his 18th year, Josiah begins temple repairs. The workers are faithful, and the funds are used properly.
Hilkiah the priest finds the Book of the Law. When Josiah hears it read, he tears his clothes in grief, realizing Judah’s guilt.
Josiah sends messengers to the prophetess Huldah. She confirms judgment is coming but says Josiah will be spared because of his humility.
Josiah gathers the people, reads the Law, and renews the covenant. He removes all detestable things and leads Judah to serve the LORD.

Josiah celebrates the Passover with unmatched devotion. Priests and Levites are organized, and thousands of offerings are made. The feast is observed according to the Law, and no Passover like it had been kept since Samuel’s time.
Josiah goes to battle against Pharaoh Neco despite warnings. He is wounded at Megiddo and dies in Jerusalem.
Jeremiah laments Josiah’s death. His deeds are recorded, and he is remembered for his faithfulness.
Jehoahaz becomes king but is deposed by Pharaoh Neco after three months. Neco installs Eliakim (renamed Jehoiakim) as king.
Jehoiakim reigns 11 years and does evil. Nebuchadnezzar takes him to Babylon and installs Jehoiachin, who reigns three months before being exiled. Nebuchadnezzar appoints Zedekiah as king.
Zedekiah rebels against Babylon and does evil. The people mock God’s messengers until there is no remedy. God’s wrath rises.
Babylon invades, destroys Jerusalem and the temple, and exiles the people. The land enjoys its sabbath rest for 70 years, fulfilling prophecy.
Cyrus of Persia issues a decree allowing the Jews to return and rebuild the temple, fulfilling Jeremiah’s prophecy and ending the exile with hope.

In fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy, the LORD moves King Cyrus of Persia to issue a decree allowing the Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. Cyrus encourages the people to contribute silver, gold, goods, and livestock for the work.

The heads of Judah and Benjamin, along with priests and Levites, prepare to return. Neighbors support them with donations. Cyrus returns the temple articles taken by Nebuchadnezzar, totaling 5,400 items, and gives them to Sheshbazzar, the appointed leader.

A detailed list of the exiles who return from Babylon, organized by family and region. The list includes priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and descendants of Solomon's servants. Some cannot prove their ancestry, including certain priests who are excluded from service.
The total number of exiles is 42,360, not including servants and singers. They bring offerings for the temple and settle in their towns.
In the seventh month, the people gather in Jerusalem. Jeshua and Zerubbabel rebuild the altar and resume regular burnt offerings in accordance with the Law of Moses, despite surrounding fear.

They fund materials and labor for temple construction. When the temple foundation is laid, priests and Levites lead a celebration. Many rejoice, but older priests who remembered the former temple weep aloud.
Enemies of Judah offer to help build but are rejected. They then work to discourage and frighten the people, hindering construction throughout Cyrus’s reign.
Accusations are sent to Persian kings, warning that rebuilding Jerusalem threatens imperial control. Under Artaxerxes, the opposition succeeds in halting construction until the reign of Darius.
Prophets Haggai and Zechariah encourage rebuilding. Zerubbabel and Jeshua resume work on the temple with prophetic support.
Tattenai, the Persian governor, questions their authority and sends a letter to King Darius requesting confirmation of their right to rebuild.
King Darius orders a search of the archives and finds Cyrus’s original decree authorizing the rebuilding of the temple and the return of its articles.

Darius commands Tattenai and others not to interfere with the work. He orders full support for the temple’s construction and worship, including funding and supplies, and issues a curse on anyone who alters the decree.
Tattenai and his associates obey Darius’s decree. The temple is completed and dedicated with joy. Priests and Levites are appointed according to the Law of Moses.
The returned exiles celebrate the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread with purity and joy, thanking God for turning the king’s heart to support them.
Ezra, a skilled scribe and descendant of Aaron, comes to Jerusalem during Artaxerxes’s reign. He is devoted to studying, practicing, and teaching the Law of the LORD.

Artaxerxes issues a decree granting Ezra authority to lead a group of Israelites to Jerusalem, manage temple affairs, and appoint judges. The decree includes financial support and exemption from taxes for temple workers.
Ezra praises God for the king’s favor and gathers courage to lead the return, assembling leaders from Israel.
A list is given of the family heads and numbers of men returning with Ezra from Babylon.
Ezra gathers the group at the Ahava Canal and realizes no Levites are present. He sends for Levites and temple servants, who respond willingly.
Ezra proclaims a fast to seek God’s protection for the journey, choosing not to request military escort out of faith in God’s care.
Ezra entrusts the temple offerings to twelve priests, charging them to guard the silver, gold, and sacred vessels until they reach Jerusalem.
God protects the group on their journey. Upon arrival, the offerings are weighed and presented at the temple. The king’s orders are delivered to the regional governors.
Leaders report that Israelites, including priests and Levites, have intermarried with surrounding pagan nations, compromising their holiness.
Ezra is devastated by the news. He tears his garments, pulls out hair, and sits appalled. Others who fear God gather around him.
Ezra prays a heartfelt confession, acknowledging the people’s guilt and God’s mercy. He expresses shame and fear over their repeated unfaithfulness.
While Ezra prays and weeps, a large crowd gathers. Shecaniah proposes a covenant to separate from foreign wives and children, and urges Ezra to lead the reform.
Ezra makes the leaders swear to the covenant. A proclamation is issued requiring all returned exiles to gather in Jerusalem or face excommunication and property loss.
The people assemble in Jerusalem, trembling from guilt and rain. Ezra confronts them, and they agree to investigate and resolve the issue case by case.
A committee examines the cases over three months. The chapter ends with a list of men who had married foreign women and pledged to send them away.
Nehemiah receives a report from Hanani about the dire state of Jerusalem’s walls and the affliction of the returned exiles.
The report emphasizes the broken walls and burned gates, symbolizing vulnerability and disgrace.
Nehemiah mourns, fasts, and prays, confessing the sins of Israel and his father's house.
He recalls God’s covenant with Moses and pleads for mercy and success before the king.
Nehemiah appears sad before King Artaxerxes and explains his grief over Jerusalem.
He requests permission to rebuild the city and is granted leave and a timeframe.
Nehemiah secures letters for safe passage and timber, and arrives in Jerusalem with an escort.
Sanballat and Tobiah are displeased by Nehemiah’s arrival to seek the welfare of the Jews.
Nehemiah surveys the walls at night without informing the officials, assessing the damage firsthand.
He rallies the leaders and people to rebuild, sharing how God’s hand and the king’s favor are with him.
Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem mock the effort, but Nehemiah declares God’s support and their exclusion.
Priests and nobles begin rebuilding the Sheep Gate and adjacent sections, though some nobles refuse to help.
Various families and individuals repair gates and walls, including the Old Gate and the Broad Wall.
The work continues around the Valley Gate, Dung Gate, and Fountain Gate, with detailed assignments by family and region.
Repairs near the Horse Gate and East Gate are completed, with goldsmiths and merchants contributing.
Sanballat mocks the Jews’ rebuilding efforts, and Tobiah ridicules the wall’s strength, saying even a fox could break it down.
Nehemiah prays for justice against their enemies and continues the work; the people build the wall to half its height with unified determination.
As opposition intensifies from surrounding nations, Nehemiah stations guards and the people pray and remain vigilant.
Discouragement spreads among the workers due to rubble and threats; Jews living nearby report enemy plots to attack.
Nehemiah arms the people and encourages them to remember the Lord and defend their families and homes.
Half the men work while the other half guard; builders carry weapons, and Nehemiah ensures everyone is prepared for battle.
Nehemiah organizes a trumpet warning system and keeps his men close; none remove their clothes except for washing, staying ready at all times.
A great outcry arises as poorer Jews complain of debt, famine, and being forced to mortgage land and sell children into servitude.
Nehemiah is angered by the injustice and rebukes the nobles and officials for charging interest; he demands they restore lands and forgive debts.
The leaders agree to Nehemiah’s demands and take an oath; Nehemiah shakes out his garment as a symbolic warning against breaking the promise.
Nehemiah describes his own example of leadership refusing the governor’s allowance, working on the wall, and feeding many at his own expense.
Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem invite Nehemiah to meet in Ono, intending harm; he refuses four times, citing the importance of his work.
A fifth message accuses Nehemiah of plotting rebellion and wanting to be king; the letter is open to spread fear.
Nehemiah denies the accusations and prays for strength, recognizing the enemy’s intent to weaken the people.
A false prophet, Shemaiah, urges Nehemiah to hide in the temple; Nehemiah discerns the trap and refuses to sin by fleeing.
He prays against the conspirators, including the prophetess Noadiah and others who tried to intimidate him.
The wall is completed in 52 days; surrounding nations are disheartened, recognizing God’s hand in the work.
Despite the success, Tobiah maintains influence through family ties and correspondence with nobles, continuing to undermine Nehemiah.
Nehemiah appoints gatekeepers, singers, and Levites to oversee Jerusalem. He instructs that the gates remain closed until the sun is hot and assigns guards from among the inhabitants.
Though the city is large, few people live in it. Nehemiah is moved by God to register the genealogies of the returned exiles.
A detailed list is given of the families and individuals who returned from exile under Zerubbabel, including the number of people in each group.
The list continues with priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants, each group named and numbered.
Some individuals could not prove their lineage, including certain priests who were excluded from priestly duties until a priest could consult the Urim and Thummim.
The total number of the congregation is given, along with their servants and animals.
Leaders and families contribute generously to the temple treasury for its restoration.
The people settle in their towns, and by the seventh month, the Israelites are back in their cities.
All the people gather at the Water Gate and ask Ezra to read the Book of the Law. He reads from morning until midday to attentive listeners.
Ezra stands on a wooden platform with leaders beside him. He blesses the Lord, and the people respond with lifted hands and bowed heads.
Levites help the people understand the Law by reading and explaining it clearly.
The people weep upon hearing the Law, but Nehemiah, Ezra, and the Levites encourage them to rejoice, for the joy of the Lord is their strength.
On the second day, leaders study the Law and discover the command to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.
The people gather branches and build booths, reviving a practice not observed since Joshua’s time. The feast is celebrated with great joy, and Ezra reads the Law daily.
On the 24th day, the people fast, wear sackcloth, and separate from foreigners. They confess their sins and read from the Law for a quarter of the day, then worship.
Levites stand and lead the people in praise, calling them to bless the Lord forever.
The prayer recounts God’s greatness in creation, His covenant with Abraham, deliverance from Egypt, and provision in the wilderness.
Despite Israel’s rebellion, God remains merciful, giving them laws, sustenance, and victory in the Promised Land.
The cycle of disobedience, oppression, and deliverance is acknowledged. God’s patience and compassion are emphasized.
The prayer appeals to God’s mercy, recognizing the current servitude under foreign kings due to past unfaithfulness.
In response, the people make a firm covenant, putting it in writing and sealing it with their leaders’ names.
A list of leaders, priests, Levites, and officials who seal the covenant, including Nehemiah and other prominent figures.
The rest of the people priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and all who separated themselves from foreign influence join in the oath to follow God's Law.
They vow not to intermarry with foreign peoples and to observe the Sabbath, including refraining from trade on holy days.
They commit to an annual temple tax and to supporting the daily offerings, feasts, and other temple needs.
The people pledge to bring firstfruits, tithes, and offerings to the temple, ensuring the Levites and priests are supported and the house of God is not neglected.
Lots are cast to bring one-tenth of the people to live in Jerusalem, while others bless those who willingly offer to dwell there.
A list of the leaders and families from Judah and Benjamin who settle in Jerusalem.
Priests who serve in the temple are listed, including those responsible for sacrifices and temple oversight.
Levites, gatekeepers, and singers are named, along with their duties and royal appointments.
The chapter concludes with a list of towns and villages where the rest of the Israelites, priests, and Levites live throughout Judah and Benjamin.
A list of priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel, including heads of priestly families.
The genealogy of Levites and priests is continued, including those who served during the time of Joiakim, Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua.
The Levites and priests purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall in preparation for the dedication ceremony.
Two great choirs are appointed to give thanks, marching in opposite directions along the top of the wall.
The choirs meet at the temple, and the dedication concludes with great sacrifices and rejoicing, with the sound of celebration heard far away.
Men are appointed to oversee temple storerooms and offerings. The people give their portions faithfully, and temple service is restored as in David’s time.
Upon reading the Law, the people separate themselves from foreigners, recalling the exclusion of Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly.
Nehemiah discovers that Eliashib the priest gave Tobiah a room in the temple. Nehemiah throws out Tobiah’s belongings and restores the room for sacred use.
Nehemiah finds that Levites were not receiving their portions and had returned to their fields. He rebukes the officials and restores proper support for temple workers.
He observes Sabbath violations people working and merchants selling goods. Nehemiah rebukes the nobles, closes the gates on the Sabbath, and stations guards to enforce observance.
Nehemiah confronts intermarriage with foreign women, rebukes the offenders, and reminds them of Solomon’s downfall due to such alliances.
He drives out a priest who had married Sanballat’s daughter and prays for God to remember those who defiled the priesthood.
Nehemiah purifies the people, appoints duties for priests and Levites, and concludes with a prayer for God to remember him for good.
King Ahasuerus reigns over 127 provinces and hosts a lavish 180-day feast to display his wealth and glory.
A seven-day banquet follows for all in Susa, with royal decor and abundant wine served without compulsion.
Queen Vashti holds a separate feast for the women in the royal palace.
On the seventh day, the king commands Vashti to appear before the guests, but she refuses, angering him.
Advisors suggest Vashti’s disobedience could inspire rebellion; they recommend her removal and a royal decree.
The king agrees and sends letters to all provinces affirming male authority in every household.
After his anger subsides, the king seeks a new queen; young virgins are gathered and prepared for selection.
Mordecai, a Jew in Susa, raises his cousin Esther, a beautiful orphan.
Esther is taken to the palace and gains favor with Hegai, the keeper of women; Mordecai checks on her daily.
Each woman undergoes a year of beauty treatments before meeting the king; they return to a different harem afterward.
Esther pleases the king and is crowned queen; a great feast is held in her honor.
Esther keeps her Jewish identity secret as Mordecai advised; he continues to sit at the king’s gate.
Mordecai uncovers a plot to assassinate the king; Esther reports it in his name, and the conspirators are executed.
King Ahasuerus promotes Haman above all officials; all bow to him except Mordecai.
The king’s servants question Mordecai’s defiance; he explains it is due to his Jewish identity.
Haman, enraged, plots not only to punish Mordecai but to destroy all Jews in the empire.
In the first month, Haman casts lots (Pur) to determine the day for the Jews’ destruction.
Haman persuades the king to issue a decree against the Jews, offering silver for the royal treasury; the king agrees.
Decrees are sent throughout the empire, setting the 13th day of the 12th month for annihilation; the city of Susa is bewildered.
Mordecai learns of the decree and mourns publicly in sackcloth and ashes; Jews throughout the provinces fast and lament.
Esther is distressed by Mordecai’s appearance and sends clothes, which he refuses. She sends Hathach to learn what’s wrong.
Mordecai explains Haman’s plot and urges Esther to plead with the king, giving her a copy of the decree.
Esther replies that approaching the king uninvited is punishable by death unless he extends the golden scepter.
Mordecai warns that silence won’t save her and suggests she may have come to the kingdom for such a time as this.
Esther agrees to approach the king, asking Mordecai to gather the Jews to fast for three days. She resolves, 'If I perish, I perish.'
On the third day, Esther dresses in royal robes and approaches the king, who welcomes her by extending the golden scepter.
The king offers to grant her request; she invites him and Haman to a banquet that day.
At the banquet, the king again asks her request. Esther invites them to a second banquet the next day, where she will reveal it.
Haman leaves joyful but becomes enraged when Mordecai doesn’t bow. He vents to his wife and friends about his frustration.
Zeresh and Haman’s friends suggest building a gallows 50 cubits high to hang Mordecai. Haman is pleased and proceeds with the plan.
That night, the king cannot sleep and has the royal chronicles read. He discovers Mordecai was never rewarded for saving his life.
Haman enters to request Mordecai’s execution, but before he can speak, the king asks how to honor someone deserving.
Thinking the honor is for himself, Haman suggests a royal robe, horse, and public parade led by a noble.
The king commands Haman to do exactly that for Mordecai. Haman obeys, humiliated, and leads the procession.
Mordecai returns to the gate; Haman rushes home in grief. His wife and advisors ominously predict his downfall.
While they speak, the king’s eunuchs arrive to escort Haman to Esther’s second banquet.
At the second banquet, the king again asks Esther for her petition, offering up to half the kingdom.
Esther pleads for her life and her people, revealing that they have been sold to be destroyed, slain, and perished.
The king demands to know who is responsible. Esther identifies Haman as the adversary and enemy.
The king rises in wrath and walks into the palace garden; Haman stays to beg Esther for his life.
Returning, the king sees Haman fallen on Esther’s couch and accuses him of assaulting the queen.
Harbonah suggests hanging Haman on the gallows he built for Mordecai. The king agrees, and Haman is executed.
The king gives Haman’s estate to Esther. Mordecai is promoted and receives the king’s signet ring.
Esther pleads again with the king to revoke Haman’s decree against the Jews, weeping before him.
The king allows Esther and Mordecai to write a new decree in his name, since the original cannot be revoked.
On the 23rd day of the third month, scribes write a new decree allowing Jews to defend themselves.
The decree permits Jews to gather, protect themselves, and destroy any who attack them. Couriers deliver it swiftly.
Mordecai leaves the palace in royal robes. The Jews rejoice, and many people convert out of fear.
On the 13th day of the 12th month, the Jews defend themselves and gain the upper hand over their enemies.
They strike down their foes, including Haman’s ten sons, but take no plunder.
The king informs Esther of the outcome. She requests a second day of defense in Susa and the public hanging of Haman’s sons.
The Jews in Susa kill 300 more on the second day. Throughout the provinces, 75,000 enemies are slain.
The Jews rest and celebrate with feasting and gladness, establishing the 14th and 15th days of Adar as days of joy.
Mordecai writes to all Jews to institute the annual feast of Purim to commemorate their deliverance.
The Jews agree to observe Purim each year, remembering how sorrow was turned to joy.
Esther confirms the decree of Purim in writing, and it is recorded in official records.
King Ahasuerus imposes tribute across the empire. The acts of his power and Mordecai’s greatness are recorded in the chronicles.
Mordecai, second only to the king, is honored among the Jews and seeks the welfare of his people and peace for all.
Job is introduced as a blameless and upright man in Uz, blessed with wealth and a large family. He regularly offers sacrifices on behalf of his children, fearing they may have sinned.
A heavenly scene unfolds where Satan appears before God. God praises Job’s righteousness.
Satan challenges Job’s integrity, claiming he is faithful only because of his blessings. God permits Satan to test Job by taking his possessions, but not harming him physically.
In rapid succession, Job receives news that his oxen, donkeys, sheep, camels, servants, and all ten children have been destroyed by raiders and natural disasters.
Job mourns deeply but worships God, declaring, 'The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord.' He does not sin or charge God foolishly.
Another heavenly council convenes. Satan argues that Job’s faith will fail if his health is attacked. God allows Satan to afflict Job physically but forbids taking his life.
Satan strikes Job with painful boils from head to toe. Job sits among ashes, scraping himself with a potsherd.
Job’s wife urges him to curse God and die. Job rebukes her, accepting both good and evil from God without sinning.
Job’s three friends Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar arrive to comfort him. They are shocked by his appearance and sit with him in silence for seven days.
Job breaks his silence and curses the day of his birth, wishing it had never existed.
He laments not dying at birth, imagining death as a place of rest for kings, prisoners, and the weary.
Job questions why life is given to those in misery, who long for death but cannot find it.
He confesses his deep anguish, saying his worst fears have come true and he has no peace or rest.
Eliphaz the Temanite begins his speech, gently rebuking Job. He reminds Job that he has encouraged others in the past, and now that he suffers, he seems dismayed.
Eliphaz argues that the innocent do not perish and that suffering is the result of wrongdoing. He uses imagery of lions to describe the fate of the wicked.
He recounts a mysterious vision in the night that questioned whether a mortal can be more just or pure than God.
Eliphaz concludes that humans are fragile and perishable, likening them to dwellings of clay easily crushed without wisdom.
Eliphaz challenges Job to call on anyone who can help. He asserts that trouble does not come from nowhere   man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward.
He urges Job to seek God, who does great and unsearchable things, lifts the lowly, and frustrates the plans of the crafty.
Eliphaz declares that God disciplines those He loves. He promises restoration, protection, and peace if Job accepts God's correction.
Job responds, lamenting that his grief is heavier than the sand of the sea. He feels his friends’ words are tasteless and unhelpful.
He wishes God would crush him and end his life, seeing it as a relief. He feels he has no strength or help within himself.
Job criticizes his friends for being unreliable, like a dried-up brook. He accuses them of failing to show kindness in his time of need.
He insists he never asked for their help or bribes. He challenges them to show him his error, asserting his words are not false.
Job compares life to hard labor, filled with weariness and sleepless nights. His flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust, and his skin breaks out afresh.
He laments the swiftness of life and the finality of death, saying that once a person dies, they do not return to their house.
Job refuses to restrain his complaint. He questions why God targets him and expresses a desire to be left alone, even asking God to let him die.
He wonders why God pays such close attention to man, visiting him every morning. Job pleads for pardon before he dies and is no more.
Bildad the Shuhite responds, defending God’s justice. He suggests Job’s children died because of their sin and urges Job to seek God for restoration.
He appeals to the wisdom of the ancients, warning that those who forget God are like reeds without water destined to wither.
Bildad describes the fate of the godless: their confidence is fragile, their homes unstable, and they are uprooted from the earth.
He concludes that God will not cast away the blameless and will fill the righteous with laughter, while the wicked will be clothed with shame.
Job agrees that no one can be righteous before God. He describes God’s power over creation and His ability to act without being questioned.
Job feels powerless and unjustly afflicted. Even if he were innocent, he says he could not answer God or believe he would be heard.
He asserts that God destroys both the blameless and the wicked, and that the earth is given into the hand of the wicked.
Job laments the fleeting nature of life and the futility of trying to cleanse himself, as God would still plunge him into the ditch.
He longs for a mediator between himself and God someone to remove God’s rod and allow him to speak without fear.
Job pleads with God, asking why He contends with him and questions whether it pleases God to oppress the work of His hands.
He asks if God sees as man sees and insists that God knows he is not guilty, even if no one can deliver him from God's hand.
Job reflects on how God formed him with care, granting him life and favor, and preserving his spirit.
He accuses God of hiding intentions and watching for faults, punishing him regardless of innocence or guilt.
Job laments being born, wishing God would let him alone before he descends into the land of darkness and shadow of death.
Zophar the Naamathite rebukes Job for his bold words, claiming Job deserves even worse and that God’s wisdom is deeper than Job can grasp.
He challenges Job’s understanding of God’s mysteries, asserting that man is born foolish and cannot comprehend divine perfection.
Zophar urges Job to repent and stretch out his hands to God, promising restoration, security, and brightness if he puts away iniquity.
Job sarcastically responds, claiming his friends think they alone have wisdom, though he is not inferior to them.
He laments that the righteous are mocked while the wicked live in ease, seemingly secure in their defiance of God.
Job points to nature beasts, birds, earth, and sea as witnesses that all life is in God’s hand.
He affirms that wisdom is found with the aged, and understanding comes with long life.
Job extols God’s unmatched power and wisdom, describing how He overthrows counselors, judges, kings, and nations, bringing darkness and confusion upon them.
Job asserts that he has understanding equal to his friends and criticizes them as forgers of lies and worthless physicians.
He urges them to be silent and listen as he prepares to argue his case before God, warning them not to speak wickedly on God's behalf.
Job declares his willingness to take his life in his hands, saying, 'Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.' He is confident in his integrity and readiness to defend himself.
He pleads with God to remove His hand of terror and allow him to speak freely, asking to know his sins and transgressions.
Job laments God's harsh treatment, feeling like a decaying thing pursued and punished, even for the sins of his youth.
Job reflects on the frailty of human life, comparing it to a flower that withers and a shadow that does not endure. He pleads with God to look away and let man rest.
He contrasts human mortality with a tree that may sprout again. Once a man dies, he does not rise until the heavens are no more.
Job wishes God would hide him in the grave until His wrath passes, then remember him. He imagines a time when God would long for the work of His hands and forgive his sins.
He returns to despair, noting that mountains erode and hope is destroyed. Man dies, and his body decays while his soul mourns in silence.
Eliphaz rebukes Job for his bold speech, accusing him of undermining piety and condemning himself with his own words.
He sarcastically asks if Job was the first man born or privy to God's counsel, accusing him of turning his spirit against God.
Eliphaz emphasizes human impurity, stating that even angels are not pure before God. He appeals to ancient wisdom passed down by the fathers.
He describes the torment of the wicked: constant fear, distress, and eventual ruin, even if they seem powerful for a time.
Eliphaz warns that trusting in vanity leads to deception and destruction. The wicked conceive mischief and bring forth iniquity.
Job calls his friends 'miserable comforters' and says he could speak as they do if their roles were reversed, but he would strengthen and comfort them instead.
He laments that speaking brings no relief. He describes how God has worn him out, shriveled him, and delivered him to mockers.
Job feels God has handed him over to the wicked, shattered him, and broken him with blow after blow like a warrior.
He has mourned in sackcloth and wept without violence or deceit, yet his face is red with weeping and his eyelids dark.
Job calls on the earth not to cover his blood and declares that his witness is in heaven. He pleads for God to mediate for him before death comes.
Job says his spirit is broken and his days are extinguished. He accuses his friends of mockery and betrayal.
He feels like a byword among people, spit upon and scorned. Yet the righteous will hold to their way and grow stronger.
Job sees no wise man among them. He despairs of hope and sees only the grave as his house, with corruption as his father and worms as his family.
Bildad rebukes Job for his words, accusing him of tearing himself in anger and demanding that Job listen before speaking.
He describes the fate of the wicked: their light is extinguished, their steps are trapped, and snares lie in their path.
Terrors surround the wicked, disease consumes their strength, and they are driven from their homes to dwell with destruction.
Their memory perishes, they are forgotten, and horror seizes those who hear of their fate. Such is the destiny of those who know not God.
Job rebukes his friends for tormenting him with words and insists that God has wronged him and surrounded him with His net.
He cries out for justice but receives no answer. He describes how God has stripped him of honor and treated him as an enemy.
Job laments his isolation family, friends, and servants have all turned away. He is physically wasted and barely recognizable.
He pleads with his friends for pity, asking why they persecute him as God does.
Job longs for his words to be recorded forever. He declares, 'I know that my redeemer liveth,' and expresses hope in seeing God after death.
He warns his friends against continuing to judge him, for judgment belongs to God and wrath may come upon them.
Zophar responds, provoked by Job’s words. He insists that the triumph of the wicked is short and the joy of the godless momentary.
Even if the wicked rise high, they will perish like dung. Their children will seek the poor for favors, and their bones will lie in the dust.
Zophar describes how evil is sweet in the mouth but turns to poison. The wicked swallow riches but vomit them up, and their greed leads to ruin.
He concludes that the wicked will face God's wrath, lose their possessions, and be consumed by fire. This is the portion appointed by God.
Job urges his friends to listen carefully. He is troubled not by their rebukes but by the prosperity of the wicked.
He questions why the wicked live long, grow powerful, and enjoy peace. They reject God, yet their lives seem blessed.
Job challenges the idea that punishment always comes swiftly to the wicked. Often, their children suffer instead, which seems unjust.
He observes that both the prosperous and the afflicted die alike, lying in the dust and consumed by worms.
Job accuses his friends of offering empty comfort. He knows their arguments are false and do not reflect reality.
Eliphaz accuses Job of being unprofitable to God and suggests that Job’s fear of God is insincere. He claims Job’s wickedness is great and his iniquities endless.
He lists alleged sins: withholding pledges, denying water and bread to the weary, oppressing widows and orphans. He says this is why Job is surrounded by darkness and disaster.
Eliphaz reminds Job that God sees all from heaven and that the wicked once prospered but were swept away. He implies Job is following the same path.
He urges Job to return to God, promising restoration, prosperity, and the power to intercede for others if he repents and removes iniquity.
Job longs to find God and present his case. He believes he could reason with God and be acquitted by Him.
He searches in every direction but cannot perceive God. Yet he trusts that God knows his way and that he will come forth as gold. He has kept God’s commandments faithfully.
Job acknowledges God’s unchangeable will and feels overwhelmed by His presence. He is terrified, yet silenced by God’s hidden purposes.
Job questions why God does not set times for judgment. He describes how the wicked oppress the poor, widows, and orphans without consequence.
He details the suffering of the needy wandering for food, lacking shelter, and being wounded by injustice yet God seems to ignore their cries.
He describes those who rebel against the light: murderers, adulterers, and thieves who operate in darkness, avoiding exposure.
Job asserts that the wicked are ultimately cursed and forgotten, though they may seem secure for a time. He challenges anyone to prove him wrong.
Bildad speaks briefly, declaring that dominion and fear belong to God, who makes peace in His high places. He asks who can be justified before such a majestic being.
He emphasizes human impurity, stating that even the moon and stars are not pure in God’s sight how much less man, who is like a worm.
Job sarcastically rebukes Bildad for offering no real help or wisdom, questioning whose spirit inspired his words.
Job describes God’s immense power over creation: the dead tremble beneath the waters, the heavens are stretched out, and the pillars of heaven tremble. These are only the fringes of His ways.
Job maintains his integrity, swearing by God that he will not speak wickedness or deceit. He refuses to admit guilt falsely and holds fast to his righteousness.
He declares that the hope of the hypocrite will perish. Though his friends claim wisdom, Job insists they’ve seen the same things and should know better.
Job outlines the fate of the wicked: their children may suffer, their wealth vanish, and terror overtake them. God will strike them down, and people will clap and hiss at their downfall.
Job describes how humans mine the earth for precious metals and stones, exploring deep and dangerous places to uncover hidden treasures.
He asks where wisdom can be found, declaring it cannot be bought with gold or jewels. Its value surpasses all earthly riches.
Wisdom is hidden from all living things and even from the realm of the dead. No creature knows its path.
Only God understands the way to wisdom. He established it at creation and declared: 'The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding.'
Job nostalgically recalls the days when God watched over him, his children were around him, and his steps were bathed in butter.
He remembers his respected place in society when he sat in the gate, young men withdrew, and elders rose in his presence.
Job recounts his acts of justice and mercy: helping the poor, fathering the fatherless, and breaking the jaws of the wicked.
He once believed he would die in peace, with strength renewed like a tree planted by water.
People listened to his counsel in silence, valued his words like rain, and followed him as a leader and comforter.
Job laments that now he is mocked by younger men, the sons of those he once would not have hired to watch his sheep.
He is the subject of songs and scorn. They spit at him, attack him without restraint, and his dignity is stripped away.
Job describes his physical and emotional torment his bones ache, his skin blackens, and he cries to God without answer, believing death is near.
He questions why his cries for help are ignored, despite his past compassion for others. His harp is turned to mourning, and his joy to weeping.
Job declares he made a covenant with his eyes not to look lustfully at a woman and affirms that God sees all his ways.
He denies walking in falsehood or deceit and calls for punishment if he has turned aside from righteousness.
Job denies adultery, calling it a heinous crime deserving judgment and destruction.
He claims he treated his servants justly, recognizing that all are made by the same Creator.
Job lists acts of compassion: feeding the poor, clothing the naked, and not exploiting the fatherless or widows. He fears God’s judgment if he had failed in these.
He denies trusting in wealth or worshiping the sun or moon, calling such idolatry punishable by judges.
Job says he never rejoiced at an enemy’s downfall, always welcomed strangers, and never hid his sins out of fear of public shame.
He longs for someone to hear his case and sign his defense before God, confident in his integrity.
He concludes by declaring his innocence regarding land and laborers. If he is guilty, let thorns grow instead of wheat. The words of Job are ended.
Job’s three friends stop answering him because he considers himself righteous. Elihu, a younger man, burns with anger at both Job and the friends for their failure to speak rightly.
Elihu explains that though he is young, he must speak because wisdom comes from the breath of the Almighty, not age alone.
He waited patiently for the elders to speak but found no one who refuted Job. He now feels compelled to offer his own perspective.
Elihu insists he will speak without flattery or partiality, for he is full of words and cannot hold back.
Elihu addresses Job directly, asking him to listen. He claims to speak sincerely and without fear, as one formed from clay like Job.
He quotes Job’s claim of innocence and challenges him, asserting that God is greater than man and not accountable to human questioning.
Elihu says God speaks in various ways through dreams or warnings to turn people from pride and preserve them from destruction.
He describes how God uses suffering to humble and redeem a person, sending a mediator to restore them to righteousness and health.
Elihu concludes that God works repeatedly to save souls from the pit. He urges Job to listen, promising to teach him wisdom.
Elihu addresses the wise and accuses Job of claiming innocence while suggesting that righteousness brings no benefit. He criticizes Job’s words as irreverent.
He defends God’s justice, declaring that the Almighty cannot do wickedness. God repays each person according to their deeds and sustains all life.
Elihu asks if one who hates justice can govern. He emphasizes that God shows no partiality and brings down the mighty without inquiry.
God sees all human ways and judges without needing investigation. He strikes down the wicked in public view and prevents the godless from ruling.
Elihu urges Job to repent and learn from affliction rather than complain. He accuses Job of adding rebellion to his sin by multiplying words against God.
Elihu challenges Job’s claim that righteousness is useless. He argues that human actions do not affect God directly sin harms others, and righteousness benefits fellow humans.
He observes that people cry out under oppression but do not seek God their Maker. Because of pride, God does not answer empty cries.
Elihu tells Job that though he waits for judgment, his case is not before God. He accuses Job of speaking without knowledge and multiplying words in vain.
Elihu continues, claiming to speak on God’s behalf with perfect knowledge and upright motives.
He declares that God is mighty and just, exalting the righteous and disciplining the wicked to turn them from evil. If they obey, they prosper; if not, they perish.
The godless harbor anger and die in youth. Elihu warns Job not to be enticed by riches or bribes and not to let wrath lead him astray.
He asks if Job’s wealth or strength can deliver him and reminds him that no one teaches like God, who is supreme in judgment.
Elihu urges Job to magnify God’s works. He describes God’s control over the weather rain, lightning, and thunder as signs of His greatness and care for the earth.
Elihu describes the awe-inspiring voice of God in thunder and lightning, declaring that His works are marvelous and beyond understanding.
He explains how God commands snow, rain, and storms to accomplish His purposes whether for correction, mercy, or blessing.
Elihu challenges Job to consider the wonders of creation: the balance of clouds, the warmth of the south wind, and the brightness of the sky. He asks how Job dares to speak before such majesty.
Though the sun is hidden by clouds, God comes in golden splendor. Elihu concludes that God is great in power and justice, and men should fear Him.
The Lord answers Job out of the whirlwind, challenging him to prepare himself like a man and answer divine questions.
God asks where Job was when He laid the earth’s foundations, set its measurements, and commanded the sea to halt at its boundaries.
He questions Job about the dawn, the depths of the sea, the gates of death, and the breadth of the earth things Job cannot comprehend.
God asks about the storehouses of snow and hail, the paths of lightning, and the origins of ice and frost.
He challenges Job to bind the stars, command the clouds, or send lightning demonstrating Job’s lack of cosmic control.
God asks if Job provides food for lions or ravens, emphasizing His care for even the wildest creatures.
God asks if Job knows the timing of mountain goats giving birth or watches over the calving of deer.
He describes the wild donkey, free from human control, living in the wilderness by its own will.
God asks if the wild ox will serve Job or plow his fields, highlighting its untamable strength.
He speaks of the ostrich, which lacks wisdom yet runs faster than a horse, defying expectations.
God describes the horse’s strength, fearlessness in battle, and eagerness to charge into war.
He ends with the hawk and eagle, who soar by God’s command and dwell in high places, feeding on the slain.
The Lord asks Job if he still contends with the Almighty. Job responds humbly, saying he is unworthy and will speak no more.
God continues from the whirlwind, challenging Job to adorn himself with majesty and judge the proud if he can. If Job can do this, then God will acknowledge his power.
God describes Behemoth, a powerful creature made by Him, emphasizing its strength, fearlessness, and dependence on God for life.
God asks if Job can catch Leviathan with a hook or control it. No one dares to stir it up who then can stand before God?
Leviathan’s limbs, scales, and fierce nature are described in detail. Its heart is hard as stone, and it fears nothing.
It breathes fire, churns the sea, and leaves a shining wake. Nothing on earth is its equal; it is king over all the proud.
Job responds with repentance, acknowledging God’s power and wisdom. He says, 'I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear, but now mine eye seeth thee.'
God rebukes Eliphaz and his friends for not speaking rightly about Him. He instructs them to offer sacrifices, and Job prays for them.
God restores Job’s fortunes, giving him twice as much as before. His family returns, and he lives 140 more years, seeing four generations. Job dies old and full of days.
Blessed is the one who avoids the counsel of the wicked and delights in the law of the Lord, meditating on it day and night.
Such a person is like a tree planted by rivers of water, yielding fruit in season and prospering in all they do.
The wicked are like chaff blown by the wind and will not stand in judgment or among the righteous.
The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish.
Nations and rulers conspire against the Lord and His Anointed, seeking to break free from divine authority.
God laughs at their rebellion and declares that He has set His King on Zion, His holy hill.
The Lord proclaims the decree: 'You are my Son; this day have I begotten thee.' He promises the nations as inheritance.
Kings are warned to serve the Lord with fear and rejoice with trembling. Blessed are all who take refuge in Him.
David laments the multitude of enemies rising against him and their claim that God will not deliver him.
He declares the Lord as his shield and glory, confident that God hears his cry from His holy hill.
David sleeps and wakes in safety, unafraid of thousands set against him.
He calls on the Lord to arise and save, affirming that salvation belongs to the Lord and His blessing is upon His people.
David pleads for God to hear his prayer and show mercy, recalling past deliverance.
He rebukes those who love vanity and assures that the Lord sets apart the godly for Himself.
He urges self-examination, reverence, and trust in the Lord through righteous offerings.
While others seek worldly good, David rejoices in God's presence and sleeps in peace, trusting in divine safety.
David asks the Lord to hear his morning prayer and considers God as his King and God.
He affirms that God does not delight in wickedness and will destroy liars and bloodthirsty men.
David enters God’s house in reverence and asks for guidance in righteousness because of his enemies.
He describes the deceitfulness of the wicked and calls for their downfall.
He blesses those who trust in the Lord, rejoicing in His protection and favor like a shield.
David pleads with the Lord not to rebuke him in anger but to have mercy, for he is weak and troubled in soul.
He appeals to God's steadfast love and asks for deliverance, noting that the dead cannot praise God.
David describes his grief he is weary with groaning, floods his bed with tears, and his eyes are consumed with sorrow.
He declares that the Lord has heard his prayer and that his enemies will be ashamed and turned back in defeat.
David seeks refuge in the Lord, asking for deliverance from those who pursue him like a lion.
He declares his innocence, saying if he has done wrong, let his enemy overtake him.
David calls on God to rise in judgment and vindicate the righteous according to integrity.
He affirms that God is a righteous judge who is angry with the wicked and prepares weapons of judgment.
The wicked fall into their own traps, and David praises the Lord for His righteousness and justice.
David marvels at the majesty of God's name and how He uses the praise of children to silence enemies.
He reflects on the heavens and wonders why God is mindful of humanity.
God has made humans a little lower than angels, crowned them with glory, and given them dominion over creation.
The psalm closes by repeating the praise: 'O Lord our Lord, how excellent is thy name in all the earth!'
David gives thanks with his whole heart, rejoicing in God's marvelous works.
He praises God for judging righteously and rebuking the nations, causing the wicked to perish.
The Lord reigns forever, judging with equity and being a refuge for the oppressed.
David calls others to praise God and asks for mercy so he may declare God's praise in Zion.
The wicked are caught in their own traps; the needy will not be forgotten, and hope will not perish.
David asks God to arise and judge the nations, reminding them they are but men.
David questions why God seems distant while the wicked persecute the poor and boast of their desires.
He describes the arrogance and cruelty of the wicked, who believe God does not see or care.
David calls on God to arise, see the affliction of the helpless, and break the arm of the wicked.
He affirms that the Lord is King forever, hears the desire of the humble, and defends the fatherless and oppressed.
David affirms his trust in the Lord and rejects the advice to flee like a bird. He questions what the righteous can do when foundations are destroyed.
He declares that the Lord is in His holy temple, observing all people and testing both the righteous and the wicked.
God will rain fire and brimstone on the wicked, but the righteous will behold His face, for He loves righteousness.
David laments the disappearance of the faithful and the prevalence of flattering lips and double-hearted speech.
He calls on the Lord to cut off boastful lips and those who claim mastery over their own tongues.
God promises to arise and protect the poor and needy from oppression.
The Lord’s words are pure, like refined silver. Though the wicked prowl, God will preserve the righteous forever.
David cries out, feeling forgotten by God and overwhelmed by sorrow and inner turmoil.
He pleads for God to consider and answer him, lest he sleep the sleep of death and his enemies rejoice.
Despite his anguish, David trusts in God’s mercy, rejoices in salvation, and sings because the Lord has dealt bountifully with him.
The fool says in his heart there is no God. All have turned aside and become corrupt; none do good.
Evildoers devour God’s people and do not call on the Lord. They mock the righteous, but God is their refuge.
David longs for salvation to come from Zion and anticipates joy when the Lord restores His people.
David asks who may dwell in God’s tabernacle and holy hill.
He answers: one who walks uprightly, speaks truth, honors the faithful, keeps oaths, lends without interest, and rejects bribes. Such a person will never be moved.
David seeks refuge in God, declaring that apart from Him, he has no good thing.
He delights in the saints of the land but warns against those who chase after other gods.
The Lord is his portion and cup; his inheritance is secure and pleasant.
David blesses the Lord for counsel and sets the Lord always before him, confident he will not be shaken.
His heart rejoices, and he rests in hope, for God will not abandon him to the grave but will show him the path of life and eternal joy in His presence.
David pleads for God to hear his righteous cause, affirming his integrity and asking for divine examination.
