He calls on God for protection, asking to be kept as the apple of His eye and hidden under His wings.
He describes the wicked as arrogant and violent, seeking to destroy him. He asks God to deliver him from them.
David expresses hope in seeing God’s face in righteousness and being satisfied upon awakening with His likeness.
David declares his love for the Lord, his rock and deliverer, in whom he finds refuge and salvation.
He recalls being overwhelmed by death and calling upon the Lord, who heard his cry.
God responds with a dramatic display of power earthquakes, thunder, and fire to rescue David.
God delivers David because of his righteousness and obedience, rewarding him according to his integrity.
David praises God’s justice and guidance, describing how God equips him with strength and makes his path secure.
He recounts victories over enemies, attributing them to God’s empowerment and deliverance.
David exalts the Lord as the living God who gives triumph and shows steadfast love to His anointed.
The heavens declare God’s glory, and the skies proclaim His handiwork, speaking without words to all the earth.
David extols the perfection of God’s law, which revives the soul, brings wisdom, and is more desirable than gold.
He asks to be cleansed from hidden faults and kept from willful sins, so they do not rule over him.
He prays that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart be acceptable to the Lord, his rock and redeemer.
A prayer for the Lord to answer in times of trouble, protect His anointed, and remember offerings.
The people ask God to grant the king’s desires and rejoice in His salvation.
They express confidence that the Lord saves His anointed, contrasting trust in chariots with trust in the name of the Lord.
A final plea for the Lord to save and answer when His people call.
The king rejoices in the Lord’s strength and celebrates the fulfillment of his heart’s desires and requests.
God blesses the king with rich blessings, a crown of gold, long life, and joy in His presence.
The king trusts in the Lord, and through God’s mercy, he will not be moved.
God’s hand will find and destroy His enemies. They will be consumed like fire, and their evil plans will fail.
The psalm ends with a call to exalt the Lord in His strength and sing praise to His power.
David cries out, feeling forsaken by God and unheard despite his constant prayers.
He recalls God’s faithfulness to Israel’s ancestors, who trusted and were delivered.
David feels scorned and mocked, with people ridiculing his trust in God.
He appeals to God’s past care from birth and pleads for help in his present distress.
David vividly describes his suffering surrounded by enemies, physically broken, and stripped of dignity.
He pleads for God’s nearness and deliverance from danger and death.
A shift to praise: David vows to declare God’s name and worship among the congregation.
All nations will remember and turn to the Lord. Future generations will proclaim His righteousness.
The Lord is David’s shepherd, providing rest, restoration, and guidance in righteousness.
Even in the valley of the shadow of death, David fears no evil, for God is with him.
God prepares a table before David in the presence of enemies, anointing his head with oil and overflowing his cup.
David is confident that goodness and mercy will follow him, and he will dwell in the Lord’s house forever.
The earth and everything in it belong to the Lord, who founded it upon the seas.
Only those with clean hands and pure hearts may ascend God’s hill and receive blessing from Him.
A triumphant call for the gates to open for the King of glory the Lord strong and mighty in battle.
David lifts his soul to God, trusting in Him and asking not to be put to shame.
He asks for guidance in God’s paths and pleads for mercy, remembering God’s love rather than his youthful sins.
David praises God’s goodness and asks for pardon, acknowledging his great iniquity.
He reflects on the blessings of those who fear the Lord and keep His covenant.
David pleads for deliverance from affliction, loneliness, and enemies, ending with a prayer for Israel’s redemption.
David asks the Lord to vindicate him, affirming his integrity and trust in God, and declaring that he walks in truth.
He avoids the company of evildoers and expresses love for God’s house and the place where His glory dwells.
David pleads not to be gathered with sinners and affirms his uprightness, declaring that he will bless the Lord in the congregation.
David proclaims the Lord as his light and salvation, expressing confidence even in the face of enemies and war.
He desires to dwell in the house of the Lord, to behold His beauty, and to be hidden in His shelter in times of trouble.
David pleads for God’s mercy and guidance, trusting that even if forsaken by others, the Lord will receive him.
He asks for instruction in God’s way and expresses hope in seeing the Lord’s goodness, encouraging others to wait on Him with courage.
David cries out to the Lord, pleading not to be silent or counted among the wicked.
He asks for justice against those who speak peace but harbor evil, trusting that God will repay them according to their deeds.
David blesses the Lord for hearing his cry, declaring that the Lord is his strength and shield.
He affirms that the Lord is the strength of His people and prays for their salvation, blessing, and guidance forever.
David calls on heavenly beings to ascribe glory and strength to the Lord and worship Him in holiness.
He describes the powerful voice of the Lord over waters, forests, and wilderness, shaking creation with majesty.
The Lord sits enthroned over the flood and gives strength and peace to His people.
David praises God for lifting him up, healing him, and sparing him from death.
He calls others to praise the Lord, affirming that His anger is momentary but His favor lasts a lifetime.
David recalls his former confidence and how he cried out to God when troubled, asking for mercy and preservation.
God turned his mourning into dancing. David vows to give thanks forever and not be silent.
David seeks refuge in God, asking for deliverance in righteousness and committing his spirit into God's hands.
He rejects idols and rejoices in God's steadfast love, acknowledging divine protection in distress.
David laments his affliction, grief, and social rejection, feeling forgotten and slandered by enemies.
Despite fear, he trusts in God and pleads for deliverance from enemies and shame for the wicked.
He praises God's goodness, protection, and hidden shelter for the faithful.
David exhorts the saints to love the Lord and be strong, for God preserves the faithful.
Blessed is the one whose sins are forgiven and in whom there is no deceit.
David recalls the burden of unconfessed sin and the relief that came with confession and forgiveness.
He encourages the godly to pray and describes God as a hiding place who preserves from trouble.
God promises to instruct and guide, warning not to be stubborn like a horse or mule.
Many sorrows come to the wicked, but steadfast love surrounds those who trust in the Lord. The righteous are called to rejoice.
The righteous are called to rejoice in the Lord, praising His upright word and faithful works.
God created the heavens by His word and commands reverence from all the earth.
The Lord frustrates the plans of nations but establishes His own counsel forever. Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord.
God sees all from heaven; no king is saved by great armies or strength.
The Lord watches over those who fear Him. The psalm ends with a prayer for mercy and a declaration of trust.
David vows to bless the Lord at all times and invites others to magnify Him together.
He testifies that God delivered him from fear and affliction, and that the angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him.
David urges others to taste and see the Lord’s goodness, promising that those who seek Him lack no good thing.
He teaches the fear of the Lord: to keep the tongue from evil, depart from evil, and pursue peace.
The Lord watches over the righteous and hears their cries, drawing near to the brokenhearted.
Though the righteous face many afflictions, the Lord delivers them. Evil will slay the wicked, but the Lord redeems His servants.
David asks the Lord to contend with those who fight against him and to come to his aid.
He prays for his enemies to be put to shame and fall into the traps they set.
David rejoices in the Lord’s salvation and praises Him for defending the poor and needy.
He laments being repaid with evil for good, describing how his kindness was met with mockery and cruelty.
David pleads for God to rescue him from unjust enemies who gloat and speak maliciously.
He calls on God not to be silent, asking for vindication and rejoicing in the Lord’s righteousness.
David describes the wicked as having no fear of God, flattering themselves, speaking deceit, and plotting evil even on their beds.
He contrasts this with God’s steadfast love, faithfulness, righteousness, and judgments, which are vast and life-giving. God is a fountain of life and light.
David prays for continued love to the upright and protection from the proud, confident that evildoers will fall and not rise again.
David urges trust in the Lord and not to envy the wicked, who will soon fade. The meek will inherit the earth.
The wicked plot against the righteous, but the Lord laughs, knowing their day is coming. The righteous are preserved, while the wicked perish.
The righteous are generous and blessed. God upholds them, guides their steps, and His law is in their hearts.
Though the wicked lie in wait, the Lord delivers the righteous. Salvation comes from Him; He is their strength in trouble.
David pleads for mercy, overwhelmed by God’s discipline. His body and soul are in anguish due to sin.
He confesses his sorrow and isolation, as friends and enemies alike avoid or attack him. He remains silent like one who cannot hear.
David waits for the Lord, confessing guilt and acknowledging that his enemies repay good with evil.
He ends with a desperate plea for God not to forsake him and to come quickly to his aid.
David resolves to guard his tongue, especially in the presence of the wicked, but his silence becomes a burning burden.
He reflects on the brevity of life, asking God to help him understand how fleeting his days are.
David places his hope in the Lord, asking for deliverance from transgressions and acknowledging God’s discipline.
He pleads for God to hear his prayer and give him relief before he departs this life.
David praises God for lifting him from the pit and setting his feet on solid ground. Many will see and trust in the Lord.
He declares that God desires obedience over sacrifice and proclaims God’s righteousness and faithfulness publicly.
David asks for God’s mercy and deliverance, as troubles surround him and enemies seek his ruin.
He prays that all who seek the Lord rejoice, and humbly asks God not to delay in helping him, for he is poor and needy.
Blessed is the one who considers the poor; the Lord delivers him in trouble, preserves him, and strengthens him on his sickbed.
David pleads for healing and confesses sin. He laments that his enemies speak evil and wait for his downfall.
He is betrayed by close companions, even one who shared his bread.
David asks for mercy and vindication, ending with praise to the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting.
The psalmist longs for God like a deer for water, remembering joyful worship in God's house while now in sorrow.
He questions his soul’s despair and urges hope in God, his salvation and help.
Though cast down, he remembers God from distant places. Deep calls to deep amid waves, yet God’s love remains.
He asks why God seems absent and why enemies taunt him, but again resolves to hope in God.
The psalmist asks for vindication and laments feeling rejected by God.
He prays for God’s light and truth to lead him to the holy hill and altar, where he will praise with joy.
He repeats the refrain: 'Why art thou cast down, O my soul?' and affirms hope in God.
The psalmist recalls how God gave victory to their ancestors, not by their own strength but by His favor.
He declares trust in God, not in weapons, and boasts in the Lord continually.
Yet now they feel rejected and defeated, scorned by nations and covered in shame.
Despite faithfulness, they suffer as if slaughtered sheep. The psalmist insists they have not forgotten God.
He pleads for God to awake, arise, and redeem them for His mercy’s sake.
A royal psalm celebrating the king’s majesty, grace, and military might. The psalmist’s heart overflows with praise.
The king is addressed as divine, anointed with gladness above others, clothed in splendor and fragrance.
The bride is urged to forget her people and honor the king, who desires her beauty.
The bride, adorned in gold, is led to the king with joy and gladness.
The king’s sons will be princes, and his name will be remembered in all generations. Nations will praise him forever.
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore, we will not fear, even if the earth gives way and mountains fall into the sea.
There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God. God is in her midst; she shall not be moved. The Lord of hosts is with us.
Come behold the works of the Lord. He makes wars cease and says, 'Be still, and know that I am God.' The Lord is exalted among the nations.
All peoples are called to clap and shout to God with joy, for He is the great King over all the earth.
God has ascended with a shout. Sing praises to our King, for He reigns with understanding.
God reigns over the nations and sits on His holy throne. The princes of the people gather to worship the God of Abraham.
Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised in Zion, His holy mountain, beautiful in elevation and the joy of the whole earth.
Kings assembled and fled in fear at the sight of God’s city. God establishes it forever.
In the temple, the people meditate on God’s steadfast love. His praise reaches to the ends of the earth.
Walk about Zion and consider her strength. This God is our God forever and will be our guide even to death.
All peoples are called to hear wisdom, as the psalmist speaks a parable with understanding.
He warns against fear of the rich, for no one can ransom another or give to God the price of life.
The wise and foolish alike die. The proud trust in themselves, but death is their shepherd.
God will redeem the psalmist from the grave. Though the rich seem honored, they perish like beasts without understanding.
The Mighty One, God the Lord, summons the earth and shines from Zion. He comes in fire and tempest to judge His people.
God rebukes Israel not for sacrifices, but for thinking He needs them. He owns all and desires thanksgiving and trust in trouble.
To the wicked, God declares their hypocrisy reciting His statutes while hating discipline and joining with thieves and slanderers.
God warns those who forget Him and promises salvation to those who offer thanksgiving and walk uprightly.
David pleads for mercy after his sin with Bathsheba, acknowledging his transgressions and that he has sinned against God alone.
He confesses his sinful nature from birth and asks for cleansing, desiring to be made whiter than snow.
David asks for a clean heart and a steadfast spirit, praying not to be cast away. He vows to teach sinners God's ways.
He seeks deliverance from guilt and declares that God desires a broken spirit more than sacrifice.
David prays for Zion’s restoration and that God would delight in righteous sacrifices once again.
David rebukes the mighty man who boasts in evil, describing his love for lies and deceit.
He declares that God will destroy the wicked, who trusted in riches rather than God.
David contrasts himself as a green olive tree in God’s house, trusting in His mercy and praising Him forever.
The fool denies God, and all have turned aside; none do good.
Evildoers oppress God’s people, but God is with the righteous and will scatter the wicked.
David longs for salvation to come from Zion and rejoices in the hope of Israel’s restoration.
David calls on God to save him from strangers and oppressors who do not regard God.
He affirms that God is his helper and will repay his enemies.
David promises to offer sacrifices and praises God for delivering him from trouble.
David pleads for God to hear him as he is overwhelmed by fear and wishes to flee like a dove.
He asks God to confuse the wicked and laments betrayal by a close companion.
David turns to God in prayer, confident that He will hear and save him from his enemies.
He describes the treachery of his betrayer and urges others to cast their burdens on the Lord, who will sustain the righteous.
David pleads for mercy as enemies pursue him. Despite fear, he declares trust in God, whose word he praises.
He describes the constant twisting of his words and asks God to bring justice upon his adversaries.
David finds comfort in God’s awareness of his tears and affirms that he will not fear man, for God is with him.
He vows to fulfill his offerings of thanks, confident that God has delivered him from death and will keep his feet from falling.
David seeks refuge under God’s wings until danger passes, trusting that God will send help from heaven.
He describes his soul among lions and enemies who set traps, but he remains steadfast in praise.
David’s heart is fixed on praising God among the nations, exalting His mercy and truth above the heavens.
David denounces unjust rulers who speak lies and act wickedly from birth, likening them to venomous serpents.
He calls on God to break their teeth and render them powerless, like melting snails or stillborn children.
The righteous will rejoice when justice is done, affirming that there is a God who judges the earth.
David asks for deliverance from bloodthirsty enemies, appealing to God’s strength and justice.
He describes the enemies prowling like dogs, but declares that God will laugh at them and be his defense.
David asks God not to kill them outright but to scatter them, exposing their lies and pride.
He ends with praise, singing of God’s mercy and strength each morning.
David laments God’s apparent rejection in battle and pleads for restoration and help.
God speaks from His sanctuary, claiming dominion over Israel and mocking enemy nations.
David asks who will lead them to victory and affirms that only through God can they triumph over their foes.
David cries out to God from the ends of the earth, asking to be led to the rock that is higher than he.
He recalls God as his refuge and vows to dwell in His tent forever, trusting in His protection and heritage.
David prays for the king’s long life and faithfulness, promising to sing praise and fulfill his vows daily.
David declares that his soul waits silently for God alone, his rock and salvation.
He warns of those who plot to topple others with lies and hypocrisy.
He exhorts himself and others to trust in God at all times, pouring out their hearts before Him.
David reflects on the vanity of human strength and riches, affirming that power and mercy belong to God.
In the wilderness, David thirsts for God, longing to see His power and glory as in the sanctuary.
He finds satisfaction in God’s presence, meditating on Him through the night and clinging to Him for help.
David declares that his enemies will fall, while the king will rejoice in God and all liars will be silenced.
David asks for protection from secret plots and sharp tongues. He describes how the wicked lay traps with cunning words.
God will shoot them with arrows, bringing sudden ruin. The righteous will rejoice and trust in the Lord.
Praise awaits God in Zion. He hears prayer, forgives sins, and blesses those He draws near to dwell in His courts.
God answers with awesome deeds, stilling the roaring seas and inspiring awe from east to west.
He waters the earth abundantly, crowning the year with bounty. The hills, pastures, and valleys shout for joy.
All the earth is called to shout joyfully to God, sing His name, and declare His awesome works.
The psalmist invites others to see God’s deeds how He turned the sea into dry land and rules by His power forever.
He blesses God for testing and refining His people, bringing them through fire and water into abundance.
The psalmist vows to offer sacrifices and fulfill promises made in distress.
He invites others to hear his testimony of answered prayer and praises God for not turning away His mercy.
A prayer for God’s grace and blessing so that His way may be known among all nations.
The peoples are called to praise God, who judges with equity and guides the nations.
The earth yields its increase, and all the ends of the earth will fear God.
God arises and scatters His enemies. He is a father to the fatherless and sets the lonely in families.
The psalm recalls God’s mighty acts at Sinai and in battle, providing for His people and scattering kings.
God’s choice of Zion is exalted, and He is praised for ascending on high and receiving gifts among men.
Blessed be the Lord who daily bears burdens. God crushes His enemies and brings justice.
A procession of worshipers is described, with singers and musicians praising God in the sanctuary.
God is called to strengthen His people. Kings will bring tribute, and all nations will acknowledge His power.
David cries out from deep distress, overwhelmed by enemies and false accusations.
He confesses his sins and describes how zeal for God’s house has brought reproach.
David pleads for God’s mercy and deliverance, asking not to be ashamed.
He recounts insults and rejection, including being given gall and vinegar to drink.
He calls for judgment on his enemies, asking that their names be blotted from the book of life.
Despite suffering, David praises God, confident that the Lord hears the needy and will restore Zion.
David urgently asks God to deliver him and put to shame those who seek his harm.
He prays that all who seek God rejoice and magnify Him continually.
David confesses his need and asks God not to delay in helping him.
The psalmist seeks refuge in God, asking for deliverance from the wicked and unjust.
He recalls God as his hope and trust since youth, praising Him continually.
He pleads not to be forsaken in old age and asks for shame upon his accusers.
He vows to hope continually and declare God’s wondrous works to the next generation.
The psalmist praises God’s greatness and faithfulness, confident that He will revive and comfort him again.
A prayer for the king to rule with righteousness and justice, bringing peace and prosperity to the people.
The king’s dominion will extend from sea to sea, and all nations will serve him.
He will deliver the needy and have compassion on the poor and oppressed.
The king will be honored, and his name will endure as long as the sun, bringing blessing to all nations.
The psalm ends with praise to the Lord God, declaring His glory and concluding Book II of Psalms.
The psalmist confesses envy of the wicked, who seem to prosper despite their arrogance.
He describes their ease, pride, and scoffing, questioning the value of righteousness.
He struggles with doubt until he enters God’s sanctuary and perceives the wicked’s end.
He realizes their downfall is sudden and that his own bitterness was foolish.
He affirms God’s continual presence, guidance, and ultimate strength, declaring that nearness to God is his good.
A lament over God’s apparent rejection and the destruction of the sanctuary by enemies.
The psalmist recalls God’s past acts of salvation and power over creation.
He pleads for God to remember the covenant and rise up to defend His cause against the enemy.
The psalmist gives thanks to God, declaring that His name is near and His works are wondrous.
God declares that He will judge uprightly and warns the proud not to exalt themselves.
Exaltation comes from God alone, who holds a cup of judgment for the wicked to drink.
The psalmist vows to praise God and declares that the horns of the wicked will be cut off, but the righteous will be exalted.
God is known in Judah and His name is great in Israel. His dwelling is in Zion, where He broke the weapons of war.
God is more glorious than mountains full of prey. The stouthearted are plundered, and none can stand before His anger.
From heaven, God pronounced judgment, and the earth feared. Even human wrath will praise Him.
All are called to make vows and bring gifts to the Lord, who cuts off the spirit of princes and is feared by kings.
The psalmist cries aloud to God in the day of trouble, remembering Him and groaning.
He reflects on sleepless nights and questions whether God has rejected him forever.
He resolves to remember God’s mighty deeds and meditate on His wonders and power.
The psalmist recalls God’s deliverance at the Red Sea, where His path was through the waters and He led His people like a flock.
A call to teach the next generation about God’s works so they won’t repeat the rebellion of their ancestors.
Despite God’s miracles in Egypt and the wilderness, the people sinned and tested Him, leading to judgment.
Though they repented, their hearts were not steadfast. God showed mercy, recalling the plagues and deliverance from Egypt.
Israel continued to rebel, but God chose Judah and David to shepherd His people with integrity and skill.
The nations have defiled God’s temple and laid Jerusalem in ruins. His people are mocked and scorned.
The psalmist pleads for God’s anger to relent and not remember past sins.
He asks for deliverance and vengeance on the nations for their reproach and violence.
The people vow to give thanks forever and declare God’s praise to all generations.
A plea to the Shepherd of Israel to shine forth and restore His people.
The psalmist laments God’s anger and the tears of His people, asking for restoration.
He recalls how God brought a vine out of Egypt and planted it, but now it is broken and ravaged.
He pleads for God to return, strengthen His chosen one, and revive His people so they may call on His name.
A call to sing joyfully to God, the strength of Jacob, and to celebrate with music during the appointed feast.
God reminds Israel of His deliverance from Egypt and urges them to listen and worship no foreign god.
God laments Israel’s disobedience and declares that if they had listened, He would have subdued their enemies and fed them with the finest wheat and honey.
God stands in judgment among the 'gods' (earthly rulers), rebuking them for injustice and failure to defend the weak and needy.
Though they are called 'gods,' they will die like men and fall like any ruler.
A plea for God to rise and judge the earth, for all nations belong to Him.
The psalmist asks God not to remain silent as enemy nations conspire against Israel.
He recalls past victories over enemies and asks God to do the same to these current foes.
He prays for their defeat so that they may seek God’s name and know that He alone is Most High over all the earth.
The psalmist longs for the courts of the Lord, declaring that even sparrows find a home near His altar.
Blessed are those whose strength is in God; they go from strength to strength as they journey toward Zion.
He prays for God’s favor and declares that one day in God’s courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. God is a sun and shield to those who walk uprightly.
The psalmist recalls God’s past restoration and forgiveness toward His people.
He pleads for renewed mercy and revival, asking God to show steadfast love and grant salvation.
He listens for God’s peace and envisions a future where righteousness and peace embrace, and the land yields its increase under God’s blessing.
David pleads for God to hear him, acknowledging his need and God's mercy. He calls on God in the day of trouble, confident He will answer.
David declares that no other gods compare to the Lord, who alone does wondrous things and is worthy of worship from all nations.
He asks for an undivided heart to fear God's name and praises Him for great mercy and deliverance from death.
David describes the proud rising against him but affirms God's compassion. He asks for a sign of favor to shame his enemies.
The psalmist celebrates Zion, the city founded by God, and declares it more glorious than all other places.
Nations like Egypt and Babylon are counted as born in Zion, showing God's inclusive grace and the honor of being His people.
All sources of joy are found in Zion, the city of God.
A psalm of deep lament. The psalmist cries out day and night, feeling overwhelmed and abandoned even by God.
He laments isolation from friends and questions whether the dead can praise God or experience His wonders.
Despite continued prayer, he feels rejected and surrounded by darkness. The psalm ends without resolution, expressing raw sorrow.
The psalmist begins by praising God's covenant with David, promising to establish his throne forever.
He extols God's power, faithfulness, and justice, declaring that blessed are those who walk in His light.
God’s covenant with David is recalled in detail, affirming that his line will endure like the sun and moon.
Yet the psalmist laments that God has rejected and cast off His anointed, allowing enemies to triumph.
He pleads for God to remember His covenant and restore His servant, ending with a doxology: 'Blessed be the Lord forevermore. Amen and Amen.'
A prayer of Moses reflecting on God’s eternal nature and humanity’s fleeting life, like grass that withers.
He acknowledges God’s wrath against sin and the brevity of life under divine judgment.
Moses asks God to teach us to number our days, to show compassion, and to establish the work of our hands.
Those who dwell in the secret place of the Most High find refuge under His wings. God is a shield and fortress.
The faithful need not fear terror, pestilence, or destruction. Though thousands fall, they will be protected and see the punishment of the wicked.
Because they trust in God, no evil will befall them. Angels will guard them, and they will tread upon lions and serpents.
God promises deliverance, protection, and long life to those who love and know His name.
It is good to give thanks to the Lord and sing praises, rejoicing in His steadfast love and faithfulness.
God’s works are great and deep. The wicked may flourish briefly, but they will perish.
The righteous flourish like palm trees and cedars, bearing fruit even in old age, proclaiming that the Lord is upright.
The Lord reigns in majesty and strength. His throne is established from everlasting.
Though floods lift their voice, the Lord is mightier than the raging waters.
God’s testimonies are sure, and holiness adorns His house forever.
The psalmist calls on God to avenge the proud and wicked who oppress His people and deny His justice.
He rebukes the foolish, affirming that the Creator sees and knows all.
Blessed is the one disciplined by God, for the Lord will not forsake His people or abandon justice.
The psalmist finds comfort in God amid anxiety and injustice. The Lord is his defense and will bring judgment on the wicked.
A joyful call to worship the Lord, the great King above all gods, who formed the earth and sea.
An invitation to bow in reverence before the Lord, our Maker and Shepherd.
A warning not to harden hearts like Israel did at Meribah, lest they forfeit rest in God’s presence.
A call to sing a new song to the Lord and declare His glory and marvelous works among all nations.
The Lord is great and to be feared above all gods. He made the heavens, and splendor and strength are in His sanctuary.
Families of nations are called to ascribe glory to the Lord and worship Him in the beauty of holiness.
The world is firmly established under God’s reign. Let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad, for He comes to judge with righteousness and truth.
The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice. Clouds and darkness surround Him, and His lightning lights up the world.
All idolaters are put to shame. Zion rejoices because the Lord is exalted far above all gods.
Those who love the Lord hate evil. Light is sown for the righteous, and they are called to rejoice and give thanks.
Sing a new song to the Lord, for He has done marvelous things and revealed His salvation to the nations.
All the earth is called to make a joyful noise with instruments and singing before the King.
Let the sea, rivers, and hills rejoice, for the Lord comes to judge the world with righteousness and equity.
The Lord reigns and is enthroned between the cherubim. Let the nations tremble and praise His great and awesome name.
The King loves justice and has established equity. Exalt the Lord and worship at His footstool.
Moses, Aaron, and Samuel called on the Lord and He answered them. Worship at His holy hill, for the Lord is holy.
Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth. Serve the Lord with gladness and come before Him with singing.
Know that the Lord is God; He made us, and we are His people, the sheep of His pasture.
Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise. Give thanks and bless His name.
For the Lord is good; His mercy is everlasting, and His truth endures to all generations.
David vows to sing of mercy and justice and to walk with integrity in his house.
He declares he will set no wicked thing before his eyes and will not tolerate slander, pride, or deceit.
David promises to favor the faithful and to cut off evildoers from the city of the Lord.
A prayer of affliction. The psalmist pours out his lament, describing his physical weakness and isolation.
He shifts to hope, affirming that the Lord will arise and have mercy on Zion, rebuilding it in His appointed time.
The psalmist envisions future generations praising the Lord for His deliverance and restoration.
Though his strength fades, he trusts in God’s eternal nature and faithfulness to future generations.
David blesses the Lord for His benefits healing, redemption, love, and renewal.
The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and full of compassion. He remembers our frailty.
Human life is fleeting, but God’s steadfast love endures for those who fear Him and keep His covenant.
The Lord rules over all. All creation is called to bless His holy name.
The psalmist praises God for His majestic creation light, heavens, waters, and boundaries of the sea.
He describes God’s provision for all creatures springs, grass, food, and the rhythms of day and night.
All creation depends on God’s Spirit for life and renewal. His wisdom is seen in all His works.
The psalmist rejoices in the Lord’s glory and prays that sinners be consumed. He ends with praise and joy.
A call to give thanks, sing, and remember God’s wondrous works and covenant with Abraham.
God protected the patriarchs and warned kings not to harm His anointed ones.
He sent Joseph ahead to Egypt, where he rose to power and prepared for famine.
God multiplied Israel in Egypt, sent plagues on the Egyptians, and brought His people out with wealth.
He guided them with cloud and fire, fed them with manna and quail, and gave them the promised land to keep His statutes.
The psalm opens with praise for God’s enduring mercy and a prayer to be remembered with His people and share in their joy.
Israel’s sins in Egypt and at the Red Sea are confessed, yet God saved them for His name’s sake.
Despite God’s wonders, the people quickly forgot and rebelled craving meat, envying Moses, and worshiping the golden calf. Yet Moses interceded.
They despised the promised land, grumbled, and provoked God at Meribah, leading to judgment even on Moses.
Israel mingled with the nations, adopted idolatry, and shed innocent blood. Yet God repeatedly showed mercy when they cried out.
A closing plea for salvation and a doxology: 'Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting.'
A call to give thanks to the Lord for His steadfast love and redemption of the exiles.
He delivered wanderers in the desert who cried out in hunger and thirst.
He freed prisoners who sat in darkness because of rebellion.
He healed the sick who were afflicted due to sin.
He calmed the storm for sailors who cried out in distress.
God turns rivers into deserts and deserts into springs, humbling the proud and lifting the needy. The wise will consider His steadfast love.
David’s heart is steadfast. He praises God among the nations and asks for deliverance by His right hand.
God declares His dominion over Israel and surrounding nations Shechem, Moab, Edom, and Philistia.
David asks who will lead them to victory and affirms that with God they will triumph over their enemies.
David pleads for God to respond to false accusers who repay his love with hatred.
He calls down severe imprecations on his enemy desiring judgment, loss, and disgrace for their cruelty.
David appeals to God’s mercy, asking for deliverance and vindication so others may know the Lord’s hand.
He ends with praise, confident that God stands at the right hand of the needy to save them from condemnation.
The Lord says to David’s Lord, 'Sit at my right hand.' The Messiah will rule in power, and His people will offer themselves willingly.
God swears that the Messiah is a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
The Lord will shatter kings in the day of His wrath, judge the nations, and lift His head in triumph.
The psalmist praises the Lord with his whole heart, declaring that God’s works are great, honorable, and remembered for His graciousness.
God provides for those who fear Him, remembers His covenant, shows power to His people, and sends redemption. His precepts are trustworthy.
The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; all who follow His commandments have good understanding.
Blessed is the one who fears the Lord and delights in His commands. His descendants will be mighty, and wealth and righteousness will endure.
The righteous are gracious, generous, and steadfast. They are not afraid of bad news and give freely to the poor.
The wicked see and are vexed; their desires perish.
Servants of the Lord are called to praise His name from sunrise to sunset.
The Lord is exalted above all nations and stoops to behold the heavens and the earth.
He lifts the poor from the dust and seats them with princes. He gives the barren woman a home and children.
When Israel came out of Egypt, God’s presence caused the sea to flee and the mountains to skip like rams.
The psalmist marvels at creation’s response to God and recalls how He turned rock into water for His people.
Not to us, but to God be the glory. He is in heaven and does whatever pleases Him.
Idols are lifeless and those who trust in them become like them.
Israel is exhorted to trust in the Lord, their help and shield. He will bless all who fear Him.
The heavens belong to the Lord, but the earth He gave to humanity. The dead do not praise Him, but the living will bless Him forever.
The psalmist loves the Lord for hearing his cry for mercy and deliverance from death.
He praises God’s graciousness and declares that the Lord preserved him when he was brought low.
Though afflicted and disillusioned by men, he resolves to fulfill his vows and call on the Lord.
Precious in God’s sight is the death of His saints. The psalmist offers thanksgiving and worship in the courts of the Lord.
A universal call to praise the Lord for His steadfast love and enduring truth. The shortest psalm, yet globally expansive in scope.
A call for Israel, the house of Aaron, and all who fear the Lord to give thanks for His enduring mercy.
The psalmist recounts deliverance from distress and affirms that trust in the Lord is better than in man or princes.
Surrounded by enemies, he triumphed in the name of the Lord. Though disciplined, he was not given over to death.
He enters the gates of righteousness, declaring that the rejected stone has become the cornerstone this is the day the Lord has made.
A plea for salvation and blessing. The psalm ends with joyful praise and thanksgiving for God’s goodness.
Aleph: Blessed are those who walk in God’s law and seek Him wholeheartedly.
Beth: A young person keeps pure by guarding God’s word and delighting in His statutes.
Gimel: The psalmist asks for understanding and strength amid scorn and exile.
Daleth: He clings to the dust but finds life through God’s word and chooses the way of truth.
He: A prayer for instruction, heart transformation, and revival in righteousness.
Vav: He trusts in God’s salvation and speaks boldly of His testimonies.
Zayin: God’s word is his comfort in affliction and song in the night.
Heth: The Lord is his portion; he keeps God’s commands and rises at midnight to give thanks.
Teth: Affliction taught him to value God’s law more than riches.
Yodh: He asks for understanding and hopes that others who fear God will rejoice with him.
Kaph: His soul faints for salvation, yet he clings to God’s commandments amid persecution.
Lamedh: God’s word is eternal, sustaining creation and the psalmist’s life.
Mem: He loves God’s law, which gives wisdom and keeps him from evil.
Nun: God’s word is a lamp to his feet; he commits to obeying it even in danger.
Samekh: He rejects double-mindedness and trembles at God’s judgments.
Ayin: He pleads for justice and affirms that God’s precepts are right.
Pe: God’s words give light; the psalmist weeps over those who do not keep them.
Tsadhe: God is righteous, and His law is trustworthy even in trouble.
Qoph: He cries out before dawn, hoping in God’s word and remembering His statutes.
Resh: He asks for deliverance and affirms that God’s word is true from the beginning.
Shin: Princes persecute him, but he rejoices in God’s word like great spoil.
Tav: He pleads for understanding and deliverance, confessing that he has gone astray like a lost sheep.
The psalmist cries to the Lord in distress and is answered, asking for deliverance from lying lips.
He warns of judgment for deceitful tongues sharp arrows and burning coals.
He laments dwelling among hostile people and longs for peace, though he is surrounded by war.
The psalmist lifts his eyes to the hills, affirming that his help comes from the Lord, the Maker of heaven and earth.
God will not let your foot slip. He who watches over Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps. The Lord is your shade and protector from all harm.
The Lord will preserve you from all evil and guard your going out and coming in, now and forevermore.
The psalmist rejoices at the invitation to go to the house of the Lord, standing within Jerusalem’s gates.
Jerusalem is described as a well-built city, the place where the tribes go up and where thrones of judgment are set.
A call to pray for the peace of Jerusalem, seeking its prosperity and security for the sake of God’s house.
The psalmist lifts his eyes to God enthroned in heaven, like a servant watching the hand of a master.
He pleads for mercy, weary of contempt and scorn from the proud and arrogant.
If the Lord had not been on Israel’s side, they would have been swallowed by enemies and overwhelmed by raging waters.
Blessed be the Lord who did not let them be prey. Their help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.
Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion unshakable and enduring. The Lord surrounds His people forever.
The wicked will not rule over the righteous. The Lord will do good to the upright but lead evildoers away with the wicked.
The psalmist recalls the joy of Israel’s restoration, likening it to a dream. The Lord has done great things, and the people rejoice.
A prayer for renewed restoration. Those who sow in tears will reap with joy, carrying sheaves after faithful labor.
Unless the Lord builds the house or guards the city, human effort is in vain. God gives rest to His beloved.
Children are a heritage from the Lord, like arrows in a warrior’s hand. A man with many sons is blessed and unashamed before his enemies.
Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord and walks in His ways. They will enjoy the fruit of their labor, and their family will flourish.
The Lord will bless from Zion. May you see Jerusalem’s prosperity and your children’s children peace upon Israel.
Israel reflects on long-standing affliction from youth, yet affirms that the Lord has cut the cords of the wicked.
A prayer that those who hate Zion be put to shame, like withered grass. Let none bless them in the name of the Lord.
From the depths, the psalmist cries for mercy, acknowledging that if God marked iniquities, none could stand but with Him is forgiveness.
He waits for the Lord more than watchmen for morning. Israel is called to hope in the Lord, who will redeem from all iniquities.
The psalmist humbly declares that he does not concern himself with lofty matters but has calmed his soul like a weaned child with its mother.
Israel is exhorted to hope in the Lord from now and forever.
A plea for the Lord to remember David’s devotion and his vow to find a dwelling place for God.
The people recall finding the ark and ask God to arise to His resting place with His priests and saints rejoicing.
God’s covenant with David is affirmed his throne will endure, Zion is chosen as God’s dwelling, and blessings will abound.
A celebration of unity among brethren, likened to precious oil on Aaron’s beard and the dew of Hermon. There the Lord commands the blessing life forevermore.
Servants of the Lord who stand by night in the house of the Lord are called to bless Him and lift their hands in worship.
A blessing is spoken: May the Lord, Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.
A call to praise the Lord for His goodness and greatness, who does whatever pleases Him in heaven and earth.
God’s mighty acts in Egypt and Canaan are recalled, and His enduring name and justice are praised.
Idols are described as lifeless, and those who trust in them become like them.
All of Israel house of Aaron, Levi, and all who fear the Lord are called to bless Him from Zion.
A call to give thanks to the Lord, the God of gods and Lord of lords, for His mercy endures forever.
Praise for God’s wonders in creation heavens, earth, sun, moon, and stars all shaped by His enduring mercy.
God’s mighty acts in history: striking Egypt, dividing the Red Sea, leading Israel, and giving them the promised land all because His mercy endures forever.
He remembered us in our low estate, rescued us from enemies, and provides food for all. Give thanks to the God of heaven His mercy endures forever.
By the rivers of Babylon, the exiles weep and cannot sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land.
A vow never to forget Jerusalem, with a plea that the psalmist’s right hand forget its skill if he does.
A cry for justice against Edom and Babylon, ending with a harsh imprecation reflecting the pain of exile.
David gives thanks with his whole heart, praising God for His steadfast love and truth.
All kings will praise the Lord when they hear His words. Though exalted, God regards the lowly.
David trusts God to preserve him in trouble and fulfill His purpose 'Your mercy endures forever; do not forsake the work of Your hands.'
The psalmist marvels at God’s intimate knowledge He knows every thought, word, and action.
There is nowhere to flee from God’s presence He is with us in heaven, Sheol, darkness, and light.
God formed the psalmist in the womb; His thoughts are precious and vast beyond number.
A plea for God to slay the wicked, followed by a request to search and lead the psalmist in the everlasting way.
David asks for deliverance from evil men who stir up war and lay traps with their tongues and hands.
He declares God as his strength and shield, asking Him not to grant the desires of the wicked.
David prays for judgment on his enemies that their schemes fall back on them and slanderers be silenced.
He affirms that the Lord maintains justice for the afflicted and that the righteous will dwell in His presence.
David calls on the Lord quickly, asking that his prayer be accepted like incense and his uplifted hands like the evening sacrifice.
He asks God to guard his mouth and heart, to keep him from wickedness, and welcomes righteous correction as kindness.
David contrasts the fate of the wicked with his own trust in God, asking for protection from traps and for the wicked to fall into their own snares.
David pours out his complaint to the Lord from a cave, feeling abandoned and without refuge.
He declares the Lord as his portion and cries for deliverance from persecutors, promising to praise God when rescued.
David pleads for mercy, acknowledging that no one is righteous before God. He feels crushed and overwhelmed.
He remembers God’s past works and stretches out his hands in thirst for divine help.
David urgently asks for God’s presence, guidance, and deliverance, desiring to do His will.
He appeals to God’s righteousness and mercy to preserve his life and silence his enemies.
David blesses the Lord, his rock and trainer for battle, and marvels that God cares for frail humanity.
He asks God to come down in power, rescue him from foreign enemies who speak lies.
David vows to sing a new song and asks for deliverance from deceitful foes.
He envisions a blessed nation with flourishing children, abundant provision, and peace declaring that such a people are truly happy.
David extols God’s greatness, declaring that His mighty acts and abundant goodness will be praised from generation to generation.
The Lord is gracious, slow to anger, and full of mercy. His kingdom is everlasting, and His dominion endures through all generations.
God upholds the fallen and satisfies every living thing with His open hand.
The Lord is righteous and near to all who call on Him sincerely. He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him and preserves the faithful.
The psalmist commits to praising the Lord all his life.
He warns not to trust in princes or mortal men, who cannot save and whose plans perish.
Blessed is the one whose help is the God of Jacob. The Lord executes justice, feeds the hungry, frees prisoners, and reigns forever.
Praise the Lord who builds up Jerusalem, heals the brokenhearted, and lifts the humble while casting down the wicked.
Sing to the Lord who provides rain and food. He delights not in strength but in those who fear Him.
Jerusalem is called to praise God for His protection, provision, and unique revelation of His word to Israel.
All heavenly beings angels, sun, moon, stars are called to praise the Lord who created and established them.
All earthly creatures sea monsters, weather, mountains, animals, kings, and children are summoned to praise.
The Lord’s name alone is exalted. He has raised a horn for His people, a praise for the faithful of Israel.
A new song of praise is sung by Israel, rejoicing in their Maker and King with dancing and instruments.
The faithful are armed with praise and judgment, executing vengeance on nations and binding kings an honor for all His saints.
Praise God in His sanctuary and mighty heavens for His acts of power and surpassing greatness.
Praise Him with trumpet, harp, tambourine, strings, flutes, and cymbals let every instrument resound.
Let everything that has breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah!
Introduction to the book’s purpose: to impart wisdom, discipline, and insight. 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge.'
A father's warning not to follow sinners who entice with violent gain, for their path leads to destruction.
Wisdom personified cries out in the streets, warning that those who reject her will suffer, but those who heed her will dwell in safety.
If one seeks wisdom earnestly, the Lord gives it, guarding the paths of justice and protecting the upright.
Wisdom helps discern righteousness and guards against the ways of evil men who rejoice in perversity.
It also protects from the seductress who forsakes her covenant. The upright will inhabit the land; the wicked will be cut off.
Trust in the Lord with all your heart. Obedience and generosity lead to blessing, healing, and prosperity.
Don't despise God's discipline He corrects those He loves. Wisdom is more precious than riches and is foundational to creation.
Wisdom brings peace and confidence. Be kind to neighbors, avoid envy and violence. The Lord blesses the righteous and scorns the proud.
A father's appeal to gain understanding and not forsake wisdom, which brings honor and life.
Choose the path of righteousness over the way of the wicked, which is darkness and ruin.
Guard your heart, speak truth, and stay on the straight path without turning to evil.
A warning against the seductress whose lips drip honey but whose path leads to death and regret.
Rejoice in the wife of your youth; find satisfaction in marital love instead of straying.
God sees all paths; the wicked are ensnared by their own sin and die for lack of discipline.
A father warns his son against becoming entangled in another’s debt. If he has made a rash financial promise, he must humble himself and urgently seek release before it traps him.
The sluggard is urged to learn from the ant’s diligence and foresight. Laziness leads to sudden poverty, like a thief who strikes without warning.
A portrait of the wicked man: deceitful in speech and action, always stirring up trouble. His downfall will be swift and beyond remedy.
Seven things the Lord hates are listed pride, lying, violence, wicked schemes, eagerness to do evil, false testimony, and sowing discord among brothers.

A passionate warning against adultery. The father urges his son to treasure wisdom and avoid the seductress, whose flattery leads to ruin, disgrace, and even death. No compensation can undo the damage of betrayal.
The father pleads with his son to internalize his words and keep wisdom close like a sister or trusted friend to guard against the allure of the adulteress.

A vivid parable: the father watches from his window as a naive young man is seduced by a bold woman. Her flattery and timing are calculated, but her path leads him like an ox to slaughter unaware it will cost him his life.
A final plea: listen and turn away from her path. Her house is a gateway to death, and many strong men have fallen there.
Wisdom is personified as a noble woman calling out from the heights and crossroads. She offers truth, righteousness, and instruction more valuable than silver or gold.
Wisdom dwells with prudence and gives sound counsel, justice, and strength. Kings and rulers govern rightly by her, and those who love her inherit enduring riches and honor.
Wisdom speaks of her origin created before the world, present at creation, rejoicing in God’s works and delighting in humanity.
Wisdom urges all to listen and keep her ways. Those who find her find life and favor from the Lord; those who reject her harm themselves and embrace death.
Wisdom builds her house and prepares a feast, inviting the simple to leave their folly and live by walking in understanding.
A reflection on how people respond to correction: mockers reject it, but the wise grow wiser. 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.'
Folly is also personified as a loud, seductive woman. She offers stolen pleasures, but her guests do not know they are descending into the depths of Sheol.

A wise child brings joy to their parents, but a foolish one causes grief. Righteousness preserves life, while dishonest gain is worthless. The Lord provides for the upright and frustrates the desires of the wicked. Diligence leads to abundance; laziness brings shame and missed opportunity.

Blessings crown the righteous, but the wicked are overwhelmed by violence. The memory of the righteous is cherished; the wicked are forgotten. Integrity brings security, while deceit leads to exposure. The righteous speak life; the wicked conceal harm. Love covers offenses; hatred fuels division.

Hatred stirs up conflict, but love fosters peace. Wisdom is found in the discerning; fools invite discipline. The wise store knowledge; the foolish squander it. Righteousness leads to life; wickedness to ruin. Those who accept correction walk in life; those who reject it mislead others.

Concealed hatred and slander mark a fool. Too many words lead to sin, but restraint is wise. The words of the righteous are precious and nourishing; the wicked offer little of value. Fools perish for lack of understanding.

The Lord’s blessing brings true wealth without sorrow. Fools delight in wrongdoing; the wise find joy in understanding. The wicked’s fears come upon them; the righteous receive their desires. When storms pass, the wicked vanish, but the righteous remain secure.

A lazy person is as irritating as vinegar to teeth or smoke to eyes. The fear of the Lord prolongs life; the wicked are cut short. The righteous find joy and stability; the wicked face disappointment and removal. The Lord is a refuge to the upright but a ruin to evildoers.
The mouth of the righteous speaks wisdom and what is fitting; the wicked speak perversity and will be silenced.

The Lord detests dishonest scales but delights in accurate weights. Pride leads to disgrace, but humility brings wisdom. Integrity guides the upright, while the treacherous are destroyed by their own deceit. Riches cannot save in the day of wrath, but righteousness delivers from death and directs the blameless path.

When the wicked die, their hope perishes. The righteous are rescued from trouble, which falls on the wicked instead. Hypocrites destroy with their mouths, but the righteous are delivered by knowledge. A city rejoices when the righteous prosper, but it crumbles under the rule of the wicked.

Those who belittle others lack sense, but the prudent remain silent. A gossip betrays confidence, while the trustworthy keep secrets. Wise counsel leads to safety, but lack of guidance brings ruin. Guaranteeing another’s debt is risky; avoiding it shows wisdom.

A gracious woman gains honor, and strong men retain wealth. Kindness benefits oneself, but cruelty harms the doer. The wicked earn deceptive wages, while the righteous reap a sure reward. God delights in those who pursue righteousness and promises that the offspring of the righteous will be delivered.

Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout is beauty without discretion. The righteous desire good; the wicked expect wrath. One gives freely and gains more, while another withholds and ends in poverty. A generous soul will prosper, and those who refresh others will be refreshed. People curse hoarders but bless those who sell grain.

Those who seek good find favor; those who pursue evil will be overtaken by it. Trusting in riches leads to downfall, but the righteous flourish like a green leaf. Those who trouble their households inherit the wind. The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and the wise win souls. If the righteous are repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner.

Loving discipline shows a love for knowledge, while hating correction is foolish. The righteous gain favor and stability, but the wicked are condemned and uprooted. A noble spouse is a crown, while a disgraceful one brings decay. The righteous speak truth and justice; the wicked plot harm.

The wicked are overthrown, but the righteous stand firm. Wisdom earns respect; pretension leads to shame. The righteous care for animals, while the wicked are cruel. Hard work brings provision; chasing fantasies shows a lack of judgment.

The wicked envy evil, but the righteous flourish. Words can trap or deliver. Wise speech brings good, while fools are deceived by their own ways. A fool vents quickly; the prudent overlook insults. Truthful witnesses save lives; liars spread deceit.

Reckless words wound, but wise words heal. Truth endures; lies are short-lived. Deceit brings sorrow; peace brings joy. The righteous are protected; the wicked face trouble. God delights in truthfulness. The prudent guard knowledge; fools broadcast folly.

Diligence leads to leadership; laziness to forced labor. Anxiety weighs down, but kind words lift up. The righteous choose friends wisely; the wicked mislead. The diligent value what they gain. Righteousness leads to life; its path is secure.

A wise child listens to correction; a mocker ignores it. Good speech brings reward; rash words bring ruin. Diligence satisfies; laziness leaves empty. The righteous hate lies; the wicked bring shame. Righteousness guards the blameless; sin destroys the wicked.

Appearances can deceive some seem rich but have nothing. Wealth can protect, but the wicked’s light goes out. Pride breeds conflict; wisdom listens. Ill-gotten gain fades; steady work prospers. Hope deferred brings sorrow; fulfilled desire is life-giving.

Despising instruction leads to ruin; reverence brings reward. Wise teaching is life-giving. Good sense earns favor; treachery is hard. The prudent act with knowledge; fools flaunt folly. Discipline brings honor; fulfilled desire is sweet, but fools hate turning from evil.

Walking with the wise brings wisdom; fools bring harm. Trouble chases sinners; the righteous are rewarded. A good person leaves a legacy; the sinner’s wealth benefits the righteous. Injustice can rob the poor. Loving discipline shows true care. The righteous are satisfied; the wicked go hungry.

A wise woman builds her home; a foolish one tears it down. Uprightness honors God; deceit shows contempt. Fools speak pridefully and invite punishment; the wise protect themselves with their words. Avoid fools they offer no knowledge.

The wise consider their steps; fools are deceived. Fools mock guilt; the upright seek goodwill. Each heart knows its own sorrow. The wicked’s house will fall; the upright will flourish. What seems right may lead to death. Even laughter can hide pain. The simple believe anything; the prudent think carefully.

The wise fear evil; fools are reckless. Quick tempers lead to folly. The prudent gain knowledge; fools inherit shame. The evil will bow to the good. Kindness to the poor honors God. Planning good brings love; hard work brings profit.

Wisdom is a crown to the wise; folly is its own reward. A truthful witness saves lives. Reverence for God brings security. Patience shows understanding; envy rots the bones. Oppressing the poor insults their Maker; kindness honors Him.

The wicked fall in disaster; the righteous find refuge even in death. Wisdom rests in the discerning. Righteousness exalts a nation; sin is a disgrace. A wise servant pleases the king; shameful conduct brings wrath.

A gentle answer calms anger; harsh words stir it up. The wise use knowledge well; fools pour out folly. God sees everything. Healing words are life-giving; deceit crushes the spirit. The wise accept correction; fools despise it. The righteous have treasure; the wicked face trouble.

God detests the wicked’s sacrifices but delights in the upright’s prayers. He loves those who pursue righteousness. Discipline is life-giving; rejecting it leads to death. The heart shapes one’s outlook joy brings continual feasting.

Better a little with reverence than great wealth with turmoil. Love with simplicity is better than hatred with luxury. Patience calms conflict; anger stirs it. The upright walk a clear path; the lazy face obstacles. Wise counsel brings success. Timely words bring joy.

The wise walk an upward path, avoiding death. God tears down the proud but protects the humble. He detests wicked thoughts but delights in pure words. Greed brings ruin. The righteous weigh their words; the wicked speak evil. The fear of the Lord teaches wisdom; humility precedes honor.

People make plans, but the Lord directs outcomes. God weighs motives. Commit your work to Him, and your plans will succeed. Pride leads to destruction; humility brings honor. The Lord works all things for His purpose even the wicked for judgment. Righteousness and love atone for sin.
Kings should speak with justice and uphold righteousness. Honest scales are from the Lord. Rulers detest evil and delight in upright speech. Their favor brings life; their wrath brings death.

Wisdom is better than gold; understanding than silver. The upright avoid evil. Pride leads to downfall. The wise speak graciously and persuade with pleasant words. Understanding is a fountain of life.
There’s a way that seems right but ends in death. Hunger drives labor. A scoundrel plots evil and spreads strife. Violent people mislead others. Perverse speech corrupts.
Gray hair is a crown of glory when found in righteousness. Patience is better than power. The lot is cast, but every decision is from the Lord.

Better a dry crust with peace than a feast with strife. A wise servant may rule over a disgraceful son. The Lord tests hearts like silver in a crucible. The wicked listen to evil lips. Mocking the poor insults their Maker. Grandchildren are a crown to the aged; parents are the pride of their children.

Arrogant speech is unfitting for a fool. Bribes may influence outcomes. Love overlooks faults; repeating offenses separates friends. A rebuke impresses the wise more than a hundred lashes on a fool. Evil seeks rebellion and invites punishment. Starting a quarrel is like breaching a dam stop before it breaks.

Justifying the wicked and condemning the righteous are both detestable. Fools find no joy in understanding. A friend loves at all times. A person lacking sense shakes hands on foolish pledges. A perverse heart finds no good; a deceitful tongue leads to trouble. A foolish child brings grief to their parents.

A joyful heart is good medicine; a crushed spirit dries the bones. Bribes corrupt justice. The discerning keep wisdom in view; fools wander. A foolish child brings bitterness. Even a fool is thought wise if silent discretion is shown by holding the tongue.

The self-isolated seek their own desires and reject sound judgment. Fools find no pleasure in understanding. Wickedness brings contempt. Words can be deep waters wise speech is a bubbling brook. Partiality in judgment is wrong. A fool’s mouth invites ruin. Gossip is like tasty morsels that sink deep.

Slackness is like destruction. The Lord’s name is a strong tower for the righteous. Wealth is a false security. Pride precedes downfall. Listening before speaking is wise. A person’s spirit sustains them in sickness. A gift opens doors and brings access to the great.

The first to speak seems right until cross-examined. Casting lots settles disputes. Offended people are harder to win than fortified cities. Words satisfy like food. Life and death are in the tongue’s power. A man who finds a wife finds favor. Friends may fail, but a true friend sticks closer than a brother.

Better to be poor and blameless than a fool with deceit. Zeal without knowledge is not good. A person’s own folly ruins their life. Wealth attracts friends; the poor are deserted. A false witness will not go unpunished. Wisdom brings success; loving wisdom brings life.

A false witness will perish. It’s not fitting for a fool to live in luxury. A person’s wisdom makes them slow to anger. A king’s wrath is like a lion’s roar. A foolish child is a parent’s ruin. Discipline your child while there is hope. Kindness to the poor is lending to the Lord.

Discipline your children; don’t be a willing party to their death. A hot-tempered person must bear the consequences. Listen to advice and accept instruction. Many plans fill a heart, but the Lord’s purpose prevails. The fear of the Lord leads to life. A lazy person won’t even feed themselves. Mockers face judgment; fools invite beatings.

Wine is a mocker; beer a brawler. Avoid provoking kings. Sluggards don’t plow in season. Counsel is deep water; the wise draw it out. Many claim loyalty, but who can find a faithful person? The righteous walk with integrity. Who can say, 'I have kept my heart pure'?

The Lord detests dishonest weights. Even children show their character by their actions. Ears and eyes are from the Lord. Don’t love sleep or you’ll grow poor. 'It’s no good!' says the buyer then boasts. Gossip betrays confidence; avoid those who talk too much.

Cursing parents brings darkness. An inheritance gained too soon won’t be blessed. Don’t say, 'I’ll get even' wait for the Lord. The Lord directs steps. It’s a trap to make rash vows. A wise king winnows out the wicked. The human spirit is God’s lamp. Blows and wounds cleanse away evil.

The king’s heart is in the Lord’s hand. Doing right pleases God more than sacrifice. Haughty eyes and proud hearts are sin. Diligent plans lead to profit. The wicked’s violence drags them away. The guilty walk a crooked path. Better to live on a roof than with a quarrelsome wife.

The wicked crave evil. The wise consider the house of the wicked. Whoever shuts their ears to the poor will not be heard. A gift in secret soothes anger. Justice brings joy to the righteous. Whoever strays from wisdom rests among the dead. The wise store up treasure; fools devour it.

Whoever pursues righteousness and love finds life and honor. The wise scale the city of the mighty. Guard your tongue and preserve your life. The proud and arrogant are mockers. The lazy crave but get nothing. Sacrifices from the wicked are detestable. Victory belongs to the Lord.

A good name is more valuable than riches. God is the Maker of both rich and poor. The prudent foresee danger and avoid it. Humility and reverence bring wealth and honor. Thorns await the perverse. Train children early, and they will not depart from the path.

The borrower is servant to the lender. Sowing injustice reaps trouble. Generosity is blessed. Drive out mockers to end strife. The Lord preserves knowledge but overthrows the unfaithful. Laziness and adultery lead to ruin. Oppressing the poor or flattering the rich both end in loss.
An introduction to the sayings of the wise: listen carefully, keep them in your heart, and trust in the Lord. These words are reliable and meant to teach truth and sound answers.
Do not exploit the poor or associate with the hot-tempered. Avoid moving boundary stones or pledging what you can’t repay. Diligent people will stand before kings, not obscure men.
Be cautious when dining with rulers don’t crave delicacies. Don’t wear yourself out chasing wealth. Don’t eat with the stingy; their words are deceptive and their food bitter.

Don’t waste wisdom on fools. Don’t move ancient boundaries or exploit the fatherless. Discipline your children it brings hope. Let your heart delight in wisdom. Don’t envy sinners; fear the Lord always, for your future is secure.
Avoid drunkenness and gluttony they lead to poverty. Listen to your parents and seek truth. Rejoice in a wise child. Avoid the seductress her path leads to destruction.
A vivid warning against drunkenness: it brings sorrow, strife, hallucinations, and vulnerability. Though it bites like a snake, the drunkard returns to it again.
Don’t envy the wicked. Wisdom builds a house and wins battles. Fools falter in crisis. Rescue those being led to death God weighs motives and repays everyone accordingly.
Wisdom is sweet like honey and leads to hope. The righteous may fall but rise again; the wicked stumble into ruin. Don’t rejoice at your enemy’s fall. Fear the Lord and the king don’t join rebels.

Show no partiality in judgment. Honest answers are like a kiss. Prepare your work before building your house. Don’t testify without cause or seek revenge. Laziness leads to ruin, like a neglected field overgrown with thorns.

These proverbs of Solomon were copied by Hezekiah’s men. Concealing matters is God’s glory; searching them out is a king’s. Don’t exalt yourself before rulers. Settle disputes privately to avoid shame.

A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold. Wise rebuke is like fine jewelry. Reliable messengers refresh the soul. Don’t overstay your welcome. False testimony and betrayal are painful. Singing to a heavy heart is like vinegar on soda.
Feed your enemy and you’ll heap coals on their head. A contentious spouse is like constant dripping. Self-control is better than conquest. A broken spirit or lack of restraint leaves one vulnerable.

Honor doesn’t suit a fool. Fools repeat folly like a dog returns to vomit. Don’t answer a fool according to his folly yet sometimes you must. A fool is dangerous whether speaking or silent. There’s more hope for a fool than for someone wise in their own eyes.

The lazy make absurd excuses. A door turns on its hinges like a sluggard in bed. A meddler grabs a dog by the ears. Jokes that harm are no joke. Gossip is like tasty morsels it sinks deep and spreads strife.
Fervent words can hide a wicked heart. Hatred disguises itself with speech, but it will be exposed. A lying tongue hates its victims, and flattery leads to ruin.

Don’t boast about tomorrow you don’t know what it holds. Let others praise you, not your own mouth. A fool’s provocation is heavier than stone. Open rebuke is better than hidden love. Wounds from a friend are faithful; kisses from an enemy are deceitful.

A full soul loathes honey, but to the hungry even bitter is sweet. A person who strays from home is like a bird from its nest. Iron sharpens iron so friends sharpen one another. A loud blessing early in the morning can feel like a curse.

A quarrelsome spouse is like constant dripping. As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another. The grave and human desire are never satisfied. A person is tested by the praise they receive. Though you grind a fool, folly won’t leave them.

Be diligent to know the state of your flocks and herds. Riches don’t last forever, but careful stewardship provides lasting provision. The land yields clothing, food, and sustenance for your household.

The wicked flee though no one pursues; the righteous are bold as a lion. A nation with many rulers lacks stability. Those who forsake the law praise the wicked. Evil people don’t understand justice; the righteous seek the Lord. Turning away from the law makes prayer detestable.

Those who lead the upright astray will fall into their own pit. The rich may be wise in their own eyes, but the poor with discernment see through them. Concealing sin brings no prosperity; confessing and forsaking it brings mercy. A ruler without understanding is oppressive. A murderer is haunted by guilt.

The blameless walk securely; the crooked fall suddenly. The greedy stir up conflict. Trusting in oneself is foolish; walking in wisdom brings deliverance. Giving to the poor brings blessing; ignoring them brings curses. When the wicked rise, people hide; when they perish, the righteous flourish.

A person who resists correction will be broken beyond remedy. When the righteous thrive, people rejoice; when the wicked rule, they groan. Discipline brings wisdom; indulgence brings shame. The wise bring calm to conflict; fools rage and mock.

Bloodthirsty people hate the upright. A fool vents everything; the wise hold back. The poor and oppressor have this in common the Lord gives sight to both. Discipline your child and find rest. A servant won’t respond to mere words. Hasty speech leads to folly.

Pampering a servant leads to grief. An angry person stirs up conflict. Pride brings downfall; humility brings honor. Fear of man is a trap; trusting the Lord brings safety. The righteous detest the dishonest; the wicked detest the upright.
Agur confesses his ignorance and marvels at God’s wisdom. Every word of God is pure; don’t add to His words or be proven a liar.
Agur prays for honesty and daily provision neither poverty nor riches. He warns against slandering servants and describes generations marked by arrogance, greed, and cruelty.

The leech has two daughters: 'Give! Give!' Four things never say 'Enough': the grave, the barren womb, dry land, and fire. He lists things that amaze him like an eagle in the sky or a ship at sea and warns against servants who become kings and unloved women who marry.

Four small creatures are wise: ants, rock badgers, locusts, and lizards. Four things are stately: lions, roosters, goats, and kings. Stirring up anger produces strife pressing milk brings butter, and pressing the nose brings blood.
King Lemuel shares wisdom from his mother: avoid destructive indulgence, defend the rights of the poor, and speak up for the voiceless.
A virtuous woman is priceless. She is trustworthy, diligent, generous, wise, and fears the Lord. Her family praises her, and her works bring her honor at the city gates.
The Teacher introduces himself and declares the central theme: all is vanity human toil under the sun yields no lasting gain.
Nature’s cycles continue endlessly, while human life is fleeting and forgotten. Nothing is truly new; all things repeat.
The Teacher recounts his pursuit of wisdom and knowledge, only to find it brings grief and sorrow, not satisfaction.
He tests pleasure, wealth, and great accomplishments gardens, servants, riches, and entertainment but finds them all meaningless, like chasing the wind.
He compares wisdom and folly, noting that while wisdom is better, both the wise and the fool die alike. This realization leads him to despair.
He laments that all his labor will be left to someone else, who may be wise or foolish. Yet he concludes that enjoying one’s work is a gift from God.
A poetic reflection on life’s seasons there is a time for everything: birth and death, weeping and laughing, war and peace.
Though humans cannot grasp God’s full plan, He has made everything beautiful in its time. The best we can do is rejoice and do good.
The Teacher observes injustice and death, noting that humans and animals share the same fate. He urges contentment in one’s work.
He sees oppression and suffering with no comforter, concluding that the dead or unborn are better off than the living.
Toil and success are often driven by envy. The solitary worker gains much but has no one to share it with this too is vanity.
He praises companionship: two are better than one for support, warmth, and strength. A cord of three strands is not easily broken.
A poor but wise youth may rise to power, yet even he will be forgotten. Popularity is fleeting and meaningless.
Approach God with reverence. Speak few words and fulfill your vows. Many words and dreams are empty fear God instead.
Don’t be surprised by injustice and bureaucracy. Wealth does not satisfy; the more one has, the more one worries. The laborer sleeps peacefully, but the rich are restless.
Hoarding wealth can lead to harm. One may lose everything and leave the world as they entered it. The Teacher concludes that enjoying one’s work and portion is a gift from God.
The Teacher describes a grievous evil: a man blessed with wealth, honor, and children, yet unable to enjoy them. Even a stillborn child is better off, for it finds rest without toil or sorrow.
Human appetite is never satisfied. The wise gain no lasting advantage over fools, and wandering desires are emptier than contentment with what one has.
Whatever exists has already been named. Humans cannot contend with God or know what is truly good or what the future holds. Life is fleeting and uncertain.
A good name and the day of death are better than birth. Mourning refines the heart more than laughter. The wise embrace sorrow and rebuke, while fools chase mirth.
Oppression and bribes corrupt. Patience is better than pride. Don’t long for the past. God made both prosperity and adversity accept both, for we cannot know what comes next.

The Teacher warns against extremes in righteousness or wickedness. No one is sinless. Wisdom strengthens, but even the wise fall short. Don’t take every word to heart others may have cursed you as you have them.
The Teacher sought wisdom but found it elusive. He discovered that people have gone astray from uprightness, and that folly and deceit are traps. True wisdom is rare.
Wisdom brightens the face and softens harshness. Obey the king’s command, for his word is powerful. No one can control the wind, avoid death, or escape the consequences of wickedness.
