The righteous and the wicked often experience the same fate, yet the Teacher affirms that it will go well for those who fear God, even if justice seems delayed.
Life under the sun is full of paradoxes righteous people suffer, and the wicked prosper. The Teacher commends joy in life’s simple pleasures, for God’s work is beyond human comprehension.
The same fate death awaits all, whether righteous or wicked. The living still have hope, but the dead know nothing and have no further share in life.
Enjoy life: eat, drink, love your spouse, and work with all your might. These are God’s gifts, for there is no activity or reward in the grave.
Time and chance affect everyone. The swift, strong, or wise don’t always succeed. No one knows their time death can come suddenly, like a trap.
Wisdom is better than strength, as shown by a poor man who saved a city. Yet his wisdom was forgotten. Quiet wisdom is more powerful than loud folly, though often ignored.
A little folly can outweigh wisdom and honor. The wise act with calm and discernment, even under pressure; the fool reveals his lack of sense.
Foolishness in high places leads to disorder. Proper skill and timing are essential whether splitting logs or charming snakes, wisdom is needed to avoid harm.
The words of the wise are gracious; the fool’s talk consumes him. He multiplies words without knowledge and wearies himself with aimless effort.

Woe to the land ruled by immature leaders; blessed is the land with noble rulers. Laziness leads to decay. Money answers many needs, but don’t curse rulers even in private for your words may be overheard.

Be generous and take risks cast your bread upon the waters, for you don’t know what will return. Just as you can’t predict the wind or the growth of a child in the womb, you can’t fully understand God’s work. So sow your seed morning and evening, not knowing which effort will prosper.
Light is sweet, and life is a gift to be enjoyed. Rejoice in your youth, but remember that all will be judged. Remove sorrow and evil from your heart, for youth and vigor are fleeting.

Remember your Creator in the days of youth, before the difficult days of aging come. Through vivid metaphors darkened sun, trembling keepers, broken pitcher the Teacher describes the decline of the body and the return of the spirit to God. All is vanity, he repeats.
The Teacher was wise and taught knowledge with care, crafting proverbs and truths like goads and well-driven nails. Yet endless study can be wearisome beware of going beyond what is written.
The conclusion of the matter: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole duty of humanity. God will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing, whether good or evil.
The bride longs for her beloved's love, describing it as more delightful than wine. She yearns for intimacy and rejoices in his affection.
She speaks of her dark beauty and asks where he pastures his flocks, longing to be near him without shame or confusion.
The beloved responds with admiration, likening her to a noble mare and adorning her with jewelry and praise.
Their affections blossom as they exchange compliments fragrant and lush, they delight in each other’s presence and beauty.
She calls herself a rose of Sharon, and he elevates her above other women like a lily among thorns.
She delights in his presence, describing his love as shade and sweetness. She is lovesick and urges restraint love should not be awakened prematurely.
She joyfully recounts hearing his voice and seeing him come like a gazelle. He invites her into the blooming landscape of spring.
He calls her his dove, hidden and lovely. She urges him to be like a young stag leaping through the mountains at day’s end.
In a dream, the bride searches for her beloved through the city. When she finds him, she won’t let him go. Again, she urges not to awaken love before its time.
A royal procession is described Solomon’s palanquin, guarded by warriors. The bride is adorned like royalty, and the scene celebrates their union.
The bridegroom lavishly praises her physical beauty from her eyes to her stature declaring her altogether lovely, without flaw.
He calls her to journey with him and describes her love as intoxicating. He likens her to a locked garden precious and pure, full of fragrant delight.
She invites the winds to blow upon her garden so that its fragrance may spread, welcoming her beloved to come and enjoy its fullness.
The bridegroom rejoices in the consummation of love, inviting friends to celebrate the fullness of their union.

The bride dreams of her beloved knocking, but hesitates to respond. When she opens the door, he is gone. She searches for him, is wounded by the watchmen, and pleads with the daughters of Jerusalem to help her find him.
Asked what makes her beloved so special, the bride describes him in vivid, majestic detail his appearance, strength, and sweetness declaring him altogether lovely and her closest friend.
The daughters of Jerusalem ask where her beloved has gone. She replies that he is in his garden, and affirms their mutual belonging: 'I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine.'
The bridegroom praises her beauty, comparing her to majestic cities and noble women. She is unique and radiant among many.
The bride reflects on going to the garden and being swept up in love’s chariot. The daughters call her to return, marveling at her grace.
The bridegroom extols the bride’s beauty from head to toe her stature, grace, and allure. He is captivated by her love and desires her deeply.
The bride declares her devotion and invites him to the countryside to enjoy love’s fruits in the blossoming vineyards.
The bride longs to express her love openly, without shame. She desires to bring her beloved into her mother’s house and awaken love in its proper time.
Love is described as strong as death, unyielding as the grave, a blazing flame that cannot be quenched. It is priceless and enduring.
The bride’s brothers reflect on her early innocence. She declares her maturity and faithfulness, and Solomon is contrasted with her own vineyard her love, which she gives freely.
The bridegroom listens for her voice, and she calls him to hurry to her like a gazelle on the mountains of spices love’s final invitation.
The vision of Isaiah, son of Amoz, concerning Judah and Jerusalem during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah.
God accuses His rebellious children of forsaking Him. Despite their corruption, a faithful remnant remains, or they would have been destroyed like Sodom.
God rejects empty rituals. He calls the people to repentance, promising cleansing and blessing if they obey, but judgment if they resist.
Jerusalem is described as once faithful but now corrupt. God promises to purge it through judgment, restoring righteousness, while the unrepentant will be consumed.
A vision of the future: all nations will stream to the mountain of the Lord to learn His ways. Peace will prevail, and weapons will be transformed into tools of cultivation.
God has forsaken His people because they have filled themselves with pagan practices and pride. He will humble all human arrogance.
The day of the Lord will bring terror to the proud and lofty. God alone will be exalted. People will flee to caves, abandoning idols, as God shakes the earth.
Judah’s leadership will collapse. With capable rulers gone, inexperienced and oppressive ones will arise, leading to disorder and shame.
Jerusalem’s downfall stems from public sin and defiance. God holds the leaders accountable for plundering His people and crushing the poor.
God rebukes the vanity and pride of Zion’s daughters. He will strip away their finery, leaving them in disgrace and mourning.
In the wake of judgment, social disorder continues women seek to erase reproach by uniting with one man.
A future hope emerges: the Branch of the Lord will be glorious. The remnant will be holy, cleansed by judgment, and sheltered by God's presence like Israel in the wilderness.
God sings a love song for His vineyard Israel. Despite His careful cultivation, it yielded only bad fruit. Therefore, He will remove its protection and allow it to fall into ruin.
A series of woes condemn greed, drunkenness, deception, pride, and injustice. People call evil good and good evil, provoking God’s anger.
Because of their rejection of God’s word, judgment will come like fire consuming straw. A distant and powerful nation will swiftly overtake them like a roaring storm.

Isaiah sees the Lord exalted in the temple, surrounded by seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy.' Overwhelmed by his sin, he is purified by a burning coal from the altar, symbolizing cleansing and readiness for divine service.
God asks whom to send, and Isaiah responds, 'Here am I, send me.' He is commissioned to preach to a people who will not listen, yet a holy remnant will remain like a stump after judgment.
During a political crisis, Isaiah tells King Ahaz not to fear the alliance of Syria and Israel. Their plans will fail, and faith not fear is the path to stability.
Ahaz refuses to ask for a sign, so God gives one: a virgin will conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, meaning 'God with us.' This child is a sign of divine presence amid looming judgment.
God warns that Assyria, the very nation Ahaz trusts, will bring devastation. The land will become desolate, and prosperity will be reduced to survival.
Isaiah names his son Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz as a sign that Assyria will swiftly conquer Syria and Israel. Though enemies plot, their plans will fail because 'God is with us' (Immanuel).
Isaiah is warned not to follow the fearful ways of the people. He urges trust in God’s word, not in mediums or conspiracies. Those who reject God will face darkness and distress.
A great light will shine on those in darkness. A child will be born Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace who will reign with justice forever.
Despite repeated warnings, Israel remains proud and unrepentant. God’s anger is not turned away, and judgment continues through internal strife and external enemies.
Woe to those who write unjust laws and oppress the poor. Judgment will come, and no one will escape the day of reckoning.
Assyria is God’s instrument of judgment, but its arrogance will lead to its own downfall. God will punish its pride and reduce its army like a forest stripped bare.
A remnant of Israel will return and trust in the Lord. Though Assyria threatens, God will protect Zion. The enemy’s advance will be halted, and the proud will be cut down like trees.

A shoot will come from Jesse’s stump a righteous ruler filled with the Spirit of the Lord. He will judge with equity, defend the poor, and strike the wicked with His word. Righteousness and faithfulness will be His belt.

Under His reign, creation will be at peace wolves with lambs, children with serpents. The earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord. The Root of Jesse will be a banner for the nations, and Gentiles will seek Him.
God will gather His scattered people from all nations. Judah and Ephraim will be reconciled. A highway will be made for the remnant, like the path from Egypt in the Exodus.
A song of thanksgiving: the people praise God for His salvation, strength, and comfort. They draw joyfully from the wells of salvation and proclaim His greatness among the nations.

An oracle against Babylon: God summons nations to execute His wrath. The day of the Lord will bring terror, cosmic upheaval, and judgment on the proud and wicked. Babylon’s people will be dismayed and scattered.
The Medes will destroy Babylon without regard for silver or mercy. The once-glorious city will become desolate, inhabited only by wild creatures.
God will have compassion on Jacob and restore Israel. Foreigners will join them, and Israel will rule over former oppressors.

A taunt against the king of Babylon: his fall is mocked as he descends to Sheol. His pride is shattered, and he is likened to the fallen morning star. God will sweep Babylon with destruction and leave it desolate.
The Lord declares His unshakable plan to break Assyria and protect His people. His purpose will stand, and no one can thwart it.
An oracle against Philistia: though Assyria’s king has died, worse is coming. The Lord will establish Zion as a refuge for the afflicted, while Philistia will face ruin.

An oracle concerning Moab: its cities are laid waste overnight. The people mourn in sackcloth and weep over their ruined land. Refugees flee with sorrow, and the rivers run red with blood. God expresses deep grief over Moab’s downfall.
Moab is urged to send tribute and seek refuge in Judah. A throne will be established in steadfast love, and a righteous ruler from David’s line will judge with justice.
Moab’s pride and arrogance are exposed. Despite its former glory, Moab will wail over its ruined vineyards and lost harvests. The prophet mourns for its downfall.
The Lord declares that within three years, Moab’s splendor will fade, and only a small, feeble remnant will remain.
An oracle against Damascus: the city will become a ruin, and its alliance with Israel will fail. Both nations will lose their strength and glory.
Israel’s glory will fade like a harvest left to gleaners. Because they forgot their Maker and trusted in idols, their efforts will fail and their gardens will wither.
Though many nations roar like the sea, God will rebuke them, and they will flee like chaff before the wind terror by night, gone by morning.

A message to Cush (Ethiopia): swift messengers are sent to a tall, smooth-skinned people. God watches quietly until the right moment, then acts decisively. In the end, Cush will bring tribute to the Lord in Zion.
An oracle against Egypt: the Lord will strike Egypt with civil war, confusion, and drought. Its idols will tremble, and its wisdom will fail. Leaders will stagger like drunkards.

Yet a future hope is declared: Egypt will fear the Lord, speak His language, and worship Him. Along with Assyria and Israel, Egypt will be blessed as God’s people 'Blessed be Egypt my people, Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.'

Isaiah walks barefoot and stripped for three years as a sign against Egypt and Cush. This symbolizes how Assyria will lead their captives away in shame. Judah is warned not to rely on these nations for help.

A prophecy against Babylon: Isaiah sees a terrifying vision of its fall, likened to a desert storm. The watchman reports, 'Babylon is fallen, is fallen!' a cry of judgment against its pride and cruelty.
A brief oracle to Dumah (Edom): a voice asks the watchman about the night. The answer is cryptic morning comes, but also night hinting at uncertainty and coming judgment.
A prophecy against Arabia: caravans seek refuge, but within a year, Kedar’s glory will fade. Only a few archers will remain, for the Lord has spoken.

An oracle concerning Jerusalem: the city rejoices even as destruction looms. Instead of repentance, the people indulge in revelry 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.' God declares their sin will not be forgiven.

A rebuke to Shebna, a proud official who builds a grand tomb for himself. God will replace him with Eliakim, a servant who will carry the key of David. Yet even Eliakim’s support will eventually give way, showing that no human leader is ultimate.
A lament over Tyre: the great trading city is silenced. Its merchants and allies mourn. God humbles its pride, and its wealth is forgotten for seventy years.
After seventy years, Tyre will return to trade, but her profits will be set apart for the Lord to provide for those who dwell in His presence.
A global judgment is declared: the earth is laid waste because of its inhabitants’ sin. Joy fades, cities are desolate, and only a remnant remains like olives after harvest.
Amid judgment, a song rises from the ends of the earth praising God’s majesty. Yet Isaiah mourns the devastation. The earth reels like a drunkard. In the end, the Lord will reign gloriously in Zion.
A song of praise: the Lord has done marvelous things, bringing down ruthless nations and becoming a refuge for the poor and needy.
On Mount Zion, God will prepare a rich feast and destroy the shroud of death. He will wipe away every tear and remove His people’s disgrace.
The people will rejoice in God’s salvation. Moab, representing prideful opposition, will be trampled down. Human arrogance will be brought low, and the Lord alone will be exalted.
A song of trust in God’s protection: the righteous nation enters the strong city whose walls are salvation. The steadfast in mind are kept in perfect peace because they trust in the Lord.
The path of the righteous is level, and they wait for God’s name and justice. Even in distress, they seek Him. Other lords ruled them, but only God is remembered and exalted.
In suffering, the people cry out like a woman in labor, but their efforts bring no deliverance. Yet God promises resurrection and calls His people to hide until His wrath passes.
God will punish Leviathan, the fleeing serpent symbol of chaos and evil with His mighty sword.

A song of the fruitful vineyard: God watches over it and no longer pours out wrath. He calls for reconciliation. Though Israel was struck, it was to purge sin. The fortified city will be desolate, for its people lack understanding.
God will gather His people one by one from exile. A great trumpet will sound, and the outcasts will worship the Lord in Jerusalem.

Woe to Ephraim’s proud drunkards: their fading beauty will be trampled. God offers a crown of glory to the remnant. But Judah mocks His word, so He will speak to them through foreign tongues, and they will stumble.
The leaders of Jerusalem have made a covenant with death, thinking they’ll escape judgment. But God lays a tested cornerstone in Zion. Justice will sweep away their refuge of lies.
A parable of the farmer: God’s judgments are measured and wise, like a farmer who knows how to thresh each grain properly. His counsel is wonderful and excellent.
Woe to Ariel (Jerusalem): though it celebrates its festivals, it will be besieged. Yet its enemies will vanish like a dream, and God will defend His city.
The people are blind and honor God with lips but not hearts. Their worship is rote, and their wisdom is upside down thinking they can hide from God.
Yet hope arises: Lebanon will become fertile, the deaf will hear, and the humble will rejoice. The ruthless will vanish, and those who err in spirit will gain understanding.

Woe to the rebellious children who seek Egypt’s help without consulting God. Their alliance will bring shame. They reject God’s word and prefer illusions, but their trust in oppression will collapse suddenly.
Yet the Lord longs to be gracious. When His people cry out, He will answer. Though they face hardship, He will guide and heal them. Idols will be cast away, and the land will flourish.
The Lord comes in wrath to strike Assyria with His voice and fire. His judgment is prepared like Topheth, a burning place, for the king.
Woe to those who rely on Egypt for help instead of trusting the Holy One of Israel. Egypt is human, not divine, and both helper and helped will fall together.
God will defend Jerusalem like a lion or hovering birds. He calls His people to return to Him and promises to strike down the Assyrian invaders with fire, not human weapons.

A righteous king will reign, and princes will rule justly. The eyes and ears of the people will be opened. Fools and scoundrels will no longer be honored, but noble people will be recognized for their integrity.
Complacent women are warned of coming desolation. Fields and cities will be abandoned until the Spirit is poured out.
When the Spirit is poured out, justice and righteousness will flourish. Peace, security, and fruitfulness will return to the land, and God’s people will dwell in quiet confidence.
Woe to the destroyer who has not yet been destroyed. The Lord will rise and bring stability, salvation, and wisdom to those who fear Him.
Jerusalem trembles as enemies approach, but God will arise and scatter them. Sinners fear His presence, but the righteous will dwell with Him in safety and abundance.
The people will see the King in His beauty and a peaceful Zion. No enemy will invade again. The Lord will be their judge, lawgiver, and king He will save them and heal their wounds.
All nations are summoned to witness God’s wrath. His sword is filled with blood, and Edom is singled out for total destruction a sacrifice of judgment.
Edom will become a desolate wasteland, inhabited by wild creatures. Its land will burn and never be quenched. God’s judgment is precise and permanent, fulfilling His book of destiny.
The wilderness will rejoice and blossom. The weak are encouraged: 'Be strong, do not fear! Your God will come with vengeance and save you.'
The blind will see, the deaf will hear, and the lame will leap. A highway of holiness will lead the redeemed to Zion with everlasting joy sorrow and sighing will flee away.

In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Assyria’s king sends the Rabshakeh to Jerusalem. He mocks Judah’s trust in Egypt and questions their reliance on the Lord, claiming God Himself sent Assyria to destroy them.

Hezekiah’s officials ask the Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, but he speaks loudly in Hebrew to intimidate the people. He urges surrender, promising comfort and mocking trust in God. The people remain silent, and the officials report to Hezekiah in distress.
Hezekiah tears his clothes and seeks Isaiah’s counsel. Isaiah assures him that the Lord will cause the Assyrian king to retreat and fall by the sword in his own land.

The Rabshakeh returns to find the Assyrian king fighting elsewhere but sends another message mocking God. Hezekiah prays earnestly, exalting God’s uniqueness and asking for deliverance so all nations may know the Lord alone is God.

God responds through Isaiah: Assyria’s pride will be humbled, and it will not enter Jerusalem. That night, the angel of the Lord strikes down 185,000 Assyrians. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh and is later killed by his own sons.

Hezekiah becomes deathly ill. Isaiah tells him to prepare for death, but Hezekiah prays with tears. God hears and grants him fifteen more years, confirming the promise with a miraculous sign: the shadow on the sundial moves backward.
Hezekiah writes a psalm reflecting on his near-death experience. He praises God for healing him and vows to walk humbly all his days, declaring that the living give thanks not the dead.

Envoys from Babylon visit Hezekiah after his recovery. He proudly shows them all his treasures. Isaiah rebukes him, prophesying that all will be carried off to Babylon, including his descendants. Hezekiah accepts the word but finds comfort that there will be peace in his days.

A voice of comfort declares that Jerusalem’s sin has been paid for. A herald cries, 'Prepare the way of the Lord!' Every valley will be lifted, and God’s glory will be revealed. The Lord comes with power and tenderness, like a shepherd gathering lambs.

God’s greatness is unmatched He measures the seas, weighs mountains, and needs no counselor. Nations are like dust before Him. Idols are nothing. Lift your eyes and see: the Creator calls the stars by name.

God does not grow weary. He gives strength to the faint. Even youths stumble, but those who wait on the Lord will renew their strength they will soar on wings like eagles, run and not grow weary, walk and not faint.
God calls the nations to listen as He raises up one from the east (likely Cyrus). Though the nations forge idols in fear, God alone directs history.
God reassures Israel, His chosen servant, not to fear. He will strengthen, help, and uphold them. The poor and needy will be refreshed, and creation itself will testify to God’s hand.
God challenges idols to prove their power. They are empty and powerless, unlike the One who foretells and fulfills His word. He alone raises up the deliverer.
A servant is introduced gentle, just, and chosen by God. He will bring justice to the nations and be a light to the Gentiles. God declares new things before they spring forth.
A new song rises to the Lord from all creation. God will act mightily, turning darkness to light. Those who trust in idols will be put to shame.
Israel is blind and deaf, though chosen to carry God’s law. Because of disobedience, they are plundered and exiled, yet they do not understand why.
God declares His love and redemption for Israel. He formed them, calls them by name, and promises to be with them through fire and flood. He will gather them from all directions.
God alone is Savior. He calls witnesses to testify that there is no other god. He is doing a new thing making a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert for His people.
Despite God’s grace, Israel has not called on Him but has burdened Him with sin. Yet He promises to blot out their transgressions for His own sake.
God reaffirms His love for Jacob and promises to pour out His Spirit. Israel will flourish and proudly bear His name. He alone is the first and the last there is no other Rock.
A vivid satire of idol-making: people use the same wood to cook food and carve gods. They are blind and deceived, worshiping what cannot save.
God calls Israel to remember that He formed and redeemed them. He confirms His word and names Cyrus as the one who will rebuild Jerusalem and lay the temple’s foundation.

God speaks to Cyrus, His anointed, whom He will empower to subdue nations and release Israel. Though Cyrus does not know God, he is chosen for Israel’s sake. God alone forms light and darkness, and His purposes will stand.
The nations will come to Israel, acknowledging that God is with them. Idols are powerless, but the Lord is a righteous Savior. Every knee will bow, and every tongue will swear allegiance to Him.

Bel and Nebo, Babylon’s idols, are carried off as burdens they cannot save themselves or others. In contrast, God carries His people from birth to old age. Unlike lifeless idols, He is living and dependable.

God calls His people to remember His unmatched power and faithfulness. He declares the end from the beginning and will bring His purpose to pass. He is bringing righteousness near and will save Zion through His chosen one.

A taunt against Babylon: once proud and luxurious, she will be humbled and exposed. Her sorceries and false security will not save her. Disaster will strike suddenly, and no one will be able to deliver her from God’s judgment.
God rebukes Israel for their stubbornness. He foretold events so they couldn’t credit idols. Though they are obstinate, He refines them for His name’s sake, not because of their righteousness.

God alone is the Creator and Redeemer. He calls His people to listen and obey, promising peace like a river if they had followed His commands. He urges them to leave Babylon and proclaim His redemption with joy 'There is no peace for the wicked.'
The Servant speaks: called from the womb, hidden and prepared by God. Though he feels his labor is in vain, God honors him and expands his mission to restore Israel and be a light to the nations.
God promises to restore His people and guide them with compassion. The afflicted will be comforted, and the heavens and earth will rejoice at the Lord’s mercy.

Zion feels forgotten, but God compares His love to a mother’s unfailing and tender. He will gather her children, shame her oppressors, and make her enemies feed on their own flesh. All will know He is the Redeemer.
God asks why His people think He abandoned them. Their exile was due to their own sin, not His rejection. His power to redeem remains, but they refused to respond.

The Servant speaks again: he is taught by God, obedient even in suffering. He offers his back to beatings and his face to shame, yet trusts the Lord to vindicate him. Those who fear the Lord should walk in His light, not their own fire.
God calls His people to remember their roots Abraham and Sarah and trust in His power to comfort and restore. His righteousness and salvation are everlasting, unlike the fading strength of men.
A prayer rises for God to awaken as in ancient days, when He defeated the sea monster Rahab. God responds with assurance: He will redeem Zion, guide His people, and plant His words in their hearts.
Jerusalem is pictured as a drunken woman, reeling from God’s wrath. But now the cup of judgment will pass to her tormentors, and she will rise again.
Zion is called to awaken and clothe herself in strength and splendor. God’s people, once sold for nothing, will be redeemed without money. His name will be known again.
Beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news peace, salvation, and the reign of God. The Lord will go before and behind His people as they depart Babylon in holiness.
The Servant will be exalted, but first marred beyond recognition. Kings will be silenced by what they see something once unheard and now revealed.
The Servant is despised and rejected unremarkable in appearance, acquainted with grief, and dismissed by men.
He bears our pain and punishment. Though we strayed like sheep, the Lord laid on Him the iniquity of us all.
Silent in suffering, He is led like a lamb to slaughter. Though innocent, He is cut off and buried with the wicked and the rich.
It was the Lord’s will to crush Him, yet He will see His offspring and prolong His days. Through His suffering, He justifies many and receives a portion among the great.
The barren woman is called to sing her children will outnumber the married. God promises everlasting compassion, unlike the fleeting flood of Noah. His covenant of peace will not be removed.
Afflicted Jerusalem will be rebuilt with precious stones. Her children will be taught by the Lord and enjoy great peace. No weapon formed against her will succeed, for her righteousness is from God.
An invitation to all who thirst: come, buy without money. God offers an everlasting covenant like that made with David. Nations will be drawn to the glory of the Lord.
Seek the Lord while He may be found. His thoughts and ways are higher than ours. His word will not return void. Joy and peace will mark the return of His people, and creation will rejoice.

God calls for justice and righteousness, promising blessing to all who keep His covenant including foreigners and eunuchs. His house will be a house of prayer for all nations, and He will gather others to His people beyond the exiles of Israel.
A rebuke to Israel’s leaders: they are blind, greedy, and self-indulgent, failing to shepherd the people. Like mute dogs, they seek their own gain and ignore the danger approaching.

The righteous perish unnoticed, but they enter peace. In contrast, the wicked pursue idolatry and sexual immorality, making alliances with false gods. God exposes their hypocrisy and declares that their idols will not save them when trouble comes.
God promises to revive the lowly and contrite, offering healing and peace to the repentant. But there is no peace for the wicked, who are like a restless sea churning up mire and dirt.

God confronts false fasting rituals without righteousness. True fasting is to loose injustice, free the oppressed, and care for the needy. Then light will break forth, healing will come, and the Lord will guide continually.
Honoring the Sabbath by delighting in the Lord brings joy and blessing. God promises to lift up those who find their pleasure in Him rather than in selfish pursuits.
God’s arm is not too short to save, but sin has separated the people from Him. Their hands are stained with violence, and their paths are filled with injustice and ruin. They do not know peace.
The people confess their guilt and recognize the absence of justice and truth. They grope like the blind and mourn their condition. Truth has stumbled in the streets, and honesty cannot enter.

Seeing no one to intervene, God arms Himself with righteousness and salvation. He repays His enemies and makes a covenant with His people: His Spirit and words will remain with them and their descendants forever.

Zion is called to arise and shine, for God’s glory has come. Though darkness covers the earth, nations will be drawn to her light. Sons and daughters will return, and the wealth of nations will flow in.

Foreigners will rebuild Zion’s walls, and kings will serve her. Violence and sorrow will end. The Lord will be her everlasting light, and her people will be righteous. The least will become a mighty nation, for the Lord will hasten it in its time.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon the Servant to proclaim good news to the poor, bind up the brokenhearted, and announce liberty and comfort. He exchanges ashes for beauty, mourning for joy, and despair for praise.
The ruined cities will be rebuilt. Foreigners will serve Israel, and the people will be called priests of the Lord. God loves justice and will make an everlasting covenant with them.
The prophet rejoices in God, who clothes him with salvation and righteousness like a bridegroom and bride. Just as the earth brings forth growth, so the Lord will cause righteousness to spring up.
For Zion’s sake, the prophet will not be silent until her righteousness shines. She will be called by a new name and no longer forsaken. God delights in her like a bridegroom rejoices over his bride.

Watchmen are appointed to pray continually. The Lord swears He will no longer let enemies devour Zion’s harvest. Salvation is coming, and the people will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of the Lord.
The Lord comes from Edom, garments stained from treading the winepress of wrath alone. In His anger, He trampled nations and poured out judgment.
The prophet recalls God’s steadfast love and mercy in redeeming Israel. Though they rebelled, He became their Savior, carrying them through the wilderness.
A plea for God to look down from heaven and act. The people feel abandoned and long for His presence. They ask why He lets them wander and why enemies possess His sanctuary.

The prophet cries for God to rend the heavens and come down. He acknowledges their sin and unworthiness, yet appeals to God as Father and potter. The desolation of Zion and the temple is mourned, and mercy is sought.
God reveals He was found by those who did not seek Him, while His own people provoked Him with idolatry. Judgment will fall on the rebellious, but His servants will rejoice and be blessed.
A new heavens and new earth are promised. Former troubles will be forgotten. Jerusalem will be a place of joy, long life, peace, and harmony even between wolf and lamb.
God declares that heaven is His throne and He looks to the humble and contrite. Empty rituals are condemned. Those who tremble at His word will be vindicated, while mockers will be shamed.
Zion gives birth to a nation in a moment. God comforts her like a mother. His indignation will come with fire against His enemies, and those who follow abominations will be consumed.
God will gather all nations to see His glory. Survivors will proclaim His name among the nations. From new moon to new moon, all flesh will worship Him. The wicked will be a perpetual warning.

Jeremiah, a priest from Anathoth, is called by God as a prophet to the nations. Though young and hesitant, God assures him of divine presence, touches his mouth, and appoints him to uproot and plant by proclaiming His word.

God shows Jeremiah two visions an almond branch (watchfulness) and a boiling pot (impending northern invasion). He warns of opposition but promises to make Jeremiah a fortified city, protected by the Lord.
God recalls Israel’s early devotion and confronts their betrayal. They have exchanged the fountain of living water for broken cisterns idolatry and self-reliance.
Israel’s slavery and desolation are the result of forsaking God. Despite divine deliverance, they now run after foreign gods, forgetting their Redeemer.
God indicts His people for constant rebellion and hypocrisy. Their alliances with Egypt and Assyria are futile, and they will be humiliated because of their faithlessness.
God compares Israel to an unfaithful wife who returns to idols. Though Judah witnessed Israel's downfall, she remains unrepentant and insincere in her return.

God invites backsliding Israel to return. He promises shepherds after His heart and a time when the Ark won’t be remembered Jerusalem will be called the throne of the Lord, and all nations will gather.
God longs to treat Israel as sons, but they rebel. The people confess their sin and acknowledge that salvation is only from the Lord, not the false gods they once served.
God pleads with Judah to return wholeheartedly, remove the idols from their midst, and break up fallow ground repentance must be deep and genuine.
A warning trumpet sounds disaster is coming from the north. Destruction looms because of the people’s rebellion. Jeremiah’s anguish reflects the devastation he foresees.
The prophet’s heart aches as he sees chaos: the earth is desolate, the heavens darkened. Judah is likened to a woman in labor writhing in judgment due to relentless sin.
God searches Jerusalem for a single righteous person but finds none. The people speak falsely of God, deny His judgment, and are deeply corrupted from the least to the greatest.

God makes Jeremiah’s words a consuming fire. Foreign nations will invade as punishment. Though the people have eyes and ears, they refuse to see or hear. Prophets lie, priests rule by deceit, and the people love it so yet judgment is coming.
Jerusalem is warned to flee impending disaster from the north. God compares the city to a well that pours out wickedness. He calls for correction, but the people refuse to listen.
God will glean the remnant like grapes. From the least to the greatest, all are greedy and deceitful. Prophets and priests cry 'Peace!' when there is no peace. They are shameless in their sin.

God urges the people to walk in the ancient paths of righteousness, but they refuse. He sets watchmen, yet they ignore the warnings. Their offerings are rejected, and they are called 'rejected silver' worthless in His sight.

Jeremiah delivers the Temple Sermon: God rejects empty rituals and demands justice, mercy, and obedience. The people trust in the temple but live in sin. God warns that He will cast them out like He did at Shiloh.

God tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people. They burn incense to false gods and sacrifice their children. Their disobedience has spanned generations. God calls them to obedience, but they have turned their backs.
Judah has defiled God’s house and built altars to Baal. The Valley of Hinnom will become the Valley of Slaughter. Joy and gladness will cease, and the land will become desolate.

The bones of kings and priests will be exposed as judgment. The people prefer death to life because of their persistent rebellion. Even animals know their seasons, but Judah does not know God’s judgment.
The people claim wisdom, but they have rejected God’s word. Prophets and priests deal falsely. They cry 'Peace!' while wounds fester. God will give them bitter judgment and scatter them.
Jeremiah mourns deeply for his people. He hears their cries and laments their spiritual sickness. 'Is there no balm in Gilead?' he asks no healing for the brokenness of the nation.
Jeremiah wishes he could weep endlessly for the slain. The land is full of adultery, deceit, and treachery. God will refine and punish them, and Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins.
The people have forsaken God’s law and followed idols. God calls for mourning women to wail over the devastation. Death has entered through the windows, and corpses lie like dung in the streets.
Let not the wise, mighty, or rich boast but let those who boast, boast in knowing the Lord. God will punish all who are circumcised in flesh but uncircumcised in heart.
God warns against the customs of the nations idols made by human hands are worthless. In contrast, the Lord is the true and living God, the Creator of all. He alone is worthy of fear and praise.
Jeremiah laments the coming exile. He acknowledges God’s justice and pleads for correction with mercy. He asks God to pour out wrath on the nations that do not know Him and have devoured Jacob.

God reminds Judah of the covenant made with their ancestors obedience brings blessing, disobedience brings curse. Yet the people have conspired against Him, following other gods. Judgment is coming, and even intercession will not avert it.
Jeremiah learns of a plot against his life by the people of Anathoth, his hometown. God reveals their intentions and promises to punish them for their treachery.
Jeremiah questions why the wicked prosper. God responds that Jeremiah must brace for greater trials if he struggles now, how will he endure what’s coming?
God laments forsaking His beloved people, likening them to a lion turned against Him. He promises to uproot the wicked nations, but if they learn His ways, they too may be restored.
God instructs Jeremiah to bury a linen belt, which becomes ruined symbolizing how Judah, once close to God, has become useless through pride and idolatry.

God warns of drunkenness and shame as judgment. The people are urged to humble themselves before exile comes. Their lewdness and stubbornness have made them incapable of change 'Can the Ethiopian change his skin?' God asks.
A severe drought strikes Judah. The people and even animals suffer. Jeremiah pleads with God, acknowledging their sin but appealing to His covenant and presence.

God rejects their superficial repentance and forbids Jeremiah from interceding. False prophets promise peace, but God declares sword, famine, and plague. Jeremiah continues to plead for mercy, asking, 'Are there any among the idols who can bring rain?'
Even if Moses and Samuel interceded, God would not relent. Four forms of judgment are appointed: sword, dogs, birds, and beasts. Judah’s sins especially under Manasseh have sealed their fate.

Jeremiah laments his calling, feeling cursed and isolated. God reassures him: if he returns and speaks what is precious, not worthless, he will stand strong. Though opposed, he will be delivered and redeemed.
God commands Jeremiah not to marry or have children, for death and disaster are coming. Joy and celebration will vanish from the land as judgment falls on this generation.
When the people ask why judgment is coming, Jeremiah is to answer: because of their ancestors’ idolatry and their own stubborn evil. They have forsaken God and followed their own ways.

Yet hope remains: God will bring His people back from exile, greater than the Exodus. But first, He will send many 'fishers and hunters' to gather them for judgment. The nations will one day know His name and power.

Judah’s sin is engraved on their hearts. Cursed is the one who trusts in man; blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord. The heart is deceitful above all things. God searches hearts and repays each according to their deeds.
Jeremiah prays for deliverance, declaring the Lord as his refuge and hope. He asks for shame to fall on his persecutors, not on him.
God commands Jeremiah to warn the people to honor the Sabbath. If they obey, kings will enter Jerusalem in glory. If not, the city will be consumed by fire.

At the potter’s house, Jeremiah sees clay reshaped in the potter’s hands. God declares He can do the same with nations blessing or destroying based on their response. But Judah refuses to turn from evil.
God laments Judah’s unnatural rebellion. They’ve forgotten Him and stumbled on ancient paths. The people plot against Jeremiah, but he calls on God to judge them for their schemes.

God tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar and break it before the elders in the Valley of Hinnom. This symbolizes how God will shatter Judah for their idolatry and child sacrifice. The valley will be renamed the Valley of Slaughter.
Jeremiah returns to the temple and declares that God will bring disaster because the people have stiffened their necks and refused to hear His words.
Pashhur the priest beats Jeremiah and puts him in stocks. Jeremiah renames him 'Terror on Every Side' and prophesies his exile and death in Babylon.

Jeremiah laments his calling. He feels deceived and mocked, yet cannot hold back God’s word it burns in his bones. He praises God for deliverance but also curses the day he was born, overwhelmed by sorrow and rejection.

King Zedekiah sends messengers to Jeremiah to inquire about Nebuchadnezzar’s siege, hoping for divine intervention. But God declares He will fight against Jerusalem, not for it. The people are given a choice: surrender to Babylon and live, or stay and die by sword, famine, or plague.

A message to the house of David: administer justice and rescue the oppressed, or face divine wrath. God warns that if they persist in evil, He will punish them with unquenchable fire, and no fortress will protect them.

God commands the king of Judah to uphold justice and protect the vulnerable. If they obey, the throne will endure; if not, the palace will become desolate. The nations will ask why God judged Jerusalem, and the answer will be their covenant-breaking.

Judgment is pronounced on three kings: Shallum (Jehoahaz), who will die in exile; Jehoiakim, condemned for oppression and selfish luxury; and Coniah (Jehoiachin), cursed so that none of his descendants will sit on David’s throne. The monarchy is disgraced due to persistent disobedience.

God denounces the corrupt shepherds who have scattered His flock. He promises to gather a faithful remnant and raise up a righteous Branch from David’s line who will reign wisely and bring salvation to Judah and Israel.

Jeremiah grieves over the false prophets who commit adultery, speak lies, and lead the people into sin. They claim to speak for God but prophesy from their own imagination. God declares He is against them and will bring judgment.
God forbids the people from using the phrase 'the burden of the Lord' in a mocking or manipulative way. Those who twist His words or falsely claim divine messages will be cast out and disgraced.

Jeremiah sees a vision of two baskets of figs one with good figs representing the exiles whom God will restore, and one with bad figs symbolizing Zedekiah and those who remain in Jerusalem or flee to Egypt, who will face sword, famine, and disgrace.

After twenty-three years of ignored warnings, Jeremiah announces that Judah will serve Babylon for seventy years. Then, Babylon itself will be punished, and the nations will be judged for their iniquity.

God gives Jeremiah a symbolic cup of wrath to deliver to all nations, starting with Jerusalem. The Lord will roar from heaven, and the slain will cover the earth. No nation will escape the judgment of the Almighty.

Jeremiah preaches in the temple, warning that if the people do not repent, the temple will become like Shiloh. The priests and prophets demand his death, but Jeremiah defends himself, urging them to amend their ways and obey God.

The officials and elders defend Jeremiah, recalling how earlier prophets like Micah warned of judgment. Another prophet, Uriah, is killed for a similar message. Jeremiah is spared, protected by Ahikam son of Shaphan.

God commands Jeremiah to wear a yoke and send messages to surrounding nations, urging them to submit to Nebuchadnezzar. False prophets claim the exile will end soon, but Jeremiah warns that resisting Babylon means destruction. The temple vessels will remain in Babylon until God restores them.

Hananiah, a false prophet, breaks Jeremiah’s yoke and proclaims that Babylon’s power will end in two years. Jeremiah responds that true prophecy is proven by fulfillment. God tells Jeremiah to replace the wooden yoke with an iron one and declares Hananiah will die that year for leading the people to trust a lie.

Jeremiah sends a letter to the exiles in Babylon, urging them to settle down, seek the city’s welfare, and not listen to false prophets. God promises to bring them back after seventy years, declaring, 'I know the plans I have for you... plans to prosper you and not to harm you.'

Shemaiah, another false prophet, writes from Babylon to oppose Jeremiah. God rebukes him and declares that Shemaiah and his descendants will not see the promised return because he has led the people astray.

God tells Jeremiah to write down His words of restoration. Though Jacob’s trouble is great, God will save His people and break their yoke. He will discipline them justly, but not destroy them completely.
Though Judah’s wounds seem incurable, God promises healing. He will restore Zion, punish her oppressors, and raise up a ruler from among them. In the latter days, they will understand His purposes.

God promises to restore Israel and Judah. He declares everlasting love for His people and pledges to rebuild them. Joy will return to Zion, and mourning will be turned into gladness. The people will come with weeping and supplication, and God will lead them with compassion.

A voice is heard in Ramah Rachel weeping for her children. Yet God offers hope: the exiles will return, and Ephraim (representing the northern tribes) is called His dear son. God urges repentance and promises restoration, likening Israel to a wayward daughter who will be brought back.

God declares a new covenant: unlike the one broken before, this covenant will be written on their hearts. He will be their God, and they will be His people. All will know Him, and He will forgive their iniquity. God affirms the permanence of Israel with cosmic imagery and promises Jerusalem will be rebuilt and never uprooted again.

During the Babylonian siege, God tells Jeremiah to buy a field from his cousin Hanamel as a sign that houses, fields, and vineyards will again be possessed in the land. Jeremiah obeys, even though the city is about to fall.
Jeremiah prays, acknowledging God’s power and justice, but also expressing confusion about why he was told to buy land when destruction is imminent.

God responds: though Jerusalem will fall due to the people’s sins, He will gather them from exile, give them one heart and one way, and make an everlasting covenant with them. Fields will again be bought in Judah as a sign of restoration.

God promises to restore Judah and Jerusalem. Though the city is filled with death and desolation, He will cleanse His people, forgive their sins, and bring health and healing. Joy and thanksgiving will return to the streets.

God reaffirms His covenant with David: a righteous Branch will reign, and the Levitical priests will never lack a man to offer sacrifices. Just as day and night are fixed, so is His promise to David and the descendants of Jacob.

God tells Jeremiah to warn King Zedekiah that Jerusalem will fall to Babylon. Though Zedekiah will not die by the sword, he will be taken captive and die in peace, with people mourning him as they did for his ancestors.

The people had made a covenant to free their Hebrew slaves, and initially obeyed. But they later reversed their decision and re-enslaved them. God condemns this betrayal, reminding them of the law to release slaves in the seventh year. Because of their disobedience, He declares judgment: sword, pestilence, and famine will come, and Zedekiah and Jerusalem will fall to Babylon.

God tells Jeremiah to invite the Rechabites to drink wine. They refuse, honoring their ancestor Jonadab’s command to abstain from wine, live in tents, and not own land. Their obedience is contrasted with Judah’s disobedience to God.

God uses the Rechabites as an example of faithfulness. While they obeyed their ancestor, Judah has ignored God’s prophets. As a result, disaster is coming upon Judah. But the Rechabites are promised a lasting legacy: Jonadab’s descendants will always have someone to stand before God.
God commands Jeremiah to write all His words on a scroll. Jeremiah dictates to Baruch, who reads the scroll aloud in the temple during a fast day, hoping the people will repent.

Officials hear the scroll and bring it to King Jehoiakim. As it is read, the king cuts it up and burns it, showing contempt for God’s word. He orders the arrest of Jeremiah and Baruch, but God hides them.

God tells Jeremiah to rewrite the scroll with even more words. He pronounces judgment on Jehoiakim: none of his descendants will sit on David’s throne, and his body will be exposed to the elements. The rewritten scroll is preserved.

Zedekiah becomes king but does not listen to God’s word. He sends messengers to Jeremiah to pray for them. Egypt’s army causes the Babylonians to withdraw temporarily, but God warns that Babylon will return and destroy the city.

Jeremiah tries to leave Jerusalem but is accused of defecting to the Babylonians and is imprisoned. He pleads his innocence but is beaten and thrown into a dungeon. Later, Zedekiah secretly brings him out to ask for a word from God. Jeremiah warns of Babylon’s return and asks not to be sent back to the dungeon. He is placed in a more tolerable prison and given bread daily.

Jeremiah’s message of surrender to Babylon angers the officials, who accuse him of weakening morale. With Zedekiah’s permission, they throw him into a muddy cistern. Ebed-Melech, an Ethiopian official, courageously appeals to the king and rescues Jeremiah with ropes and rags.

Zedekiah secretly consults Jeremiah again. Jeremiah urges him to surrender to Babylon to save the city and his life. Zedekiah fears betrayal by his own people and refuses. Jeremiah is returned to the court of the guard, where he remains until Jerusalem is captured.

In the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign, Jerusalem falls to the Babylonians. Zedekiah attempts to flee but is captured near Jericho. He watches his sons executed, is blinded, and taken to Babylon. The city is burned, the elite are exiled, and only the poor are left to farm the land, reversing Jerusalem's social order.
Nebuchadnezzar orders that Jeremiah be protected and given into the care of Gedaliah. Jeremiah is freed and resides among the people. God’s favor preserves His prophet amid national judgment.

God sends a message to Ebed-Melech, the Ethiopian who rescued Jeremiah. Because he trusted in God, he will be delivered from the coming disaster and spared from the sword. This personal promise highlights God’s intimate justice for the faithful.

At Ramah, Jeremiah is formally released by Nebuzaradan and given the choice to go to Babylon or stay in Judah. Choosing to remain, he joins Gedaliah at Mizpah to live among the remnant, signaling Jeremiah’s enduring commitment to his people.

When local military leaders hear Gedaliah is governor, they return to him. Gedaliah encourages peaceful cooperation with Babylon. Exiles in nearby nations also begin to return, and a brief period of peace and harvest begins.

Johanan warns Gedaliah that Ishmael plans to kill him, urging a preemptive strike. Gedaliah refuses to believe him, tragically dismissing the danger and unwittingly opening the door to future disaster.

Ishmael assassinates Gedaliah and slaughters Judeans and Babylonian officials at Mizpah. He also kills pilgrims from the north and takes the surviving townspeople captive. The fragile hope of stability is shattered by treachery.

Johanan intercepts Ishmael, frees the captives, but Ishmael escapes. Fearing Babylonian reprisal for Gedaliah’s death, Johanan gathers the remnant and heads south toward Egypt, stopping near Bethlehem, unsure of the next step.
Johanan and the leaders ask Jeremiah to seek God’s guidance, vowing obedience whether the answer is favorable or not. Their outward humility masks inward resistance.

After ten days, Jeremiah delivers God’s answer: stay in Judah, and God will plant and protect them; flee to Egypt, and they will face sword, famine, and plague. The people are rebuked for their hypocrisy they sought confirmation, not correction and warned that rejecting God's word will bring ruin.

Despite their promise, the people accuse Jeremiah of deceit and forcibly lead the entire remnant, including Jeremiah and Baruch, to Egypt. Disobedience replaces discernment, sealing their fate in exile.

In Egypt, God instructs Jeremiah to bury stones at Pharaoh’s palace in Tahpanhes, a sign that Nebuchadnezzar will set up his throne there. Egypt, once seen as a refuge, will become a place of conquest and judgment.

God sends Jeremiah to rebuke the Jews living in Egypt those in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph, and Pathros for continuing to burn incense to other gods. He reminds them of the destruction of Jerusalem as a direct result of idolatry, yet they persist in the same sins. Their refusal to humble themselves or fear the Lord reveals a hardened rebellion.

Jeremiah warns that God will bring disaster upon the remnant in Egypt: they will perish by sword and famine. The people, however, defiantly respond that they will continue worshiping the 'queen of heaven,' claiming that their troubles began only after they stopped offering to her. This exchange exposes their deep spiritual blindness and misplaced nostalgia for false security.

Jeremiah rebukes the people for their idolatry, reminding them that their offerings provoked God’s wrath. He prophesies that none of the Jews in Egypt will return to Judah except a few fugitives. As a sign, God declares that Pharaoh Hophra will be handed over to his enemies, just as Zedekiah was. This chapter marks a tragic moment of final rejection, where the people openly choose idolatry over covenant faithfulness.

This brief chapter is a personal message to Baruch, Jeremiah’s scribe. Baruch is discouraged by the suffering he endures while faithfully serving the prophet. God acknowledges his pain but warns him not to seek great things for himself. Instead, God promises to preserve Baruch’s life wherever he goes. This intimate word highlights God’s care for individuals amid national judgment.

A prophecy against Egypt: God declares judgment on Pharaoh Necho and his army, which will be defeated at Carchemish by Nebuchadnezzar. Despite Egypt’s confidence and preparations, they will stumble and fall. The imagery of a beautiful heifer being bitten by a gadfly symbolizes Egypt’s vulnerability.

Jeremiah prophesies Babylon’s invasion of Egypt. The cities will be laid waste, and Egypt’s gods will be powerless. Yet, God promises that Egypt will eventually be inhabited again. This dual message of judgment and future restoration reflects God’s sovereignty over all nations.

God reassures Israel not to fear. Though He disciplines them, He will not destroy them completely. In contrast, the nations He judges will face total ruin. This closing promise affirms God’s enduring covenant with His people, even in exile.

A prophecy against the Philistines: The Lord declares that a flood of destruction will come from the north, overwhelming the land of the Philistines, including Gaza and Ashkelon. The sword of the Lord will not be quiet until His judgment is complete. The imagery evokes relentless devastation, and the chapter ends with a rhetorical cry for the sword to rest, though it cannot until God’s purpose is fulfilled.

Moab is condemned for its pride and idolatry. Cities like Nebo and Kiriathaim will fall, and Chemosh, Moab’s god, will go into exile. The nation’s strength and wealth will not save it from destruction.

Moab has lived undisturbed, like wine left on its dregs, but now it will be poured out and shattered. The Lord mocks Moab’s false confidence and foretells the fall of its fortified cities and warriors.
Moab’s arrogance is its downfall. The Lord calls for mourning over its ruin, describing widespread weeping and shame. The once-proud nation will be ridiculed and broken.

An eagle (Babylon) will swoop down on Moab. Panic and flight will follow. Yet, in the final verse, God promises to restore Moab’s fortunes in the latter days, offering a glimmer of hope amid judgment.
A prophecy against Ammon: Because they took Israel’s land and worshiped Milcom, they will face judgment. Yet, like Moab, Ammon is promised restoration in the future.
Edom will be laid waste due to its pride and wisdom. Its cities will become desolate, and its people will flee. The destruction will be swift and total, likened to a lion attacking from the thickets.
Damascus is gripped by fear and will become feeble. Its famed city will be consumed by fire, and its young men will fall in battle.
Kedar and Hazor, nomadic desert tribes, will be attacked by Nebuchadnezzar. Their tents and flocks will be plundered, and they will scatter in fear.
Elam will be broken and scattered to the four winds. Yet, like Moab and Ammon, Elam is also promised restoration in the latter days, showing God’s long-term plan for mercy.
A prophecy against Babylon: Though Babylon was God’s instrument of judgment, it will now face its own downfall. Israel and Judah will return to seek the Lord and reunite in covenant faithfulness.
Babylon is condemned for rejoicing over Israel’s fall. God promises to punish Babylon and restore His people, cleansing them from sin and guilt.
God commands an attack on Babylon’s land. Its warriors will be broken, and its pride will be humbled. The arrogant one will stumble and fall with no one to lift him up.
Israel and Judah are oppressed, but God will redeem them. Babylon’s destruction will be so complete that the earth will tremble, and the nations will hear of its fall.

God declares that He will stir up a destroying wind against Babylon and its inhabitants. He calls for archers and warriors to attack, promising that Babylon’s sins have reached heaven. The city that once devoured others will now be devoured. This opening salvo sets the tone for Babylon’s total downfall.

Jeremiah praises God’s power as Creator and Judge. Babylon is likened to a hammer that shattered nations, but now it will be broken. God will repay Babylon for all the evil it has done to Zion. The imagery of vengeance and divine justice is vivid and unrelenting.

God summons nations to rise against Babylon Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz. The Medes are named as His instrument of judgment. Babylon’s idols are powerless, and her gods will be shamed. The city will become a haunt for jackals, a symbol of utter desolation.

God warns His people to flee Babylon to avoid sharing in her punishment. Babylon’s pride and cruelty are condemned, and her destruction is portrayed as sudden and irreversible. The chapter ends with a dramatic image: a stone tied to a scroll of judgment and thrown into the Euphrates, symbolizing Babylon’s sinking fate.

Jeremiah gives a scroll of these prophecies to Seraiah, who is to read them aloud in Babylon and then cast the scroll into the Euphrates, declaring that Babylon will sink and rise no more. This symbolic act seals the prophecy with a visual demonstration of Babylon’s doom.

This historical appendix recounts the fall of Jerusalem under King Zedekiah. After an 18-month siege, the Babylonians breach the city. Zedekiah tries to escape but is captured, blinded, and taken to Babylon after witnessing the execution of his sons.

Nebuzaradan, the Babylonian captain, burns the temple, palace, and houses of Jerusalem. He dismantles the temple’s bronze pillars and sacred furnishings, carrying them off to Babylon. The detailed inventory underscores the magnitude of what was lost.
Key leaders and officials are executed at Riblah. The chapter lists the number of people exiled in three waves, totaling over 4,600. This grim tally reflects the completeness of Judah’s judgment.

In a surprising epilogue, King Jehoiachin exiled for decades is released from prison by Evil-Merodach, king of Babylon. He is given a place of honor and daily provisions. This final note of mercy hints at future hope and restoration.

Jerusalem, once full of people, sits desolate like a widow. She has no comforters and is betrayed by former allies. The people are in exile, and Zion's roads mourn. Her priests groan, and her children are in captivity. All her splendor is gone because of rebellion and affliction.

Jerusalem pleads for pity, lamenting that no one understands her pain. She recognizes that the Lord is just in punishing her sins. Her enemies triumph, her people perish, and she calls on the Lord to witness her anguish and bring judgment on those who gloat over her fall.

The Lord’s anger has brought Zion low. He has withdrawn His protection, destroyed His temple, and allowed enemies to triumph. The leaders sit in silence, and the elders cast dust on their heads. The city once glorious is left in ruin.

The poet grieves over the suffering, especially the starving children. False prophets have misled the people. God has fulfilled His warnings, and now there is no escape. The people cry out in sorrow, asking the Lord to see their plight and show mercy.
The speaker suffers under God's wrath isolated, broken, and surrounded by darkness. He describes his affliction vividly and confesses that his soul is bowed down within him.

In the midst of despair, the speaker remembers God's steadfast love and mercies, which are new every morning. He acknowledges that it is good to wait quietly for salvation. God is just and does not afflict willingly but allows discipline for correction.

The call is given to examine one’s heart and return to the Lord. The speaker recounts answered prayers and asks God to judge his enemies. The chapter closes with confidence that the Lord sees injustice and will act.

The glory of Jerusalem is gone gold is dimmed, the sacred stones scattered. Children cry for food, the rich and noble are reduced to ruin, and compassionate mothers resort to desperate acts. The city’s suffering surpasses that of Sodom.

The Lord’s wrath consumed Jerusalem, and her prophets and priests are defiled. The people are rejected by all nations. Edom is warned of its future judgment, while Zion is told her punishment is ending, and exile will not last forever.

A communal prayer pleads with God to remember the suffering of His people. Their inheritance has been seized, their lives are ruled by foreigners, and their joy has turned to mourning. They cry out for restoration, asking God not to abandon them forever.

Ezekiel, a priest in exile by the Kebar River, receives a divine vision in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin’s captivity. The word of the Lord comes to him, marking the beginning of his prophetic ministry.

Ezekiel sees a stormy wind and a great cloud with flashing fire and brilliant light. Four living creatures appear, each with four faces and four wings, moving with wheels within wheels. Above them is a throne with a radiant figure like a man, glowing with fire and surrounded by a rainbow-like radiance. Overwhelmed, Ezekiel falls facedown as he beholds the glory of the Lord.

God commands Ezekiel to stand and commissions him as a prophet to a rebellious people. He is told not to fear their resistance. God gives him a scroll filled with lamentation, mourning, and woe, instructing him to eat it symbolizing his full acceptance of the prophetic message.

Ezekiel eats the scroll, which tastes sweet like honey. God sends him to speak to the house of Israel, not to foreign nations. Though the people are stubborn, Ezekiel is made resolute. He is taken by the Spirit to Tel Abib, where he sits overwhelmed for seven days among the exiles.

God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman for Israel. He is responsible for warning the wicked and the righteous alike. If he fails to warn them, their blood is on his hands. Ezekiel is then bound and silenced, only to speak when God opens his mouth to deliver His word.

Ezekiel is instructed to build a model of Jerusalem under siege and lie on his side 390 days for Israel’s sin and 40 days for Judah’s. This symbolic act represents the years of their iniquity and the certainty of judgment.
He is told to eat a meager diet of bread and water, cooked over cow dung, to symbolize the scarcity and defilement of food during the siege. The people’s disobedience will lead to famine and despair.

Ezekiel is commanded to shave his head and beard, dividing the hair into thirds burning, striking, and scattering it to represent the fate of Jerusalem’s people. God declares that Jerusalem has been more rebellious than surrounding nations, and therefore His judgment will be fierce and without pity. Famine, pestilence, and the sword will devastate the city.

God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where idolatrous altars and high places have been built. The Lord declares that He will destroy these places, slay the idolaters, and scatter their bones around their altars. This judgment is a direct response to the nation’s spiritual adultery and serves as a warning to all who defile His name.

Despite the coming destruction, God promises that a remnant will survive. These survivors will remember their sins and loathe themselves for their iniquities. This section reveals God’s desire for repentance and restoration, even amid judgment.

Ezekiel is told to strike his hands and stamp his feet in mourning over the abominations of Israel. God reiterates that sword, famine, and plague will consume the land. The devastation will be so complete that the desolate land will testify to the Lord’s justice and power.

God declares that the end has come upon the land of Israel. The time of judgment is now, and there will be no more delay. The people’s abominations have reached their limit, and God will show no pity. This section emphasizes the certainty and severity of divine retribution.

The chapter vividly describes the chaos and terror that will accompany the judgment: violence, economic collapse, and the failure of religious and political leaders. The people will seek peace but find none. God’s wrath will be poured out, and they will know that He is the Lord. This passage underscores the futility of trusting in wealth or human institutions when God’s judgment is at hand.

Ezekiel is taken in a vision to Jerusalem, where he sees an idol that provokes God’s jealousy standing at the entrance of the temple. God shows Ezekiel the abominations being committed in secret by the elders of Israel, revealing the spiritual corruption that has defiled the sanctuary.

Ezekiel is shown a hidden chamber where seventy elders are worshiping carved images of animals and creeping things. They claim that the Lord does not see them, exposing their disbelief in God’s presence and justice.

Ezekiel witnesses women weeping for the Babylonian god Tammuz and men bowing to the sun in the temple courtyard. God declares that these abominations have filled the land with violence and provoked His wrath. He will act in fury and show no pity.

God calls six executioners and a man clothed in linen with a writing kit. The man is instructed to mark the foreheads of those who grieve over the abominations in Jerusalem. The others are commanded to kill without pity everyone who lacks the mark, beginning at the sanctuary. This vision emphasizes divine justice and the protection of the righteous remnant.

Ezekiel intercedes for the people, asking if God will destroy all of Israel. God responds that the guilt of the land is exceedingly great and that He will not relent. The man in linen reports that he has completed the marking, affirming God’s control over judgment and mercy.

Ezekiel sees the glory of God above the cherubim and a man in linen commanded to take burning coals from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city. This act symbolizes the coming judgment by fire upon Jerusalem.

Ezekiel describes the wheels and cherubim in detail, emphasizing their coordinated movement and the presence of the Spirit within them. The vision mirrors the one in chapter 1, reinforcing the majesty and mobility of God’s glory.

The glory of the Lord departs from the threshold of the temple and stands above the cherubim, who then lift off and move to the east gate. This marks the beginning of God’s withdrawal from Jerusalem, a profound moment of divine judgment.

Ezekiel is shown 25 leaders of the people who give wicked counsel. God condemns them for their false confidence and violence. One of the leaders, Pelatiah, dies during the vision, prompting Ezekiel to cry out in fear that all of Israel will be destroyed.

God reassures Ezekiel that He will preserve a remnant among the exiles. He promises to gather them, give them a new heart and spirit, and restore them to the land. The chapter ends with the glory of the Lord departing from the city and Ezekiel returning from the vision to speak to the exiles.

God instructs Ezekiel to act out the exile by packing his belongings and digging through a wall in the sight of the people. This symbolic act represents the coming captivity of Jerusalem’s inhabitants, including the prince, who will attempt to flee but be captured.

God explains the meaning of Ezekiel’s actions: the prince in Jerusalem (Zedekiah) will try to escape but will be caught and taken to Babylon, though he will not see it. The people will be scattered, and their suffering will be a sign of God’s judgment. Yet a few will be spared to declare their sins among the nations.

Ezekiel is told to eat and drink with trembling and anxiety to symbolize the fear and desolation that will grip the people during the siege. The land will be stripped of its abundance because of the violence of its inhabitants.

God rebukes the people for saying that visions never come to pass. He declares that His words will no longer be delayed every prophecy will be fulfilled in its time. This section emphasizes the certainty and imminence of divine judgment.

God condemns false prophets who speak lies and claim divine authority. They build flimsy spiritual defenses, likened to whitewashed walls that will collapse in the storm of judgment. These prophets mislead the people with false visions of peace, and God declares that they will be excluded from His people and their names erased from Israel’s records.

God also denounces false prophetesses who use magic charms and veils to deceive and control others. They profane God’s name for personal gain and kill the innocent while sparing the guilty. God promises to rescue His people from their grip and expose their lies.

Elders come to inquire of God, but He exposes their idolatry. God declares that anyone who sets up idols in their heart and then seeks Him will be answered according to their deception. Even prophets who are deceived will be judged. This passage stresses personal responsibility and the danger of hypocrisy.

God declares that even if righteous men like Noah, Daniel, and Job were in the land, they could only save themselves by their righteousness. The land would still face judgment sword, famine, wild beasts, and plague. Yet a remnant will survive, and their conduct will justify God’s actions in the eyes of the exiles.

Jerusalem is compared to a useless vine good for nothing but fuel for fire. Just as vine wood is consumed and discarded, so will the inhabitants of Jerusalem be judged and made desolate for their unfaithfulness. This metaphor underscores the city’s failure to fulfill its purpose.

God describes Jerusalem as an abandoned infant whom He rescued, nurtured, and adorned with beauty. He raised her into a queen, lavishing her with fine clothing and jewels. Her fame spread because of His splendor bestowed upon her. This allegory highlights God’s grace and the intimate covenant He made with His people.

Despite God’s care, Jerusalem turns to prostitution trusting in her beauty and engaging in idolatry with surrounding nations. She sacrifices her children to idols and builds high places for pagan worship. Unlike other prostitutes, she pays her lovers instead of receiving payment. This section emphasizes the depth of her betrayal and spiritual adultery.

God declares judgment on Jerusalem for her unfaithfulness. Her lovers will turn against her, strip her bare, and stone her. God compares her sins to those of Samaria and Sodom, declaring that Jerusalem has acted even more wickedly. Her pride and detestable practices have surpassed those infamous cities.

Despite the severity of judgment, God promises eventual restoration. He will bring back the captives of Sodom and Samaria along with Jerusalem. The people will be ashamed of their past and remember their disgrace. God reaffirms His everlasting covenant, and Jerusalem will know that He is the Lord, not because of her righteousness, but because of His mercy.

God presents a parable of two eagles and a vine. The first eagle represents Babylon, which takes the top of a cedar (King Jehoiachin) and plants a seed (Zedekiah) in fertile soil. The vine grows but later turns toward another eagle (Egypt), seeking help. This allegory illustrates Judah’s political alliances and betrayal of Babylon.

God explains the parable: Zedekiah broke his covenant with Babylon by turning to Egypt for support. As a result, he will be captured and die in Babylon. His army will be scattered, and his rebellion will not succeed. This section underscores the seriousness of breaking oaths made in God’s name.

God promises to plant a tender sprig from the top of a cedar on a high mountain. It will grow into a majestic tree under which birds will dwell. This messianic prophecy points to the future reign of Christ, who will bring restoration and exaltation from humble beginnings.

God refutes the proverb that children suffer for their parents’ sins. Each person is responsible for their own actions. A righteous man will live, a wicked man will die, and a righteous son of a wicked father will not bear his father’s guilt. This passage emphasizes personal accountability before God.

God declares that if a wicked person repents, they will live, and their past sins will not be remembered. Conversely, if a righteous person turns to sin, they will die. God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that all turn from their ways and live. This section highlights divine justice and mercy.

This lamentation compares Israel’s leaders to lion cubs. One cub (likely Jehoahaz) is captured and taken to Egypt. Another (possibly Jehoiachin) becomes a fierce predator but is also captured and taken to Babylon. The imagery mourns the downfall of Judah’s kings and the loss of national strength.

Israel is likened to a fruitful vine, once strong and flourishing. But it is uprooted in fury, cast to the ground, and consumed by fire. The lament ends with a bleak note: there is no strong branch left, symbolizing the end of the Davidic line’s rule in Jerusalem.

Elders come to inquire of the Lord, but God refuses to answer them. He recounts Israel’s rebellion in Egypt, where they rejected His laws and profaned His name. Yet for the sake of His name, He did not destroy them.

God continues recounting Israel’s history of rebellion in the wilderness. Despite His provision and laws, they defiled His Sabbaths and turned to idols. He disciplined them but did not annihilate them, preserving a remnant.

The pattern of rebellion continues even after entering the land. Israel adopts the detestable practices of the nations. God declares that He will not allow them to be like other nations or serve idols.

God promises to gather Israel from the nations with a mighty hand. He will purge the rebels and bring the faithful into covenant relationship. Ultimately, they will loathe their past sins and know that He is the Lord.
God commands Ezekiel to prophesy against the south (Judah), warning of an unquenchable fire of judgment. The people mock Ezekiel’s parables, failing to grasp the seriousness of the message.

God declares that His sword of judgment is drawn against Jerusalem. It will strike the righteous and the wicked alike. The imagery is intense flashing, polished, and ready to slay. Ezekiel is told to cry and wail, for the sword is coming swiftly.
