God describes Nebuchadnezzar’s decision-making at a crossroads using divination to choose between attacking Rabbah or Jerusalem. He chooses Jerusalem, and God affirms that the city’s guilt demands judgment. The crown will be removed until the rightful one comes.
A prophecy against the Ammonites declares that their mocking will not save them. They too will face the sword, and their destruction will be final.
God lists Jerusalem’s sins: bloodshed, idolatry, oppression of the poor, and profaning the Sabbath. Leaders, priests, and prophets are all corrupt. The city is defiled and will face judgment.
God compares the people to dross the worthless residue from smelting metal. He will gather them into the furnace of His wrath and melt them in judgment.
God searches for someone to stand in the gap and intercede for the land, but finds none. Therefore, His wrath will be poured out, and the people will suffer the consequences of their actions.

Two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), represent the divided kingdoms of Israel and Judah. Both commit spiritual adultery with foreign nations. Oholah is judged and falls, yet Oholibah becomes even more corrupt, lusting after the Babylonians.
God declares that Oholibah will be handed over to the very nations she lusted after. They will strip her, shame her, and destroy her. Her cup of judgment will be bitter and desolate.

God commands Ezekiel to confront the sisters for their lewdness and bloodshed. Their judgment will be public and severe, serving as a warning to others. The chapter ends with a declaration that they shall bear the penalty of their sins and know that He is the Lord.

On the very day Babylon begins its siege of Jerusalem, God gives Ezekiel a parable of a boiling pot filled with choice meat. The pot represents Jerusalem, and the meat symbolizes its people. The scum and corrosion that cling to the pot signify the city’s deep-seated sin. God declares that judgment is now irreversible He will not relent or show pity. The parable underscores the certainty and severity of divine justice.

God tells Ezekiel that his wife the delight of his eyes will die, but he must not mourn publicly. This shocking command is a sign to the exiles: just as Ezekiel remains silent, so too will they be stunned and unable to grieve when Jerusalem falls. Ezekiel’s personal loss becomes a prophetic symbol of national catastrophe. The chapter ends with a promise that Ezekiel will speak again when a fugitive arrives with news of the city’s destruction.

A prophecy against Ammon: Because they rejoiced over Israel’s downfall, God will hand them over to the people of the East. Their land will become a pasture for camels and a dwelling for nomads. This judgment reflects God’s intolerance for gloating over His people’s suffering.

Moab is condemned for claiming that Judah is no different from other nations. God will expose Moab’s borders and give them to the people of the East. This judgment highlights the danger of dismissing God’s covenant with Israel.

Edom is judged for taking vengeance on Judah. God will punish them through His people Israel, who will act as His instrument of retribution. This section emphasizes divine justice through human agency.

Philistia is condemned for its ancient hostility and revenge. God declares that He will stretch out His hand against them and execute great vengeance. The chapter closes with a reminder that all these judgments are meant to reveal God’s identity and sovereignty.

God declares judgment against the city of Tyre for rejoicing over Jerusalem’s fall. Tyre, a coastal trading hub, believed it would benefit from Judah’s destruction. God promises that many nations will come against Tyre like waves, breaking down its walls and scraping it bare like a rock.

Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is named as the instrument of Tyre’s destruction. He will bring a massive army, destroy the city’s towers, and cast its debris into the sea. Tyre will become a place for spreading nets a symbol of total desolation.

The fall of Tyre will cause trembling among the coastal nations. God describes the city’s descent into the pit, where it will be forgotten among the ruins of the ancient world. This prophecy emphasizes the finality of Tyre’s judgment and its removal from prominence.

Ezekiel delivers a lament for Tyre, describing it as a beautiful ship made of the finest materials. The city’s glory and craftsmanship are praised, highlighting its former splendor and strategic importance.

A detailed list of Tyre’s trade partners and goods is presented, showcasing its vast commercial empire. The city traded with nations far and wide, dealing in precious metals, livestock, spices, and luxury items.

Despite its greatness, Tyre’s ship is wrecked by the east wind symbolizing divine judgment. The merchants and mariners mourn its fall. The chapter ends with a dirge, as the world laments the loss of such a powerful and wealthy city.

God rebukes the prince of Tyre for his pride and self-deification. Though he claims to be a god, he is merely a man. God promises that foreigners will bring him down, and he will die a disgraceful death.

A lament is directed at the king of Tyre, using imagery that echoes the fall of a glorious being from Eden. This poetic section portrays the king as once perfect and adorned with beauty, but corrupted by pride and violence. His downfall is inevitable.

A prophecy against Sidon, another Phoenician city. God declares judgment upon it for its sins and promises that it will no longer be a thorn to Israel. This section reinforces God’s sovereignty over all nations.
God promises to restore Israel. After judging the surrounding nations, He will gather His people from exile and bring them back to their land. They will live in safety and know that He is the Lord.

God pronounces judgment on Pharaoh and Egypt, likening Pharaoh to a great sea monster who claims the Nile as his own creation. Because of his arrogance, God will bring Nebuchadnezzar against Egypt. The land will be desolate for forty years, and its people scattered. Yet after this period, Egypt will be restored, though it will remain a lowly kingdom, never again to rule over nations.

In a later prophecy, God declares that since Nebuchadnezzar received no reward for his campaign against Tyre, He will give Egypt to him as compensation. This act fulfills God’s justice and affirms His sovereignty. The chapter ends with a promise that Israel’s strength will rise again, and Ezekiel will speak once more.

A lamentation over Egypt and its allies: God declares that the 'Day of the Lord' is near, a day of doom for Egypt. He will break the arms of Pharaoh and bring ruin to cities like Memphis, Pathros, and Zoan. Allies such as Cush, Put, and Lydia will fall with Egypt. The devastation will be widespread, and the pride of Egypt will be shattered.

God reiterates His judgment by declaring that He will break Pharaoh’s arms while strengthening the arms of Babylon’s king. Egypt will know that the Lord is God when He scatters them among the nations and uses Babylon as His instrument of judgment.

God compares Assyria to a mighty cedar of Lebanon, tall and beautiful, nourished by abundant waters. Yet because of its pride, it was cut down and cast into the pit. This allegory warns Egypt that it too will fall like Assyria. The chapter ends with a vivid picture of the nations trembling at Assyria’s fall, foreshadowing Egypt’s similar fate.

Nahum opens with a declaration of God’s character jealous, avenging, slow to anger, yet great in power. He will not leave the guilty unpunished. The imagery is vivid: storms, earthquakes, and withering nature reflect His wrath. Yet for those who trust in Him, He is a stronghold in times of trouble.

God promises to completely destroy Nineveh, the enemy of His people. Though they may seem strong, their end is certain. Judah is encouraged to celebrate, for the wicked will no longer pass through them. The chapter ends with a vision of deliverance and the fall of the oppressor.

The chapter vividly describes the siege and fall of Nineveh. The attacker is advancing, shields are red, chariots flash like fire, and the city’s defenses crumble. The queen is led away, and the palace collapses. The once-mighty city is now vulnerable and exposed.

Nineveh is likened to a drained pool its people flee, and no one turns back. The city is plundered, its treasures looted. God mocks its former strength, comparing it to a lion’s den now deserted. The chapter ends with a divine declaration: 'I am against you,' says the Lord, sealing Nineveh’s fate.

Woe is pronounced on Nineveh, the city of blood, full of lies and plunder. The scene is chaotic whips crack, wheels rumble, horses charge. Corpses pile up. The city’s shame is exposed, and God declares He will treat Nineveh with contempt, making it a spectacle to the nations.

Nineveh is compared to Thebes, a once-great city that fell despite its strength. The same fate awaits Nineveh. Its fortresses are weak, its leaders scattered, and its people helpless. The book ends with a final blow: there is no healing for Nineveh’s wound, and all who hear of its fall will rejoice.

Zephaniah opens with a sweeping declaration of judgment. God announces that He will utterly consume everything from the face of the earth humans, animals, birds, and fish because of widespread idolatry and rebellion. Judah and Jerusalem are specifically targeted for their syncretism and neglect of the Lord.

The 'Day of the Lord' is described as imminent and terrifying. God warns of distress, devastation, and darkness. Wealth and status will not save anyone. The chapter ends with a vivid portrayal of divine wrath, emphasizing that the whole earth will be consumed by the fire of God's jealousy.
A call to repentance is issued to the humble and righteous. Zephaniah urges the people to seek the Lord, righteousness, and humility in hopes that they may be hidden on the Day of the Lord’s anger.

Judgment is pronounced on surrounding nations Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria. Each is condemned for pride, violence, or mocking God’s people. The chapter highlights God's sovereignty over all nations and His intent to humble the arrogant.

Jerusalem is rebuked for its corruption. Its leaders are compared to roaring lions and evening wolves. Prophets are reckless, priests profane the sanctuary, and the people ignore God’s discipline. Despite His justice, they remain unrepentant.

God declares that He will gather the nations for judgment but also promises to purify the lips of the peoples so they may call on His name. A humble and faithful remnant will remain, characterized by honesty and trust in the Lord.

The book ends with a song of joy and restoration. God promises to remove judgment, defeat enemies, and dwell among His people. He will gather the outcasts, restore their fortunes, and turn their shame into praise. The tone shifts from wrath to hope, highlighting God's mercy and faithfulness.

God rebukes the people for neglecting the rebuilding of His temple while focusing on their own homes. Through the prophet Haggai, He explains that their hardships drought, poor harvests, and economic struggles are a direct result of their misplaced priorities. The Lord calls them to consider their ways and resume work on the temple.

Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and the remnant of the people respond in obedience to God’s message. They fear the Lord and begin work on the temple. Haggai assures them that God is with them, marking a turning point in their spiritual renewal.

God encourages the people who feel discouraged by the modest appearance of the new temple compared to Solomon’s. He promises that the glory of this latter house will surpass the former, and that He will fill it with peace. This prophecy points to a future spiritual fulfillment beyond physical splendor.

Haggai delivers a message about holiness and defilement, using a priestly analogy. He explains that while holiness doesn’t transfer easily, defilement does. The people’s past disobedience brought hardship, but now that they’ve resumed the temple work, God promises to bless them from this day forward.

God speaks directly to Zerubbabel, declaring that He will shake the heavens and the earth, overthrowing kingdoms. Zerubbabel is called God’s 'signet ring,' symbolizing divine authority and favor. This messianic promise hints at future leadership and restoration through his lineage.

Zechariah opens with a call to repentance. God urges the people not to be like their ancestors who ignored the prophets and suffered judgment. The message is clear: return to God, and He will return to you. This sets the tone for the book’s themes of restoration and divine presence.

Zechariah receives his first vision: a man among myrtle trees with red, sorrel, and white horses. These symbolize God’s patrol over the earth. The angel explains that the earth is at peace, and God is now ready to show mercy to Jerusalem. He promises that the temple will be rebuilt and prosperity will return.

In a second vision, Zechariah sees four horns representing the nations that scattered Judah. Then four craftsmen appear to terrify and cast down the horns. This symbolizes God’s plan to overthrow the oppressors and restore His people.

Zechariah sees a man with a measuring line going to measure Jerusalem. An angel tells him that Jerusalem will be a city without walls because of the multitude of people and livestock. God Himself will be a wall of fire around it and its glory within.

God calls His people to flee from Babylon and return to Zion. He promises to dwell among them and that many nations will join themselves to the Lord. The chapter ends with a call for all flesh to be silent before the Lord, for He is stirring from His holy dwelling.

Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest standing before the Angel of the Lord, with Satan accusing him. The Lord rebukes Satan and removes Joshua’s filthy garments, symbolizing the removal of sin. Joshua is given clean clothes and a charge to walk in God’s ways. The vision ends with a messianic prophecy about the Branch and a stone with seven eyes, pointing to future cleansing and peace.

Zechariah sees a golden lampstand with a bowl on top and seven lamps, flanked by two olive trees. The angel explains that this vision represents God’s Spirit empowering Zerubbabel to complete the temple not by might, nor by power, but by the Spirit. The two olive trees symbolize the anointed ones who serve the Lord.

Zechariah sees a flying scroll, representing a curse going out over the land. It will enter the house of every thief and perjurer, consuming it completely. This vision emphasizes God’s judgment against sin.

He then sees a woman in a basket, symbolizing wickedness. The basket is sealed and carried by two winged women to the land of Shinar (Babylon), where a house will be built for it. This vision portrays the removal of wickedness from the land.

Zechariah sees four chariots coming from between two bronze mountains, each pulled by different colored horses. These represent the four spirits of heaven sent to patrol the earth. The vision emphasizes God’s sovereign control over the nations and His active presence in world affairs.

God commands Zechariah to crown Joshua the high priest, symbolizing the coming of the Branch a messianic figure who will unite the roles of priest and king. This act foreshadows the future reign of Christ, who will build the temple of the Lord and rule in peace.

A delegation asks whether they should continue fasting in remembrance of the temple’s destruction. God responds by questioning their motives, pointing out that their fasts were self-serving. He reminds them that true obedience is better than ritual observance.

God calls for justice, mercy, and compassion, condemning the hard-heartedness of the people’s ancestors. Because they refused to listen, God scattered them among the nations. This section reinforces the importance of sincere devotion and ethical living.

God declares His passionate love for Zion and promises to return to Jerusalem. The city will be called the Faithful City, and its streets will be filled with old men and children a symbol of peace and restoration.

God encourages the people to be strong and continue rebuilding the temple. He promises to bless their work and calls them to speak truth, pursue justice, and avoid evil. These ethical commands are tied to the blessings He intends to pour out.

God transforms the fasts of mourning into joyful feasts. He promises that many nations will come to seek the Lord in Jerusalem, and people from all languages will grasp the robe of a Jew, saying, 'Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.'

God pronounces judgment on Israel’s neighboring nations Hadrach, Damascus, Tyre, and others for their pride and oppression. Tyre’s wealth and fortifications will not save it. God promises to protect His people and encamp around His house, ensuring no oppressor will pass through again.

A messianic prophecy foretells the coming of a righteous and humble king riding on a donkey fulfilled in Jesus’ triumphal entry into Jerusalem. This king will bring peace to the nations and rule from sea to sea. God promises to restore His people, making them strong and victorious like warriors. Their prosperity and joy will overflow as they are saved by the Lord.

God urges the people to seek rain from Him, not from idols or false prophets. He condemns the shepherds (leaders) who mislead the flock and promises to strengthen Judah and restore both Judah and Joseph (Israel). God will gather His scattered people, redeem them, and bring them back to their land. They will walk in His name with strength and unity.

Zechariah enacts a prophetic allegory of shepherding a doomed flock. He breaks two staffs Favor and Union symbolizing the breaking of God’s covenant and the unity of Israel and Judah. He is paid thirty pieces of silver, which he throws into the temple foreshadowing Judas’s betrayal of Jesus. The chapter ends with a warning against a foolish shepherd who will exploit the flock, representing corrupt leadership.

God declares that He will make Jerusalem a cup of trembling and a burdensome stone to the nations. Though all nations gather against it, God will defend Jerusalem and empower its people. The house of David will be strengthened, and God will pour out a spirit of grace and supplication. The people will mourn deeply for the one they pierced, pointing to the crucified Messiah.

A fountain will be opened to cleanse sin and impurity. Idolatry and false prophecy will be cut off from the land. Even family members will reject false prophets. This purification reflects God’s desire for holiness among His people.

God calls for the sword to strike the shepherd another messianic prophecy fulfilled in Jesus. The sheep will scatter, but a remnant will be refined like silver and tested like gold. They will call on God, and He will answer, affirming their identity as His people.

The Day of the Lord arrives with Jerusalem under siege. God will fight for His people, and His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives, splitting it in two. Living waters will flow from Jerusalem, and the Lord will be king over all the earth. The city will be secure and inhabited in peace.

God will strike the enemies of Jerusalem with a plague. Survivors from the nations will come yearly to worship the King and celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles. Holiness will permeate everything, even the bells on horses and cooking pots. The book ends with a vision of universal worship and sanctification.

God declares His love for Israel, contrasting His favor toward Jacob with His rejection of Esau. Though Edom may try to rebuild, God will tear it down. This opening affirms God's covenant love and sets the stage for confronting Israel’s ingratitude.

God rebukes the priests for dishonoring Him by offering blemished sacrifices. They treat worship with contempt, offering blind, lame, and sick animals. God declares that His name will be great among the nations, and He will not accept defiled offerings. The chapter ends with a warning that cursed sacrifices dishonor the Lord.

God issues a stern warning to the priests: if they do not honor His name, He will curse their blessings and shame them publicly. He reminds them of His covenant with Levi, which was based on reverence and truth. The priests have turned from the path, causing many to stumble.

Malachi condemns Judah for breaking faith with one another and with God. The people have married foreign women who worship other gods, profaning the covenant. God also rebukes them for divorcing their wives treacherously. He declares, 'I hate divorce,' and calls for faithfulness in marriage.
The people weary God with their words, claiming that those who do evil are good in His sight. They question God's justice, revealing their spiritual blindness and moral confusion.

God promises to send a messenger to prepare the way before Him. The Lord will come suddenly to His temple, purifying the Levites like a refiner’s fire. Though God will bring judgment, He affirms that He does not change this is why Israel has not been consumed.

God calls the people to return to Him, accusing them of robbing Him through withheld tithes and offerings. He challenges them to test Him: if they give faithfully, He will open the windows of heaven and pour out blessings. Obedience will bring protection and fruitfulness.

God confronts those who speak arrogantly, claiming it is useless to serve Him. Yet a faithful remnant fears the Lord, and their names are written in a book of remembrance. God promises to spare them as His treasured possession on the day of judgment.

The Day of the Lord is coming like a burning furnace. The arrogant and wicked will be consumed like stubble, but those who fear the Lord will experience healing and victory. They will tread down the wicked like ashes underfoot.

God urges the people to remember the Law of Moses. He promises to send Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful Day of the Lord. Elijah will turn hearts of fathers to children and children to fathers, preventing total destruction. This final prophecy bridges the Old and New Testaments.
The genealogy of Jesus begins with Abraham and traces through David, highlighting key patriarchs and royal lineage.
The line continues through the kings of Judah, ending with the Babylonian exile.
Post-exile descendants lead to Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born.
Matthew summarizes the genealogy in three sets of fourteen generations.
Mary is found with child by the Holy Spirit; an angel tells Joseph to name Him Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins.
Jesus’ birth fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy of the virgin birth; Joseph obeys and names the child Jesus.
Wise men arrive in Jerusalem seeking the newborn King; Herod consults the chief priests about the Messiah’s birthplace.
Herod secretly meets the magi; they find Jesus in Bethlehem, worship Him, and are warned in a dream not to return to Herod.
Joseph is warned in a dream to flee to Egypt with Mary and Jesus, fulfilling Hosea’s prophecy.
Herod orders the massacre of Bethlehem’s male infants; Matthew links this to Jeremiah’s lamentation.
After Herod’s death, the family returns and settles in Nazareth, fulfilling the prophetic theme that He would be called a Nazarene.
John the Baptist preaches repentance in the wilderness, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy; people from all Judea come to be baptized.
John rebukes the Pharisees and Sadducees, warning them to bear fruit in keeping with repentance.
John contrasts his baptism with the coming One who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, bringing judgment.
Jesus comes to be baptized; John hesitates, but Jesus insists to fulfill all righteousness.
As Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends like a dove and the Father declares Him His beloved Son.
Jesus is led by the Spirit into the wilderness and resists Satan’s temptation to turn stones into bread, quoting Scripture to affirm dependence on God’s Word.
Satan tempts Jesus to test God’s protection by leaping from the temple; Jesus rebukes him, refusing to put God to the test.
Satan offers Jesus the kingdoms of the world in exchange for worship; Jesus commands him to leave, affirming worship belongs to God alone.
After John’s arrest, Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy and proclaiming, 'Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.'
Jesus calls Simon Peter, Andrew, James, and John to follow Him; they immediately leave their nets and families to become His disciples.
Jesus teaches, preaches, and heals throughout Galilee; large crowds from surrounding regions begin to follow Him.
The Beatitudes: Jesus blesses the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, and others who reflect Kingdom values, promising them comfort, inheritance, and reward.
Believers are called to be salt and light preserving truth and illuminating righteousness in the world.
Jesus declares He came to fulfill the Law, not abolish it, and calls for a righteousness that exceeds that of the Pharisees.
Jesus deepens the commandment against murder, teaching that anger and insult also bring judgment and urging reconciliation.
He equates lust with adultery of the heart and calls for radical purity, even if it means figurative self-amputation.
Jesus teaches that divorce, except for sexual immorality, causes adultery and undermines covenant faithfulness.
He warns against swearing oaths and urges simple, honest speech: 'Let your yes be yes and your no be no.'
Jesus overturns the principle of retaliation, calling for nonresistance, generosity, and going the extra mile.
He commands love for enemies and prayer for persecutors, modeling the perfection of the Father’s mercy.
Give to the needy in secret, not for public praise; God rewards what is done in private.
Pray sincerely and privately, not with empty repetition or for show.
Jesus teaches the Lord’s Prayer, emphasizing God’s holiness, provision, forgiveness, and deliverance.
Fast without drawing attention to yourself; God sees and rewards hidden devotion.
Store treasures in heaven, not on earth; your heart follows your treasure. You cannot serve both God and money.
Do not worry about food, drink, or clothing; seek first God’s kingdom and righteousness, and all needs will be provided.
Do not judge hypocritically; remove the plank from your own eye before addressing another’s speck.
Do not give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine exercise discernment in sharing sacred truths.
Ask, seek, and knock God responds generously to persistent, trusting prayer.
The Golden Rule: Treat others as you want to be treated; this sums up the Law and the Prophets.
Enter through the narrow gate; the path to life is hard and few find it, while the broad road leads to destruction.
Beware of false prophets; you will know them by their fruits good trees bear good fruit.
Not everyone who calls Jesus 'Lord' will enter the Kingdom, but only those who do the Father’s will.
The wise build on the rock by hearing and doing Jesus’ words; the foolish build on sand and fall in the storm.
The crowds are astonished at Jesus’ teaching, for He speaks with divine authority, not like the scribes.
Jesus heals a leper who approaches Him in faith, demonstrating His authority over disease and His willingness to cleanse the unclean.
A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant from afar; Jesus marvels at his faith and grants the request, declaring that many Gentiles will enter the Kingdom.
Jesus heals Peter’s mother-in-law of a fever; she rises and serves Him, showing immediate restoration and gratitude.
Jesus heals many who are sick and demon-possessed, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy that He bore our infirmities.
Jesus challenges would-be followers, warning them of the cost of discipleship and the need for total commitment.
Jesus calms a violent storm on the sea, rebuking the winds and waves and revealing His divine authority over nature.
Jesus casts demons out of two men in the region of the Gadarenes; the demons enter a herd of pigs, which rush into the sea, prompting the townspeople to ask Jesus to leave.
Jesus heals a paralyzed man and forgives his sins, revealing His authority to heal both body and soul.
Jesus calls Matthew the tax collector and dines with sinners, declaring that He came to call the sick, not the righteous.
Jesus explains why His disciples do not fast, using metaphors of new cloth and new wine to illustrate the newness of His mission.
Jesus raises a synagogue leader’s daughter and heals a woman with a bleeding condition who touches His garment in faith.
Two blind men are healed after expressing faith in Jesus as the Son of David; He warns them not to tell others, but they spread the news.
Jesus casts out a demon from a mute man, restoring his speech; the crowds marvel, but the Pharisees accuse Jesus of using demonic power.
Jesus travels through towns teaching and healing, moved with compassion for the crowds; He urges prayer for more laborers in the harvest.
Jesus calls and names His twelve apostles, giving them authority to heal and cast out demons.
He sends them to the lost sheep of Israel with instructions to preach, heal, and rely on hospitality, warning of judgment for those who reject them.
Jesus warns of persecution, betrayal, and suffering, but assures them of the Spirit’s help and promises salvation to those who endure.
He encourages boldness, reminding them of their value to God and the importance of confessing Him before others.
Jesus declares that His message will divide families and calls for radical allegiance even above family ties.
He promises reward for those who receive His messengers, even with small acts of kindness.
John the Baptist, imprisoned, sends disciples to ask if Jesus is the Messiah. Jesus responds by pointing to His miracles and preaching as fulfillment of prophecy.
Jesus honors John as the greatest born of women and identifies him as the prophesied forerunner, yet says the least in the Kingdom is greater than he.
Jesus critiques the fickle generation that rejected both John’s asceticism and His own approach, likening them to children who refuse to be satisfied.
Jesus denounces unrepentant cities like Chorazin and Capernaum, warning that Gentile cities would have repented if they had seen such miracles.
Jesus praises the Father for revealing truth to the humble and affirms His unique relationship with the Father as the revealer of divine knowledge.
Jesus invites the weary to find rest in Him, offering a gentle yoke and a light burden to those who follow Him.
Jesus defends His disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath, declaring Himself Lord of the Sabbath and prioritizing mercy over sacrifice.
He heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, exposing the Pharisees’ hardness of heart and prompting them to plot against Him.
Jesus withdraws and heals many, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy of the gentle Servant who brings justice to the nations.
Jesus casts out a demon, prompting accusations of using Satan’s power. He refutes them and warns against blasphemy of the Holy Spirit.
Jesus teaches that words reveal the heart, and people will be judged by their speech good trees bear good fruit.
When asked for a sign, Jesus offers only the sign of Jonah, pointing to His death and resurrection as the ultimate proof.
He warns that spiritual emptiness invites greater evil, likening it to a house swept clean but left unoccupied.
Jesus redefines family as those who do the will of His Father, emphasizing spiritual kinship over blood ties.
Jesus tells the Parable of the Sower, describing how different hearts receive the Word like different soils receive seed.
He explains why He speaks in parables to reveal truth to seekers and conceal it from the hard-hearted, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy.
Jesus interprets the Parable of the Sower, identifying the four types of hearers and their responses to the Word.
The Parable of the Weeds illustrates the coexistence of good and evil until the final judgment.
The Parables of the Mustard Seed and Leaven show the Kingdom’s small beginnings and expansive, transformative power.
Matthew notes that Jesus spoke in parables to fulfill prophecy about hidden truths being revealed.
Jesus explains the Parable of the Weeds, identifying the sower, the enemy, the harvest, and the judgment of the wicked.
The Parables of the Hidden Treasure and the Pearl emphasize the incomparable value of the Kingdom, worth sacrificing everything to obtain.
The Parable of the Net depicts the final separation of the righteous and the wicked at the end of the age.
Jesus affirms that those trained in the Kingdom bring out treasures both old and new truths from the Law and the Gospel.
Jesus is rejected in His hometown of Nazareth, where familiarity breeds unbelief, and He does few miracles due to their lack of faith.
Herod hears of Jesus’ fame and fears He is John the Baptist raised from the dead.
Flashback: John the Baptist is imprisoned and beheaded at Herod’s birthday feast due to Herodias’ manipulation through her daughter’s dance.
Jesus withdraws to grieve, but crowds follow Him; moved with compassion, He heals their sick.
Jesus feeds over 5,000 people with five loaves and two fish, demonstrating divine provision and abundance.
Jesus walks on water toward the disciples’ boat during a storm; they are terrified, but He calms them with His presence.
Peter walks on water toward Jesus but begins to sink when he doubts; Jesus rescues him and calms the sea.
In Gennesaret, people bring their sick to Jesus, and many are healed simply by touching His garment.
Pharisees confront Jesus about handwashing traditions; He rebukes them for elevating human tradition over God’s commandments.
Jesus teaches that defilement comes from the heart, not from what enters the mouth.
A Canaanite woman pleads for her daughter’s healing; Jesus tests her faith, then praises it and grants her request.
Jesus heals many on a mountainside lame, blind, mute, and crippled causing the crowd to glorify God.
Jesus feeds 4,000 men (plus women and children) with seven loaves and a few fish, again showing His compassion and power.
Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign; Jesus refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah.
Jesus warns the disciples about the 'leaven' the corrupting influence of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ; Jesus blesses him and speaks of building His church on this confession.
Jesus predicts His suffering and death; Peter rebukes Him, and Jesus sharply corrects him for opposing God’s plan.
Jesus teaches the cost of discipleship: deny self, take up your cross, and follow Him, for eternal reward outweighs worldly gain.
Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John; His divine glory is revealed alongside Moses and Elijah.
Jesus explains that Elijah has already come in the person of John the Baptist, who was rejected.
Jesus heals a demon-possessed boy after the disciples fail; He teaches that faith and prayer are essential.
Jesus again predicts His betrayal, death, and resurrection; the disciples are distressed.
To avoid offense, Jesus tells Peter to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth to pay the temple tax for both of them.
The disciples ask who is greatest in the Kingdom. Jesus places a child before them, teaching that humility and childlike faith are essential for entering the Kingdom.
Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and urges radical action against personal sin, emphasizing the seriousness of eternal consequences.
The Parable of the Lost Sheep illustrates God's deep concern for each individual, especially those who go astray.
Jesus outlines a process for confronting a sinning brother: private correction, small group confirmation, and finally church involvement if unrepentant.
He affirms the authority of believers gathered in unity and promises His presence where two or three gather in His name.
Peter asks how often to forgive; Jesus replies not seven times, but seventy-seven times signifying limitless forgiveness.
The Parable of the Unforgiving Servant teaches that those forgiven by God must extend the same mercy to others, or face judgment.
Pharisees test Jesus on divorce. He affirms God’s original design for marriage as a lifelong union between one man and one woman.
Jesus explains that Moses permitted divorce due to hardened hearts, but it was not God’s intent. He also speaks of celibacy for the sake of the Kingdom.
Jesus welcomes little children and blesses them, declaring that the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to such as these.
A rich young man asks how to gain eternal life. Jesus challenges him to sell his possessions and follow Him, but the man walks away sorrowful.
Jesus teaches that it is difficult for the rich to enter the Kingdom, but with God all things are possible.
Peter asks about the disciples’ reward. Jesus promises thrones and eternal life to those who have left everything for His sake, and warns that the last will be first.
The Parable of the Workers in the Vineyard illustrates God’s generosity and the reversal of human expectations: the last will be first, and the first last.
Jesus again predicts His betrayal, suffering, death, and resurrection as He heads toward Jerusalem.
The mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit beside Jesus in His Kingdom. Jesus responds that greatness comes through suffering and service.
Jesus teaches that true greatness is found in serving others, just as He came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom for many.
Two blind men cry out to Jesus as He passes by. Moved with compassion, He heals them, and they follow Him.
Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah’s prophecy. The crowds welcome Him with palm branches and shouts of 'Hosanna to the Son of David!'
Jesus cleanses the temple, overturning the tables of money changers and declaring it a house of prayer. He heals the blind and lame, while children praise Him, angering the chief priests.
Jesus curses a barren fig tree, which withers immediately. He teaches the disciples about faith and the power of prayer.
Religious leaders question Jesus’ authority. He counters with a question about John the Baptist, exposing their hypocrisy.
The Parable of the Two Sons: One son refuses to obey but later repents; the other agrees to obey but does not. Jesus applies this to the religious leaders’ rejection of repentance.
The Parable of the Wicked Tenants: Tenants kill the landowner’s servants and son. Jesus warns that the Kingdom will be given to others who bear fruit. The leaders realize He is speaking about them.
The Parable of the Wedding Feast: Many reject the king’s invitation; one guest is cast out for lacking proper attire. Jesus warns that many are called, but few are chosen.
Pharisees try to trap Jesus with a question about taxes. He replies, 'Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s,' silencing them.
Sadducees challenge Jesus on the resurrection with a hypothetical marriage. He corrects their misunderstanding and affirms that God is the God of the living.
A lawyer asks about the greatest commandment. Jesus answers: Love God with all your heart, and love your neighbor as yourself on these hang all the Law and Prophets.
Jesus questions the Pharisees about the Messiah’s identity, showing that the Christ is both David’s son and David’s Lord. They are unable to respond.
Jesus warns the crowds about the scribes and Pharisees, who preach but do not practice. He calls for humility and servant leadership.
Jesus pronounces seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees for hypocrisy, legalism, greed, and spiritual blindness. He compares them to whitewashed tombs beautiful outside, but full of death within.
Jesus laments over Jerusalem, longing to gather its people like a hen gathers her chicks, but they were unwilling. He foretells their desolation until they welcome Him again.
Jesus foretells the destruction of the temple, declaring that not one stone will be left upon another.
On the Mount of Olives, Jesus outlines signs of the end: false messiahs, wars, famines, earthquakes, persecution, and the global preaching of the gospel.
He warns of the 'abomination of desolation' spoken of by Daniel, urging urgent flight and describing a time of great tribulation.
Jesus cautions against deception by false Christs and false prophets, emphasizing that His return will be unmistakable.
After the tribulation, cosmic signs will precede the visible return of the Son of Man, who will gather His elect with a trumpet call.
The Parable of the Fig Tree teaches that the signs will indicate the nearness of His return, and His words will never pass away.
Jesus stresses that no one knows the day or hour of His coming, likening it to the days of Noah unexpected and sudden.
He contrasts the faithful and wicked servants, urging readiness and warning of judgment for those who are unprepared.
The Parable of the Ten Virgins: Five wise virgins bring extra oil and are welcomed into the wedding feast; five foolish ones are shut out, symbolizing the need for spiritual preparedness.
The Parable of the Talents: A master entrusts his servants with talents; two invest and are rewarded, while one hides his and is condemned highlighting faithful stewardship.

The Final Judgment: The Son of Man separates the nations like sheep and goats based on their treatment of 'the least of these,' revealing that acts of compassion reflect one’s relationship with Christ.
Jesus predicts His imminent crucifixion during Passover. Meanwhile, the chief priests and elders conspire to arrest and kill Him, but not during the feast to avoid public unrest.
At Bethany, a woman anoints Jesus with expensive perfume. Though the disciples criticize the act, Jesus praises her, saying she has prepared Him for burial and her deed will be remembered.
Judas Iscariot agrees to betray Jesus to the chief priests in exchange for thirty pieces of silver.
During the Passover meal, Jesus reveals that one of the disciples will betray Him. Each asks, 'Is it I?' and Jesus confirms it is Judas.
Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper, symbolizing His body and blood as the new covenant. They sing a hymn and go to the Mount of Olives.
Jesus predicts that all the disciples will fall away and that Peter will deny Him three times before dawn. Peter insists he will never deny Him.
In Gethsemane, Jesus prays in deep anguish, asking the Father to let the cup pass, yet submits to His will. The disciples repeatedly fall asleep.
Judas arrives with a crowd and betrays Jesus with a kiss. Jesus is arrested, and the disciples flee.
Jesus is brought before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin. False witnesses accuse Him, and He is condemned for blasphemy after affirming He is the Son of God.
Peter denies Jesus three times as predicted. When the rooster crows, he remembers Jesus’ words and weeps bitterly.
Jesus is handed over to Pilate. Judas, filled with remorse, returns the silver and hangs himself. The priests use the money to buy a potter’s field.
Pilate questions Jesus and offers to release Him or Barabbas. The crowd chooses Barabbas. Pilate washes his hands and delivers Jesus to be crucified.
Roman soldiers mock Jesus, placing a crown of thorns on His head and striking Him before leading Him away.
Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two criminals. Bystanders and religious leaders mock Him, challenging Him to save Himself.
Darkness covers the land. Jesus cries out and dies. The temple veil is torn, the earth quakes, and many recognize Him as the Son of God.
Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus in his own tomb. Mary Magdalene and the other Mary watch where He is laid.
The chief priests secure the tomb with a guard and seal, fearing the disciples might steal the body and claim resurrection.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary find the tomb empty. An angel announces Jesus’ resurrection. Jesus appears to them and tells them to inform the disciples.
The guards report the resurrection to the chief priests, who bribe them to spread the false story that the disciples stole the body.
Jesus meets the disciples in Galilee and gives the Great Commission: to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them, with the promise of His presence always.
John the Baptist prepares the way for the Messiah, preaching repentance and baptizing in the wilderness. He foretells the coming of one greater who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.
Jesus is baptized by John in the Jordan. As He emerges from the water, the Spirit descends like a dove and the Father declares Him His beloved Son.
Immediately after His baptism, Jesus is driven into the wilderness where He is tempted by Satan for forty days, yet remains without sin.
Following John’s arrest, Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, proclaiming the arrival of God’s Kingdom and calling for repentance and belief in the gospel.
Jesus calls His first disciples Simon, Andrew, James, and John who leave their nets and follow Him immediately.
In Capernaum, Jesus teaches with authority and casts out an unclean spirit in the synagogue, astonishing the people.
Jesus heals Simon’s mother-in-law and many others who are sick or demon-possessed, drawing crowds to the door.
Jesus rises early to pray in solitude. When found by His disciples, He insists on continuing His mission to preach in other towns.
A leper approaches Jesus in faith and is healed. Jesus instructs him to remain silent, but the man spreads the news, causing Jesus to stay in secluded places.
Jesus heals a paralyzed man lowered through the roof, first forgiving his sins. The scribes accuse Him of blasphemy, but Jesus proves His authority by healing the man.
Jesus calls Levi (Matthew) the tax collector and dines with sinners. He explains that He came to call sinners, not the righteous.
When questioned about fasting, Jesus compares His presence to a wedding feast and uses metaphors of new cloth and new wine to illustrate the newness of His ministry.
Jesus defends His disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath, declaring that the Sabbath was made for man and that He is Lord of the Sabbath.
Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, provoking the Pharisees to conspire with the Herodians to destroy Him.
Large crowds follow Jesus from many regions. He heals many and commands unclean spirits not to reveal His identity.
Jesus appoints twelve apostles to be with Him, to preach, and to have authority to cast out demons.
Jesus is accused by scribes of casting out demons by Beelzebul. He refutes them, warning that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is an unforgivable sin.
When His family comes to take Him home, Jesus redefines true kinship as those who do the will of God.
Jesus teaches the Parable of the Sower to a large crowd from a boat, illustrating how different hearts receive the Word like various types of soil.
Privately, Jesus explains that parables reveal truth to those open to it, but conceal it from the hard-hearted, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy.
He interprets the Parable of the Sower: the seed is the Word, and the soils represent hearts some hardened, shallow, distracted, or fruitful.
Jesus teaches that truth is meant to be revealed, like a lamp on a stand. The measure of attention given to His words determines spiritual understanding.
The Parable of the Growing Seed shows the mysterious, God-driven growth of the Kingdom, independent of human control.
The Parable of the Mustard Seed illustrates how the Kingdom starts small but grows into something vast and sheltering.
Jesus calms a violent storm on the Sea of Galilee, rebuking the wind and waves. The disciples marvel, asking, 'Who is this, that even the wind and sea obey Him?'
Jesus heals a man possessed by a legion of demons in the region of the Gerasenes. The demons enter pigs, which rush into the sea. The man is restored and sent to proclaim what Jesus has done.
Jairus, a synagogue leader, pleads with Jesus to heal his dying daughter. Jesus agrees and begins the journey with him.
A woman with a twelve-year bleeding condition touches Jesus’ garment in faith and is instantly healed. Jesus commends her faith and calls her 'daughter.'
News arrives that Jairus’s daughter has died, but Jesus tells him to believe. He raises the girl from the dead, astonishing all present.
Jesus is rejected in His hometown of Nazareth. The people are offended by His wisdom and miracles, and their unbelief limits what He does there.
Jesus sends out the twelve disciples two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits and instructing them to travel simply and preach repentance.
Herod hears of Jesus and fears He is John the Baptist raised from the dead. The narrative recounts John’s beheading at Herod’s banquet due to Herodias’ grudge.
Jesus feeds over 5,000 people with five loaves and two fish, demonstrating His compassion and divine provision.
Jesus walks on water toward the disciples’ boat during a storm. They are terrified, but He calms them and the wind, revealing His divine authority.
Wherever Jesus goes, people bring the sick to Him. Many are healed simply by touching the fringe of His garment.
Pharisees and scribes confront Jesus about His disciples eating with unwashed hands. Jesus rebukes them for elevating human tradition above God’s commandments, exposing their hypocrisy.
Jesus teaches the crowd that true defilement comes not from external things but from within the heart evil thoughts, immorality, and pride.
In Tyre, a Syrophoenician woman pleads for her daughter’s healing. Jesus tests her faith, then commends it and heals her daughter from afar.
In Decapolis, Jesus heals a deaf and mute man by touching his ears and tongue and saying, 'Be opened!' The crowd is amazed, declaring, 'He has done all things well.'
Jesus feeds 4,000 people with seven loaves and a few fish, demonstrating His compassion and divine provision.
Pharisees demand a sign from heaven. Jesus refuses, sighing deeply at their unbelief.
Jesus warns the disciples about the 'leaven' of the Pharisees and Herod. They misunderstand, thinking He refers to bread, revealing their spiritual dullness.
In Bethsaida, Jesus heals a blind man in two stages, symbolizing the gradual opening of spiritual eyes.
At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ. Jesus instructs them not to tell anyone yet.
Jesus predicts His suffering, death, and resurrection. Peter rebukes Him, but Jesus rebukes Peter for opposing God’s plan.
Jesus teaches the cost of discipleship: deny self, take up your cross, and follow Him. Gaining the world is worthless if one loses their soul.
Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John. Moses and Elijah appear, and a voice from heaven declares, 'This is my beloved Son; listen to Him.'
Jesus heals a boy possessed by a mute spirit after the disciples fail. The father cries, 'I believe; help my unbelief!' Jesus teaches that such power comes through prayer.
Jesus again predicts His death and resurrection. The disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask.
The disciples argue about who is greatest. Jesus teaches that true greatness is found in humility and welcoming the lowly, like a child.
John reports someone casting out demons in Jesus’ name. Jesus says not to stop him whoever is not against us is for us.
Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and urges radical action against sin. He calls for purity, peace, and preserving one’s witness like salt.
Jesus teaches on marriage and divorce, affirming God’s original design for lifelong union and rejecting the Pharisees’ attempts to justify easy divorce.
Jesus welcomes little children, rebuking the disciples and declaring that the Kingdom of God belongs to those who receive it with childlike faith.
A rich young man asks how to inherit eternal life. Jesus challenges him to sell all and follow Him, but the man walks away sorrowful, unable to part with his wealth.
Jesus teaches that it is hard for the rich to enter the Kingdom, but with God all things are possible. He promises great reward for those who leave everything for His sake.
Jesus again predicts His suffering, death, and resurrection as they journey toward Jerusalem.
James and John request seats of honor in Jesus’ glory. He teaches that true greatness comes through servanthood, just as He came to give His life as a ransom for many.
Blind Bartimaeus cries out to Jesus and is healed because of his persistent faith. He immediately follows Jesus on the way.
Jesus enters Jerusalem riding a colt, fulfilling prophecy. The crowds shout 'Hosanna!' and welcome Him as the coming King.
Jesus curses a fig tree for bearing no fruit, symbolizing judgment on fruitless religion.
Jesus cleanses the temple, driving out merchants and declaring it a house of prayer for all nations. The religious leaders begin plotting His death.
The withered fig tree becomes a lesson on faith, prayer, and forgiveness.
Religious leaders question Jesus’ authority. He counters with a question about John the Baptist, exposing their fear and hypocrisy.
The Parable of the Tenants: A landowner’s servants and son are rejected and killed by tenants. Jesus warns that the Kingdom will be given to others who bear fruit.
Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus with a question about taxes. He replies, 'Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.'
Sadducees challenge Jesus on the resurrection. He corrects their misunderstanding and affirms that God is the God of the living.
A scribe asks about the greatest commandment. Jesus answers: Love God with all your being, and love your neighbor as yourself.
Jesus questions how the Messiah can be both David’s son and Lord, revealing His divine identity.
Jesus warns against the scribes who seek honor but exploit the vulnerable. They will receive greater condemnation.
Jesus praises a poor widow who gives two small coins, saying she gave more than all others because she gave all she had.
As the disciples admire the temple’s grandeur, Jesus foretells its complete destruction 'not one stone will be left upon another.'
On the Mount of Olives, Jesus warns of false messiahs, wars, earthquakes, and famines calling them the beginning of birth pains.
He prepares the disciples for persecution, betrayal, and hatred for His name’s sake, encouraging endurance to the end.
Jesus describes the 'abomination of desolation' and urges urgent flight during the great tribulation, warning of deceptive false prophets.
After the tribulation, cosmic signs will precede the coming of the Son of Man, who will gather His elect from the ends of the earth.
The Parable of the Fig Tree teaches that the signs will indicate the nearness of His return, and His words will never pass away.
Jesus emphasizes watchfulness, as no one knows the day or hour not even the Son so His followers must stay alert and ready.
The chief priests and scribes plot to arrest and kill Jesus, but not during the feast to avoid a public uproar.
At Bethany, a woman anoints Jesus with costly perfume. Though criticized, Jesus praises her act as preparation for His burial.
Judas Iscariot agrees to betray Jesus to the chief priests in exchange for money.
During the Passover meal, Jesus predicts His betrayal by one of the Twelve, causing sorrow and confusion among the disciples.
Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper, identifying the bread and wine as His body and blood of the new covenant.
Jesus predicts that all the disciples will fall away and that Peter will deny Him three times before the rooster crows twice.
In Gethsemane, Jesus prays in deep anguish, submitting to the Father’s will while the disciples repeatedly fall asleep.
Judas arrives with a crowd and betrays Jesus with a kiss. Jesus is arrested, and all the disciples flee.
Jesus is brought before the Sanhedrin. False witnesses accuse Him, and He is condemned for blasphemy after affirming His identity as the Son of God.
Peter denies Jesus three times. When the rooster crows, he remembers Jesus’ words and weeps bitterly.
Jesus is brought before Pilate. Though accused by the chief priests, He remains mostly silent, astonishing the governor.
Pilate offers to release a prisoner. The crowd, stirred by the priests, demands Barabbas and calls for Jesus’ crucifixion. Pilate, seeking to satisfy the crowd, hands Jesus over.
Roman soldiers mock Jesus, dressing Him in purple, crowning Him with thorns, and striking Him before leading Him away.
Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two criminals. Bystanders and leaders mock Him, challenging Him to save Himself.
Darkness covers the land. Jesus cries out and dies. The temple veil is torn. A centurion declares, 'Truly this man was the Son of God.' Women followers watch from a distance.
Joseph of Arimathea courageously asks Pilate for Jesus’ body and lays it in a tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses witness the burial.
Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome find the tomb empty. An angel announces Jesus’ resurrection and instructs them to tell the disciples. They flee in awe and fear.
Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, but the disciples do not believe her report.
He appears in another form to two disciples walking in the country, but they too are not believed.
Jesus appears to the Eleven, rebukes their unbelief, and commissions them to preach the gospel to all creation, promising signs to accompany believers.
Jesus ascends into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. The disciples go out and preach, with signs confirming their message.
Luke introduces his Gospel as an orderly account addressed to Theophilus, aiming to provide certainty about the events surrounding Jesus.

The angel Gabriel appears to Zechariah, announcing that his wife Elizabeth will bear a son, John, who will prepare the way for the Lord. Zechariah doubts and is rendered mute until the prophecy is fulfilled.
Gabriel visits Mary in Nazareth, announcing that she will conceive Jesus by the Holy Spirit. Mary humbly accepts her role in God’s plan.
Mary visits Elizabeth, whose baby leaps in the womb. Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, blesses Mary for her faith.
Mary praises God in the Magnificat, celebrating His mercy, justice, and faithfulness to Israel.
John is born. Zechariah confirms his name and regains his speech, causing awe among the neighbors.
Zechariah prophesies in the Benedictus, praising God for redemption and foretelling John’s role as the forerunner of the Messiah.
Joseph and Mary travel to Bethlehem for a census. Jesus is born and laid in a manger, fulfilling prophecy.
Angels announce Jesus’ birth to shepherds, who visit the newborn and glorify God. Mary treasures these events in her heart.
Jesus is circumcised and presented at the temple, in accordance with the Law of Moses.
Simeon, led by the Spirit, blesses the infant Jesus and prophesies about His role in salvation and the opposition He will face.
Prophetess Anna gives thanks to God and speaks about Jesus to those awaiting redemption.
The family returns to Nazareth, and Jesus grows strong, filled with wisdom and God’s favor.
At age twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, astonishing teachers with His understanding. He declares His devotion to His Father’s house.
John the Baptist begins his ministry, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy as the voice preparing the way of the Lord.
John preaches repentance and ethical living, calling for fruit in keeping with repentance and addressing specific groups like tax collectors and soldiers.
John clarifies that he is not the Messiah but points to One greater who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. He rebukes Herod and is imprisoned.
Jesus is baptized. As He prays, the Holy Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father affirms Him as His beloved Son.
Luke presents Jesus’ genealogy, tracing His lineage through David and Abraham all the way back to Adam, emphasizing His universal mission.
Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, is led into the wilderness and tempted by the devil for forty days. He resists each temptation by quoting Scripture, affirming His obedience to the Father.
Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit and begins teaching in synagogues, gaining widespread praise.
In Nazareth, Jesus reads from Isaiah and declares the prophecy fulfilled. The crowd initially marvels but turns hostile when He challenges their assumptions, attempting to throw Him off a cliff.
In Capernaum, Jesus teaches with authority and casts out an unclean spirit in the synagogue, astonishing the people.
Jesus heals Simon’s mother-in-law and many others. Demons are cast out, and they recognize Him as the Son of God, but He silences them.
Jesus withdraws to a solitary place, but the crowds seek Him. He insists on preaching the Kingdom of God in other towns as well.
Jesus performs a miraculous catch of fish and calls Simon Peter, James, and John to follow Him and become fishers of men.
Jesus heals a man with leprosy, instructing him to follow Mosaic law. News spreads, and crowds gather, but Jesus often withdraws to pray.
Jesus heals a paralyzed man lowered through the roof, first forgiving his sins. The Pharisees question His authority, but the healing confirms His divine power.
Jesus calls Levi (Matthew) the tax collector and dines with sinners. He declares that He came to call sinners to repentance, not the righteous.
When questioned about fasting, Jesus explains that His presence is like a wedding feast. He uses parables of new cloth and wineskins to illustrate the newness of His mission.
Jesus defends His disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath, declaring that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, provoking the Pharisees to rage and plot against Him.
After a night of prayer, Jesus selects twelve apostles from among His disciples.
Jesus delivers the Beatitudes and corresponding woes, blessing the poor and warning the rich, redefining Kingdom values.
He teaches radical love: love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and be merciful as the Father is merciful.
Jesus warns against hypocritical judgment and urges self-examination before correcting others.
He teaches that a tree is known by its fruit good hearts produce good words and actions.
Jesus concludes with the parable of the wise and foolish builders, emphasizing the importance of obeying His words.

A Roman centurion in Capernaum sends elders to ask Jesus to heal his servant. Though the centurion feels unworthy for Jesus to enter his home, he expresses great faith in Jesus’ authority. Jesus marvels at his faith and heals the servant from a distance.
In Nain, Jesus raises a widow’s only son from the dead, moved by compassion. The crowd is filled with awe, declaring that a great prophet has arisen and that God has visited His people.
John the Baptist, from prison, sends disciples to ask if Jesus is the Messiah. Jesus points to His miracles and preaching as evidence and blesses those who are not offended by Him.
Jesus praises John as more than a prophet and critiques the generation’s fickleness they rejected both John’s asceticism and Jesus’ openness.

At a Pharisee’s house, a sinful woman anoints Jesus’ feet with her tears and perfume. Jesus tells a parable about forgiveness and love, then declares her sins forgiven, saying her faith has saved her.
Jesus travels with the Twelve and several women who support His ministry, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Susanna.
Jesus tells the Parable of the Sower, explaining how different hearts receive the Word like various soils only the good soil bears lasting fruit.
He teaches that light is meant to be revealed and urges careful listening, for those who receive will be given more.
Jesus redefines family as those who hear and obey God’s Word.
Jesus calms a storm on the lake, rebuking the wind and waves. The disciples marvel at His authority over nature.
In the region of the Gerasenes, Jesus casts a legion of demons out of a man into pigs. The man is restored and sent to proclaim what God has done for him.
Jesus heals a woman with a twelve-year bleeding condition who touches His garment in faith. He then raises Jairus’s daughter from the dead, urging faith and silence.
Jesus sends out the Twelve with power to heal and preach the Kingdom, instructing them to travel simply and rely on hospitality.
Herod hears of Jesus’ miracles and is perplexed, wondering if John the Baptist has risen from the dead.
Jesus feeds over 5,000 people with five loaves and two fish, demonstrating divine provision and compassion.
Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ after Jesus asks who the disciples believe He is.
Jesus predicts His suffering and calls for self-denial and cross-bearing, warning that gaining the world is worthless if one loses their soul.
Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John. Moses and Elijah appear, and a voice from heaven declares Jesus as God’s Son.
Jesus heals a boy possessed by an unclean spirit after the disciples fail. He rebukes their lack of faith.
Jesus again predicts His betrayal, but the disciples do not understand and are afraid to ask.
The disciples argue about greatness. Jesus teaches that the least is the greatest and that whoever is not against them is for them.
As Jesus sets His face toward Jerusalem, a Samaritan village rejects Him. James and John want to call down fire, but Jesus rebukes them.
Jesus challenges would-be followers, emphasizing the cost of discipleship and the need for total commitment.

Jesus appoints seventy-two disciples and sends them out in pairs to proclaim the Kingdom, heal the sick, and prepare towns for His arrival. He warns them of rejection and pronounces judgment on unrepentant cities.
Jesus rebukes Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum for their hardness of heart despite witnessing miracles, declaring that rejecting His messengers is rejecting Him.
The seventy-two return with joy, reporting that demons submitted to them. Jesus affirms their authority but urges them to rejoice that their names are written in heaven.
Jesus rejoices in the Spirit, praising the Father for revealing truth to the humble. He blesses the disciples for witnessing what prophets longed to see.
A lawyer asks how to inherit eternal life. Jesus tells the Parable of the Good Samaritan, redefining 'neighbor' as anyone in need and highlighting mercy over religious status.
Jesus visits Martha and Mary. While Martha is distracted with serving, Mary sits at His feet. Jesus affirms that Mary has chosen the better portion listening to His word.
In response to a disciple’s request, Jesus teaches the Lord’s Prayer, emphasizing reverence, provision, forgiveness, and deliverance.
Through a parable and teaching, Jesus urges persistence in prayer and assures that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask.
Jesus casts out a mute demon. Some accuse Him of using Beelzebul’s power, but He refutes them, declaring that a divided kingdom cannot stand and that He casts out demons by God’s power.
Jesus warns that an unclean spirit may return with greater force if a person’s life remains spiritually empty after deliverance.
A woman blesses Jesus’ mother, but He replies that true blessedness belongs to those who hear and obey God’s Word.
Jesus rebukes the crowd for seeking a sign, offering only the sign of Jonah His death and resurrection as the ultimate proof.
He teaches that the eye is the lamp of the body and urges spiritual clarity, warning against inner darkness.
At a Pharisee’s dinner, Jesus pronounces woes on the Pharisees and experts in the law for hypocrisy, legalism, and hindering others from knowing God.
Jesus warns against the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, declaring that all hidden things will be revealed.
He urges fearless confession of faith, trusting in God’s care and the Spirit’s help in times of persecution.
Jesus tells the Parable of the Rich Fool, warning against greed and storing up earthly wealth without being rich toward God.
He teaches not to worry about material needs, assuring that the Father provides and calling His followers to seek the Kingdom first.
Jesus urges readiness for His return, likening it to servants awaiting their master. Faithful servants are rewarded; negligent ones face judgment.
He declares that His coming will bring division even within families as people respond differently to His message.
Jesus rebukes the crowds for failing to interpret the spiritual signs of the times and urges reconciliation before judgment.
Jesus responds to tragic events by emphasizing that all must repent or perish, rejecting the idea that suffering always reflects personal guilt.
The Parable of the Barren Fig Tree illustrates God’s patience and the urgency of bearing spiritual fruit before judgment comes.
Jesus heals a woman crippled for eighteen years on the Sabbath. When criticized, He defends the act as a work of mercy, silencing His opponents.
The Parables of the Mustard Seed and the Leaven show how the Kingdom of God starts small but grows expansively and transforms everything it touches.
Jesus teaches about the narrow door to salvation, warning that many will seek to enter too late and be excluded despite their familiarity with Him.
Pharisees warn Jesus about Herod. He remains undeterred, laments over Jerusalem’s rejection of prophets, and foretells its desolation.
Jesus heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath in a Pharisee’s home, challenging their legalism with a question about rescuing animals on the Sabbath.
He teaches guests to choose the lowest seat at a banquet, illustrating that those who humble themselves will be exalted.
Jesus urges hosts to invite the poor, crippled, and blind those who cannot repay promising reward at the resurrection of the righteous.
The Parable of the Great Banquet shows that many invited guests reject the call, so the host invites the outcasts instead, symbolizing God’s open invitation to all.
Jesus teaches the cost of discipleship, calling for total allegiance even above family and self and urging people to count the cost before following Him.
He warns that salt without flavor is useless, symbolizing disciples who lose their distinctiveness and commitment.
The Parable of the Lost Sheep: A shepherd leaves ninety-nine to find one lost sheep, illustrating God’s joy over one sinner who repents.
The Parable of the Lost Coin: A woman searches diligently for a lost coin and rejoices when she finds it, symbolizing heaven’s joy over repentance.
The Parable of the Prodigal Son: A younger son squanders his inheritance but returns in repentance. The father runs to welcome him, celebrating his restoration.
The elder brother resents the celebration, revealing self-righteousness. The father pleads with him, showing that God’s grace is for all who return.

The Parable of the Shrewd Manager: A dishonest steward secures his future by reducing debts. Jesus commends his foresight not his dishonesty and teaches that believers should wisely use worldly wealth for eternal purposes, for no one can serve both God and money.
Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for their love of money and self-justification. He affirms the enduring authority of the Law and addresses the seriousness of divorce and remarriage.

The Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus: A rich man lives in luxury while a poor man, Lazarus, suffers. After death, Lazarus is comforted in Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man is tormented. The story emphasizes the finality of judgment and the sufficiency of Scripture for repentance.
Jesus warns against causing others to stumble and commands repeated forgiveness for those who repent even seven times in a day.
The apostles ask for more faith. Jesus replies that even faith as small as a mustard seed can uproot a mulberry tree highlighting the power of genuine belief.
He teaches that servants should not expect praise for doing their duty, emphasizing humble obedience in discipleship.
Jesus heals ten lepers, but only one a Samaritan returns to give thanks. Jesus commends his faith and gratitude.
Jesus teaches that the Kingdom of God is not coming with visible signs it is already among them. He warns of sudden judgment, likening it to the days of Noah and Lot, and urges readiness.
The Parable of the Persistent Widow: A widow secures justice from an unjust judge through persistence. Jesus encourages continual prayer and faith, assuring that God will respond to His elect.
The Parable of the Pharisee and the Tax Collector: A proud Pharisee and a humble tax collector pray in the temple. The tax collector is justified, teaching that humility leads to righteousness.
Jesus welcomes little children and teaches that the Kingdom of God belongs to those who receive it with childlike faith.

A rich ruler asks how to inherit eternal life. Jesus challenges him to sell all and follow Him. The man walks away sorrowful. Jesus teaches that with God, even the impossible like a rich man entering the Kingdom is possible.
Jesus predicts His suffering, death, and resurrection for the third time. The disciples do not understand His words.
As Jesus approaches Jericho, a blind beggar cries out for mercy. Jesus heals him, and the man follows, glorifying God.

Jesus enters Jericho and calls Zacchaeus, a wealthy tax collector, down from a sycamore tree. Zacchaeus repents and pledges restitution. Jesus declares that salvation has come to his house, affirming His mission to seek and save the lost.

The Parable of the Ten Minas: A nobleman entrusts servants with money before leaving to receive a kingdom. Upon return, he rewards the faithful and punishes the unproductive, warning of judgment for those who reject his rule.
Jesus makes His triumphal entry into Jerusalem on a colt, fulfilling prophecy. The crowds praise Him as King, but the Pharisees object. Jesus says if they were silent, the stones would cry out.
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, foreseeing its destruction because it did not recognize the time of its visitation.
Jesus cleanses the temple, driving out merchants and declaring it a house of prayer. The religious leaders seek to destroy Him, but the people are captivated by His teaching.
Religious leaders challenge Jesus’ authority. He counters by asking about John the Baptist’s origin, exposing their fear and hypocrisy.
The Parable of the Wicked Tenants: Tenants kill the landowner’s servants and son. Jesus warns that the Kingdom will be given to others. The leaders realize He is speaking against them.
Spies try to trap Jesus with a question about taxes. He replies, 'Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s,' astonishing them.
Sadducees question Jesus about the resurrection. He affirms that God is the God of the living and explains that resurrection life is different from earthly marriage.
Jesus asks how the Christ can be both David’s son and Lord, revealing His divine identity.
He warns the people about the scribes, who seek honor but exploit the vulnerable. They will receive greater condemnation.
Jesus observes a poor widow giving two small coins and declares she gave more than all others because she gave all she had.
As the disciples admire the temple, Jesus foretells its total destruction.
Jesus describes signs of the end: false messiahs, wars, earthquakes, persecution, and betrayal. He urges endurance and promises that not a hair of their heads will perish.
He warns of Jerusalem’s siege and destruction, urging flight and lamenting the city’s downfall under Gentile rule.
Cosmic signs will precede the coming of the Son of Man in glory. Jesus urges His followers to lift their heads, for their redemption is near.
The Parable of the Fig Tree teaches that the signs will indicate the nearness of the Kingdom. Jesus affirms that His words will never pass away.
Jesus warns against spiritual complacency and urges watchfulness and prayer to stand before the Son of Man. He continues teaching daily in the temple, drawing eager crowds.
As Passover approaches, the chief priests and scribes plot to kill Jesus. Judas Iscariot agrees to betray Him for money, setting the stage for the arrest.
Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover meal. They follow His instructions and find a furnished upper room, where they make ready.
At the Last Supper, Jesus institutes the New Covenant through bread and wine, symbolizing His body and blood. He reveals that one of the disciples will betray Him.
A dispute arises among the disciples about who is greatest. Jesus teaches that true greatness is found in servanthood and promises them a place in His Kingdom.
Jesus warns Peter that Satan will sift him, but He has prayed for his restoration. He also prepares the disciples for coming trials, urging readiness.
In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays in agony, submitting to the Father’s will. The disciples struggle to stay awake during His distress.
Judas arrives with a crowd and betrays Jesus with a kiss. Jesus is arrested but heals the servant’s ear and confronts the injustice of the moment.
Peter follows at a distance but denies Jesus three times. When the rooster crows, he remembers Jesus’ words and weeps bitterly.
Jesus is mocked, beaten, and brought before the council. When asked if He is the Son of God, He affirms it, and they declare Him guilty.
Jesus is brought before Pilate, accused of misleading the nation. Pilate finds no guilt in Him.
Pilate sends Jesus to Herod, who mocks Him and sends Him back. Pilate and Herod, previously enemies, become friends that day.
Pilate tries to release Jesus, but the crowd demands Barabbas instead. Pilate gives in and delivers Jesus to be crucified.
Simon of Cyrene is compelled to carry the cross. Jesus speaks to the mourning women, warning of coming judgment.
Jesus is crucified between two criminals. One mocks Him; the other asks to be remembered. Jesus promises him paradise that very day.
Darkness covers the land. Jesus dies, committing His spirit to the Father. The centurion declares Him righteous, and the crowd departs in sorrow.
Joseph of Arimathea places Jesus’ body in a new tomb. The women prepare spices and rest on the Sabbath.
On the first day of the week, women find the tomb empty. Angels announce Jesus’ resurrection. The disciples are skeptical, but Peter runs to see for himself.
On the road to Emmaus, Jesus walks with two disciples, explaining the Scriptures. They recognize Him when He breaks bread, and He vanishes from their sight.
Jesus appears to the disciples, shows His wounds, and eats with them. He opens their minds to understand the Scriptures and commissions them to preach repentance and forgiveness.
Jesus leads them to Bethany, blesses them, and ascends into heaven. The disciples return to Jerusalem with great joy, continually praising God.
The Word (Logos) existed from the beginning, was with God, and was God. Through Him all things were made. He is the source of life and light, which darkness cannot overcome.
John the Baptist is sent to bear witness to the Light. Though the world was made through the Word, it did not recognize Him. Yet those who receive Him are given the right to become children of God.
The Word became flesh and dwelled among us, full of grace and truth. John testifies to His preeminence. Through Him, we receive grace upon grace.
Religious leaders question John the Baptist. He denies being the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet, and identifies himself as the voice crying in the wilderness.
John sees Jesus and declares Him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. He testifies that the Spirit descended on Jesus, confirming Him as the Son of God.
John’s disciples follow Jesus. Andrew brings his brother Simon to Jesus, who renames him Peter.
