Jesus calls Philip and Nathanael. Nathanael is amazed by Jesus’ supernatural knowledge and confesses Him as the Son of God and King of Israel.
At a wedding in Cana, Jesus performs His first miracle by turning water into wine, revealing His glory and strengthening His disciples’ faith.
Jesus clears the temple in Jerusalem, driving out merchants and money changers. He declares, 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me.'
When challenged for a sign, Jesus speaks of destroying the temple and raising it in three days referring to His body and resurrection.
Many believe in Jesus because of His signs, but He does not entrust Himself to them, knowing what is in each person’s heart.
Nicodemus, a Pharisee, visits Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that one must be born again of water and the Spirit to enter the Kingdom of God.
Jesus explains spiritual rebirth using earthly and heavenly analogies, referencing Moses lifting the serpent as a foreshadowing of His crucifixion.
Jesus declares God’s love in sending His Son to save the world. Those who believe are not condemned; those who reject the Light remain in darkness.
John the Baptist affirms Jesus’ supremacy, saying, 'He must increase, but I must decrease.' He rejoices as the friend of the bridegroom.
John testifies that Jesus speaks the words of God and has the Spirit without measure. Belief in the Son brings eternal life; rejection brings God’s wrath.
Jesus leaves Judea for Galilee, passing through Samaria. Weary from travel, He rests at Jacob’s well in Sychar around noon.

Jesus engages a Samaritan woman in conversation, breaking cultural norms. He offers her 'living water' and reveals intimate knowledge of her life. He teaches about true worship in spirit and truth and openly declares Himself the Messiah.

The disciples return and are surprised to find Jesus speaking with a woman. Meanwhile, the woman shares her encounter in town. Jesus teaches His disciples about spiritual harvest and the joy of sowing and reaping.
Many Samaritans believe in Jesus first through the woman’s testimony, then through their own experience, declaring Him the Savior of the world.
Jesus continues to Galilee, where He is welcomed by those who had seen His signs in Jerusalem.
In Cana, Jesus heals a royal official’s son from a distance. The man believes Jesus’ word, and his entire household comes to faith.
At the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem, Jesus heals a man who had been an invalid for 38 years, commanding him to rise and walk.
The healing occurs on the Sabbath, provoking controversy. Jesus defends His actions, claiming unity with the Father, which intensifies opposition.
Jesus teaches about His divine authority: He does what the Father does, gives life, and will judge all. Those who hear His voice and believe will have eternal life.
Jesus cites multiple witnesses to His identity John the Baptist, His works, the Father, and the Scriptures. He rebukes the religious leaders for rejecting Him despite their knowledge of the Law.
Jesus feeds over 5,000 people with five loaves and two fish, demonstrating divine provision. The crowd wants to make Him king by force, but He withdraws.
That night, Jesus walks on water toward the disciples’ boat during a storm. He calms their fears and brings them safely to shore.
The crowd seeks Jesus for more bread. He teaches that He is the Bread of Life, sent from heaven to give eternal life to those who believe.
The Jews grumble at Jesus’ claim to be the Bread from heaven. He insists that eternal life comes through eating His flesh and drinking His blood symbolizing deep union with Him.
Many disciples find His teaching hard and leave. Jesus asks the Twelve if they will go too. Peter responds, 'Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.'
Jesus delays going to the Feast of Tabernacles in Judea because of threats from the Jews. His brothers, who do not yet believe, urge Him to show Himself publicly.
Jesus goes to the feast in secret and begins teaching. The crowd is divided about who He is. He defends healing on the Sabbath and challenges them to judge rightly, not by appearances.
Some Jerusalem residents question how Jesus speaks openly despite the authorities’ hostility. Jesus hints at His divine origin and speaks of going where they cannot follow, confusing His listeners.
On the last day of the feast, Jesus cries out, offering living water to those who believe referring to the future gift of the Holy Spirit.
The crowd is divided: some believe Jesus is the Prophet or Messiah, others reject Him because of His Galilean background. The Pharisees scorn the masses, and Nicodemus cautiously defends Jesus.
A woman caught in adultery is brought to Jesus. He challenges her accusers: 'Let him who is without sin cast the first stone.' They leave one by one, and Jesus tells her to go and sin no more.
Jesus declares, 'I am the light of the world.' The Pharisees challenge His testimony, but He affirms His divine mission and relationship with the Father.
Jesus warns that those who do not believe will die in their sins. He speaks of His coming death and promises that His identity will be revealed when He is 'lifted up.'
To Jews who believe, Jesus speaks of true discipleship and freedom through truth. He challenges their claim to be Abraham’s children, saying their actions reveal a different father.
Jesus confronts accusations of demon-possession. He declares that Abraham rejoiced to see His day and boldly affirms, 'Before Abraham was, I AM' prompting an attempt to stone Him.

Jesus encounters a man born blind. He explains the man’s condition is for God’s works to be displayed. He makes mud, applies it to the man’s eyes, and tells him to wash in the Pool of Siloam resulting in healing.
Neighbors question the man’s identity after his healing. He confirms it and explains how Jesus healed him.
The Pharisees investigate the healing, offended that it occurred on the Sabbath. The formerly blind man defends Jesus, even under pressure. In frustration, they expel him from the synagogue.
Jesus finds the man and reveals Himself as the Son of Man. The man believes and worships Him. Jesus speaks of spiritual blindness those who claim to see are, in fact, blind.

Jesus begins with a parable about the sheepfold, contrasting the true shepherd who enters by the gate with thieves and robbers. His sheep recognize His voice and follow Him, but the audience does not understand the metaphor.
Jesus declares, 'I am the door of the sheep.' He contrasts Himself with false leaders and promises that those who enter through Him will be saved and find abundant life.

Jesus proclaims, 'I am the Good Shepherd.' He lays down His life for the sheep, unlike hired hands who flee. He knows His sheep intimately and speaks of His authority to lay down and take up His life again.
His words cause division among the Jews some accuse Him of being demon-possessed, while others are moved by His miracles and teaching.
At the Feast of Dedication, Jesus affirms His identity: 'My sheep hear My voice... I and the Father are one.' He promises eternal life and security to His followers.
The Jews attempt to stone Jesus for blasphemy. He defends His works and retreats across the Jordan, where many believe in Him.
Jesus learns that Lazarus is sick but delays visiting. He tells the disciples that the illness is for God’s glory. After Lazarus dies, Jesus decides to go to Bethany, despite the danger.
Jesus arrives and speaks with Martha, who expresses faith in the resurrection. Jesus declares, 'I am the resurrection and the life,' and asks if she believes.
Mary meets Jesus and weeps. Moved deeply, Jesus also weeps. The crowd marvels at His love for Lazarus but questions why He didn’t prevent his death.
Jesus commands the stone to be removed and calls Lazarus out of the tomb. Lazarus emerges alive, still wrapped in grave clothes.
Many believe, but some report the miracle to the Pharisees. The Sanhedrin plots to kill Jesus. Caiaphas prophesies that Jesus will die for the nation. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim.
At Bethany, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with expensive perfume. Judas objects, but Jesus defends her act as preparation for His burial.
A large crowd comes to see Jesus and Lazarus. The chief priests plot to kill Lazarus because many are believing in Jesus through him.
Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, fulfilling prophecy. The crowd hails Him with palm branches, shouting 'Hosanna!' The Pharisees despair at His growing influence.
Some Greeks seek Jesus. He speaks of His impending death, comparing it to a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit. He calls His followers to die to self and serve Him.
Jesus is troubled but submits to the Father’s will. A voice from heaven affirms Him. He speaks of being 'lifted up' and urges the crowd to walk in the light while they have it.
Despite His many signs, most do not believe, fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy. Some leaders believe but remain silent out of fear of the Pharisees.
Jesus declares that He came to save, not judge. His words are from the Father, and those who reject them will be judged on the last day.
During the Last Supper, Jesus washes His disciples’ feet, demonstrating humble service. He teaches that true greatness is found in serving others and calls them to follow His example.
Jesus predicts His betrayal and identifies Judas by giving him a piece of bread. Judas departs into the night to carry out his plan.
After Judas leaves, Jesus speaks of His glorification and gives a new commandment: 'Love one another as I have loved you.' This love will mark them as His disciples.
Peter asks where Jesus is going. Jesus says Peter cannot follow now but will later. Peter insists he will lay down his life, but Jesus predicts Peter’s denial before the rooster crows.
Jesus comforts His disciples, telling them not to be troubled. He is going to prepare a place for them and will return to bring them to Himself.
Thomas asks how they can know the way. Jesus replies, 'I am the way, the truth, and the life.' He explains His unity with the Father and promises that those who believe will do greater works.
Jesus promises the Holy Spirit, the Advocate, who will dwell with and in believers. He emphasizes that love for Him is shown through obedience.
Jesus assures them that the Spirit will teach and remind them of His words. He gives them His peace and urges them not to be afraid. He prepares them for His departure and the coming conflict.
Jesus declares, 'I am the true vine.' He calls His disciples to abide in Him, for apart from Him they can do nothing. Fruitfulness comes through connection to Him.
He commands them to remain in His love and love one another as He has loved them. He calls them friends, not servants, and reminds them that He chose them to bear lasting fruit.
Jesus warns that the world will hate them because it hated Him first. This fulfills what was written in the Law: 'They hated Me without cause.'
He promises that the Spirit of truth will testify about Him, and the disciples will also bear witness because they have been with Him from the beginning.

Jesus warns His disciples of coming persecution they will be expelled from synagogues and even killed by those thinking they serve God. He tells them this in advance so they won’t stumble when it happens.

Jesus explains that His departure is for their benefit, as it will bring the Holy Spirit. The Spirit will convict the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment, and guide believers into all truth, glorifying Christ.

Jesus tells them they will soon experience sorrow, but it will turn to joy like a woman in labor rejoicing after birth. He assures them that after His resurrection, they will ask the Father in His name and receive.

Jesus speaks plainly about His return to the Father. Though the disciples claim to understand, He predicts they will scatter. Yet He assures them of peace in Him, saying, 'Take heart; I have overcome the world.'
Jesus prays to the Father, asking to be glorified so He may glorify the Father. He speaks of eternal life as knowing the Father and Himself, and of completing the work He was given.

Jesus prays for His disciples, thanking the Father for them and asking for their protection, unity, and sanctification through the truth. He does not ask for their removal from the world, but for their preservation in it.
Jesus prays for all future believers, asking that they may be one as He and the Father are one. He desires that they see His glory and experience the love the Father has for Him.

Jesus is betrayed by Judas and arrested in the Garden of Gethsemane. He steps forward willingly, identifying Himself as 'I am He,' causing the arresting party to fall back. Peter cuts off the ear of Malchus, but Jesus rebukes him and submits to arrest.
Jesus is taken to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who had advised that it was better for one man to die for the people.
Peter follows Jesus into the high priest’s courtyard but denies being His disciple when questioned by a servant girl.
Annas questions Jesus about His teaching. Jesus responds that He taught openly and invites them to ask His listeners. An officer strikes Him, and He is sent to Caiaphas.
Peter denies Jesus two more times. As the rooster crows, Jesus’ earlier prophecy about Peter’s denial is fulfilled.

Jesus is brought before Pilate. The Jewish leaders avoid entering the praetorium to remain ceremonially clean. Pilate questions Jesus about His kingship. Jesus declares His kingdom is not of this world. Pilate finds no guilt in Him but offers to release a prisoner Barabbas is chosen instead.

Pilate has Jesus flogged. Soldiers mock Him with a crown of thorns and a purple robe. Pilate presents Jesus to the crowd, hoping to release Him, but the chief priests demand crucifixion. Pilate, pressured by their appeal to Caesar, hands Jesus over.

Jesus carries His cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others. Pilate’s inscription reads, 'Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.' Soldiers divide His garments. Jesus entrusts His mother to the beloved disciple.
Knowing all is fulfilled, Jesus says, 'I thirst.' He is given sour wine, then declares, 'It is finished,' and dies.

To hasten death before the Sabbath, soldiers break the legs of the others but find Jesus already dead. A soldier pierces His side, fulfilling Scripture: 'Not one of His bones will be broken' and 'They will look on Him whom they pierced.'
Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus prepare Jesus’ body with spices and wrap it in linen. They lay Him in a new tomb in a nearby garden.

Mary Magdalene discovers the stone rolled away from the tomb and runs to tell Peter and John. They race to the tomb, find the linen cloths, and believe, though they do not yet understand the resurrection fully.

Mary remains at the tomb, weeping. She sees two angels and then Jesus Himself, though she doesn’t recognize Him until He says her name. Jesus tells her not to cling to Him and sends her to announce His resurrection to the disciples.

That evening, Jesus appears to the disciples behind locked doors, offers them peace, shows His wounds, and breathes on them, saying, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' He gives them authority to forgive sins.

Thomas, absent at the first appearance, doubts the resurrection. Eight days later, Jesus appears again and invites Thomas to touch His wounds. Thomas believes, declaring, 'My Lord and my God!' Jesus blesses those who believe without seeing.
John concludes by stating that Jesus did many other signs not recorded, but these are written so readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ and have life in His name.

Jesus appears to seven disciples at the Sea of Tiberias. After a fruitless night of fishing, He tells them to cast the net on the right side, resulting in a miraculous catch. Peter jumps into the water to meet Him. They eat breakfast together on the shore.
Jesus restores Peter by asking three times, 'Do you love Me?' mirroring Peter’s three denials. Each time, Jesus commissions him to feed His sheep and foretells Peter’s future martyrdom.
Peter asks about John’s future. Jesus replies, 'If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me.' A rumor spreads that John would not die, but Jesus had not said that.
The Gospel ends affirming the testimony’s truth and noting that Jesus did many other things so many that the world could not contain the books that would be written.
Luke opens by summarizing Jesus’ post-resurrection appearances and teachings. Jesus instructs the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Spirit.

The disciples ask if Jesus will restore the kingdom to Israel. He redirects their focus to the coming Spirit and their mission as witnesses. Jesus then ascends into heaven, and two angels promise His return.
The apostles return to Jerusalem and gather in the upper room with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and His brothers, devoting themselves to prayer.
Peter addresses the group of 120 believers about replacing Judas. After prayer and casting lots, Matthias is chosen to join the Twelve.
On Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descends with wind and fire. The apostles speak in various languages, astonishing the international crowd. Some are amazed; others mock.
Peter boldly preaches, explaining the event as fulfillment of Joel’s prophecy. He proclaims Jesus’ death, resurrection, and exaltation, declaring Him both Lord and Christ.
Convicted, the crowd asks what to do. Peter calls them to repent and be baptized. About 3,000 respond and are added to the Church.
The early believers devote themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer. They share possessions, experience signs and wonders, and enjoy favor with the people.
Peter and John heal a man lame from birth at the temple gate. The man leaps and praises God, drawing a crowd filled with awe.
Peter addresses the crowd, attributing the healing to Jesus. He calls them to repent so their sins may be wiped away and times of refreshing may come from the Lord.
Peter and John are arrested for preaching the resurrection. Before the Sanhedrin, Peter boldly proclaims that Jesus whom they crucified is the only name by which we must be saved.
The leaders are astonished by Peter and John's boldness, recognizing them as uneducated men who had been with Jesus. Unable to deny the miracle, they threaten them but release them.
The believers pray for boldness rather than protection. The place is shaken, and they are filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking the word of God courageously.
The early believers share everything in common. Barnabas sells a field and gives the proceeds to the apostles, setting a positive example of generosity.
Ananias and Sapphira lie about the proceeds from a land sale and fall dead after Peter confronts them, instilling great fear in the Church.
The apostles perform many signs and wonders. People bring the sick in hopes that even Peter’s shadow might fall on them. All who are brought are healed.

The high priest and Sadducees arrest the apostles, but an angel frees them. Brought again before the council, Peter insists, 'We must obey God rather than men,' proclaiming Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation.
Gamaliel advises caution, arguing that if the movement is not from God, it will fail. The apostles are flogged and ordered not to speak in Jesus’ name but they rejoice and keep preaching.

As the Church grows, conflict arises over food distribution to widows. The apostles appoint seven men, including Stephen, to oversee the task so they can focus on prayer and teaching. The word of God spreads rapidly.
Stephen, full of grace and power, performs signs and is falsely accused of blasphemy. He is seized and brought before the council, where his face shines like an angel’s.

Stephen responds to the high priest by recounting Israel’s history from Abraham to Moses to Solomon emphasizing God’s presence beyond the temple and Israel’s repeated rejection of His messengers. He accuses the council of resisting the Holy Spirit and betraying the Righteous One, Jesus.

Enraged, the council drags Stephen out and stones him. Filled with the Spirit, Stephen sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand and prays for his killers as he dies becoming the first Christian martyr. Saul watches and approves.
A great persecution breaks out in Jerusalem after Stephen’s death. Believers scatter throughout Judea and Samaria, while Saul zealously hunts down Christians.
Philip preaches in Samaria, performing miracles and bringing joy. Many believe, including Simon the sorcerer, who later tries to buy the power of the Holy Spirit and is rebuked by Peter.
An angel sends Philip to meet an Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah. Philip explains the gospel, and the eunuch is baptized. The Spirit then carries Philip away to continue preaching elsewhere.
On the road to Damascus, Saul is blinded by a heavenly light and hears Jesus ask, 'Why are you persecuting Me?' He is led into the city, unable to see, eat, or drink.
God sends Ananias to heal Saul and baptize him. Saul regains his sight, is filled with the Holy Spirit, and begins to eat and regain strength.
Saul boldly preaches Jesus in Damascus and later in Jerusalem, astonishing believers. After threats on his life, he is sent to Tarsus. The Church enjoys peace and growth.
Peter heals a paralyzed man named Aeneas in Lydda and raises Tabitha (Dorcas) from the dead in Joppa. Many believe in the Lord as a result.
Cornelius, a Roman centurion and God-fearing Gentile, receives a vision from an angel instructing him to send for Peter in Joppa.

As Cornelius' messengers approach, Peter receives a vision of unclean animals and is told to eat. This prepares him to understand that God shows no partiality. When the messengers arrive, Peter welcomes them.
Peter travels to Caesarea. Cornelius gathers relatives and friends, and Peter shares how God taught him not to call anyone impure or unclean.
Peter proclaims the gospel. As he speaks, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles. The Jewish believers are astonished, and Peter baptizes them, recognizing that God has given them the same gift.

Peter returns to Jerusalem and is criticized for eating with Gentiles. He recounts the entire story, emphasizing the Spirit’s work. The assembly glorifies God, realizing that repentance and life are also for the Gentiles.

The scattered believers from the persecution spread the gospel as far as Antioch. Some speak to Greeks, and many believe. Barnabas is sent from Jerusalem, rejoices, and brings Saul from Tarsus to help teach for a year. The disciples are first called Christians in Antioch.
Prophets come from Jerusalem, and one named Agabus foretells a famine. The believers in Antioch send relief to Judea, entrusting it to Barnabas and Saul.
King Herod (Agrippa I) begins persecuting the Church. He kills James (John’s brother) and imprisons Peter, intending to bring him to trial after Passover.

On the night before his trial, Peter is miraculously freed by an angel. He goes to the house of Mary, where the believers are praying. Meanwhile, Herod executes the guards when Peter is found missing.

Herod gives a speech and is praised as a god. Because he does not give glory to God, an angel strikes him down, and he dies. The word of God continues to grow and spread. Barnabas and Saul return from Jerusalem, taking John Mark with them.
In the church at Antioch, while prophets and teachers worship and fast, the Holy Spirit calls Barnabas and Saul for missionary work. The church lays hands on them and sends them off.

In Cyprus, they preach in synagogues. In Paphos, they confront Elymas the sorcerer, who opposes them. Paul, filled with the Spirit, strikes him blind. The proconsul Sergius Paulus believes, amazed at the teaching.
In Pisidian Antioch, Paul preaches in the synagogue, recounting Israel’s history and proclaiming Jesus as the promised Savior. He emphasizes forgiveness and justification through Him.

The next Sabbath, nearly the whole city gathers. Jealous Jews oppose them, so Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles. Many rejoice and believe, but persecution forces them to leave. They shake the dust off their feet and move on.
In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas preach boldly, performing signs and wonders. A divided city leads to threats of stoning, so they flee to Lystra and Derbe.

In Lystra, Paul heals a crippled man. The crowd mistakes them for gods Zeus and Hermes and tries to offer sacrifices. Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes and redirect them to the living God. Later, Jews from Antioch and Iconium incite the crowd to stone Paul, leaving him for dead. He survives and continues on.

They preach in Derbe, then revisit the cities to strengthen disciples and appoint elders. They return to Antioch in Syria, reporting all God had done and how He opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.
Some men from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised. Paul and Barnabas dispute this and are sent to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders.

At the Jerusalem Council, Peter testifies that God gave the Spirit to Gentiles without requiring the Law. James agrees and proposes a letter asking Gentiles to abstain from idolatry, sexual immorality, and blood.
The council sends Judas (Barsabbas) and Silas with Paul and Barnabas to deliver the letter to Antioch. The believers rejoice at the encouragement and clarity.
Paul and Barnabas plan to revisit the churches, but disagree over taking John Mark. They part ways Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus, and Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia.

Paul meets Timothy in Lystra and invites him to join the mission. Timothy is circumcised to avoid offense among Jews. They deliver the Jerusalem Council’s decisions, and the churches are strengthened.
The Holy Spirit prevents them from preaching in Asia and Bithynia. In Troas, Paul receives a vision of a Macedonian man pleading for help prompting their journey into Europe.
In Philippi, they meet Lydia, a seller of purple cloth. The Lord opens her heart to Paul’s message, and she and her household are baptized.
Paul casts a spirit of divination out of a slave girl, angering her owners. Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned.

At midnight, Paul and Silas pray and sing. An earthquake opens the prison. The jailer, fearing escape, is stopped by Paul and asks how to be saved. He and his household believe and are baptized. The next day, Paul reveals his Roman citizenship, prompting an apology from the magistrates.
In Thessalonica, Paul reasons from Scripture that Jesus is the Christ. Some believe, but jealous Jews incite a mob. Jason, their host, is dragged before the authorities.
In Berea, the Jews are more noble, examining the Scriptures daily. Many believe. But agitators from Thessalonica arrive, and Paul is sent to Athens while Silas and Timothy remain.

In Athens, Paul is distressed by the idolatry. He debates in the synagogue and marketplace. At the Areopagus, he proclaims the 'Unknown God' as the Creator and Judge. Some mock, others believe including Dionysius and Damaris.
In Corinth, Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla and works with them as a tentmaker. He preaches in the synagogue. When opposed, he turns to the Gentiles. Crispus, the synagogue leader, believes.
The Lord encourages Paul in a vision to keep speaking. He stays 18 months. When Jews bring him before Gallio, the proconsul dismisses the case.
Paul sails to Ephesus with Aquila and Priscilla, then returns to Antioch, completing his second journey. He begins a third journey, strengthening churches in Galatia and Phrygia.

Apollos, an eloquent teacher from Alexandria, arrives in Ephesus. He knows only John’s baptism. Aquila and Priscilla instruct him more fully. He then ministers powerfully in Achaia, refuting Jews and proving Jesus is the Christ.
Paul finds disciples in Ephesus who only knew John’s baptism. He explains the gospel, baptizes them in Jesus’ name, and they receive the Holy Spirit, speaking in tongues and prophesying.
Paul teaches boldly in the synagogue for three months. When opposition arises, he moves to the lecture hall of Tyrannus and teaches daily for two years, reaching all in Asia.
God performs extraordinary miracles through Paul. Jewish exorcists misuse Jesus’ name and are overpowered by a demon. Fear spreads, and many repent, burning their magic scrolls.
A riot erupts in Ephesus, led by Demetrius the silversmith, who fears loss of income from idol-making. The crowd chants for Artemis, but the town clerk calms them and dismisses the assembly.
Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, encouraging believers. He avoids a plot against him by returning through Macedonia and reunites with his companions in Troas.
In Troas, Paul preaches late into the night. A young man named Eutychus falls from a window and dies, but Paul raises him to life. The believers are greatly comforted.
Paul continues his journey, sailing past Ephesus to avoid delay, aiming to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.
In Miletus, Paul gives a heartfelt farewell to the Ephesian elders. He recounts his ministry, warns of future dangers, and entrusts them to God’s grace. They weep and pray together before parting.
Paul travels to Jerusalem, despite repeated warnings including a prophecy from Agabus that he will be bound. Paul remains resolute, ready to suffer for Jesus.
In Jerusalem, Paul meets James and the elders. To ease tensions, he joins in a purification ritual to show respect for Jewish customs.
Jews from Asia falsely accuse Paul of defiling the temple. A riot breaks out, and Roman soldiers rescue Paul from the mob.
As Paul is taken into the barracks, he asks to speak to the crowd. The commander is surprised Paul speaks Greek, and Paul prepares to address the people in Hebrew.

Paul addresses the Jerusalem crowd in Hebrew, recounting his strict Jewish upbringing, persecution of Christians, and dramatic conversion on the road to Damascus. He shares how Jesus appeared to him, and how he was commissioned to preach to the Gentiles.

The crowd erupts in fury when Paul mentions his mission to the Gentiles. The Roman commander prepares to flog him, but Paul reveals his Roman citizenship. Alarmed, the commander halts the proceedings.
The next day, to determine the charges against Paul, the commander brings him before the Jewish Sanhedrin.

Before the council, Paul causes division by declaring his belief in the resurrection a doctrine held by Pharisees but not Sadducees. The dispute turns violent, and the commander removes him for safety.
That night, the Lord appears to Paul and encourages him, saying he must also testify in Rome.
A group of Jews forms a plot to kill Paul, vowing not to eat or drink until he is dead. Paul’s nephew learns of the plot and warns the commander.
The commander sends Paul under heavy guard to the governor Felix in Caesarea with a letter explaining the situation. Felix agrees to hear the case when the accusers arrive.
Five days later, the high priest and lawyer Tertullus accuse Paul before Felix, charging him with stirring unrest and profaning the temple.
Paul defends himself, denying the accusations and asserting his belief in the resurrection a hope shared by many Jews.

Felix postpones the decision. He frequently calls for Paul, hoping for a bribe, but keeps him in custody for two years. When Porcius Festus succeeds him, Felix leaves Paul imprisoned to gain favor with the Jews.

Festus, the new governor, travels to Jerusalem where Jewish leaders request Paul be transferred planning to ambush him. Festus denies the transfer and invites them to Caesarea. At Paul’s hearing, unable to secure justice, Paul appeals to Caesar, invoking his right as a Roman citizen.

King Agrippa and Bernice arrive in Caesarea to visit Festus. Festus explains Paul’s case, noting the lack of clear charges and Paul's appeal to the emperor. Agrippa expresses interest in hearing from Paul directly.

The next day, with great pomp, Agrippa and Bernice enter the audience room. Festus introduces Paul, highlighting the oddity of having a prisoner with no concrete accusation against him to send to Caesar.

Paul begins his defense before Agrippa, respectfully recounting his upbringing as a Pharisee and his zeal in persecuting Christians, reflecting the very hope promised to the Jewish ancestors the resurrection.
He describes his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to Damascus, where Jesus commissioned him to open eyes, turn people from darkness to light, and bring forgiveness through faith in Him.

Paul explains his obedience to the heavenly vision preaching repentance to Jews and Gentiles alike. He emphasizes that his message aligns with Moses and the prophets: that the Christ must suffer and rise from the dead.

Festus interrupts, accusing Paul of madness, but Paul affirms his clarity. Agrippa deflects Paul’s invitation to believe. The leaders confer afterward and agree that Paul has done nothing deserving death or imprisonment, and say he could have been released if he hadn't appealed to Caesar.

Paul, under the custody of a centurion named Julius, sets sail for Rome with other prisoners. They make several stops, including Sidon (where Paul is allowed to visit friends), Myra, and Fair Havens on Crete. The journey is slow and increasingly dangerous due to seasonal weather.

Despite Paul’s warning that continuing the voyage would lead to disaster, the crew decides to press on. A violent storm (the Northeaster) strikes, and after many days without sun or stars, the crew loses all hope of survival.
Paul encourages everyone, sharing that an angel assured him they would all survive, though the ship would be lost. He urges them to take heart and trust God’s promise.

After two weeks adrift, the sailors sense land. Paul urges everyone to eat. The ship runs aground and begins to break apart. Soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but Julius intervenes to save Paul. All 276 people on board reach shore safely, just as God had promised.

Shipwrecked on Malta, the locals show kindness. Paul is bitten by a viper but suffers no harm, astonishing the islanders. He heals the father of Publius (the chief official) and many others, gaining great respect.
After three months, they sail to Rome via Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli. Believers come to meet Paul, encouraging him. In Rome, he is allowed to live under house arrest with a guard.

Paul meets with local Jewish leaders, explaining his situation and proclaiming Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel’s hope. Some believe, others reject. Paul quotes Isaiah, warning that salvation has been sent to the Gentiles.
For two years, Paul lives in his own rented house, welcoming all who come. He proclaims the Kingdom of God and teaches about Jesus Christ with boldness and without hindrance.
Paul introduces himself as a servant and apostle, set apart for the gospel of God concerning Jesus Christ. He greets the believers in Rome, calling them saints loved by God.
Paul expresses gratitude for the Roman believers and his longing to visit them to strengthen and be encouraged by their mutual faith.
He declares he is not ashamed of the gospel, which is the power of God for salvation to all who believe. Righteousness is revealed from faith to faith.
God’s wrath is revealed against all ungodliness. Though people knew God, they suppressed the truth, exchanged His glory for idols, and were given over to degrading passions and a depraved mind.
Paul warns against judging others while doing the same things. God’s kindness is meant to lead to repentance, but stubbornness stores up wrath.
God will judge everyone impartially according to their deeds eternal life for those who do good, wrath for those who do evil.
Those without the law will perish without it; those under the law will be judged by it. Gentiles show the law written on their hearts, and God will judge secrets through Christ.
Paul confronts Jews who boast in the law but break it. True Jewish identity and circumcision are inward, of the heart, by the Spirit not merely outward.
Paul addresses objections: Does Jewish unfaithfulness nullify God’s faithfulness? No God remains true. But human unrighteousness does not excuse sin.
All Jews and Gentiles are under sin. Paul strings together Scripture to show that no one is righteous. The law reveals sin but cannot justify.
Now, apart from the law, God’s righteousness is revealed through faith in Jesus Christ. All have sinned, but are justified freely by grace through Christ’s atoning sacrifice.
Boasting is excluded. Justification is by faith, not works. God is God of both Jews and Gentiles, and faith upholds the law.
Abraham justified by faith before circumcision his righteousness counted apart from works.
David speaks of the blessedness of the one whose sin is forgiven apart from works.
Promise to Abraham came before circumcision, making him father of all who believe by faith.
The promise rests on faith so it extends to Gentiles; Christ was delivered for our trespasses and raised for our justification.
Peace with God through faith; we boast in tribulations because they produce hope.
Christ died for the ungodly; we are reconciled and saved by His life.
Sin entered through Adam and spread to all death reigned from Adam to Moses.
One man’s trespass brought death; one Man’s act of righteousness brings life and reigns through grace.
Dead to sin, baptized into Christ’s death, raised to walk in newness of life.
United with Him by resurrection; count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God.
Sin must not reign; slaves either to sin resulting in death or to obedience resulting in righteousness.
Not under law but grace slaves to righteousness lead to holiness and eternal life.
Released from the law’s jurisdiction through Christ’s death, believers now bear fruit for God, not sin.
The law reveals sin but also arouses it; death brings law’s purpose to light, yet sin’s death-dealing power is exposed.
We struggle: sin lives in us, yet we know the good we ought to do even if we can’t do it apart from Christ.
Paul laments the flesh’s rebellion against the mind and worships deliverance through Jesus Christ our Lord.
No condemnation for those in Christ Jesus life in the Spirit fulfills what the law could not do.
Living according to the Spirit sets minds on life and peace; the Spirit raises Christ and will give life to our mortal bodies.
We are debtors to the Spirit, not the flesh adopted as God’s children and heirs with Christ, sharing His sufferings and glory.
Future glory far outweighs present sufferings. The Spirit helps our weakness and intercedes. All things work for good to those who love God; nothing can separate us from His love.
Paul’s sorrow over Israel’s unbelief even with all their privileges reveals God’s sovereign purposes.
Not all descended from Israel are true Israel; God’s promise rests on His calling and mercy, not human descent.
God’s compassion and justice stand He hardens or shows mercy to fulfill His plan and display His glory.
Scripture shows inclusion of Gentiles by faith; Christ is the stumbling stone for those who insist on works.
Paul longs for Israel’s salvation; Christ is the culmination of the law so that righteousness comes to everyone who believes.
Righteousness is by faith, not works; confession and belief in Jesus as Lord bring salvation everyone who calls on Him will be saved.
Faith requires hearing the message; Paul stresses the necessity of preaching so others can believe, for faith comes through the word of Christ.
Though Paul quotes Isaiah ‘How beautiful are the feet…’ he laments Israel’s unbelief, showing God’s patience met with disobedience.
God preserves a remnant of Israel by grace; the rest are hardened so Gentiles might be grafted in, provoking Israel to jealousy.
Israel’s stumbling brought salvation to the Gentiles Paul uses the olive tree metaphor to urge Gentile believers not to boast over broken branches.
A partial hardening of Israel continues until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in; then all Israel will be saved God’s mercy extends to all.
Doxology: Paul marvels at the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge ‘For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things.’”
Paul urges believers to present their bodies as living sacrifices, not conformed to this world but transformed by renewing their minds.
Using the body metaphor, he exhorts humility and sober judgment in exercising diverse gifts service, teaching, encouragement, generosity, leadership, mercy.
Marks of authentic love: sincere affection, abhorrence of evil, devotion, honor, zeal, rejoicing in hope, endurance in suffering, prayer, and hospitality.
Respond to persecution with blessing, live in harmony, empathize, overcome evil with good, and leave vengeance to God.
Submit to governing authorities they’re instituted by God. Love pays taxes and fulfills civic duties.
Owe only love, for love fulfills the law: commandments against adultery, murder, coveting, etc.
The hour to wake from slumber is now cast off works of darkness and clothe yourselves with Christ.
Accept weaker believers in matters of food and sacred days; each accountable to God.
Don’t judge or put stumbling blocks; pursue peace and mutual edification.
Build one another up. Whatever is not from faith is sin; avoid actions that violate conscience.
Strong should bear the failings of the weak, following Christ’s example to glorify God together.
Welcome one another as Christ welcomed you live in harmony, hoping in Christ, filled with joy and peace.
Paul commends the Romans’ goodness, explains his gospel ministry to the Gentiles as fulfilling prophecy.
Paul plans to visit Spain and now goes to Jerusalem with Gentile offerings; he asks for their prayers.
Paul sends personal greetings to over two dozen believers Phoebe, Priscilla and Aquila, Andronicus and Junia, and many others.
Warn against divisive people who oppose the gospel; God will soon crush Satan under your feet.
Final greetings from Paul’s co-workers; doxology celebrating the mystery of the gospel revealed and obeyed by all nations.
Paul, called as an apostle of Christ, greets the Corinthian believers, thanking God for their gifts and faithfulness.
He urges unity no divisions over Paul, Apollos, or Cephas and reminds them Christ sent him to preach the gospel, not to baptize.
The message of the cross is foolishness to the world but the power of God to those being saved; God’s wisdom transcends human wisdom.
God chose the lowly and despised to shame the strong; therefore, let no one boast except in the Lord.
Paul came in weakness and fear, relying not on human eloquence but on the Spirit’s power so their faith rests on God’s wisdom.
God’s wisdom is hidden to the world but revealed by the Spirit to believers Christ crucified is God’s secret wisdom, discerned by spiritual minds.
They are still worldly like infants in Christ because of jealousy and strife. Paul and Apollos are merely servants through whom they came to faith.
Paul laid the foundation Jesus Christ and others build on it. Each builder’s work will be tested by fire; quality work endures.
Believers are God’s temple, and God’s Spirit dwells in them; destroying this temple brings divine judgment.
Do not deceive yourselves with worldly wisdom or boast in human leaders everything belongs to you in Christ: Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death.
Think of apostles as servants and stewards of mysteries; it is the Lord’s faithfulness that ultimately judges them, not human opinion.
Paul and apostles have become a spectacle insults, hardships, poverty, yet proclaim Christ with spiritual abundance.
Paul appeals as a spiritual father, warning against arrogance. He plans to visit soon, bringing the authority of Christ, perhaps with a demonstration of power.
Paul rebukes the church for tolerating incest, commands them to expel the immoral brother to purge sin.
Using leaven as a metaphor: purge the old leaven of malice, celebrate the feast of sincerity and truth.
Do not associate with sexually immoral believers; judge those inside, not outsiders, to maintain church purity.
Believers suing one another before unbelievers is shameful; disputes should be settled within the church.
All things permissible but not beneficial; the body is a temple of the Spirit honor God with your body.
Instructions on marriage: each spouse has conjugal duties; singleness is good but marriage avoids immorality.
Guidance for the married, unmarried, and mixed marriages do not divorce; a believing spouse sanctifies the unbeliever.
Remain in the state you were called circumcision and slavery are irrelevant; serve God as you are.
Advice for virgins and widows: singleness fosters devotion, but marriage is honorable if one cannot exercise self-control.
About food offered to idols: we know there is one God, but knowledge puffs up love builds up.
Some eat idol food unaware, but if it causes a brother to stumble, abstain for his sake.
Paul defends his apostleship claims the right to food, drink, a believing wife, and financial support, yet chooses not to exercise these rights.
Using examples of soldiers, farmers, and priests, Paul argues that ministers of the gospel deserve material support, though he has foregone this right.
Despite being free and an apostle, Paul refuses to burden anyone; he becomes all things to all people to save some by any means.
The Christian life is like an athletic contest run to win, exercise self-control, and discipline the body to obtain an imperishable crown.
Israel’s history under the cloud and through the sea serves as a warning though they shared God’s provisions, many displeased Him and fell.
God did not spare the disobedient; believers must flee idolatry, for God is faithful and provides a way of escape in every temptation.
Flee from idols participation in Christ’s table is communion with Him, not compatible with participation in demonic feasts.
All things may be lawful, but not all are helpful; do all for God’s glory, avoid causing others to stumble, and live to serve everyone.
Instructions on head coverings worship order reflects creation and mutual honor between men and women before the Lord.
Critique of the Corinthian Lord’s Supper divisions, selfish indulgence, and unequal sharing show lack of discernment.
Paul recounts the institution of the Lord’s Supper: Christ’s body and blood given for the church, to be proclaimed until His return.
Warning to examine oneself before partaking unworthy participation brings judgment; eat in order and wait for one another.
Spiritual gifts are given by the one Spirit for the common good wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues, interpretation.
Christians form one body with many members; each part matters if one suffers all suffer, if one is honored all rejoice.
God has appointed apostles, prophets, teachers, miracles, gifts of healing, helping, guidance, tongues; eagerly desire the greater gifts.
Without love, the most eloquent speech, greatest faith, or self-sacrifice profit nothing.
Love is patient, kind, not envious or boastful; it bears, believes, hopes, and endures all things.
Prophecies, tongues, knowledge will cease, but love never fails; faith, hope, and love abide, and the greatest is love.
Pursue love and desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy, which builds up, encourages, and comforts the church.
Unintelligible tongues benefit only the speaker; prophecy clarifies God’s word better to speak words everyone understands.
Children think tongues are madness, but prophecy convicts and converts unbelievers, revealing hearts and leading to worship.
In gatherings, each contributes orderly: psalm, teaching, revelation, tongue, interpretation; all done for edification and peace.
Paul reiterates the gospel: Christ died for sins, was buried, raised on the third day, and seen by many witnesses, affirming the foundation of our faith.
If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised; without it, preaching and faith are in vain, and believers are still in their sins.
Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep; at His coming, He will hand over the kingdom to God the Father after destroying all opposing powers, even death itself.
Paul appeals to the Corinthians: why undergo baptism for the dead or risk peril? Urges self-examination, sober living, and focus on the resurrection hope.
Answers the nature of the resurrection body perishable vs. imperishable, natural vs. spiritual; proclaims victory over death through the risen Christ and exhorts steadfast service.
Instructions for the collection: set aside funds weekly and deliver them to the saints in Jerusalem to avoid improvised donations when Paul arrives.
Paul’s itinerary: plans to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost and hopes to pass through Macedonia, though faces many adversities in his work.
Commends Timothy and Apollos: urges the church to welcome them; greets the household of Stephanas for their devoted leadership.
Paul praises the Corinthians for imitating him in word and deed, warns them to watch out for those who cause divisions, and urges unity and love.
Final personal greeting written by Paul’s own hand; he blesses them with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ amid challenges.
Doxology: the mystery of the gospel now revealed and obeyed among all nations, to the glory of God’s eternal wisdom.

Paul greets the church in Corinth and all the saints in Achaia, praises God as the Father of mercies and comfort, and explains how their afflictions lead to God’s consolation, equipping them to comfort others.
He recalls being under deadly peril in Asia, how they despaired of life yet were delivered by God through the Corinthians’ prayers, affirming God’s power to save and strengthen.
Paul defends his integrity before God, expresses confidence in the Corinthians’ understanding of him, and looks forward to mutual boasting in Christ on the Day of the Lord.
He explains his change of travel plans to spare them sorrow by delaying his visit then reaffirms his promise, highlights God’s seal on them, and underscores his ministry’s authenticity by the Spirit.
Paul explains why he did not make another painful visit: he chose to write a loving, tearful letter instead, to spare the Corinthians sorrow and show his deep affection.
He urges the church to forgive and comfort the repentant offender so Satan won’t gain ground, emphasizing communal responsibility for restoration and love.
Paul rejoices in God’s triumphal procession in Christ, spreading the fragrance of the gospel; he contrasts his sincere service with those who preach for selfish gain.
Rejecting the need for letters of commendation, Paul calls the Corinthians his living epistle, written by the Spirit on human hearts, visible to all.
His sufficiency and boldness come from God; as minister of the new covenant, he serves by the Spirit who gives life, not by the letter that kills.
He contrasts the fading glory of Moses’ ministry under the old covenant with the far greater, permanent glory of the new covenant in Christ.
With confidence and unveiled faces, we behold the Lord’s glory and are progressively transformed into His image by the Spirit, moving from glory to glory.
By God’s mercy, Paul and his team do not lose heart; they renounce secret dishonesty and handle the word of God with integrity, commending themselves to every conscience.
Though the gospel is veiled to unbelievers blinded by the god of this age, God shines the light of Christ’s glory in the hearts of those being saved.
We are jars of clay carrying the treasure of the gospel; though hard-pressed, perplexed, persecuted, and struck down, we are not crushed because Christ’s life is revealed in us.
Paul affirms his spirit’s witness, rejoices amid trials, and contrasts momentary light afflictions with an eternal weight of glory, fixing eyes on unseen realities.
Earthly bodies are tents destined to perish; God gives us an eternal heavenly dwelling through the Spirit.
We walk by faith, confident of our heavenly dwelling; all will appear before Christ’s judgment seat for deeds done in the body.
Motivated by Christ’s love and death for all, we persuade others, living not for ourselves but for Him who died and rose again.
No longer regard anyone from a worldly view; Christ became sin for us so we might become God’s righteousness and serve reconciliation.
We urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain; now is the time of salvation.
Paul’s ministry proves genuine through hardships and blessings honor and disgrace, sorrow and joy, poverty and abundance, having nothing yet possessing all things.
Paul’s open heart towards the Corinthians he speaks freely, inviting them to open their hearts to him likewise.
By perfecting holiness in reverence for God, Paul encourages the Corinthians, recalling past affliction and the comfort Titus brought.
Godly sorrow from Paul’s letter led to earnest repentance; Paul rejoices in Titus’s report of their godly earnestness and longing for Paul.
Macedonian churches, in deep poverty yet overflowing in joy, gave generously according to their ability beyond expectation.
Paul urges excellence in generosity, citing Christ’s self-giving; distribution is to be fair those who have plenty share with those in need.
Titus is commended for his integrity; Paul sends trusted brothers to arrange the collection with care, ensuring transparency and honor.
Paul commends the Corinthians’ readiness to give for the Jerusalem saints and instructs Titus and companions to complete their pledge without reluctance.
He unfolds the principle of sowing and reaping those who give generously will reap generously and urges cheerful, voluntary giving, reminding them that God provides and multiplies grace.
Their service supplies the needs of the saints and overflows in thanksgiving to God; Paul rejoices in God’s indescribable gift and the joy their generosity brings.
Paul appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, then explains that his warfare is spiritual, using divine weapons to demolish strongholds and take every thought captive.
He rebukes those who judge by outward appearance and self-commendation, reminding them that true apostolic authority is shown by Christ’s power, not human showmanship.
Paul limits his boasting to God’s assigned sphere among the Corinthians and expresses hope to preach further; he insists that commendation comes only from the Lord.
Paul, with godly jealousy, likens the church to a bride betrothed to Christ, fearing they may be led astray by false apostles preaching a different Jesus.
He recounts preaching the gospel free of charge to shame deceitful workers, warns that even Satan masquerades as an angel of light, and exposes false apostles.
Engaging in ‘foolish’ boasting, Paul lists credentials he could boast of Hebrew lineage, labors, sufferings to match the so-called super-apostles.
He details the hardships endured for Christ imprisonments, beatings, dangers, shipwrecks, hunger culminating in being lowered in a basket to escape Damascus.
Paul speaks of a man caught up to the third heaven, hearing inexpressible revelations fourteen years prior, yet refrains from boasting.
To keep him humble, Paul was given a ‘thorn in the flesh’; God’s answer ‘My grace is sufficient’ teaches him to boast in weakness.
Defending his apostleship, Paul contrasts his patient, self-sacrificial ministry and concern for the Corinthians with the claims of the super-apostles.
Paul warns that on his third visit he will not spare those who persist in sin, invoking two or three witnesses and the power of Christ living in him.
He urges self-examination ‘Test yourselves to see if you are in the faith’ and prays for their restoration, willing to seem weak if it brings their spiritual maturity.
Final exhortations: rejoice, be perfect, live in peace; he sends greetings from the saints and closes with the trinitarian benediction of grace, love, and fellowship.
Paul greets the Galatian churches, asserts his apostolic calling not from men but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.
He marvels that they so quickly desert the true gospel for a different one and pronounces a curse on any who pervert it.
Paul clarifies that the gospel he preaches is received by revelation of Jesus Christ, not taught by human agency.
He recounts his former zeal in Judaism, his conversion on the Damascus road, and his initial meetings with Peter and James in Jerusalem.
Paul describes his visit to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, securing apostolic approval that Gentiles need not follow the law.
He confronts Peter in Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile brothers under pressure from the circumcision party.
Justification comes by faith in Christ, not law; we are crucified with Him and live by faith in His Son.
Paul rebukes their foolishness having begun by the Spirit, they now seek perfection by the flesh; Abraham’s faith was credited as righteousness.
The law brings a curse on those who rely on works; Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, blessing the Gentiles.
The promise to Abraham and his Seed (Christ) predates the law and remains unaltered by it.
The law served as a guardian until Christ came; now all who are in Christ are Abraham’s seed and heirs according to promise.
Heirs under guardianship are like believers under the law; at Christ’s coming we were adopted as God’s children and heirs.
Paul laments their return to weak elemental principles and fears for their spiritual stability.
He makes a heartfelt appeal, recalling their care for him despite his illness and urging them not to abandon the gospel he preached.
The allegory of Hagar and Sarah illustrates two covenants: slavery under the law versus freedom through the promise; believers are children of the free woman.
Stand firm in the freedom Christ gives; accepting circumcision severs you from Christ true righteousness is through faith working in love.
Paul reproaches those hindering their gospel progress and warns that reliance on the law forfeits Christ’s benefit.
Called to freedom, they must serve one another in love and walk by the Spirit to avoid gratifying the flesh.
The works of the flesh enmity, strife, jealousy, etc. contrast with the fruit of the Spirit: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.
Restore the fallen gently, mindful of your own weakness; each should carry their own load while bearing one another’s burdens.
Share all good things with those who teach you, sow to the flesh or the Spirit and reap accordingly; do good to all, especially the household of faith.
Paul writes in large letters, warns against circumcision advocates, boasts only in the cross of Christ, and pronounces peace and grace on his readers.
Paul greets the saints in Ephesus, affirming his apostleship and extending grace and peace.
Doxology of spiritual blessings: chosen, predestined, redeemed, sealed with the Spirit, united under Christ.
Paul prays for wisdom, revelation of hope, riches of inheritance, and power of God for the believers.
Christ’s resurrection and exaltation: head over all, body is the church, fullness dwelling in Him and given to the church.
Made alive in Christ by grace: dead in sins but saved through faith, God’s workmanship created for good works.
Gentiles were once separated but brought near by Christ’s blood.
Christ is our peace, breaking down the dividing wall and granting access to the Father by one Spirit.
Believers are fellow citizens and God’s household, built on apostles and prophets with Christ as cornerstone.
Paul, a prisoner for the Gentiles, reveals the mystery: Gentiles are fellow heirs and part of one body through the gospel.
Paul’s stewardship: ministering by grace to make known God’s wisdom in the church and encourage boldness despite trials.
Prayer for believers to be strengthened in the Spirit, Christ to dwell in their hearts, grasp love and fullness of God.
Doxology: praise to God who can do immeasurably more than we ask, to Him be glory in the church and Christ Jesus.
Unity of the Spirit: walk worthy, one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God.
Diverse gifts given by Christ apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers equip the saints for unity and maturity.
Put off the old self and be renewed in mind, putting on the new self created in righteousness and holiness.
Instructions for Christian conduct: truthfulness, anger management, work ethic, wholesome speech, kindness, forgiveness.
Be imitators of God and walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave Himself as a fragrant sacrifice.
Live as children of light: avoid immorality, impurity, dishonesty; expose darkness and walk wisely.
Be filled with the Spirit: live wisely, redeem time, speak with psalms, be thankful and submit to one another.
Marriage parallels: wives submit to husbands, husbands love wives as Christ loved the church mutual sacrifice and unity.
Children obey parents, and fathers do not provoke but nurture them in the Lord’s instruction.
Bondservants obey masters with respect, and masters treat servants without threats, knowing God shows no partiality.
Put on the full armor of God truth, righteousness, gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word, and prayer readiness.
Pray in the Spirit for all saints, Paul’s bold proclamation, and final greetings of peace, love, faith, and grace.
Paul and Timothy greet the Philippians, express thanksgiving for their partnership in the gospel, and pray for their spiritual growth.
Paul rejoices that his imprisonment has advanced the gospel as others preach Christ, regardless of motives.
Paul declares that to live is Christ and to die is gain, torn between departing to be with Christ and remaining for their benefit.
Exhortation to conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel, standing firm in one spirit and sharing in Christ’s sufferings.
Call to unity and humility: fulfill my joy by being like-minded, esteeming others above yourselves.
Christ’s example of humility: though in the form of God, He emptied Himself and was exalted by the Father.
Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; shine as lights, rejoicing amid sacrifice and cold drink offerings.
Commendation of Timothy for genuine care and Epaphroditus for risking his life in service to Christ.
Warning against Judaizers: true worshippers are those of the Spirit, rejoicing in Christ and placing no confidence in the flesh.
Paul counts all his former gains as loss for Christ, pressing on to know Him and the power of His resurrection.
Press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ and live up to what you have already attained.
Imitate Paul’s example, watch those who live as citizens of heaven, awaiting Christ’s transformation of our bodies.
Exhortation to stand firm in the Lord and reconcile Euodia and Syntyche, enlisting a true companion to help them.
Rejoice in the Lord always, let your gentleness be known, pray with thanksgiving, and God’s peace will guard your hearts.
Think on what is true, noble, right, pure, lovely, admirable and practice these things, and the God of peace will be with you.
Paul thanks them for their renewed concern, shares the secret of contentment in every circumstance through Christ’s strength.
Gratitude for their gifts, assurance that God will supply all needs, and final greetings and benediction of grace.
Paul and Timothy greet the holy brothers and sisters in Colossae, extending grace and peace from God our Father.
Thanksgiving for the Colossians’ faith, love, and hope; continuing prayer that they be filled with spiritual wisdom.
Paul prays they may walk worthy filled with knowledge of God’s will, bearing fruit, strengthened by His power, and rescued from darkness.
Christ is the image of the invisible God, creator and head of the church; once alienated, believers now reconciled by His blood.
Paul rejoices in his sufferings for the church, proclaiming the mystery of Christ in us, laboring to present everyone mature in Him.
Paul struggles and prays for the Colossians to be encouraged in love and to grasp the riches of full assurance in Christ.
Warning against hollow philosophy; believers are complete in Christ spiritually circumcised, forgiven, and triumphant over rulers.
Freedom from judgment on food, festivals, or Sabbath these shadows point to Christ alone, the substance of all reality.
Believers died with Christ to elemental rules; asceticism and angel‐worship have no power to curb sinful indulgence.
Seek the things above where Christ is seated; you have died, and your life is now hidden with Him in God.
Put to death earthly sins immorality, anger, greed and put on the new self, renewed in knowledge, unity, and Christ’s likeness.
Clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience; let Christ’s peace and word dwell richly among you.
Household code: wives submit, husbands love, children obey, fathers nurture; bondservants work heartily for the Lord.
Devote yourselves to prayer, watchfully with thanksgiving; pray also for Paul’s boldness to proclaim the mystery of Christ.
Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the most of opportunities; let your speech be gracious and seasoned with salt.
Tychicus and Onesimus are sent to update and encourage the Colossians trusted servants bringing comfort and news.
Final greetings from Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke, and others; instructions to share letters and complete entrusted ministry.

Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the church, give thanks for their work of faith, labor of love, and steadfast hope, and recall their turning from idols to serve the living God and the rapid spread of the gospel.
Paul defends his ministry: boldness under persecution, purity of motives, and tender care like a nursing mother, urging them to live lives worthy of God.
He thanks God for their reception of the word as God’s and acknowledges the persecutions they endured, likening their sufferings to those of Judean churches.
Paul expresses his longing to visit but is hindered; he affirms that the Thessalonians are his glory, joy, and crown in Christ.
Unable to endure separation, Paul sends Timothy to strengthen and encourage them in faith amid afflictions.
Timothy’s good report of their steadfastness brings Paul great joy; he prays earnestly for them and longs to see them.
Paul prays for their continual growth in love, holiness, and blamelessness at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Exhortation to live in holiness: pursue sexual purity and sanctification as God’s will for you.
Continue in brotherly love, lead a quiet life, work with your hands, and win the respect of outsiders.
Comfort regarding believers who have died: at Christ’s return the dead in Christ will rise first and the living will join them to meet the Lord forever.
Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the church with grace and peace from God and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Thanksgiving for the Thessalonians’ growing faith and love amid persecutions, boasting of their endurance.
God’s righteous judgment is revealed through their suffering; at Christ’s return He will repay persecutors and bring relief and glory to believers.
Prayer that God would make them worthy of their calling, fulfill every good purpose by power, and glorify Jesus in them.
Warning not to be shaken or alarmed by claims that the Day of the Lord has already come.
The rebellion must come first and the man of lawlessness be revealed, who opposes God and exalts himself.
The lawless one is restrained until the proper time; when revealed he will deceive many with false signs and be destroyed by Christ.
Thanksgiving for their election through the gospel, encouragement to stand firm, and exhortation to hold to apostolic traditions.
Request for prayer that the word of the Lord may spread quickly, that they may be delivered from evil, and confidence in God’s faithfulness.
Command to withdraw from those living disorderly and instructions to work quietly and earn their keep, warning the idle that they shall not eat.
Exhortation not to grow weary in doing good and to treat idle brethren as brothers through loving admonition.
Paul’s prayer for the Lord of peace to grant them peace at all times, his final greeting in his own hand, and benediction of grace.
Paul greets Timothy, affirming his apostolic calling and Timothy’s role as his true child in the faith.
He urges Timothy to remain in Ephesus to oppose false teachers who promote myths and endless genealogies, highlighting the law’s true purpose to foster love from a pure heart and good conscience.
Paul explains that the law is good when used properly designed not for the righteous but for lawbreakers and rebels and aligns with the gospel of the blessed God.
He gives thanks for Christ’s mercy, recounts his own transformation from blasphemer to apostle, and celebrates grace’s overflow toward him.
Paul charges Timothy to fight the good fight, holding faith and a clear conscience, and warns of those like Hymenaeus and Alexander who have shipwrecked their faith.
Paul urges prayers, intercessions, supplications, and thanksgivings for all people, including kings and authorities, so that believers may lead peaceful, godly lives.
He affirms there is one God and one mediator Jesus Christ who gave Himself as ransom for all, and Paul was appointed a herald, apostle, and teacher of the Gentiles.
Men are to pray everywhere with holy hands free from anger; women are to adorn themselves modestly, learn quietly, and submit respectfully.
Women must not teach or assume authority over men, grounded in the creation order and Eve’s deception; they will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness.

Paul states that aspiring to be an overseer is noble, then lists qualifications: above reproach, monogamous, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, and well-managed household.
He outlines deacons’ qualifications: dignified, sincere, not indulging in much wine or dishonest gain, holding to the faith with a clear conscience; proven blameless before serving.

Paul expresses hope to visit soon, reminds them the church is God’s household, and proclaims the mystery of godliness: Christ manifested in the flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed to the nations, believed in the world, and taken up in glory.

Paul warns that in later times some will abandon the faith, following deceiving spirits and demonic doctrines that forbid marriage and certain foods, though everything God created is good and to be received with thanksgiving.

He instructs Timothy to point believers to sound teaching, become a good servant nourished by the word of faith, and to recognize that godliness with contentment is valuable for both this life and the next.

Timothy is told to command these things, set the believers an example in speech, conduct, love, faith, and purity, devote himself to reading Scripture, preaching, and teaching, and keep watch on himself and his teaching.
Treat older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, all with absolute purity.
Honor true widows those without family support by caring for them; younger widows should remarry to avoid idleness and slander; family members must first show piety by caring for their own.
Elders who lead well, especially preaching and teaching, deserve double honor; accusations against them require two or three witnesses, and persistent sin must be rebuked publicly.
Timothy must observe these rules impartially, avoid hasty ordinations, and remember that some sins are obvious while others emerge later, though nothing is hidden from God.
Bondservants are urged to honor their masters so that God’s name and doctrine are not blasphemed; those with believing masters must serve even more earnestly.
Paul warns against false teachers who promote controversies and exploit godliness for gain, emphasizing that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
Timothy is exhorted to flee youthful passions, pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, and gentleness, fight the good fight, and keep the commandment until Christ’s appearing.
The wealthy are instructed not to be arrogant or put hope in wealth but to be rich in good deeds, generous, and ready to share, storing up a good foundation for the coming age.
Paul charges Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him, avoid godless chatter and opposing ideas, which some have professed and thus gone astray from the faith.
Paul, an apostle of Jesus by God’s will, and Timothy, his beloved child, greet with grace, mercy, and peace.
He recalls Timothy’s sincere faith, urges him to rekindle God’s gift within, not be timid but live in power, love, and self-discipline.
Paul encourages solidarity in suffering for the gospel, not to be ashamed, and trusts God’s call and ability to guard His deposit.
Hold fast to the pattern of sound words and guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit.
Paul notes how many deserted him, yet praises Onesiphorus for seeking him, praying mercy on his house.
Be strong in the grace of Christ and entrust teachings to faithful men who can teach others also.
Endure hardship as a good soldier, compete according to the rules as an athlete, and toil patiently as a farmer.
Remember Christ’s resurrection, endure suffering, and know that if we die with Him we will also live with Him.
Avoid worthless quarrels, present yourself approved, flee youthful passions, pursue righteousness, and gently correct opponents.
In the last days people will be self-loving, money-loving, boastful, proud, abusive, disobedient, unthankful, unholy, and outwardly godly but devoid of power.
False teachers exploit the vulnerable and oppose truth, reminiscent of Jannes and Jambres, but their folly will be exposed.
Paul highlights his teachings, way of life, purpose, faith, patience, love, and endurance of persecutions as Timothy’s example.
All Scripture is God-breathed and beneficial for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness, equipping the servant for every good work.
Paul solemnly charges Timothy before God and Christ to preach the word, correct, rebuke, and encourage with patience.
Anticipating death, Paul declares he has fought the good fight, finished the race, kept the faith, and awaits the crown of righteousness.
Paul describes Demas’s desertion, commends loyal companions, and affirms the Lord’s strength amid persecution.
He sends final greetings, requests Timothy bring his cloak and books, and closes with a benediction of grace.
Paul greets Titus as his true child in the faith and affirms his authority to set in order the church on Crete.
Titus is instructed to appoint elders in every town, outlining qualifications of blameless character, family leadership, hospitality, and sound teaching.
Paul warns against false teachers and rebellious Cretans, urging Titus to rebuke them sharply so they may be sound in the faith.
Paul directs Titus to teach sound doctrine and practical conduct for older men, older women, young men, young women, and slaves.
The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all and teaching us to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives.
Titus is to declare these things with authority, exhorting and rebuking those who oppose sound teaching.
Believers are reminded to submit to rulers, be ready for good works, show humility, gentleness, and avoid slander.
Paul recalls our former sinful state and emphasizes that salvation comes by God’s mercy through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
Believers should devote themselves to good works and avoid foolish controversies, warning divisive people twice before rejecting them.
Titus is to send Zenas and Apollos, ensure these instructions are followed, and greet fellow workers before final benediction.
Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy greet Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, and the church in Philemon’s house with grace and peace.
He thanks God for Philemon’s faith and love, praising his generosity and partnership in the gospel, and expresses confidence in his obedience.
Paul appeals for Onesimus, formerly Philemon’s slave and now a believer, asking that he be welcomed as a brother and offering to repay any debt.
Paul urges Philemon to go beyond obligation in showing kindness to Onesimus, appealing to Christian love and mutual benefit.
He requests a guest room for his visit, sends greetings from fellow workers, and closes with a benediction of grace.
God’s final revelation comes through His Son, heir of all things, the exact imprint of God’s nature, who sustains the universe and sat down at the right hand of Majesty.
Christ is superior to angels: as Son He shares God’s throne forever; angels are only ministering spirits to heirs of salvation.
Warning to pay much closer attention to the salvation we heard, confirmed by signs, wonders and gifts of the Spirit.
Though destined for angels, the world to come is entrusted to humanity Jesus tasted death for everyone and was crowned with glory and honor through suffering.
Jesus, made perfect through sufferings, identifies with our humanity to destroy the devil’s power and becomes a merciful, faithful high priest at God’s right hand.
Fix your thoughts on Jesus, apostle and high priest, greater than Moses, builder rather than servant of God’s house, of which we are His family.
Quoting Psalm 95, the Spirit warns against hardening hearts in unbelief, as Israel did in the wilderness and so failed to enter God’s rest.
Call to hold firm in faith and encourage one another daily so none are hardened by sin’s deceit and barred from God’s rest.
The promise of entering God’s rest still stands; those who heard but disbelieved lost the opportunity, though God’s works were complete at creation.
Some will enter that rest today by faith; like God’s seventh-day rest, it is a Sabbath-rest for God’s people who cease their own works.
Exhortation to strive to enter rest, for God’s word is living, piercing and judges thoughts and attitudes nothing is hidden from Him.
We have a great high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses Jesus was tempted yet without sin so let us approach the throne of grace with confidence.
Every high priest is chosen from men to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, able to sympathize with ignorance; honour comes by God’s call, not self-assumption.
Christ did not appoint Himself but was called by God as Son and made perfect through suffering, becoming high priest in Melchizedek’s order for eternal salvation.
Warning of spiritual immaturity though time for solid food, readers need milk again; the mature discern good and evil by constant practice of the Word.
Leave the elementary teachings about Christ and press on to maturity rather than re-establish basics of repentance, faith, baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, and judgment.
Solemn warning: those once enlightened who fall away cannot be renewed to repentance; like land that only yields thorns, it is cursed and near burning.
Though speaking sternly, author trusts readers hold firm; urged to imitate those who inherited God’s promises through faith and patience.
God’s promise to Abraham confirmed by an unchangeable oath gives us strong encouragement and hope as an anchor for the soul, behind the curtain where Jesus is.
Melchizedek appears as king of righteousness and peace, priest of Most High God; without genealogy he resembles the Son, remaining a priest continually.
Abraham paid tithe to Melchizedek, demonstrating Melchizedek’s superiority over Levi; Levitical priests descend from Abraham yet pay tithes to this priest.
If perfection came through Levi’s priesthood, no need for another; but change in priesthood demands change in law, introducing a better hope by God’s oath.
