Jesus is made priest by divine oath, superior to mortal priests who die; He holds His priesthood permanently and perfectly intercedes for us.
Main point: we have a great high priest seated at God’s right hand in the true heavenly sanctuary, not the copy made by Moses on earth.
Jesus mediates a better covenant with better promises; if first covenant were faultless there’d be no need for a second.
New covenant foretold in Jeremiah: God will write His laws on hearts, forgive sins; by calling it new He has made the first obsolete.
Description of earthly tabernacle and rituals under first covenant only high priest enters holy of holies once yearly with blood for sins.
Christ, high priest of good things to come, enters heavenly tabernacle with His own blood once for all, obtaining eternal redemption.
Christ mediates new covenant by His death; first covenant required blood for every commandment and purification without shedding no forgiveness.
Earthly priests repeatedly offer sacrifices; Christ offered Himself once and will appear a second time for salvation of those who await Him.
Law’s sacrifices are only a shadow and cannot perfect worshipers; repeated sacrifices remind of sin but cannot take it away.
Quoting Psalm 40, God desires obedience over ritual; Christ came to do God’s will, offering His body once for all to sanctify believers.
Unlike priests’ daily offerings, Christ’s single sacrifice perfects forever; He remembers sins no more under new covenant.
Since we have confidence to enter holy place by Christ’s blood, let us hold fast, encourage love and good deeds, and not forsake gathering together.
Sober warning: willful sin after knowing truth brings fearful expectation of judgment; God is a consuming fire.
Encouragement to endure suffering as in past, drawing near, laying aside sin, and living by faith rather than shrinking back.
Definition of faith as assurance of hope and conviction of unseen; examples of Abel, Enoch and Noah show faith’s power.
Faith of patriarchs: Abraham obeys God’s call, Sarah bears Isaac, Isaac and Jacob bless, Joseph trusts God’s purposes.
Faith of Moses’ parents spares him, Moses leads exodus, Rahab trusts spies faith delivers and conquers.
Faith in Judges, David, Samuel endures victories and persecutions, often sealing testimony with suffering.
These heroes did not receive promise fully but saw it from afar; God’s plan includes us so all may reach perfection together.
Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside hindrances and run with endurance, fixing eyes on Jesus who endured shame.
God disciplines His children for training in righteousness; enduring hardship proves sonship and yields peaceable fruit.
Strengthen weak hands and knees, make straight paths; pursue peace and holiness, avoid root of bitterness as Esau did.
Contrast terrifying Sinai with joyous Zion: we come to heavenly assembly, mediator of new covenant, sprinkled blood that speaks better.
Warning not to refuse God who speaks from heaven; we receive unshakable kingdom, so worship with reverence and awe.
Brotherly love and hospitality must continue; remember prisoners; honor marriage and live contentedly trusting God’s promise never to leave you.
Remember leaders’ faith, imitate their example; Jesus Christ is unchanging do not be carried away by strange teachings.
We have altar of Christ’s sacrifice; offer praise and good deeds; obey leaders, pray for them, for they watch over your souls.
Author’s request for prayer, final greetings from Italy, benediction of grace concludes the epistle.
James encourages believers to consider trials pure joy, as testing faith produces perseverance.
God gives wisdom generously to those who ask in faith without doubting.
Believers of humble circumstances are to boast in their high position, while the rich should recognize their fading wealth.
Blessed is the one who endures temptation, for it leads to the crown of life; temptation arises from one’s own desires.
Every good and perfect gift comes from the unchanging God, who brought us forth by the word of truth.
True religion is to be quick to listen, slow to speak, slow to anger, to do the word, and care for orphans and widows.
Believers must not show favoritism but hold faith in Jesus Christ without partiality.
Fulfilling the royal law of loving one’s neighbor is essential; mercy triumphs over judgment.
Faith without works is dead; genuine faith is demonstrated through actions, as illustrated by Abraham and Rahab.
Not many should become teachers, for they will be judged more strictly; the tongue, though small, can set a forest ablaze.
The tongue is untamable, inconsistent in blessing God and cursing others, revealing the need for heart transformation.
True wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, merciful, impartial, and sincere, producing a harvest of righteousness.
Conflicts arise from selfish desires; friendship with the world is enmity with God, who gives grace to the humble.
Believers are urged to submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, and purify their hearts through repentance.
Do not slander or judge one another, and acknowledge life’s uncertainty by trusting in God’s will rather than presuming the future.
Rich oppressors are warned of miseries to come; their hoarded wealth will testify against them at judgment.
Believers are encouraged to be patient in suffering, following the examples of farmers, prophets, and Job.
Let your yes be yes and no be no; prayer is powerful for healing and restoration, as demonstrated by Elijah.
Restoring a wandering brother saves a soul from death and covers a multitude of sins.
Greeting to the elect exiles, chosen according to God’s foreknowledge and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience and sprinkling of Christ’s blood.
Praise to God for a new birth into a living hope through Jesus’ resurrection and an imperishable, undefiled inheritance reserved in heaven.
Trials serve as a refiner’s fire, proving the genuineness of faith which results in praise and glory when Christ is revealed.
Prophets longed to understand the grace now revealed in Christ; even angels long to look into these salvific mysteries.
Exhortation to prepare minds, be sober, set hope fully on grace, live as obedient children, love one another earnestly, and recall God’s enduring word.
Lay aside malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and slander, and crave pure spiritual milk so you may grow in salvation.
Come to Jesus, the living Stone rejected by men but precious to God; as living stones you’re built into a spiritual house with Christ as cornerstone.
Believers are a chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation called to proclaim God’s excellencies who once were not His people but now obtained mercy.
Live as sojourners abstaining from fleshly lusts, keeping honorable conduct among unbelievers so their good works may glorify God.
Submit to every human authority for the Lord’s sake, live as free people but not using freedom to cover evil, and honor all.
Servants submit to unjust masters; enduring suffering for doing good is commendable Christ’s example and redemptive work on the cross guide us.
Wives submit to unbelieving husbands through exemplary conduct and inner beauty of a gentle, quiet spirit, like Sarah calling Abraham lord.
Husbands live with your wives in understanding and honor as the weaker vessel, since you are heirs together of God’s grace.
All believers live in harmony, be sympathetic, love, compassionate, humble, refrain from retaliation, pursue peace, and trust God’s care.
Do not fear suffering for righteousness; sanctify Christ in your hearts, always be ready to give a defense of your hope with gentleness.
Christ suffered once for sins and was raised; baptism now saves you as an appeal to God for a good conscience, and Christ is exalted at God’s right hand.
Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same mindset, cease living for sinful passions, and live for God’s will, even in suffering.
The end of all things is near be sober, pray, love deeply, show hospitality without grumbling, and use your spiritual gifts to serve one another.
Do not be surprised by fiery trials; rejoice as partners in Christ’s sufferings, suffering for doing good aligns you with His judgment and purpose.
Elders are urged to shepherd God’s flock willingly and eagerly, not as lords but as examples, knowing they’ll receive an unfading crown.
Younger submit to elders; all clothe yourselves with humility under God’s mighty hand and cast your anxieties on Him who cares.
Be sober and vigilant against the devil who prowls; resist him steadfast in faith, and after suffering a little, God will restore and strengthen you.
The true grace of God encourages you; stand firm, receive greetings from fellow believers, and may peace be with all in Christ.
Peter greets believers, affirms their faith, and reminds them of God’s power and promises that enable participation in the divine nature.
He exhorts them to add to their faith goodness, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, mutual affection, and love to be effective.
Peter vows to remind them of these truths, recalls the Transfiguration as his eyewitness testimony, and asserts prophecy is from the Spirit.
Peter warns of false teachers who secretly introduce destructive heresies and exploit believers, assuring their swift judgment.
He cites the judgment of angels, the flood, and Sodom as examples, showing God’s justice and His rescue of the righteous.
False teachers are likened to lawless creatures: arrogant, immoral, and destined for destruction, yet they lead many astray.
Peter reminds readers of the prophets’ and apostles’ warnings, scoffers who doubt Christ’s return, and past judgment by water.
He explains God’s timing differs from ours, His patience for repentance, and the coming Day of the Lord with fire.
Believers are urged to live holy lives, hasten the Lord’s day by godliness, beware distortions of Scripture, and grow in grace.
Proclaims Jesus as the Word of life witnessed by the apostles and calls believers to fellowship in the light.
God is light with no darkness; walking in the light fosters truth, confession of sins, and cleansing by His blood.
Jesus is our Advocate and propitiation, restoring fellowship when we sin.
Obeying God’s commands proves genuine knowledge of Him and perfects love.
Reiterates the command to love one another as the mark of walking in the light.
Believers are anointed by the Spirit, warned against worldliness, and informed of antichrists.
Distinguishes truth from the spirit of antichrist; urges abiding in Christ for confidence at His coming.
God’s lavish love makes us His children; our hope of likeness to Him inspires holiness.
Sin is lawlessness; God’s children practice righteousness and love, unlike the world and the devil.
The command to love one another is underscored by action, not merely words, contrasting Cain’s example.
Assurance before God comes through love, obedience, and the Spirit’s witness enabling answered prayer.
Test every spirit: true spirits confess Jesus Christ’s incarnation; false ones align with the antichrist.
God is love; those born of God love others, reflecting His love shown in Christ’s sacrifice.
Living in God gives confidence in judgment; perfect love casts out fear and affirms our union with Him.
We love because God first loved us; genuine love for God is expressed by loving His children.
Believers born of God overcome the world through faith in Jesus Christ as the Son of God.
God’s testimony water, blood, and Spirit confirms Jesus; believing grants assurance of eternal life.
John writes so believers may know they have eternal life and assures their prayers when they align with God’s will.
Those born of God do not continue in sin; believers are kept from evil and warned to shun idols.
John the elder greets the chosen lady and her children, expressing love in the truth and extending grace and peace.
He rejoices that they walk in truth, urges them to walk in love according to God’s commandments, and remain steadfast.
Warning against deceivers who deny Christ’s incarnation; he cautions against receiving false teachers and commends hospitality to true ministers.
John hopes to visit soon for face-to-face fellowship and sends greetings from the children of the elect sister.
The elder greets Gaius, wishes him prosperity, rejoices at his faithfulness to the truth, and expresses his utmost joy.
He commends Gaius for showing hospitality to traveling brothers and urges support for those who labor for the Name.
He criticizes Diotrephes for refusing to welcome brothers and slandering the elder, and praises Demetrius for his good testimony.
John expresses his desire to see Gaius face to face soon and sends final greetings and peace.
Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, greets the called and loved, and urges them to contend for the faith against infiltrating ungodly sinners.
He recalls past judgments on Israel, angels, and Sodom; condemns false teachers as grumblers and likens them to hidden reefs.
Describes false teachers as arrogant dreamers, indulging in worldly desires, grumbling, boasting, and reviling what they do not understand.
Exhorts believers to remember apostles’ warnings, build themselves up in the faith, pray in the Spirit, and show mercy to some with fear.
Doxology: to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and present you faultless before His glory be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority forever.
Prologue and blessing for those who read, hear, and keep the words of this prophecy.
Greetings to the seven churches; doxology declaring Christ, the Alpha and Omega, sovereign over past, present, and future.
John, on Patmos for Christ’s testimony, hears a trumpet-like voice commanding him to write to the seven Asian churches.
Vision of the Son of Man among seven golden lampstands: description of Christ’s majesty white hair, fiery eyes, sword from His mouth.
Christ comforts John not to fear, identifies Himself as the First and the Last, and explains stars and lampstands as church angels and congregations.
To Ephesus: praised for works and discernment, rebuked for losing first love, urged to repent and recover.
To Smyrna: acknowledged suffering and poverty, encouraged to remain faithful under tribulation, promised crown of life.
To Pergamum: commended for holding fast in Satan’s seat, reproved for tolerating false teaching, promised hidden manna.
To Thyatira: honored for love and service, censured for tolerating Jezebel’s immorality, promised authority over nations to overcomers.
To Sardis: rebuked for dead reputation, called to wake up, strengthen what remains, and hold fast to their garments.
To Philadelphia: praised for keeping Christ’s word, promised an open door no one can shut and a secure place in God’s temple.
To Laodicea: rebuked for lukewarm faith, counseled to repent, invited to fellowship; overcomers will dine with Christ.
Door standing open in heaven; John is invited to see future events beyond the church age.
Vision of God’s throne: appearance like jasper and carnelian; twenty-four elders with crowns seated around it; a sea of glass before the throne.
Four living creatures lion, ox, man, eagle full of eyes, worship God day and night saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy.’
Elders cast crowns, worship God, and declare His worthiness as Creator and Sustainer of all things.
Scroll in God’s right hand sealed with seven seals; no one in heaven or earth found worthy to open it, causing John to weep.
One of the elders points to the Lion of Judah, the Root of David; John sees a slain Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes take the scroll.
Living creatures and elders fall before the Lamb, each holding harps and golden bowls of worship, singing a new song of redemption by His blood.
Thousands of angels join the chorus, proclaiming the Lamb’s worthiness to receive power, wealth, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and praise.
The Lamb opens the first four seals, releasing the Four Horsemen: conquest on white, war on red, famine on black, death on pale.
The third seal’s black horse brings famine with scales, and the fourth pale horse named Death follows with Hades given authority over a fourth of the earth.
Under the fifth seal, John sees the souls of martyrs under the altar crying out for justice; they are given white robes and told to wait.
The sixth seal brings cosmic upheaval earthquake, darkened sun and moon, falling stars and all hide in terror at the Lamb’s wrath.
Four angels hold back the winds until God’s servants have the seal on their foreheads, marking them for protection.
144,000 from the twelve tribes of Israel are sealed 12,000 from each tribe as God’s protected remnant.
John sees a great multitude from every nation standing before the throne and the Lamb, clothed in white robes and worshiping.
Those before the throne serve God day and night; the Lamb shepherds them, they lack nothing, and God wipes away every tear.
Opening the seventh seal brings silence in heaven; an angel offers incense with the saints’ prayers and readies seven trumpets.
The first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, destroying a third of the earth, its trees, and green grass.
The second trumpet casts a burning mountain into the sea, turning a third into blood, killing sea life and ships; the third star Wormwood poisons a third of fresh waters.
The fourth trumpet darkens a third of the sun, moon, and stars; an eagle proclaims woes for earth’s inhabitants.
The fifth trumpet opens the abyss: smoke darkens the sky and locusts with scorpion power torment the unsealed for five months under Abaddon/Apollyon.
The sixth trumpet releases four angels bound at the Euphrates who kill a third of mankind; survivors refuse to repent of idolatry and immorality.
John sees a mighty angel in a cloud with a rainbow, feet on sea and land, holding an open little scroll; seven thunders speak and are sealed.
The angel raises his hand to heaven and swears that there will be no more delay and that God’s mystery will be fulfilled in the days of the seventh trumpet.
John is told to eat the scroll it tastes sweet but turns sour in his stomach and then to prophesy again about peoples and nations.
John is given a measuring rod to measure God’s temple and altar, while the outer court is excluded and given to the nations.
Two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth; they wield authority over heaven and earth, breathe fire on foes.
When they finish, the beast rises, kills them, and their bodies lie in the street; people rejoice and send gifts to one another.
After three and a half days the witnesses are raised by God, ascend in a cloud, and a great earthquake kills many.
The seventh trumpet sounds, announcing God’s kingdom; voices in heaven praise Him, temple opens, and the ark of His covenant is seen.
A woman clothed with the sun gives birth to a son who is caught up to God; a great red dragon stands ready to devour her child.
Michael and his angels fight the dragon; he is cast down to earth with his angels, provoking woes for earth’s inhabitants.
The dragon pursues the woman, but she is protected in the wilderness; enraged, he makes war on her offspring who keep God’s commandments.
A beast rises from the sea with ten horns and blasphemous names, given authority by the dragon to persecute the saints for forty-two months.
A second beast from the earth deceives by signs, enforces worship of the first beast, and mandates the mark of the beast 666 to buy or sell.
The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 who follow Him; they are blameless and sing a new song before the throne.
Three angels proclaim the eternal gospel, Babylon’s fall, and warn against worshiping the beast, calling for patient endurance.
A voice blesses the dead in the Lord; an angel harvests the earth grain into the barn, grapes into the winepress of God’s wrath.
Seven angels with the seven last plagues stand before God’s throne; those victorious over the beast sing the song of Moses and the Lamb.
The heavenly temple opens, revealing the ark of the covenant; smoke fills the temple as the seven angels prepare to pour out bowls.
The first bowl brings painful sores; the second turns the sea to blood; the third turns rivers and springs to blood.
The fourth bowl scorches people with fire and intense heat; the fifth plunges the beast’s kingdom into darkness.
The sixth bowl dries the Euphrates, preparing Armageddon; unclean spirits gather kings for battle at the great day.
The seventh bowl produces a great earthquake, hail, and cities collapse; every island and mountain vanishes under God’s wrath.
One of the seven angels shows John the judgment of the great prostitute Babylon seated on a scarlet beast, adorned with luxury.
The angel explains the beast’s seven heads as mountains and kings; the prostitute’s fall is foretold, and the Lamb’s armies overcome them.
The waters represent peoples; the beast and prostitute rule them; the ten horns will hate Babylon and consume her flesh.
Another angel proclaims Babylon’s fall because of her immorality and greed; plagues and desolation follow.
Kings and merchants mourn Babylon’s destruction, lamenting her wealth and trade.
The merchants and sailors weep as they see smoke from Babylon’s ruin; heaven calls to rejoice over her judgment.
A mighty angel casts a millstone into the sea, declaring Babylon will be found no more; her sins reach to the skies.
A great multitude praises God for Babylon’s judgment; hallelujahs echo in heaven.
The marriage of the Lamb is announced; the Bride has made herself ready to share in His reign.
Christ appears on a white horse as Faithful and True, leading heavenly armies to judge and wage war in righteousness.
An angel calls birds to feast on the flesh of the defeated armies, including the beast and the false prophet.
An angel binds Satan for a thousand years in the abyss so he cannot deceive the nations.
Thrones appear; the martyrs reign with Christ for a thousand years this is the first resurrection and they are blessed.
After the thousand years, Satan is released, deceives the nations, and is thrown into the lake of fire with the beast and false prophet.
The great white throne appears; the dead are judged according to their works; death and Hades are cast into the lake of fire.
John sees a new heaven and new earth; the New Jerusalem descends, and God dwells with humanity, wiping away every tear.
God proclaims all things new; the thirsty receive the water of life; unrepentant sinners face the lake of fire.
One of the angels shows John the bride, the New Jerusalem, with twelve gates named for Israel’s tribes.
The city’s dimensions and foundations are described, adorned with precious stones and twelve gates of pearl.
No temple is seen, for God and the Lamb are its temple; the city needs no sun, and its gates never shut.
The river of the water of life flows from God’s throne; the tree of life yields twelve fruits, and the servants see God’s face.
An angel affirms the words of prophecy are trustworthy; blessings and warnings are pronounced for the quick and the wicked.
Christ’s imminent return is announced; the Spirit and the Bride invite all to take the free gift of the water of life.
A final warning is given against tampering with the prophecy; John closes with a plea for Christ’s coming and a benediction of grace.
